You will begin with Python and backend engineering, then add models, retrieval, tools, agents, evaluation, deployment, and operations. code.title: A dependency and Python-version check that fails visibly instead of leaving you guessing.
code.code:
import sys
from importlib.util import find_spec

required = ("httpx", "pydantic", "pytest")
print(f"Python {sys.version_info.major}.{sys.version_info.minor}.{sys.version_info.micro}")

if sys.version_info < (3, 11):
   raise SystemExit("Upgrade to Python 3.11 or newer before continuing.")

missing = [name for name in required if find_spec(name) is None]
if missing:
   print("Missing packages:", ", ".join(missing))
   raise SystemExit("Install them with: uv add " + " ".join(missing))

print("Environment ready:", ", ".join(required))
what_to_notice: The script checks importability and Python version, but it does not prove that a model provider key or network path works.
A missing package is reported once, with the exact install command, so setup failures are quick to diagnose.

Welcome to the Course
Learn how the course works, what you will build, and how to study so the skills survive contact with a real product.
AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 1 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI engineering is learned by building and operating systems, not by collecting explanations. A clear workspace and a habit
of producing evidence will matter more than watching every video. This lesson sets those expectations before the
technical work begins.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Describe the three-page lesson pattern and the artefact each module expects you to produce.
 • Set up a course workspace with Python 3.11+, Git, a virtual environment, and an organised notes folder.
 • Write a one-sentence definition of done for your first AI feature that covers quality, latency, cost, and safety.
CORE CONCEPTS
A course built around a system
Each module teaches a component or architecture decision that you can apply to one product brief. You will begin
with Python and backend engineering, then add models, retrieval, tools, agents, evaluation, deployment, and operations.
By the final module you will have a reviewable AI system, and your architecture record will explain which optional components you included or rejected. A prompt is one line inside that system, not the system itself.
How each lesson works
Page one gives you the mental model: objectives, concepts, terms, and a rule of thumb. Page two makes it concrete with
a worked example, an ordered procedure, and code where code is useful. Page three moves to production concerns, self-
checks, questions, and hands-on tasks. Read with a terminal and notebook open; answer the questions before checking
the material again.
Your learning contract
Plan for five to seven focused hours each week and protect two of them for building. Keep one repository, write short
decision records, and record the measurements behind each claim. Completion means you can explain a choice,
reproduce a result, and name its failure modes. Finishing a lesson without producing an artefact is only reading.
KEY TERMS
 Foundation model                 A large pre-trained model, usually accessed through an API or as open weights, that can be adapted to many
                                  tasks without training from scratch.
 Evaluation harness               A repeatable script and dataset that scores system outputs against explicit criteria so changes can be
                                  compared fairly.
 Capstone                         The final integrated project in which you design, build, test, and deploy the production AI platform.

  MENTAL MODEL Building an AI product is like running a restaurant: the model is a talented but unpredictable chef, while the kitchen
  workflow, suppliers, health checks, and complaints process make service dependable. Learn the kitchen, not only the chef.

lessons.title: What Is an AI Engineer?
lessons.subtitle: Separate the AI engineer's responsibilities from adjacent roles and learn the loop that turns a model into a dependable
why_it_matters: Most AI failures are integration and ownership failures rather than insufficient model intelligence. Someone must connect the model to real data, constrain its output, measure quality, and answer the pager. The AI engineer owns that seam between a probabilistic model and a dependable service.
outcomes: Classify project tasks as model work, application engineering, evaluation, or operations.
Explain the trade-offs between a hosted API, an open-weight model, and fine-tuning to a non-technical stakeholder.
Produce a one-page role map for a chosen feature, naming the owner and metric for each component.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Integration plus ownership An ML engineer commonly trains models, builds feature pipelines, and studies model quality. A researcher invents methods, while an AI engineer composes existing foundation models into a running product. The deliverable is a service with clear contracts: authenticated requests, grounded context, validated output, fallbacks, and observed cost. That engineer may fine-tune, but only when evaluation shows that prompting, retrieval, or a smaller model cannot meet the requirement. The five-part working loop Specify the user decision and the cost of being wrong; ground the model in trusted data and tools; constrain it with schemas, timeouts, and permissions; evaluate it on a representative dataset; then operate it with traces, cost limits, and incident paths. The loop repeats as evidence changes, not as a one-off launch checklist. For example, a schema failure might send you back to prompt or model choice, while a new data source may require retrieval and evaluation changes. Engineering judgement is knowing which part of the loop the evidence implicates. Judgement over model worship Start with the simplest architecture that can pass the evaluation. A rules engine, a classifier, or a fixed workflow may beat an agent on accuracy, latency, and cost for narrowly defined tasks. Add model complexity only when a measured failure justifies it, and record the trade-off. Choosing a cheaper model is an engineering decision only after quality has been tested, not before.

key_terms.definition: A single model call that produces output from an input, typically billed by input and output tokens and measured for latency.
The application code that assembles context, calls models and tools, validates results, and decides the next step.

A versioned collection of representative inputs with expected properties or labels, used to score changes consistently. MENTAL MODEL The AI engineer is the ship's engineer, not the engine designer: the engine matters, but someone must wire the fuel, alarms, steering, and maintenance so the voyage completes.
Page 7 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: Marcus leads three engineers at a logistics startup handling 8,000 support tickets a month. A vendor demo appears to resolve 90% of questions, but on 300 sampled tickets the team finds 18 intents and a tricky refund policy. A keyword baseline routes 46% correctly; a model with six worked examples, a JSON schema, and policy retrieval reaches 82%. Marcus decides against an autonomous agent and ships a fixed triage workflow with a confidence threshold and a human queue for uncertain cases. The measured cost is about USD 0.003 per ticket and p95 latency is 2.1 seconds. The decision is documented with the failed alternatives so the team can revisit it when volume doubles.
steps: Inventory one week of your work and tag each task as model, integration, evaluation, or operations; note which tasks you avoid.
Pick one feature and write the user decision, the cost of a wrong answer, and the acceptable latency and spend.
Sketch the smallest architecture: model, context sources, tools, output schema, and human escalation.
Build a baseline with a fixed prompt and a 30-case evaluation set; record accuracy, p95 latency, and cost per request.
Review the trade-off table with a stakeholder and choose the next experiment based on the biggest measured risk.

code.title: An order-of-magnitude cost model that makes model choice a measurable decision rather than a preference.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Usage:
  requests_per_month: int
  input_tokens: int
  output_tokens: int

def monthly_cost(u: Usage, in_price: float, out_price: float) -> float:
  input_cost = u.requests_per_month * u.input_tokens / 1_000_000 * in_price
  output_cost = u.requests_per_month * u.output_tokens / 1_000_000 * out_price
  return input_cost + output_cost

triage = Usage(requests_per_month=8_000, input_tokens=1_200, output_tokens=120)
print(f"USD {monthly_cost(triage, 0.50, 1.50):,.2f} per month")
what_to_notice: The estimate is driven by volume multiplied by tokens; a 20% retry rate adds 20% to the bill even when the prompt is unchanged.
Input tokens dominate here because 1,200 tokens of instructions and policy accompany every 120-token answer.

The model excludes embedding, retrieval, observability, and human-review costs, so it is a floor rather than the full unit economics. Three pages per lesson Page 8 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Comparing providers on price per million tokens without measuring token counts for your own prompts and outputs.
Calling a prototype accurate because a handful of impressive demos worked, then skipping a representative evaluation set.
Removing the human escalation path before proving that the model handles low-confidence and adversarial cases.
production_notes: Define service objectives for task success, p95 latency, error rate, and cost per successful request; review them together.
Make the evaluation set a release gate and version it alongside prompts and model identifiers.
Design an explicit escalation and fallback path for low confidence, provider failure, and policy-sensitive requests.
checklist: I can state the difference between an ML engineer's and an AI engineer's primary deliverable.
My feature has a user decision, an error cost, and numeric quality, latency, and cost targets.
I have a simple baseline and at least 30 representative evaluation cases.
The design names its system of record, fallback, and human escalation path.
I can justify the model choice with measured evidence rather than fashion.
questions: Which tasks in an AI feature belong to the model provider, and which remain your responsibility?
Why can a fixed workflow be a better engineering choice than an agent?
What does the five-part loop produce after each iteration?
How would you explain the hosted-API versus open-weight trade-off to a finance stakeholder?
Why is cost per successful request more useful than cost per token?
What evidence would justify moving from prompting to fine-tuning?
tasks: Create a role map for an AI feature you know, assigning every component an owner, an interface, and a metric (30 minutes).
Shadow a support agent for 40 minutes and record ten real requests, their ambiguity, and the consequence of a wrong answer.

Extend the cost model to compare three models with different token counts and include a 15% retry allowance; write a recommendation. lessons.title: Anatomy of a Modern AI Application
lessons.subtitle: Trace one request through six layers and learn where reliability is won or lost before a framework hides the details.
lessons.meta: AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 3 of 5 · study guide
why_it_matters: A model call is only one dependency in a distributed system that also includes authentication, databases, retrieval, tools, and networks. Real incidents often come from a missing timeout, a malformed response, or a stale index rather than a weak model. Seeing the whole request path makes those failures visible before users find them.
outcomes: Draw the six layers of an AI application and state the responsibility of each.
Follow a streamed request from client to persisted trace and name the artefacts produced.
Assign a timeout, validation rule, and fallback to every external dependency on the request path.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Six layers, six contracts The interface accepts input and explains progress; the backend authenticates, authorises, limits, and persists; orchestration assembles context and controls the model loop; model access selects a provider and accounts for usage; the data layer holds records, caches, files, and vectors; and the trust layer validates outputs, traces behaviour, and enforces policy. Each boundary should have an explicit input, output, timeout, and failure behaviour. Frameworks may collapse several boxes into one file, but the contracts still exist. One request, many hand-offs A chat turn begins with HTTPS, authentication, quota checks, and conversation history. The orchestrator retrieves two to six relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and calls a model through a gateway. Tokens stream back while the backend assembles the full response, validates schema and citations, and persists the turn with token counts, latency, model version, and a trace ID. Background work updates analytics, memory, and evaluation samples. If the client disconnects, the server should cancel downstream work rather than paying for an answer nobody receives. Failure is designed, not discovered Every remote call needs a deadline, and the total deadline must fit inside the user-facing latency target. A retrieval timeout might degrade to a plain answer with a warning; an order-service timeout must not become an invented order status. Validate model output against a schema and check that cited sources actually exist. A fallback is only useful if it has been exercised, so test it deliberately and record which path served each request.

Anatomy of a Modern AI Application
Trace one request through six layers and learn where reliability is won or lost before a framework hides the details.
AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 3 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A model call is only one dependency in a distributed system that also includes authentication, databases, retrieval, tools,
and networks. Real incidents often come from a missing timeout, a malformed response, or a stale index rather than a
weak model. Seeing the whole request path makes those failures visible before users find them.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Draw the six layers of an AI application and state the responsibility of each.
 • Follow a streamed request from client to persisted trace and name the artefacts produced.
 • Assign a timeout, validation rule, and fallback to every external dependency on the request path.
CORE CONCEPTS
Six layers, six contracts
The interface accepts input and explains progress; the backend authenticates, authorises, limits, and persists;
orchestration assembles context and controls the model loop; model access selects a provider and accounts for usage; the
data layer holds records, caches, files, and vectors; and the trust layer validates outputs, traces behaviour, and enforces
policy. Each boundary should have an explicit input, output, timeout, and failure behaviour. Frameworks may collapse
several boxes into one file, but the contracts still exist.
One request, many hand-offs
A chat turn begins with HTTPS, authentication, quota checks, and conversation history. The orchestrator retrieves two to
six relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and calls a model through a gateway. Tokens stream back while the backend
assembles the full response, validates schema and citations, and persists the turn with token counts, latency, model
version, and a trace ID. Background work updates analytics, memory, and evaluation samples. If the client disconnects,
the server should cancel downstream work rather than paying for an answer nobody receives.
Failure is designed, not discovered
Every remote call needs a deadline, and the total deadline must fit inside the user-facing latency target. A retrieval
timeout might degrade to a plain answer with a warning; an order-service timeout must not become an invented order
status. Validate model output against a schema and check that cited sources actually exist. A fallback is only useful if it has
been exercised, so test it deliberately and record which path served each request.

 Orchestrator                     The code that builds context, invokes models and tools, validates results, and controls the sequence of a
                                  request.
 Trace ID                         A unique identifier attached to every log, span, and record produced by one request so the path can be
                                  reconstructed.
 System of record                 The authoritative source for a fact, such as the order database, which must be queried rather than guessed.

  MENTAL MODEL An AI feature is a normal distributed system with one probabilistic dependency. Treat the model like a remote service
  that is slow, expensive, occasionally wrong, and can change without notice.

CODE
A boundary-focused request handler that validates citations, records a trace, and degrades safely when generation fails.
  from dataclasses import dataclass
  from uuid import uuid4
  from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
  class Draft(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    cited_chunk_ids: list[int]
  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Turn:
    trace_id: str
    answer: str
    source_ids: list[int]
  def handle(question, retrieve, generate) -> Turn:
    tid, chunks = uuid4().hex, retrieve(question, limit=4)
    try:
       draft = Draft.model_validate(generate(question, chunks, timeout_s=8))
       ids = [i for i in draft.cited_chunk_ids if 0 <= i < len(chunks)]
       if not ids:
          raise ValueError("no valid citation")
       return Turn(tid, draft.answer, ids)
    except (ValidationError, ValueError, TimeoutError):
       return Turn(tid, "I cannot verify that answer right now.", [])

 → The trust layer rejects a plausible answer with zero valid citations instead of showing it to the user.
 → The trace ID is created before retrieval, so a failure still produces a searchable record.

   must not be forgotten.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Boring infrastructure and data Start with a container runtime, a relational database, object storage, and a cache or queue only when a workload requires one. PostgreSQL with pgvector can hold millions of chunks and, more importantly, keeps metadata filtering, permissions, and transactions beside your application data. A dedicated vector database earns its place when scale, indexing features, or isolation justify another service to operate. The same logic applies to Kubernetes: three engineers serving 12,000 documents a month rarely need it. Model access through a stable boundary A gateway gives the application one interface for providers while centralising keys, quotas, retries, fallbacks, caching, and usage accounting. It also lets you switch models without editing every service. Keep the gateway thin: validate the request, enforce a timeout, route to a provider, normalise the response, and record cost. If the gateway becomes a second application with its own agent framework and business rules, it has stopped reducing complexity. Evaluation and operations are stack layers A stack is incomplete without a versioned evaluation set, a way to run it in CI, structured logs, traces, and cost dashboards. These tools answer different questions: evaluations ask whether quality changed, traces ask where a request spent time, and dashboards ask whether the service is healthy and affordable. Instrument the request path before launch, because reconstructing it after an incident is expensive. Keep prompt, model, and dataset versions linked in every result.

code.title: A provider-neutral gateway call with explicit timeouts and token accounting from the response.
code.code:
import os
import httpx
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Completion(BaseModel):
  text: str
  input_tokens: int
  output_tokens: int
async def complete(prompt: str, model: str = "small") -> Completion:
  base = os.environ["MODEL_GATEWAY_URL"].rstrip("/")
  headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['GATEWAY_TOKEN']}"}
  payload = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
  timeout = httpx.Timeout(20.0, connect=2.0)
  async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=timeout) as client:
     r = await client.post(f"{base}/v1/chat", json=payload, headers=headers)
     r.raise_for_status()
     data = r.json()
  usage = data.get("usage", {})
  return Completion(
     text=data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"],
     input_tokens=usage.get("prompt_tokens", 0),
     output_tokens=usage.get("completion_tokens", 0),
  )
what_to_notice: The connect timeout is two seconds while the read timeout is twenty, so a dead gateway fails quickly without cutting off a legitimate long generation.
Retries are intentionally absent; retrying a 401 makes an auth problem worse, and a retry policy belongs in the gateway or a wrapper that handles 429 and 5xx only.

Missing usage fields default to zero, which keeps the call working but can silently under-report cost; production should alert on absent accounting. Three pages per lesson Page 14 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Adding a dedicated vector database and Kubernetes before there is enough traffic or a feature that requires them.
Hard-coding one provider's request schema throughout the application, then discovering that a fallback needs a second schema.
Logging full prompts and responses that contain customer data, secrets, or personal information.
production_notes: Apply per-tenant quotas, budget alarms, and rate limits at the gateway; unbounded model access is an availability and finance risk.
Pin model and dependency versions, but rehearse upgrades against the evaluation set because hosted models can change behaviour.
Test backup restoration and provider failover, not just their configuration; a documented fallback that has never run is an assumption.
checklist: I can name each stack layer and the smallest tool that satisfies its contract.
Every managed service has a stated reason, owner, cost estimate, and exit or revisit condition.
The model is reached through a boundary with timeouts, quotas, and usage accounting.
Traces, logs, evaluation reports, and cost data are designed before launch.
The stack fits the team's operating capacity, not just the architecture diagram.

lessons.title: Course Roadmap
lessons.subtitle: Turn thirteen modules into a realistic plan, with artefacts that compound into a capstone instead of exercises you
why_it_matters: A broad curriculum fails when it becomes an unordered playlist. Dependencies matter: agents assume HTTP, tool calling, and state, while production work assumes a working application to observe. A plan protects the scarce resource, your attention, and turns each module into evidence rather than another unfinished tutorial.
outcomes: Sequence the modules and explain which prerequisites each later module assumes.
Map module artefacts to capstone capabilities so work is reused rather than discarded.
Create a dated study plan with module gates, buffer time, and a measurable definition of progress.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The dependency spine Modules 1 and 2 build Python and backend foundations, because every later feature needs a request, validation, storage, and tests. Modules 3 and 4 add model behaviour, prompting, structured output, streaming, and reliability. Module 5 adds retrieval; Modules 6 to 8 add agents, orchestration, and MCP; Modules 9 to 11 cover production, deployment, and system design; Module 12 integrates them. Skipping the backend or production modules does not save time, because their gaps reappear as incident work during the capstone. One product through-line Choose a capstone domain by Module 2 and keep using the same repository. Each module then adds a capability to one product: extraction to the intake path, RAG to the knowledge path, tools to actions, MCP to integration, evaluation to the release gate, and deployment to the delivery path. Reuse is not laziness; it exposes the integration problems that isolated demos hide. Write down the scope boundary so the capstone stays achievable alongside the lessons. Cadence, gates, and evidence A workable pace is five to seven hours a week for roughly twenty weeks, with at least half the time spent building. Each module ends with a small artefact, a passing self-check, an evaluation number, and a short decision record. Gate progress on demonstrated capability, not on finishing a page count: if you cannot explain and reproduce the artefact, repeat the relevant task. Two buffer weeks are part of the plan, not evidence of failure.

key_terms.definition: A skill or artefact that later material assumes you can already use without instruction.
A concrete output such as a service, evaluation report, diagram, or decision record that demonstrates a capability.

One of the thirteen stages in Module 12, each producing a reviewed part of the final platform. MENTAL MODEL A curriculum is a dependency graph, not a playlist: do not play a module until the modules it imports are working.

worked_example: Aisha is a data analyst with six hours a week and an 18-week target: a permit-document assistant for 250 colleagues. She maps Module 1 to a Python ingestion script, Module 2 to a FastAPI service, Module 5 to RAG over 4,000 pages, Module 6 to a read-only lookup tool, Module 9 to an evaluation and tracing gate, and Module 12 to a staging deployment. At week 12 she finds that retrieval answers 88% of 150 test questions correctly, but a multi-agent rewrite adds latency without improving accuracy. The decision is to keep the fixed workflow, spend the saved week on permission filtering, and document the rejected alternative. Her buffer week absorbs a provider outage instead of becoming catch-up debt.

AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 5 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A broad curriculum fails when it becomes an unordered playlist. Dependencies matter: agents assume HTTP, tool calling,
and state, while production work assumes a working application to observe. A plan protects the scarce resource, your
attention, and turns each module into evidence rather than another unfinished tutorial.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Sequence the modules and explain which prerequisites each later module assumes.
 • Map module artefacts to capstone capabilities so work is reused rather than discarded.
 • Create a dated study plan with module gates, buffer time, and a measurable definition of progress.
CORE CONCEPTS
The dependency spine
Modules 1 and 2 build Python and backend foundations, because every later feature needs a request, validation, storage,
and tests. Modules 3 and 4 add model behaviour, prompting, structured output, streaming, and reliability. Module 5 adds
retrieval; Modules 6 to 8 add agents, orchestration, and MCP; Modules 9 to 11 cover production, deployment, and system
design; Module 12 integrates them. Skipping the backend or production modules does not save time, because their gaps
reappear as incident work during the capstone.
One product through-line
Choose a capstone domain by Module 2 and keep using the same repository. Each module then adds a capability to one
product: extraction to the intake path, RAG to the knowledge path, tools to actions, MCP to integration, evaluation to the
release gate, and deployment to the delivery path. Reuse is not laziness; it exposes the integration problems that isolated
demos hide. Write down the scope boundary so the capstone stays achievable alongside the lessons.
Cadence, gates, and evidence
A workable pace is five to seven hours a week for roughly twenty weeks, with at least half the time spent building. Each
module ends with a small artefact, a passing self-check, an evaluation number, and a short decision record. Gate progress
on demonstrated capability, not on finishing a page count: if you cannot explain and reproduce the artefact, repeat the
relevant task. Two buffer weeks are part of the plan, not evidence of failure.
KEY TERMS
 Prerequisite                     A skill or artefact that later material assumes you can already use without instruction.
 Artefact                         A concrete output such as a service, evaluation report, diagram, or decision record that demonstrates a
                                  capability.
 Capstone phase                   One of the thirteen stages in Module 12, each producing a reviewed part of the final platform.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The data shapes you will meet Model APIs return nested dictionaries: a response with choices, usage, and finish_reason. Catalogues are lists of dictionaries. Your job is to move between those shapes, keep types honest, and avoid silent coercion. Know the difference between rebinding a name and mutating an object, because appending to a list while looping over that same list is how scripts double their data. Treat None as a distinct value, never as zero or an empty string. Comprehensions and lazy iteration Use a list comprehension when you need every result; use a generator when you need one pass over a large file. dict.get(key, default) beats a KeyError; enumerate and zip remove index bookkeeping. Unpacking a row into named variables documents its shape at the point of use. Sorting a list of dicts with key=lambda r: r["cost"] is stable, so equal costs keep their original order, which matters for reproducible reports. Tracebacks and the run loop Run scripts as modules (python -m package.module) so imports resolve the same way in development and CI. Read a traceback bottom-up: the last frame is where the exception surfaced, but the cause is often the line that passed a string where an integer was expected. python -c and the REPL are for one-line experiments only; anything you want to keep belongs in a file under version control.

CODE
One-pass aggregation with the type conversion kept at the edge, and a formatted report a reviewer can check.
  from collections import defaultdict

  models = [
    {"name": "Atlas-S", "provider": "Northwind", "price": "0.50"},
    {"name": "Atlas-L", "provider": "Northwind", "price": "3.00"},
    {"name": "Kestrel-8", "provider": "Cobalt", "price": "1.20"},
  ]

  def provider_average(rows: list[dict[str, str]]) -> dict[str, float]:
    totals: dict[str, list[float]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
      totals[row["provider"]].append(float(row["price"]))
    return {name: round(sum(v) / len(v), 3) for name, v in sorted(totals.items())}

  if __name__ == "__main__":
     for provider, avg in provider_average(models).items():
       print(f"{provider:<10} USD {avg:.2f} per million tokens")

   raised ValueError.

lessons.title: Python project structure
lessons.subtitle: Lay out a Python package so imports resolve the same way on your laptop, in tests, and in the container that runs your API
why_it_matters: AI clients grow from one script into a package with schemas, an HTTP layer, retries, and tests. Without a layout, imports work only from the directory you happen to be in, and the first CI run or container build fails. A deliberate structure keeps the dependency graph acyclic, makes the public surface obvious, and lets you move a module without editing every caller.
outcomes: Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
Draw the dependency direction between schemas, I/O, domain logic, and the command-line entry point.
Explain why python -m package avoids the import failures caused by running a file inside the package.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: src layout, not script soup Place the importable package under src/, for example src/model_catalog/, and keep tests, data, and configuration beside it at the repository root. The extra directory prevents Python from importing the working directory by accident, so a test can only pass by importing the installed package. pyproject.toml declares the package name, version, and dependencies; one editable install then serves your shell, editor, and CI. Boundaries follow change Group code by the reason it changes, not by technical type. schemas.py holds data shapes, loader.py owns file and network I/O, catalog.py holds pure business rules, and main.py wires them together. Dependencies point one way: main imports catalog, catalog imports schemas, and schemas import nothing from the project. When loader needs catalog you have a cycle, and the fix is usually a new module or an injected function. Entry points and import-time calm Expose one main() and guard it with if __name__ == "__main__":. Add __main__.py so python -m model_catalog works, and use absolute imports such as from model_catalog.loader import load_models everywhere inside the package. Importing a module must not read files, call an API, or start a server; those belong in main(), where tests can choose not to run them. Keep one public function per module and import helpers from their own module, not through a package re- export.

key_terms.definition: The single function or module Python runs to start the program, kept separate from the library code it calls.

A failure where two modules import each other, usually revealing that responsibilities or dependency direction are wrong. MENTAL MODEL A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb through a window to reach the database.

worked_example: At a four-person team building a model-catalogue client, loader.py starts importing catalog.py to reuse a price formatter, while catalog.py already imports loader.py to read files. Tests pass on one laptop because the modules were imported in a lucky order, then fail in CI with ImportError: partially initialized module. In the review, the team moves the formatter into formatting.py, points both modules at it, and adds __main__.py. They also replace sys.path.append("..") in the tests with an editable install. The CI run drops from four minutes to ninety seconds because tests no longer resolve three copies of the package. The decision: no module may import a module that imports it, and shared helpers get their own home.

Python project structure
Lay out a Python package so imports resolve the same way on your laptop, in tests, and in the container that runs your API
client.
Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 2 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI clients grow from one script into a package with schemas, an HTTP layer, retries, and tests. Without a layout, imports
work only from the directory you happen to be in, and the first CI run or container build fails. A deliberate structure keeps
the dependency graph acyclic, makes the public surface obvious, and lets you move a module without editing every caller.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
 • Draw the dependency direction between schemas, I/O, domain logic, and the command-line entry point.
 • Explain why python -m package avoids the import failures caused by running a file inside the package.
CORE CONCEPTS
src layout, not script soup
Place the importable package under src/, for example src/model_catalog/, and keep tests, data, and configuration beside
it at the repository root. The extra directory prevents Python from importing the working directory by accident, so a test
can only pass by importing the installed package. pyproject.toml declares the package name, version, and dependencies;
one editable install then serves your shell, editor, and CI.
Boundaries follow change
Group code by the reason it changes, not by technical type. schemas.py holds data shapes, loader.py owns file and
network I/O, catalog.py holds pure business rules, and main.py wires them together. Dependencies point one way: main
imports catalog, catalog imports schemas, and schemas import nothing from the project. When loader needs catalog you
have a cycle, and the fix is usually a new module or an injected function.
Entry points and import-time calm
Expose one main() and guard it with if __name__ == "__main__":. Add __main__.py so python -m model_catalog works,
and use absolute imports such as from model_catalog.loader import load_models everywhere inside the package.
Importing a module must not read files, call an API, or start a server; those belong in main(), where tests can choose not
to run them. Keep one public function per module and import helpers from their own module, not through a package re-
export.
KEY TERMS
 src layout                       A repository convention where the importable package lives under src/, so tests import the installed package
                                  rather than loose files.
 Entry point                      The single function or module Python runs to start the program, kept separate from the library code it calls.
 Circular import                  A failure where two modules import each other, usually revealing that responsibilities or dependency
                                  direction are wrong.

  MENTAL MODEL A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb
  through a window to reach the database.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.subtitle: Design small functions with honest inputs and outputs, so a model client stays testable when retries, parsing, and prompts
why_it_matters: A model client is mostly functions: build a prompt, call an endpoint, parse a response, validate a record, compute a cost. When one function does four of those, a failure in parsing looks like a failure in networking, and tests need a live API to tell the difference. Small, explicit functions make each step observable and let you change one decision without re- running the world.
outcomes: Write a function with an explicit contract: typed parameters, a single return shape, and documented failure behaviour.
Replace mutable default arguments and hidden global state with keyword-only parameters and injected dependencies.
Refactor a long procedure into three composable functions that can each be tested in isolation.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A function is a contract The signature states what goes in; the return statement states what comes out; the docstring states what can go wrong. Callers should not need to read the body to use it. Name the unit in the function name: parse_usage(response) returns a Usage or raises ValueError, and it never prints, retries, or writes a file. When a function needs a paragraph explaining its order of operations, it is probably two functions. Defaults and side effects Default arguments are evaluated once, at definition time, so def add(item, bucket=[]) shares one list across every call. Use None and create the list inside the body. Keep printing, network calls, and file writes at the edges; a pure function that takes data and returns data can be tested with literals. Inject collaborators such as a fetch callable instead of importing a module-level client, so a test can pass a fake. Composition over cleverness Build behaviour by calling small functions, not by adding flags. A retry parameter that changes the return type, or a mode string that selects three code paths, is a sign the caller should choose a different function. Keyword-only arguments such as *, timeout_s: float = 10.0 make call sites readable and let you add parameters without breaking positional callers. Return early on errors; keep the happy path unindented.

key_terms.definition: A function whose output depends only on its arguments and which changes no external state, so it can be tested with literals.
A parameter default such as a list or dictionary created once when the function is defined and shared by every call.

A parameter placed after the star in the signature, callable only by name, which keeps call sites readable as the API grows. MENTAL MODEL A function is a kitchen appliance: one job, a clear input, a predictable output, and a warning label for the ways it can burn you.

CODE
Per-case error isolation with an injected fetch callable, so the batch survives one bad response and tests run offline.
  from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable

  def score_case(case: dict[str, str], fetch: Callable[[str], str]) -> dict[str, object]:
    try:
       score = float(fetch(case["prompt"]))
       return {"id": case["id"], "score": score, "error": None}
    except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
       return {"id": case.get("id", "?"), "score": None, "error": type(exc).__name__}

  def run(
     cases: Iterable[dict[str, str]], fetch: Callable[[str], str]
  ) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
     return [score_case(case, fetch) for case in cases]

  def fake_fetch(prompt: str) -> str:
    return "0.8" if "safe" in prompt else "not-a-number"

  print(run([{"id": "c1", "prompt": "safe?"}, {"id": "c2", "prompt": "bad"}], fake_fetch))
WHAT TO NOTICE

lessons.title: Type hints
lessons.subtitle: Annotate the boundaries of your client so editors, mypy, and reviewers catch wrong shapes before a request reaches the
why_it_matters: Type hints are executable documentation that a checker verifies. In AI code they are especially valuable because the data is loosely typed JSON: a response may have usage or not, a finish reason is one of four strings, and a missing field becomes None three calls later. Annotations move those failures from production logs into your editor and CI, at the cost of a few minutes per function.
outcomes: Annotate functions and data shapes with builtin generics, unions, TypedDict, and Literal without resorting to Any.
Run mypy in strict mode on a package and triage errors by boundary, narrowing, and missing annotations.
Decide where runtime validation is still required despite a clean static check.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Types describe values, not variables An annotation says what a name may hold at that point, and mypy tracks it through assignments and branches. list[dict[str, float]] is a list of dictionaries with string keys and float values; dict[str, list[float]] is a different shape. Use X | None for values that may be absent and narrow with an early if value is None: return. Avoid Any, which silently disables checking for everything it touches. Model JSON with TypedDict and Literal TypedDict describes a dictionary with fixed keys and per-key types, which matches API payloads better than a wide dict[str, object]. Mark optional keys with NotRequired, or use total=False on a separate class. Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"] turns a magic string into a checked set of values. These are static shapes only: they do not validate a response at runtime, so a cast from json.loads is a promise you have not verified. Gradual typing and the checker loop Start with public functions and the data that crosses a module boundary; private helpers can stay unannotated until they are stable. Run mypy with strict = true in pyproject.toml, then fix errors by adding a missing annotation, narrowing a union, or correcting the shape. reveal_type(value) prints what the checker inferred, which is faster than guessing. Keep the checker in CI so a new Any cannot quietly spread.

key_terms.definition: An approach where some functions are fully annotated and checked while unannotated code is treated as compatible, allowing adoption over time.
The process where a type checker uses a runtime check, such as if x is not None, to prove a union has one specific member.

A typing construct describing a dictionary with known string keys and a distinct value type for each key. MENTAL MODEL Type hints are a contract sketch: cheap to draw, checked by a machine, and never a substitute for checking the parcel that actually arrived.

model.
Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 4 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Type hints are executable documentation that a checker verifies. In AI code they are especially valuable because the data
is loosely typed JSON: a response may have usage or not, a finish reason is one of four strings, and a missing field
becomes None three calls later. Annotations move those failures from production logs into your editor and CI, at the cost
of a few minutes per function.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Annotate functions and data shapes with builtin generics, unions, TypedDict, and Literal without resorting to Any.
 • Run mypy in strict mode on a package and triage errors by boundary, narrowing, and missing annotations.
 • Decide where runtime validation is still required despite a clean static check.
CORE CONCEPTS
Types describe values, not variables
An annotation says what a name may hold at that point, and mypy tracks it through assignments and branches.
list[dict[str, float]] is a list of dictionaries with string keys and float values; dict[str, list[float]] is a different shape. Use X |
None for values that may be absent and narrow with an early if value is None: return. Avoid Any, which silently disables
checking for everything it touches.
Model JSON with TypedDict and Literal
TypedDict describes a dictionary with fixed keys and per-key types, which matches API payloads better than a wide
dict[str, object]. Mark optional keys with NotRequired, or use total=False on a separate class. Literal["stop", "length",
"tool_calls"] turns a magic string into a checked set of values. These are static shapes only: they do not validate a
response at runtime, so a cast from json.loads is a promise you have not verified.
Gradual typing and the checker loop
Start with public functions and the data that crosses a module boundary; private helpers can stay unannotated until they
are stable. Run mypy with strict = true in pyproject.toml, then fix errors by adding a missing annotation, narrowing a
union, or correcting the shape. reveal_type(value) prints what the checker inferred, which is faster than guessing. Keep
the checker in CI so a new Any cannot quietly spread.
KEY TERMS
 Gradual typing                   An approach where some functions are fully annotated and checked while unannotated code is treated as
                                  compatible, allowing adoption over time.
 Narrowing                        The process where a type checker uses a runtime check, such as if x is not None, to prove a union has one
                                  specific member.
 TypedDict                        A typing construct describing a dictionary with known string keys and a distinct value type for each key.

  MENTAL MODEL Type hints are a contract sketch: cheap to draw, checked by a machine, and never a substitute for checking the parcel
  that actually arrived.

During a migration to a second model provider, a client starts failing with TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +:
'NoneType' and 'int' in the cost report. The cause: the new provider omits completion_tokens for cached responses, and

modules. They fix the boundary first: parse into Usage with a default of zero and a warning log, then let the rest of the
code use plain integers. The decision: absent fields are normalised once, where the payload enters.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Add a [tool.mypy] section with strict = true and run it on the package to capture a baseline error count.
2.    Annotate the module boundaries first: loaders, HTTP calls, and anything that builds a prompt or parses a response.
3.    Replace bare dict and Any with TypedDict, Literal, and concrete generics, then re-run the checker.
4.    Use reveal_type on three confusing values and record what mypy inferred before changing the annotation.
5.    Add mypy to CI and reject new errors, keeping a short list of ignored modules with an owner and a date.
CODE
A TypedDict that reflects the provider contract, with optional usage and a Literal finish reason checked by mypy.
  from typing import Literal, NotRequired, TypedDict

  class Usage(TypedDict):
    prompt_tokens: int
    completion_tokens: NotRequired[int]

  class Response(TypedDict):
    finish_reason: Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"]
    usage: NotRequired[Usage]

  def output_tokens(response: Response) -> int:
    usage = response.get("usage")
    if usage is None:
       return 0
    return usage.get("completion_tokens", 0)

  print(output_tokens({"finish_reason": "stop"}))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → NotRequired reflects the API contract honestly; a required completion_tokens would force every test to invent a value.
 → The None check is what lets the checker narrow usage; indexing without it fails strict mode and would fail on a real cached
   response.
 → The annotation did not validate the JSON: a payload with prompt_tokens as the string "12" type-checks here and still breaks
   at runtime.

CODE
A small client that enforces its URL invariant, injects transport, and exposes usage state without leaking secrets.
  class ModelClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str, transport, *, timeout_s=10.0) -> None:
       if not base_url.startswith("https://"):
          raise ValueError("base_url must use https")
       self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
       self.timeout_s = timeout_s
       self._transport = transport
       self._requests = 0

     @classmethod
     def from_env(cls, env, transport):
       return cls(env["MODEL_BASE_URL"], transport, timeout_s=float(env["TIMEOUT_S"]))

     def request(self, path: str, payload: dict) -> dict:
       self._requests += 1
       return self._transport(f"{self.base_url}{path}", payload, self.timeout_s)

     def __repr__(self) -> str:
       return f"ModelClient({self.base_url!r}, requests={self._requests})"

 → The constructor rejects a non-HTTPS base URL and strips a trailing slash, so every later method can trust the invariant.

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.subtitle: Replace hand-written record classes with dataclasses, and choose frozen fields, factories, and validation deliberately.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 6 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: AI pipelines are full of small records: a usage report, a scored case, a retrieved chunk, a cost summary. Writing __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ by hand for each is noise that hides bugs. Dataclasses generate those methods from the field list, so the shape of the data is visible in one place. The decisions that remain, defaults, mutability, and invariants, are where the real engineering sits.
outcomes: Define record types with the dataclass decorator, including defaults, field(default_factory=...), and computed properties.
Choose between mutable and frozen dataclasses based on whether identity or value semantics fit the data.
Explain why a dataclass is not a validation layer and where a schema model must take over.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Generated methods, visible shape The dataclass decorator reads the class annotations and generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__. Two instances with the same field values compare equal, which is what you want for records and what you rarely want for clients holding sockets. field(default_factory=list) supplies a new list per instance; a bare class-level list raises at definition because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug outright. asdict() converts nested dataclasses to dictionaries for JSON, at the cost of a deep copy. Frozen records and invariants dataclass(frozen=True) blocks attribute assignment and makes instances hashable, so a record can key a dictionary or live in a set. Use it for values that represent a fact at a point in time: a usage report does not change, a new report replaces it. Add __post_init__ to validate combinations the type system cannot express, such as a non-negative token count. Raise ValueError there; a record that exists should already be valid. Dataclass or schema model A dataclass describes data your code already trusts. It does not coerce the string "12" into 12, reject an unknown field, or explain a validation error to an API caller. Put a Pydantic model at the trust boundary, where JSON from a provider or a request body arrives, then convert to a dataclass for internal use if you want immutability and cheap construction. Using Pydantic everywhere is also defensible; mixing them without a rule creates confusion.

key_terms.definition: A dataclass whose attributes cannot be assigned after construction, making instances immutable and hashable by field value. post_init hook A method that runs after the generated initialiser, used to validate or derive fields that depend on each other. MENTAL MODEL A dataclass is a labelled parts tray: the fields are visible at a glance, each slot gets its own contents, and nothing enters the tray unvalidated.

worked_example: An evaluation harness stores one CaseResult per prompt and a RunSummary for the batch. The first version uses a plain class with errors = [] as a class attribute, so all 300 results share one list and the summary reports 41 failures instead of 3. The rewrite uses a frozen dataclass for CaseResult and a mutable dataclass with field(default_factory=list) for the summary, plus a post-init check that rejects a score outside 0 to 1. A property computes pass_rate from counts instead of storing it. The decision: records are frozen, aggregates are mutable, and invalid scores fail at construction rather than in a dashboard.

A provider offer schema with bounds, a cross-field rule, and bulk error reporting.
  from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError, model_validator

  class Price(BaseModel):
    model_config = {"extra": "forbid"}
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)
    context_window: int = Field(gt=0, le=2_000_000)
    input_usd: float = Field(ge=0)
    output_usd: float = Field(ge=0)

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def output_costs_more(self) -> "Price":
        if self.output_usd < self.input_usd:
           raise ValueError("output must cost at least as much as input")
        return self
  raw = {"name": "Atlas-S", "context_window": "128k", "input_usd": 0.5,
       "output_usd": "cheap", "region": "eu"}
  try:

  except ValidationError as exc:

lessons.title: Error handling
lessons.subtitle: Catch only failures you can act on, translate them into a small taxonomy, and make every skip visible in metrics.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 8 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Production code fails in expected ways: a provider returns 503, a file is missing, one record has no body field. A broad except Exception turns those into silence, and silence becomes wrong data. Good handling means deciding which failures are retryable, which are fatal, and which must be reported. The goal is not fewer exceptions; it is that every failure has an owner, a visible signal, and a defined outcome.
outcomes: Distinguish transient failures from permanent ones and choose retry, fallback, or fail-fast for each.
Build an exception hierarchy and re-raise with context so tracebacks preserve the original cause.
Route exhausted work to a dead-letter path and alert on skip rates instead of swallowing errors.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Catch what you can act on An exception is a typed signal, so catch the narrowest type you can handle: FileNotFoundError to fall back to defaults, httpx.TimeoutException to retry, ValidationError to quarantine one record. Let programming errors such as KeyError and AttributeError crash in development, because they indicate a bug rather than a condition. At a layer boundary, translate library exceptions into your own types with raise DomainError('...') from exc, which preserves __cause__ and keeps callers independent of the library. Retry only what can succeed twice Retry timeouts, 429, and 502/503/504 with exponential backoff and full jitter, cap attempts at three to five, and hold a total deadline. A 400, 401, 403, or 422 will fail identically on the second attempt and wastes quota. Writes need an idempotency key before retries are safe, or a retried POST can create two orders. If an outer job and an inner client both retry, four attempts become sixteen; place the policy in one layer and pass the remaining deadline down. Make every failure observable Use logging.exception inside the handler so the traceback and structured fields such as record_id, provider, and attempt travel together, and increment a counter rather than printing. Keep a dead-letter queue for records that exhausted retries, with the payload and error type, so recovery is a replay rather than a mystery. Use finally for closing files and clients, except* for concurrent task groups, and never bare except: pass. Alert on error rate and skip count, not only on process exit.

key_terms.definition: Linking a new exception to the original with raise ... from exc, so the traceback shows the cause and the translation boundary.
A caller-supplied identifier that lets a server recognise a repeated write and return the first result instead of creating a duplicate.

A holding area for messages that exhausted retries, kept with their error details so they can be inspected and replayed. MENTAL MODEL Errors are mail: sort each item into retry, return to sender, or escalate; a bin marked miscellaneous is how deliveries disappear.

  import random

  class IngestError(Exception): ...

  def with_retries(fn, attempts: int = 3, base_s: float = 0.5):

      except TransientIngestError:

  import json
  from decimal import Decimal
  from datetime import datetime, timezone

  def encode(value):
    if isinstance(value, Decimal):
       return float(value)
    if isinstance(value, datetime):
       return value.astimezone(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    raise TypeError(f"not JSON serialisable: {type(value).__name__}")

  report = {"run_id": "eval-2026-10-26", "score": Decimal("0.9167"),
        "finished_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc), "notes": None}
  text = json.dumps(report, default=encode, allow_nan=False, indent=2)
  back = json.loads(text, parse_float=Decimal)
  print(back["score"] + Decimal("0.01"))

why_it_matters: Almost every AI feature is a network client: model providers, vector databases, embedding services, and internal APIs. Those calls are slower and less reliable than local functions, and a missing timeout can hold a worker for minutes. The difference between a demo and a service is usually a few decisions about deadlines, retries, connection reuse, and malformed responses.
outcomes: Build a request with the correct method, headers, JSON body, and status handling for an AI API.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A request is a typed message A request carries a method, URL, headers, and an optional body; a response carries a status, headers, and a body. Use POST for model calls, GET for idempotent reads, and never put an API key in the query string, where proxies and logs record it. A 2xx means the transport succeeded, not that the payload is usable: check Content-Type, decode JSON, then validate against a schema. A 401 or 403 is a configuration failure, 422 is a request bug, and 5xx is the provider's problem. Deadlines and retries httpx.Timeout separates connect, read, write, and pool waits; a 3-second connect with a 20-second read handles slow generation without hanging on a dead host. Set a total deadline at the caller and shrink it for each retry. Retry only 429, 502, 503, 504, and timeouts, honour Retry-After when present, and add jitter so a fleet does not synchronise. Cap attempts at three or four and surface the final error with the provider request id. Never retry a non-idempotent write without an idempotency key. Reuse connections and verify responses Creating a client per call repeats DNS, TCP, and TLS work; one httpx.Client with Limits(max_connections=50, max_keepalive_connections=20) reuses sockets and bounds concurrency. Close it with a context manager. Disable redirects for authenticated calls so a 302 cannot forward your bearer token to another host. Stream large bodies instead of calling .json() blindly, and record status, latency, request id, and token usage. Validate the decoded object with Pydantic before use.

key_terms.definition: The property that repeating a request produces the same result as sending it once, which makes retries safe.

  import time
  import httpx

  RETRYABLE = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504}

  def fetch_completion(prompt: str, base: str, token: str) -> dict:
    body = {"model": "small", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
    auth = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
    with httpx.Client(timeout=httpx.Timeout(20.0, connect=3.0)) as client:
       for attempt in range(4):
         r = client.post(f"{base}/v1/chat", json=body, headers=auth)
         if r.status_code in RETRYABLE and attempt < 3:
            time.sleep(float(r.headers.get("retry-after", 2 ** attempt)))
            continue
         r.raise_for_status()

code.title: Typed settings that load from the environment, validate before serving, and mask the API key.
code.code:
from pydantic import Field, SecretStr, ValidationError
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
  model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")
  app_env: str = Field(pattern="^(dev|staging|prod)$")
  database_url: str = Field(min_length=1)
  api_key: SecretStr
  request_timeout_s: float = Field(default=10.0, gt=0, le=120)

try:
  settings = Settings()
except ValidationError as exc:
  raise SystemExit(f"invalid config: {exc.error_count()} field(s)")

print(settings.app_env, settings.request_timeout_s, settings.api_key)

lessons.title: Virtual environments
lessons.subtitle: Give every project its own interpreter and packages so an upgrade in one repository cannot break another.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 12 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Python installs packages into whichever interpreter is active, so a global upgrade for one tutorial can break three services that expected an older Pydantic. Virtual environments give each project its own site-packages directory, and a lockfile makes that directory reproducible on another machine. This is unglamorous work, but most works-on-my-machine incidents start with an ambiguous interpreter and end with a dependency conflict nobody can reproduce.
outcomes: Create a project virtual environment with a pinned Python version and use it without relying on activation.
Rebuild the environment from a lockfile in CI and containers, and prove the result matches.
Diagnose import shadowing and version drift using sys.prefix, pip check, and explicit interpreter paths.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Isolation is a directory on sys.path A virtual environment is a folder containing a symlink to a base interpreter, its own pyvenv.cfg, and a site-packages directory that appears early on sys.path. Activation only edits PATH and VIRTUAL_ENV for the current shell; it does not change the code. Calling .venv/bin/python -m pip or .venv/bin/python -m pytest is deterministic, while a bare python in a cron job or IDE may resolve elsewhere. Check sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix before blaming the package. Create, pin, and rebuild Create one environment per repository with python3.11 -m venv .venv, upgrade pip once, and add .venv/ to .gitignore. Record the interpreter version in .python-version and declare dependencies in pyproject.toml; a lockfile pins exact versions and hashes for every platform you support. In CI and Docker, build a fresh environment from the lock rather than copying a developer folder, because a venv contains absolute paths and native wheels tied to the machine that built it. A venv isolates but does not pin Two projects can each have a venv and still drift if both install pydantic>=2 on different days. Lockfiles, constraints, and hashed installs turn that drift into a reviewable diff. Use pip check or uv pip check to catch conflicting requirements, and run the test suite inside the same environment that deployment uses. Do not install project packages globally, do not mix conda and venv casually, and avoid --system-site-packages unless a system package genuinely cannot be installed.

  import sys
  from importlib.metadata import PackageNotFoundError, version

  REQUIRED = {"pydantic": "2.9.2", "httpx": "0.27.2", "pytest": "8.3.3"}

  def audit() -> list[str]:
    problems = [] if sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix else ["no active venv"]
    for name, expected in REQUIRED.items():
       try:
         found = version(name)
       except PackageNotFoundError:
         problems.append(f"{name}: missing")
       else:
         if found != expected:
            problems.append(f"{name}: {found} != {expected}")

  print(" | ".join(problems) or f"ok: Python {sys.version.split()[0]}")

lessons.title: Dependencies
lessons.subtitle: Treat every package you install as production code you did not write: pin it, lock it, and review it.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 13 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: An AI service inherits hundreds of transitive packages from an SDK, an HTTP client, and a test stack. An unpinned install can change behaviour between Tuesday and Friday without a line of your code changing. Dependencies are also an attack surface: a compromised release runs with your credentials. Treating them as reviewed, locked inputs keeps builds reproducible and incidents explainable.
outcomes: Separate direct, transitive, and development dependencies, and explain why only direct ones belong in pyproject.toml.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Direct, transitive, and locked A direct dependency is a package your code imports or a tool your build invokes. A transitive dependency is anything those packages require, often dozens deep. pyproject.toml declares intent with version ranges; a lockfile records the exact resolved version and hash of every package in the graph. WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS

lessons.title: Async Python
lessons.subtitle: Learn why one thread can serve hundreds of model calls, and where the event loop stops helping.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 14 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Model calls spend almost all their time waiting on a network, so a service that handles them one at a time wastes capacity. Async Python lets one thread keep hundreds of requests in flight, but only while every operation yields. Understanding the loop explains both the throughput gain and the outages caused by one synchronous library call.
outcomes: Distinguish concurrency from parallelism and decide when an AI workload needs asyncio rather than threads or processes.
Explain how the event loop schedules coroutines and why one blocking call stalls every pending request.
Choose between asyncio.gather, TaskGroup, and a bounded semaphore for fan-out model calls.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One thread, many waiting requests The event loop is a single-threaded scheduler holding a queue of ready callbacks. When a coroutine awaits network I/O, it registers a callback and yields, and the loop runs another request until the socket is ready. Concurrency comes from overlapping waits, not from doing two things at once. Two hundred pending model calls can share one thread because each is idle most of its lifetime. CPU-bound work has no await point, so it occupies the thread completely and queues everything behind it. The blocking trap Any synchronous call inside a coroutine blocks the loop: requests.get, time.sleep, a large pandas operation, or a tokenizer that releases the GIL only intermittently. One blocked loop means every request misses its deadline, which looks like a provider outage. Use async-native clients such as httpx.AsyncClient, and move unavoidable blocking work to a worker thread with asyncio.to_thread or a process pool. Enable asyncio debug mode in staging, where slow callbacks are logged with their stack. Bounded fan-out and backpressure Fan-out needs a ceiling. Two hundred simultaneous requests exhaust connection pools, trigger 429 responses, and multiply the cost of a retry storm. A semaphore around each call caps in-flight work, while a queue absorbs bursts beyond capacity. Size the cap from the provider's requests-per-second limit, your connection pool, and the latency budget. TaskGroup gives structured lifetimes; a semaphore gives backpressure. Use both, add a deadline for the whole batch, and record queue wait separately from model latency.

key_terms.definition: A single-threaded scheduler that runs ready callbacks and resumes coroutines when their awaited I/O completes.
A limit that slows producers when downstream capacity is full, preventing queues, connection pools, or providers from being overwhelmed.

A function defined with async def that can pause at await and resume later with a result or exception. MENTAL MODEL Async is one fast waiter serving many tables: he takes orders while food cooks, but stops serving entirely if he starts cooking a dish himself.

code.title: A bounded async fan-out: one shared client, a 16-slot semaphore, and a TaskGroup that cancels siblings on failure.
code.code:
import asyncio
import httpx

async def embed(client: httpx.AsyncClient, text: str, limit) -> list[float]:
  async with limit:
    r = await client.post("/v1/embeddings", json={"input": text}, timeout=20)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["data"][0]["embedding"]

async def embed_all(texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
  limit = asyncio.Semaphore(16)
  async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url="https://api.example.com") as client:
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
       tasks = [tg.create_task(embed(client, text, limit)) for text in texts]
  return [task.result() for task in tasks]
what_to_notice: The semaphore is created once per batch, so its 16-slot budget cannot be bypassed by a helper that forgets to acquire it.
TaskGroup cancels sibling tasks when one raises, which prevents a failing request from leaving 199 orphans running.

One AsyncClient is reused for connection pooling; creating a client per call pays a TLS handshake and leaks sockets. YOUR WORKING NOTES Three pages per lesson Page 60 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.title: async / await
lessons.subtitle: Read and write async code precisely: what await actually does, how errors and cancellation travel, and how to avoid
why_it_matters: Most async bugs are syntax-shaped: a missing await, a coroutine created and never scheduled, or a cancellation swallowed by a bare except. These mistakes pass review because the code looks concurrent. Precise knowledge of await, task lifetime, and cancellation turns asyncio from a source of mystery failures into predictable control flow.
outcomes: Write async functions, await coroutines, and explain why calling one without awaiting returns a coroutine object.
Propagate exceptions and cancellation correctly across tasks, timeouts, and TaskGroup boundaries.
Use async context managers and async iterators to manage clients, sessions, and streamed responses.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: await is a suspension point Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. At await, the current task suspends and the event loop runs other work until the awaitable completes. This is why two sequential awaits still take the sum of both latencies: the second call is created only after the first returns. Use asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup when calls are independent, and check for RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited in tests. Tasks own lifetimes A Task is a scheduled coroutine with its own lifecycle. asyncio.TaskGroup creates children inside a scope that waits for all of them; if one fails, the others are cancelled and the error surfaces as an ExceptionGroup at scope exit. Cancellation arrives as CancelledError at the next await point and must be allowed to propagate after cleanup. A bare except Exception swallows it, so the task appears to finish normally while the caller believes the work stopped. Async context and iteration Async context managers acquire and release resources across awaits; async with client.stream(...) guarantees the connection closes even when the body raises or is cancelled. Async iterators expose streamed tokens one chunk at a time, which matters for time-to-first-token and for stopping early. async / await
Read and write async code precisely: what await actually does, how errors and cancellation travel, and how to avoid
orphaned tasks.
Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 15 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most async bugs are syntax-shaped: a missing await, a coroutine created and never scheduled, or a cancellation
swallowed by a bare except. These mistakes pass review because the code looks concurrent. Precise knowledge of await,
task lifetime, and cancellation turns asyncio from a source of mystery failures into predictable control flow.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write async functions, await coroutines, and explain why calling one without awaiting returns a coroutine object.
 • Propagate exceptions and cancellation correctly across tasks, timeouts, and TaskGroup boundaries.
 • Use async context managers and async iterators to manage clients, sessions, and streamed responses.
CORE CONCEPTS
await is a suspension point
Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; nothing runs until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. At await, the
current task suspends and the event loop runs other work until the awaitable completes. This is why two sequential
awaits still take the sum of both latencies: the second call is created only after the first returns. Use asyncio.gather or a
TaskGroup when calls are independent, and check for RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited in tests.
Tasks own lifetimes
A Task is a scheduled coroutine with its own lifecycle. asyncio.TaskGroup creates children inside a scope that waits for all
of them; if one fails, the others are cancelled and the error surfaces as an ExceptionGroup at scope exit. Cancellation
arrives as CancelledError at the next await point and must be allowed to propagate after cleanup. A bare except Exception
swallows it, so the task appears to finish normally while the caller believes the work stopped.
Async context and iteration
Async context managers acquire and release resources across awaits; async with client.stream(...) guarantees the
connection closes even when the body raises or is cancelled. Async iterators expose streamed tokens one chunk at a time,
which matters for time-to-first-token and for stopping early. Never hold a lock across a long model call, and do not call
blocking cleanup from __aexit__. Test cancellation explicitly, because cleanup bugs appear only when a client disconnects
mid-stream.

 Awaitable                        An object usable with await, typically a coroutine, Task, or Future, that eventually produces a value or raises
                                  an exception.
 Cancellation                     A request to stop a task, delivered as CancelledError at its next await point and expected to propagate after
                                  cleanup.
 Structured concurrency           A pattern where child tasks live inside a scope that cannot exit until every child finishes, fails, or is cancelled.

  MENTAL MODEL await is a hand-off, not an ordinary call: your task pauses, the loop runs someone else, and you resume when the result
  is ready.

lessons.title: Testing with pytest
lessons.subtitle: Write fast, deterministic tests that pin behaviour at the boundaries where AI systems actually fail.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 16 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: A model response is variable, slow, and sometimes invalid, so tests that call a live provider are flaky and expensive. The reliable strategy is to test your code's decisions at the edges: request construction, schema validation, retries, and error mapping. A fast suite plus a few recorded contract tests catches regressions before users do, without turning CI into a billing event.
outcomes: Structure unit, integration, and contract tests so a failing build identifies the broken boundary.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Test the seams, not the model Unit tests cover pure transforms: prompt assembly, response parsing, retry classification, and cost calculation. Integration tests run your client against a fake transport and assert request headers, body, status handling, and timeouts. Contract tests hit a sandbox provider occasionally to detect schema drift. Never put live model quality in the default suite; that belongs to evaluation. Test your decisions, not the model's mood today. Fixtures and parametrisation A fixture prepares a client, temp directory, or environment variable and is injected by name; yield fixtures close resources after the test. Prefer function scope unless setup is genuinely expensive, because shared mutable state creates order- dependent failures. Parametrise tables of inputs and expected outcomes so each case reports separately: a 400, a 429, a 500, a timeout, and malformed JSON. Give cases readable ids. Mock at the transport Patch HTTP at the transport layer with httpx.MockTransport or respx, not your own functions. The real client then builds URLs, serialises JSON, applies auth headers, follows its retry loop, and parses the response, so a broken request is caught. Patching your own method proves only that the mock was called. For async code use pytest-asyncio or anyio, and freeze time or inject a sleep function so backoff tests finish instantly. Over-mocking is the usual reason a green suite misses a production bug.

key_terms.definition: A pytest function that prepares a resource or value, optionally with teardown, and is injected into tests by name.
Running one test body against a table of inputs and expected results, reporting each case as a separate test.

A small suite that verifies your client still matches a provider's real request and response shapes, run less often. MENTAL MODEL Tests are a contract with your future self: pin the behaviour you depend on, fake what you do not control, and keep the boundary honest.
