worked_example: Nadia owns the Python client for a translation API used by 40 internal services. The suite takes six minutes because 28 tests call the live endpoint, and two fail most Fridays when the provider is slow. She replaces those calls with transport- level fakes: a 200 response, a 429 then 200 sequence, a 500 with a malformed body, and a read timeout. Parametrised cases assert that only 429 and 5xx are retried, that backoff caps at eight seconds, and that a 400 surfaces as InvalidRequest without a retry. The suite drops to 340 tests in 4.2 seconds and immediately exposes a bug: retries were also firing on 401. Nadia makes the suite a required check and keeps three nightly contract tests against a sandbox key.
steps: List the behaviours your client promises: request shape, retry policy, error mapping, and response parsing.
Write one failing test per behaviour using a fake transport and small inline payloads, starting with error paths.
Replace duplicated setup with fixtures and collapse input variants into parametrised cases with readable ids.
Remove sleeps and network calls; assert on retry counts with a fake clock or an injected sleep function.
Mark slow contract tests, run them nightly, and require the fast suite in CI with a coverage floor on changed lines.

code.title: Two transport-level tests: a 429 is retried, a 400 fails immediately, and no socket is opened.
code.code:
import httpx
import pytest
from client import ProviderError, TranslationClient

def make_client(*responses):
  queue = list(responses)
  transport = httpx.MockTransport(lambda request: queue.pop(0))
  return TranslationClient(transport=transport, sleep=lambda _: None)

def test_429_then_success():
  client = make_client(
     httpx.Response(429, headers={"retry-after": "0"}),
     httpx.Response(200, json={"text": "bonjour"}),
  )
  assert client.translate("hello", "fr") == "bonjour"

def test_400_is_terminal():
  client = make_client(httpx.Response(400, json={"error": "bad lang"}))
  with pytest.raises(ProviderError):
     client.translate("hello", "xx")
what_to_notice: MockTransport replaces the network at the httpx layer, so request construction, headers, retry logic, and parsing all run for real.
Injecting sleep keeps the retry test instant while still exercising the backoff decision; a real sleep would add one to two seconds.

The queue handler raises IndexError if the client makes an extra call, which turns an unexpected retry into an immediate failure. Three pages per lesson Page 66 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

production_notes: Require the fast suite on every pull request and publish its duration; a suite over 90 seconds gets skipped under deadline pressure.
Run a small contract suite nightly against a sandbox key, and alert when the provider changes a response shape.
Track flaky tests explicitly and quarantine them with an owner; rerunning until green erodes trust in the gate.

lessons.title: Git & GitHub essentials
lessons.subtitle: Use Git as a reviewable history of decisions, not a backup folder, and let GitHub enforce the checks that protect main.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 17 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: AI projects change prompts, model versions, and evaluation data alongside code, so history is often the only record of why a result changed. A clean commit graph lets you bisect a quality regression, revert a bad prompt safely, and review a provider migration. Git skills also prevent the two expensive mistakes: committing a key and rewriting shared history.
outcomes: Create focused commits and branches that make a change easy to review, revert, and trace to an issue.
Resolve divergence with rebase or merge deliberately, and recover lost work with reflog and bisect.
Configure GitHub protection, review, and CI rules that keep main deployable and secrets out of history.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Commits are snapshots with intent A commit records a complete tree plus a message explaining why the tree changed. Keep commits atomic: one behaviour, one prompt, or one dependency bump, never formatting mixed with logic. Write an imperative subject under 72 characters and use the body for evidence, trade-offs, and the issue link. Small commits make review faster and revert safer, because you can undo one decision without unpicking a week of unrelated work. Divergence: rebase or merge Rebase replays your commits onto a new base, producing a linear history that is easy to read and bisect; it creates new hashes, so never rebase a branch others have pulled. Merge preserves real history and is the safer choice for shared branches. Resolve conflicts deliberately and run tests after each resolution, and use force-with-lease rather than a bare force push. Tags mark releases, because a branch head keeps moving while a tag does not. Review and repository protection A pull request is a conversation about a diff, so keep it under roughly 400 changed lines and include reproduction steps, risk, and rollback. Protect main with required reviews, passing checks, linear history, and blocked force pushes. CODEOWNERS routes sensitive paths such as prompts, infrastructure, and auth to named reviewers. Enable secret scanning and dependency alerts. If a key reaches history, rotate it: rewriting the commit does not unshare what was cloned, cached, or forked.

key_terms.definition: A merge that moves the branch pointer forward without a merge commit because the target has no new commits.
A local log of where HEAD and branch tips pointed, used to recover commits after a reset or rebase.

A binary search through commits, driven by a test command, that identifies the change that introduced a regression. MENTAL MODEL A branch is a hypothesis, a commit is a decision, and main is the current best explanation; review is how the team agrees to believe it.
Page 68 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: Owen leads a four-engineer team maintaining a legal-research assistant. After a release, accuracy on the 180-case evaluation set drops from 91% to 84%, but no test fails. The branch contains 37 commits: a prompt rewrite, a dependency bump, and a chunk-size change. Owen runs git bisect with the evaluation script as the test command; six iterations identify the prompt commit that removed the instruction to cite sources. The team reverts it on main, tags v2.4.1, and reopens the change as a small pull request with an evaluation report attached. The decision: prompt changes now require an eval run in CI and a reviewer from the retrieval group. Owen adds the prompt log command to the runbook.
steps: Create a branch named for the issue, and keep formatting or dependency updates in separate commits.
Write a subject under 72 characters in the imperative, with a body that records the reason, trade-off, and evidence.

Git & GitHub essentials
Use Git as a reviewable history of decisions, not a backup folder, and let GitHub enforce the checks that protect main.
Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 17 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI projects change prompts, model versions, and evaluation data alongside code, so history is often the only record of
why a result changed. A clean commit graph lets you bisect a quality regression, revert a bad prompt safely, and review a
provider migration. Git skills also prevent the two expensive mistakes: committing a key and rewriting shared history.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Create focused commits and branches that make a change easy to review, revert, and trace to an issue.
 • Resolve divergence with rebase or merge deliberately, and recover lost work with reflog and bisect.
 • Configure GitHub protection, review, and CI rules that keep main deployable and secrets out of history.
CORE CONCEPTS
Commits are snapshots with intent
A commit records a complete tree plus a message explaining why the tree changed. Keep commits atomic: one behaviour,
one prompt, or one dependency bump, never formatting mixed with logic. Write an imperative subject under 72
characters and use the body for evidence, trade-offs, and the issue link. Small commits make review faster and revert
safer, because you can undo one decision without unpicking a week of unrelated work.
Divergence: rebase or merge
Rebase replays your commits onto a new base, producing a linear history that is easy to read and bisect; it creates new
hashes, so never rebase a branch others have pulled. Merge preserves real history and is the safer choice for shared
branches. Resolve conflicts deliberately and run tests after each resolution, and use force-with-lease rather than a bare
force push. Tags mark releases, because a branch head keeps moving while a tag does not.
Review and repository protection
A pull request is a conversation about a diff, so keep it under roughly 400 changed lines and include reproduction steps,
risk, and rollback. Protect main with required reviews, passing checks, linear history, and blocked force pushes.
CODEOWNERS routes sensitive paths such as prompts, infrastructure, and auth to named reviewers. Enable secret
scanning and dependency alerts. If a key reaches history, rotate it: rewriting the commit does not unshare what was
cloned, cached, or forked.
KEY TERMS
 Fast-forward                     A merge that moves the branch pointer forward without a merge commit because the target has no new
                                  commits.
 Reflog                           A local log of where HEAD and branch tips pointed, used to recover commits after a reset or rebase.
 Bisect                           A binary search through commits, driven by a test command, that identifies the change that introduced a
                                  regression.

  MENTAL MODEL A branch is a hypothesis, a commit is a decision, and main is the current best explanation; review is how the team
  agrees to believe it.

lessons.subtitle: Follow one API request across DNS, TCP, TLS, and routing so you can diagnose the latency users blame on the model.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 1 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: Users experience your service through a network you do not control. Before a single token is generated, the browser resolves a name, opens a TCP connection, negotiates TLS, and only then sends bytes. Each step adds round trips that grow with distance and packet loss. Engineers who can measure these phases stop blaming the model for latency that DNS or a cold TLS handshake caused.
outcomes: Trace a request through DNS resolution, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, and HTTP exchange, naming the failure at each step.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Packets, not wires Data leaves your process as IP packets, each carrying source and destination addresses and a fragment of a TCP stream. Routers forward packets hop by hop using border gateway protocol routes, so two requests to the same hostname can travel different paths. Packets arrive out of order, get dropped, or are delayed; TCP reassembles them and retransmits losses, which turns one percent packet loss into visible tail latency rather than a clean error. DNS is the first dependency Before any connection, the client resolves api.example.com to an address. The operating system checks its cache, then asks a recursive resolver, which walks root, TLD, and authoritative servers while honouring TTLs. A records return IPv4, AAAA return IPv6, and CNAMEs alias names. Slow or misconfigured DNS adds hundreds of milliseconds or fails outright, so monitor resolution time separately from request time and choose TTLs deliberately. TCP and TLS cost round trips TCP opens with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), one round trip before data. TLS 1.3 adds another round trip, or none on a resumed session with a pre-shared key. Add the HTTP exchange and a fresh cross-Atlantic call spends roughly 150 ms on setup at 75 ms RTT. Connection pooling, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and edge termination exist to remove those repeated costs from every request.

key_terms.definition: Round-trip time: how long a packet takes to reach a peer and return, setting the minimum cost of each handshake.
A DNS server that follows referrals from root to authoritative servers and caches the answer for its TTL.

The point where encrypted traffic is decrypted, often a load balancer or CDN, after which it may travel in plaintext internally. MENTAL MODEL A request is a relay race across owned and unowned track: your code starts it, but DNS, routers, and TLS must pass the baton before the server sees a byte.

The on-call engineer runs curl -w on an Asian runner and sees dns_time 4 ms, connect 210 ms, appconnect 620 ms, starttransfer 2,350 ms. TCP is healthy; TLS negotiation is slow and the first byte is late. code.title: A phase-by-phase connection probe that separates DNS, TCP, and TLS cost from server time.
code.code:
import socket
import ssl
import time

HOST, PORT = "api.example.com", 443

def timed(label, fn):
  start = time.perf_counter()
  value = fn()
  print(f"{label}: {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f} ms")
  return value

addr = timed("dns", lambda: socket.getaddrinfo(
   HOST, PORT, type=socket.SOCK_STREAM)[0][4])
sock = socket.socket()
timed("tcp", lambda: sock.connect(addr))
ctx = ssl.create_default_context()
tls = timed("tls", lambda: ctx.wrap_socket(sock, server_hostname=HOST))
tls.sendall(f"HEAD /health HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: {HOST}\r\n\r\n".encode())
print(tls.recv(64).split(b"\r\n")[0].decode())
what_to_notice: The DNS phase is measured once and cached by the operating system afterwards, so a second run understates resolution cost.
TCP connect and TLS handshake are separate round trips; a healthy TCP time does not prove TLS is fast.

The script opens one connection without pooling, so repeated runs include setup cost a production client would amortise. Three pages per lesson Page 73 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Blaming model latency for a slow first byte that curl -w would attribute to TLS or DNS.
Serving every region from one origin and assuming a CDN edge removes all round trips.
Caching DNS for 24 hours, then needing an emergency failover during a provider outage.
production_notes: Terminate TLS at an edge close to users, then keep upstream connections pooled and reused to cut handshake cost.
Set DNS TTLs between 30 and 300 seconds so failover is possible without flooding resolvers after every change.
Monitor resolution, connect, TLS, and time-to-first-byte per region from real traffic; a single global average hides the users who suffer.
checklist: I can order the phases a request passes through before the server handles it.
My latency dashboard separates DNS, connect, TLS, and server time.
I know the RTT to each region where my users live.
Connection reuse is enabled in every client that calls my API.
I have tested what happens when DNS resolution fails or returns a stale record.
questions: Why does a fresh TLS connection cost more than a resumed session?
How can one percent packet loss produce a much larger p95 latency than one percent?
What does dig +trace reveal that a cached lookup does not?
Why is time-to-first-byte per region more useful than a global average?
What happens to in-flight connections when a DNS record changes?
Which phases of a request can your application code actually control?

Run the timing script against a local and a remote host, then explain the difference using RTT and handshake counts (40 minutes).

Write a one-page latency budget for your capstone assigning milliseconds to DNS, TLS, queueing, retrieval, and model time (45 minutes). core_concepts.content: Resources, not actions A REST API exposes nouns: /documents, /documents/481, /documents/481/chunks. The URL identifies a thing; the method says what to do with it. CODE
A minimal resource handler where the method selects the operation and the outcome selects the status.
  from http import HTTPStatus

  DOCUMENTS: dict[str, dict] = {}

  def handle(method: str, doc_id: str | None, body: dict | None = None):
    if doc_id is None:
       if method == "GET":
          return HTTPStatus.OK, {"data": list(DOCUMENTS.values())}
       if method == "POST" and body and "id" in body:
          if body["id"] in DOCUMENTS:
             return HTTPStatus.CONFLICT, {"error": "exists"}
          DOCUMENTS[body["id"]] = body
          return HTTPStatus.CREATED, body
    elif method == "GET" and doc_id in DOCUMENTS:
       return HTTPStatus.OK, DOCUMENTS[doc_id]
    elif method == "DELETE" and doc_id in DOCUMENTS:
       del DOCUMENTS[doc_id]
       return HTTPStatus.NO_CONTENT, None
    return HTTPStatus.NOT_FOUND, {"error": "not found"}

lessons.title: API Design
lessons.subtitle: Design an API that stays usable after v1: consistent naming, cursors, idempotency, and errors that clients can act on.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 4 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: API design is where future support cost is decided. An inconsistent error shape forces every client to write special cases; offset pagination duplicates or skips rows under load; unbounded filters invite expensive queries. None of these problems are visible in a demo. They appear when a second client integrates, traffic grows, or a field must be renamed without breaking the mobile app shipped last quarter.
outcomes: Produce a consistent naming, filtering, pagination, and error convention that every endpoint follows.
Choose offset or cursor pagination based on data size, mutation rate, and client needs.
Write a versioning and deprecation policy with concrete signals and removal dates.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One shape for every response Pick a convention and keep it: collections return data plus pagination metadata, single resources return the object, and errors return a stable type, message, and code. Include a request ID on every response and in logs so support can join the two. Keep machine-readable error codes separate from human text, because text will be translated and reworded. Consistency matters more than the specific convention chosen. Pagination and filtering Offset pagination is simple and fine for small, stable datasets, but rows shift when items are inserted or deleted, causing duplicates and gaps. Cursor pagination encodes the last seen sort key, such as created_at plus id, and returns the next page relative to it. Filtering, sorting, and field selection belong in query parameters with documented defaults and a hard maximum page size; never let a client request an unbounded list. Versioning and evolution Adding an optional field or a new endpoint is backward compatible. Renaming, removing, or changing a type is not. Put the major version in the path, evolve within it, and treat deprecation as a scheduled project: announce, add Sunset and Deprecation headers, measure usage by client, then remove. Prefer tolerant readers on clients, but do not rely on tolerance for changes that alter meaning.

key_terms.definition: Pagination that returns a token encoding the last seen sort position, giving stable pages while data changes.
The RFC 9457 JSON error format with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields that clients can parse consistently.

A response header announcing when an endpoint or version will be withdrawn, used with deprecation notices. MENTAL MODEL An API is a contract with every client you will never meet; design for the support ticket six months after the author has left.

API Design
Design an API that stays usable after v1: consistent naming, cursors, idempotency, and errors that clients can act on.
Backend Engineering · Lesson 4 of 21 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
API design is where future support cost is decided. An inconsistent error shape forces every client to write special cases;
offset pagination duplicates or skips rows under load; unbounded filters invite expensive queries. None of these problems
are visible in a demo. They appear when a second client integrates, traffic grows, or a field must be renamed without
breaking the mobile app shipped last quarter.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Produce a consistent naming, filtering, pagination, and error convention that every endpoint follows.
 • Choose offset or cursor pagination based on data size, mutation rate, and client needs.
 • Write a versioning and deprecation policy with concrete signals and removal dates.
CORE CONCEPTS
One shape for every response
Pick a convention and keep it: collections return data plus pagination metadata, single resources return the object, and
errors return a stable type, message, and code. Include a request ID on every response and in logs so support can join the
two. Keep machine-readable error codes separate from human text, because text will be translated and reworded.
Consistency matters more than the specific convention chosen.
Pagination and filtering
Offset pagination is simple and fine for small, stable datasets, but rows shift when items are inserted or deleted, causing
duplicates and gaps. Cursor pagination encodes the last seen sort key, such as created_at plus id, and returns the next
page relative to it. Filtering, sorting, and field selection belong in query parameters with documented defaults and a hard
maximum page size; never let a client request an unbounded list.
Versioning and evolution
Adding an optional field or a new endpoint is backward compatible. Renaming, removing, or changing a type is not. Put
the major version in the path, evolve within it, and treat deprecation as a scheduled project: announce, add Sunset and
Deprecation headers, measure usage by client, then remove. Prefer tolerant readers on clients, but do not rely on
tolerance for changes that alter meaning.
KEY TERMS
 Cursor pagination                Pagination that returns a token encoding the last seen sort position, giving stable pages while data changes.
 Problem Details                  The RFC 9457 JSON error format with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields that clients can parse
                                  consistently.
 Sunset header                    A response header announcing when an endpoint or version will be withdrawn, used with deprecation
                                  notices.

  left.

WORKED EXAMPLE
A B2B reporting API lists model runs with offset and limit parameters. At 40,000 runs, page 400 takes 3.2 seconds because
Postgres must scan 8,000 rows. The team replaces it with a cursor over (created_at, id), indexes that pair, and returns
next_cursor plus has_more. They cap limit at 100, default to 25, and reject offsets above 1,000 with a 400 that links to
migration docs. Old clients keep working for 90 days: responses carry a Deprecation header and the team emails the top
five integrators. After migration, p95 list latency falls from 3.2 seconds to 90 milliseconds and duplicate-row tickets stop.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Write the response envelope for success, collection, and error cases before writing any handler.
2.    List every list endpoint, its expected row count, and whether its data mutates during a session.
3.    Choose cursor pagination where data is large or changing, and document the sort key and tiebreaker.
4.    Define default and maximum limits, allowed filters, and the status code for invalid queries.
5.    Publish a deprecation policy with notice period, headers, usage measurement, and owner approval.
CODE
Opaque cursors that carry the sort key and tiebreaker, plus a page helper that cannot scan unbounded rows.
  import base64
  import json

  def encode_cursor(created_at: str, row_id: int) -> str:
    raw = json.dumps({"ts": created_at, "id": row_id}, separators=(",", ":"))
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(raw.encode()).decode()

  def decode_cursor(cursor: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
    data = json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(cursor.encode()))
    return data["ts"], int(data["id"])

  def page(rows: list[dict], limit: int = 25) -> dict:
    limit = max(1, min(limit, 100))
    window = rows[:limit]
    last = window[-1] if window else None
    more = len(rows) > limit
    cursor = encode_cursor(last["created_at"], last["id"]) if more else None
    return {"data": window, "has_more": more, "next_cursor": cursor}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The decoder is included so a cursor can be inspected during support work; production should still sign it.
 → limit is clamped to 100 rather than rejected, so a bad client cannot trigger an unbounded scan.
 → The cursor contains the sort key and tiebreaker, not an offset, so inserts do not shift later pages.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: ASGI, uvicorn, and the app ASGI is the interface between a Python web server and your application: each request arrives as a scope, receive, and send callable. Uvicorn runs the event loop, parses HTTP, and invokes the app. FastAPI builds routing, validation, and serialisation on top of Starlette and Pydantic. The app object is a single ASGI callable, which is why uvicorn app.main:app can serve it and why workers are separate processes rather than threads. Lifespan owns shared resources Create connection pools, HTTP clients, and caches once in a lifespan context manager, attach them to app.state, and close them on shutdown. Per-request clients pay handshake costs and leak sockets under load; module-level clients are created at import time, before the event loop in some deployments, and are hard to test. Lifespan also gives you a place to fail fast when a required dependency is unreachable at boot. Database drivers, file reads, and SDK clients must be async, or the work must be pushed to a thread pool or worker process. code.title: One shared HTTP client owned by lifespan, with a route that reuses it instead of reconnecting.
code.code:
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, Request

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
  app.state.http = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=2.0))
  yield
  await app.state.http.aclose()

app = FastAPI(title="documents", lifespan=lifespan)

@app.get("/v1/models")
async def models(request: Request) -> dict:
  r = await request.app.state.http.get("https://api.example.com/v1/models")
  r.raise_for_status()
  return {"items": r.json()["data"]}
what_to_notice: The client is created inside lifespan, so tests and reloads get a fresh pool and shutdown closes sockets deterministically.
A cold start can fail before the first request if the client constructor validates configuration; failing then is cheaper.

lessons.title: Routes
lessons.subtitle: Design route trees that stay readable as the API grows, with typed path parameters, query contracts, and predictable
why_it_matters: Route declarations are the API's table of contents. A flat file with 60 handlers makes ownership unclear and conflict resolution accidental. Typed parameters catch mistakes at the boundary, routers keep modules independent, and explicit status codes stop handlers from leaking implementation details. Most routing bugs are design bugs that appear only when two similar paths compete.
outcomes: Declare path and query parameters with types and constraints so invalid input fails before your handler runs.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Path, query, and body Path parameters identify a resource and are mandatory, such as /documents/{document_id}. Query parameters modify a collection request, such as limit, cursor, or status, and should have defaults and bounds. The request body carries the representation for create and update. FastAPI infers the source: a name in the path is a path parameter, a Pydantic model is a body, and a scalar outside the path is a query parameter. Routers compose the surface An APIRouter groups handlers that share a prefix, tags, dependencies, and response defaults. Create one router per resource or bounded context, include it in the app with include_router, and keep main.py small. Routers also make tests cheaper because a single module can be mounted on a bare app. Choose prefixes that mirror URLs, not team names, so the structure survives reorganisations. Order and conflict rules FastAPI matches routes in registration order, so /documents/export must be declared before /documents/{document_id} or the literal path is captured as an id. A path that exists with a different method returns 405, while an unknown path returns 404. Trailing slashes redirect by default, which can turn a POST into a GET in some clients; define one convention and test both forms.

key_terms.definition: A variable segment of a URL that identifies a resource, such as the document_id in /documents/{document_id}.
A FastAPI object that groups related routes with shared prefixes, tags, and dependencies before being included in the app.

A 307 response that sends a client to the same path with or without a slash, preserving the method and body. MENTAL MODEL Routes are a switchboard: each line must be unambiguous, owned by one team, and wired before a broader line can swallow it.

During a code review, a service has one 900-line router file and two handlers for /documents/{document_id}. The first,

1.    Inventory current paths, methods, and owners, then group them into routers by resource.
2.    Type every path and query parameter and add bounds such as ge=1 and le=100.
3.    Register literal routes before parameterised ones and add a test for each collision.
4.    Set a trailing-slash policy and confirm that redirects preserve both the method and the body.
5.    Mount each router with a prefix and tags, then check the generated OpenAPI groups.
CODE
A resource router where the literal export path is declared before the parameterised document route.
  from fastapi import APIRouter, HTTPException, Query

  router = APIRouter(prefix="/documents", tags=["documents"])
  DOCS: dict[int, dict] = {1: {"id": 1, "title": "Q3 report"}}

  @router.get("/export.csv")
  async def export_csv() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"url": "/exports/documents.csv"}

  @router.get("/{document_id}")
  async def get_document(document_id: int) -> dict:
    if document_id not in DOCS:
       raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="document not found")
    return DOCS[document_id]

  @router.get("")
  async def list_documents(limit: int = Query(25, ge=1, le=100)) -> dict:
    return {"data": list(DOCS.values())[:limit], "limit": limit}

from typing import Annotated, Literal
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

app = FastAPI()

class IngestRequest(BaseModel):
  model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", strict=True)
  title: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=200, pattern=r"\S")]
  pages: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=5_000)]
  source_url: Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r"^https?://")]
  kind: Literal["pdf", "html"] = "pdf"

@app.post("/v1/documents", status_code=201)
async def ingest(body: IngestRequest) -> dict[str, object]:
  return {"title": body.title, "pages": body.pages, "kind": body.kind}

lessons.subtitle: Define what leaves your API as carefully as what enters it, so internal fields never leak and clients keep a stable contract.

why_it_matters: Most FastAPI tutorials return the ORM object straight from the handler, which works until a column is added. Then password hashes, internal notes, and tenant IDs appear in JSON. Response models are the outbound contract: they decide which fields exist, how values serialise, and which changes break clients. outcomes: Separate request models from response models and explain why a shared schema leaks internal fields.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Two schemas, two jobs The request model protects your handler from bad input; the response model protects clients and internal data from your handler. They change for different reasons: adding a notes column should not alter the public payload, while adding a required output field is a versioned API change. Keep both in schemas/ and name them InvoiceCreate, InvoiceUpdate, and InvoiceOut so the direction is obvious at the call site. Serialisation is a filter When a route declares response_model, FastAPI validates the returned value against that model and serialises only its declared fields. Extra attributes on the ORM object are dropped, so password_hash never reaches the wire even if the query selected it. response_model_exclude_none removes absent optional fields, exclude_unset distinguishes 'not supplied' from 'explicitly null', and Field(exclude=True) keeps a value out of model_dump() entirely. Shapes that age well Return UUIDs and integers as their native JSON types, timestamps as ISO 8601 with an explicit UTC offset, and money as integer minor units or a decimal string, never a float. Use enums for closed sets so OpenAPI publishes the allowed values. Prefer a flat object per resource over a generic data/error envelope unless every endpoint needs pagination metadata. Every field you publish becomes a compatibility promise, so publish few.

Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A payments team has 62 integration tests that hit a shared PostgreSQL instance, take four minutes, and fail randomly
when run in parallel. Each route calls SessionLocal inside the handler. The team introduces get_db as a yield dependency
and a client fixture that overrides it with a session bound to a transaction rolled back after every test. The suite drops to

STEP BY STEP
1.    Find every handler that constructs a client, session, or settings object directly and list the resource it owns.
2.    Replace it with a module-level callable: a plain function for stateless services, a yield generator for anything needing
      cleanup.
3.    Annotate handler parameters with Depends and let sub-dependencies compose, for example get_current_user depending
      on get_db.
4.    Register a fake in app.dependency_overrides inside a pytest fixture and clear the dictionary in teardown.
5.    Add a failure-path test proving rollback and cleanup run when the handler raises an exception.
CODE
One session per request: commit on success, roll back on any exception, and close in every case.
  from collections.abc import Iterator
  from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
  from sqlalchemy.orm import Session, sessionmaker

  app = FastAPI()
  SessionLocal = sessionmaker()

  def get_db() -> Iterator[Session]:
    with SessionLocal() as db:
       try:
         yield db
         db.commit()
       except Exception:
         db.rollback()
         raise

  @app.get("/v1/invoices/{invoice_id}")
  def get_invoice(invoice_id: str, db: Session = Depends(get_db)) -> dict[str, str]:
    invoice = db.get(Invoice, invoice_id)
    return {"id": invoice.id, "status": invoice.status}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The commit sits after the yield, so a handler that raises skips it and the except branch rolls the transaction back.
 → The with block closes the session even when rollback itself fails, which prevents a connection leak under load.
 → The route never imports SessionLocal, so a test fixture can swap the session without changing this code.

why_it_matters: Authentication is the boundary every later control depends on. A forged or stolen token defeats tenant isolation, rate limits, and audit logs at once. The common failures are boring: unsalted hashes, tokens that live for thirty days, login endpoints with no rate limit, and a decoder that checks the signature but forgets the audience. Each is cheap to prevent and expensive to discover after a breach.
outcomes: Hash passwords with argon2id and verify them without ever storing or logging the plaintext value.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Credentials are verified, never stored Store only a memory-hard hash. Argon2id with roughly 64 MiB, three iterations, and parallelism 2 makes an offline guess expensive while staying under 100 ms on a normal core. On login, compare with verify, which is constant-time inside the library, and return the same 401 message and timing for an unknown email as for a wrong password, so the endpoint is not a user-enumeration oracle. Rehash silently when parameters change. Tokens carry claims, not trust A JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone holding it can read the payload, so never put secrets or personal data inside. The access token should name the subject, issuer, audience, expiry, and issued-at time, and last about fifteen minutes. The resource server must verify the signature, algorithm, exp, iss, and aud, and must reject alg none. Refresh tokens are opaque, stored hashed, rotated on every use, and revocable. Cookies or bearer tokens Browser clients are usually better served by an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax session cookie, which JavaScript cannot read, combined with CSRF protection on state-changing requests. Mobile apps and service-to-service calls use Authorization: Bearer, because they have no cookie jar and can protect a secret in the platform keystore. Whichever you choose, enforce TLS, set a short idle timeout, and give users a way to revoke every active session.

A name-value assertion inside a token, such as subject, issuer, audience, or expiry time.

A longer-lived, revocable credential exchanged for a new access token without asking for the password again. MENTAL MODEL Authentication is a passport check at the airport: it proves the name on the document, not which rooms in the building you may enter.

Argon2id verification and a signed access token whose lifetime and claims are checked by the resource server.
  import os
  from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

  import jwt
  from argon2 import PasswordHasher
  from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError
  hasher = PasswordHasher(time_cost=3, memory_cost=65536, parallelism=2)
  SECRET = os.environ["JWT_SECRET"]

  def verify(stored: str, supplied: str) -> bool:
    try:
       return hasher.verify(stored, supplied)
    except VerifyMismatchError:
       return False

  def issue(user_id: str) -> str:
    now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)
    claims = {"sub": user_id, "iss": "auth.acme.test", "aud": "api.acme.test",
          "iat": now, "exp": now + timedelta(minutes=15)}
    return jwt.encode(claims, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Who versus whether A verified token proves identity and nothing else. lessons.title: PostgreSQL
lessons.subtitle: Operate the database as a shared, stateful service: connections are scarce, snapshots define visibility, and the planner
why_it_matters: PostgreSQL will happily accept a schema and then fail under concurrency in ways SQLite never showed you. Connection exhaustion, long transactions holding vacuum back, and a sequential scan on a 40-million-row table all look like the API is slow. Knowing the server's model, snapshots, backends, WAL, and autovacuum, turns those incidents into measurements instead of guesses.
outcomes: Explain MVCC snapshots, the default read-committed isolation, and when a serialisable retry is required.
Size a connection pool against max_connections and put PgBouncer in front of a growing fleet.
Read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and identify a missing index, stale statistics, or table bloat.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: MVCC: readers do not block writers Every statement sees a snapshot of committed rows, so a long SELECT never blocks an INSERT. The cost is dead tuples: an update writes a new row version and marks the old one for vacuum. A transaction left open, even idle, holds the oldest snapshot and prevents cleanup of everything newer, which is how a forgotten BEGIN becomes table bloat. Monitor pg_stat_activity for idle in transaction and set a timeout. Connections are processes, not threads Each backend is an operating-system process with several megabytes of memory, so max_connections = 500 is a memory and context-switch decision, not a free knob. A pool of ten connections per API replica multiplied by forty replicas is four hundred backends before traffic arrives. Size the pool from concurrent query slots, not request rate; put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front as replicas grow, and set statement_timeout so one bad query cannot hold a slot forever. The planner needs statistics PostgreSQL chooses between sequential and index scans using row estimates from pg_statistic, refreshed by autovacuum's analyse phase. Bulk-load a million rows and the estimates go stale, so a query that used an index yesterday scans today. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows estimated versus actual rows and where the time went. A large gap points to stale statistics, a missing composite index, or a predicate the planner cannot use.

key_terms.definition: Multi-version concurrency control; each transaction reads a consistent snapshot while writers create new row versions.
The background process that removes dead row versions and refreshes planner statistics after enough changes.

A lightweight connection pooler that multiplexes many client connections onto a small number of PostgreSQL backends. MENTAL MODEL PostgreSQL is a busy library: snapshots are the reading rooms, backends are the staff, and autovacuum is the cleaner who must not be locked out.

worked_example: An API on 400 Fargate tasks, each with a ten-connection pool, starts returning FATAL: too many clients already at 09:10 on a Monday. The database allows 500 connections. The team adds PgBouncer in transaction mode with 40 server connections, caps each service at a quarter of that, sets statement_timeout to 3s and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 10s, and moves reporting to a read replica. The decision to pool at the server rather than shrink every client pool keeps request code unchanged while making the ceiling explicit.

lessons.title: SQL
lessons.subtitle: Write set-based queries that return one answer per request, respect NULL logic, and stay correct when two writers race.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 13 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: Most slow endpoints are not slow because PostgreSQL is slow; they are slow because the application asks it 200 times. SQL rewards thinking in sets: one query can join, group, rank, and filter what a loop does in 200 round trips. The same language also has sharp edges, including NULL comparisons, implicit casts, and read-modify-write races, that produce wrong answers silently rather than errors.
outcomes: Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.
Predict how inner and outer joins treat NULLs and use COUNT(*) and COALESCE correctly.
Write concurrent-safe updates with transactions, ON CONFLICT, and RETURNING, using bound parameters.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Think in sets A query describes the result you want, not the steps to build it. Instead of fetching fifty invoices and then querying each customer, join the tables and return fifty rows in one round trip. Aggregates collapse rows; window functions add a ranking or running total without collapsing them. The test is simple: count the queries your endpoint issues. If that count depends on the number of rows returned, you have an N+1 problem. NULL is unknown, not empty NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown, so WHERE deleted_at = NULL returns nothing; use IS NULL. An inner join drops rows with no match, while LEFT JOIN keeps them and fills columns with NULL, which is why COUNT(*) counts preserved rows and COUNT(c.id) does not. COALESCE supplies a fallback, but putting a nullable column inside NOT IN can silently empty the result because unknown propagates. Writes need a concurrency story Read-modify-write in application code loses updates when two requests overlap: both read 10, both write 9. Prefer a single statement such as UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = %s AND qty >= 1 RETURNING qty, and treat zero returned rows as a conflict. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE makes ingestion idempotent. Wrap multi-statement work in a transaction, keep it short, and pass values as bound parameters rather than formatting them into SQL.

key_terms.definition: A pattern where one query fetches a list and one additional query runs per row, multiplying round trips with result size.
A function that computes across related rows while keeping each row, such as ROW_NUMBER() partitioned by tenant.

An insert that updates the existing row when a specified conflict target is violated, expressed with ON CONFLICT. MENTAL MODEL SQL is a specification, not a recipe: describe the set you want, then let the planner choose how to walk it.

worked_example: A finance dashboard takes 6.8 seconds and issues 1,204 queries: one for the invoice list and one per invoice for its payments. The rewrite uses a single LEFT JOIN with COALESCE(SUM(p.amount_cents), 0) grouped by invoice, plus a LATERAL subquery for the latest payment, and drops the endpoint to 38 ms. A second bug appears in review: the old query used WHERE p.status != 'void', which silently excluded invoices with no payments because the comparison was unknown. The fix moves the predicate into the join condition. The team adds a query-count assertion to the endpoint test so a future ORM shortcut cannot reintroduce the loop.

SQL
Write set-based queries that return one answer per request, respect NULL logic, and stay correct when two writers race.
Backend Engineering · Lesson 13 of 21 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most slow endpoints are not slow because PostgreSQL is slow; they are slow because the application asks it 200 times.
SQL rewards thinking in sets: one query can join, group, rank, and filter what a loop does in 200 round trips. The same
language also has sharp edges, including NULL comparisons, implicit casts, and read-modify-write races, that produce
wrong answers silently rather than errors.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Replace per-row application loops with joins, aggregates, and window functions that return one result set.
 • Predict how inner and outer joins treat NULLs and use COUNT(*) and COALESCE correctly.
 • Write concurrent-safe updates with transactions, ON CONFLICT, and RETURNING, using bound parameters.
CORE CONCEPTS
Think in sets
A query describes the result you want, not the steps to build it. Instead of fetching fifty invoices and then querying each
customer, join the tables and return fifty rows in one round trip. Aggregates collapse rows; window functions add a
ranking or running total without collapsing them. The test is simple: count the queries your endpoint issues. If that count
depends on the number of rows returned, you have an N+1 problem.
NULL is unknown, not empty
NULL = NULL evaluates to unknown, so WHERE deleted_at = NULL returns nothing; use IS NULL. An inner join drops rows
with no match, while LEFT JOIN keeps them and fills columns with NULL, which is why COUNT(*) counts preserved rows
and COUNT(c.id) does not. COALESCE supplies a fallback, but putting a nullable column inside NOT IN can silently empty
the result because unknown propagates.
Writes need a concurrency story
Read-modify-write in application code loses updates when two requests overlap: both read 10, both write 9. Prefer a
single statement such as UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = %s AND qty >= 1 RETURNING qty, and treat zero
returned rows as a conflict. ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE makes ingestion idempotent. Wrap multi-statement work in a
transaction, keep it short, and pass values as bound parameters rather than formatting them into SQL.
KEY TERMS
 N+1 query                        A pattern where one query fetches a list and one additional query runs per row, multiplying round trips with
                                  result size.
 Window function                  A function that computes across related rows while keeping each row, such as ROW_NUMBER() partitioned
                                  by tenant.
 Upsert                           An insert that updates the existing row when a specified conflict target is violated, expressed with ON
                                  CONFLICT.

  MENTAL MODEL SQL is a specification, not a recipe: describe the set you want, then let the planner choose how to walk it.

lessons.subtitle: Turn business rules into tables, keys, and constraints so invalid states cannot be written in the first place.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 14 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: A schema outlives the code that first wrote it. Renaming a column is easy; removing a duplicated fact that three services update is not. Design decisions encode trust: if the database does not enforce tenant ownership and positive quantities, every service must, and one will forget. An hour on keys, constraints, and delete rules prevents months of reconciliation and corrupted reports.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Model the invariant, not the screen Start from the nouns the domain reasons about and the rules that always hold: an invoice belongs to one tenant, a line item to one invoice, a payment never exceeds the balance. Draw cardinality before naming columns. Third normal form removes duplicated facts so an address change happens once. Denormalise only with a measured read cost and a plan for keeping the copy correct, such as a trigger or outbox job. Constraints are cheapest validation NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, and CHECK run inside the database, cover every writer including scripts and migrations, and cannot be forgotten by a new service. Pydantic protects one API; constraints protect the data. Choose delete behaviour explicitly: ON DELETE CASCADE for owned children, RESTRICT for referenced records such as a product on an open order, and SET NULL only when the reference is optional. Types, time, and delete policy Use timestamptz for instants and run sessions in UTC; a naive timestamp is a bug waiting for a daylight-saving boundary. Store money as integer minor units or numeric, never double precision. Prefer text with a CHECK for small closed sets and a lookup table when labels, ordering, or translations matter. Soft deletes preserve history but complicate every unique index and query; use them only where an audit or undo requirement justifies it.

key_terms.definition: A schema where every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
A constraint that requires a column's value to exist in another table's key, protecting referential integrity.

Marking a row as deleted with a timestamp instead of removing it, preserving history at the cost of query complexity. MENTAL MODEL A schema is a contract with every future writer: the database should make the wrong shape impossible, not rely on everyone remembering the rules.

code.title: A minimal billing schema where identity, tenant ownership, positive quantities, and total calculation are enforced by the database.
code.code:
CREATE TABLE invoices (
   id      bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
   tenant_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES tenants (id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
   number      text NOT NULL,
   status    text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('draft', 'open', 'paid')),
   total_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
   created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
   UNIQUE (tenant_id, number)
);
CREATE TABLE invoice_items (
   invoice_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES invoices (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
   sku     text NOT NULL,
   quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
   unit_cents bigint NOT NULL CHECK (unit_cents >= 0),
   PRIMARY KEY (invoice_id, sku)
);
SELECT i.number, SUM(ii.quantity * ii.unit_cents) AS cents
FROM invoice_items ii JOIN invoices i ON i.id = ii.invoice_id
GROUP BY i.number;
what_to_notice: The UNIQUE (tenant_id, number) constraint allows two tenants to reuse invoice 1042 while preventing duplicates inside one tenant.
The items table has no surrogate key because (invoice_id, sku) is already unique and is the natural access path.

total_cents is stored as well as computed; that is deliberate for reporting, and a trigger or service must keep it consistent. Three pages per lesson Page 112 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

production_notes: Add the constraint as NOT VALID during the migration, then run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately on the table to avoid a long lock.
Document the delete policy for every foreign key; an accidental cascade can erase audit history in one statement.
Keep a reconciliation query for every derived total and run it on a schedule, alerting on any mismatch.

lessons.title: SQLAlchemy
lessons.subtitle: Model tables as Python classes, declare how relationships load, and keep one session and one transaction per request.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 15 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: The ORM is a productivity layer over SQL, not a replacement for knowing SQL. Used carelessly it emits hundreds of queries behind one endpoint, holds a transaction open across a network round trip, and hides the difference between a session and a connection. Used deliberately it gives typed models, parameterised queries, and one clear unit of work per request.
outcomes: Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.
Diagnose N+1 queries and fix them with selectinload, joinedload, or an explicit select of columns.
Choose transaction boundaries and pool settings that survive concurrent async requests.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Engine, session, and unit of work The engine owns the connection pool and is created once per process. A session is short-lived: it tracks loaded objects, batches their changes, and commits or rolls back one transaction. Build it with async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False) and open one per request through a dependency. Never share a session between concurrent tasks, because it is not task-safe; a leaked session holds a pooled connection until the pool is exhausted. Loading is a query decision A relationship using lazy='select' fetches related rows on first attribute access, so serialising 50 orders with their customers issues 51 queries. That N+1 is invisible in a test with two rows. Choose loading per query: selectinload for collections, which costs one extra query per relationship, joinedload for many-to-one when the parent set is small, and lazy='raise_on_sql' so an accidental load fails in tests instead of in production. Transactions and readable SQL Keep a transaction open only as long as correctness requires: never across a model call or an outbound HTTP request. Writes that must be atomic share one session and commit once, and a failure rolls the whole unit back. For reports, aggregations, and bulk updates, drop to select() with explicit columns or text() with bound parameters. The ORM adds row identity tracking and indirection you do not need, and it hides the plan you should read.

key_terms.definition: A short-lived unit of work that tracks loaded objects and turns their changes into one transaction on commit.

One query for a parent set plus one per row for a relationship, so cost grows with result size. selectinload A loader that fetches a whole collection in one extra query using WHERE id IN (...), avoiding per-row round trips. MENTAL MODEL A session is a shopping basket for one trip to the database: fill it, commit once, throw it away. The engine is the shop that stays open all day.

worked_example: Aleks supports a 12-person team running an admin API over 480,000 orders. The order-list endpoint takes 4.8 s at p95, and the database logs 1,204 queries for a 250-row page, because each order's customer and three line items loaded lazily during JSON serialisation. Aleks adds selectinload(Order.customer) and selectinload(Order.lines), cuts the page size to 50, and selects only the twelve columns the table renders. Queries fall to 3, p95 to 210 ms, and the 20-connection pool stops saturating at 40 requests per second. The decision: ORM objects stay, but every list endpoint must declare its loading strategy, and a test asserts query count.

code.title: A keyset-paginated list query that declares its loading strategy, so page size cannot change query count.
code.code:
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
from models import Order

engine = create_async_engine(
  "postgresql+asyncpg://app@db/app", pool_size=20, max_overflow=0
)
Session = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)

async def page_of_orders(session, after_id: int = 0, limit: int = 50) -> list[Order]:
  stmt = (
    select(Order)
    .where(Order.id > after_id)
    .order_by(Order.id)
    .limit(limit)
    .options(selectinload(Order.customer), selectinload(Order.lines))
  )
  return list((await session.scalars(stmt)).all())
what_to_notice: The page is keyset-paginated on id rather than OFFSET, so a deep page does not scan and discard every earlier row.
max_overflow=0 turns pool exhaustion into a visible timeout instead of letting Postgres accept unbounded connections.

selectinload adds two queries regardless of page size; a joinedload on a collection would duplicate order rows and break LIMIT. Three pages per lesson Page 115 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Leaving relationships lazy and discovering N+1 queries only when the production table holds thousands of rows.
Holding one global session across requests, so concurrent handlers see each other's uncommitted objects.
Calling commit inside a loop, producing thousands of transactions and partial writes when one iteration fails.
production_notes: Size the pool as database max_connections divided by process count; a larger pool turns overload into connection timeouts.
Set statement_timeout on the role and a request timeout in the app, so a slow query cannot hold a connection indefinitely.
Use READ COMMITTED with explicit SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for contended rows, and put retries outside the session.

SQLAlchemy
Model tables as Python classes, declare how relationships load, and keep one session and one transaction per request.
Backend Engineering · Lesson 15 of 21 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
The ORM is a productivity layer over SQL, not a replacement for knowing SQL. Used carelessly it emits hundreds of
queries behind one endpoint, holds a transaction open across a network round trip, and hides the difference between a
session and a connection. Used deliberately it gives typed models, parameterised queries, and one clear unit of work per
request.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Define mapped classes with typed columns, relationships, and a session factory bound to one engine.
 • Diagnose N+1 queries and fix them with selectinload, joinedload, or an explicit select of columns.
 • Choose transaction boundaries and pool settings that survive concurrent async requests.
CORE CONCEPTS
Engine, session, and unit of work
The engine owns the connection pool and is created once per process. A session is short-lived: it tracks loaded objects,
batches their changes, and commits or rolls back one transaction. Build it with async_sessionmaker(engine,
expire_on_commit=False) and open one per request through a dependency. Never share a session between concurrent
tasks, because it is not task-safe; a leaked session holds a pooled connection until the pool is exhausted.
Loading is a query decision
A relationship using lazy='select' fetches related rows on first attribute access, so serialising 50 orders with their
customers issues 51 queries. That N+1 is invisible in a test with two rows. Choose loading per query: selectinload for
collections, which costs one extra query per relationship, joinedload for many-to-one when the parent set is small, and
lazy='raise_on_sql' so an accidental load fails in tests instead of in production.
Transactions and readable SQL
Keep a transaction open only as long as correctness requires: never across a model call or an outbound HTTP request.
Writes that must be atomic share one session and commit once, and a failure rolls the whole unit back. For reports,
aggregations, and bulk updates, drop to select() with explicit columns or text() with bound parameters. The ORM adds
row identity tracking and indirection you do not need, and it hides the plan you should read.
KEY TERMS
 Session                          A short-lived unit of work that tracks loaded objects and turns their changes into one transaction on commit.
 N+1 query                        One query for a parent set plus one per row for a relationship, so cost grows with result size.
 selectinload                     A loader that fetches a whole collection in one extra query using WHERE id IN (...), avoiding per-row round
                                  trips.

  MENTAL MODEL A session is a shopping basket for one trip to the database: fill it, commit once, throw it away. The engine is the shop
  that stays open all day.

WORKED EXAMPLE
Aleks supports a 12-person team running an admin API over 480,000 orders. The order-list endpoint takes 4.8 s at p95,
and the database logs 1,204 queries for a 250-row page, because each order's customer and three line items loaded lazily
during JSON serialisation. Aleks adds selectinload(Order.customer) and selectinload(Order.lines), cuts the page size to 50,
and selects only the twelve columns the table renders. Queries fall to 3, p95 to 210 ms, and the 20-connection pool stops
saturating at 40 requests per second. The decision: ORM objects stay, but every list endpoint must declare its loading
strategy, and a test asserts query count.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Create one async engine per process with pool_size=20, max_overflow=0, and pool_pre_ping for stale connections.
2.    Declare models with Mapped[...] annotations and relationship(lazy='raise_on_sql') so accidental loads fail loudly.
3.    Provide the session through a FastAPI dependency that commits on success and rolls back on any exception.
4.    Capture emitted SQL for the slow endpoint with echo=True or an event listener, then count queries per request.
5.    Replace per-row lazy loads with selectinload or joinedload, verify the count, and add a regression test.
CODE
A keyset-paginated list query that declares its loading strategy, so page size cannot change query count.
  from sqlalchemy import select
  from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import async_sessionmaker, create_async_engine
  from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
  from models import Order

  engine = create_async_engine(
    "postgresql+asyncpg://app@db/app", pool_size=20, max_overflow=0
  )
  Session = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)

  async def page_of_orders(session, after_id: int = 0, limit: int = 50) -> list[Order]:
    stmt = (
      select(Order)
      .where(Order.id > after_id)
      .order_by(Order.id)
      .limit(limit)
      .options(selectinload(Order.customer), selectinload(Order.lines))
    )
    return list((await session.scalars(stmt)).all())

 → The page is keyset-paginated on id rather than OFFSET, so a deep page does not scan and discard every earlier row.
 → max_overflow=0 turns pool exhaustion into a visible timeout instead of letting Postgres accept unbounded connections.
 → selectinload adds two queries regardless of page size; a joinedload on a collection would duplicate order rows and break
   LIMIT.

lessons.title: Database Migrations
lessons.subtitle: Ship schema changes as reviewed, reversible revisions that stay compatible with the code running on either side of them.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 16 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: A schema change is a deployment to a shared stateful system and the change most likely to take an API down. Autogenerate hides decisions: it will happily add a NOT NULL column to a 40-million-row table and hold an exclusive lock while it rewrites. Migrations stay safe only when they are reviewed, versioned, applied by one runner, and rehearsed against realistic data volume.
outcomes: Generate an Alembic revision, review the autogenerated diff, and write an explicit downgrade or forward fix.
Apply expand-and-contract to rename or tighten a column while old and new code serve traffic.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A migration is versioned code Alembic records applied revisions in alembic_version, and each revision declares upgrade and downgrade steps. Revisions are applied in order by alembic upgrade head, which must be the same command in every environment. Autogenerate diffs models against the live database and writes a draft; treat that draft as a proposal, because it misses data backfills, extensions, triggers, and index options it cannot infer. Once a revision has run anywhere shared, it is immutable. Expand, then contract A column rename is three deployments: add the new column and dual-write, backfill and verify, then switch reads and drop the old column. Old and new application versions must both work during rollout, because containers restart at different times. Tightening constraints follows the same shape: allow nulls, backfill, then add NOT NULL and CHECK once no row violates them. The destructive step waits at least one release after the last reader moves. Locks and volume decide the plan In PostgreSQL, ADD COLUMN with a volatile default rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so add it nullable and set the default separately. CREATE INDEX blocks writes unless CONCURRENTLY is used, and that cannot run inside a transaction block. A backfill on millions of rows runs in batches of 5,000 with a commit and a log line per batch, never as one UPDATE. Watch pg_stat_activity and lock waits while it runs.

key_terms.definition: One versioned Alembic file with upgrade and downgrade functions, identified by a hash in an ordered graph.
A rollout that adds compatible schema first, migrates data, then removes old structures after clients stop using them.

A PostgreSQL index-build option that avoids blocking writes, at the cost of a longer build outside a transaction. MENTAL MODEL A migration is a bridge between two versions of the code: both ends must be able to stand on it while traffic crosses.

worked_example: A team must rename customers.name to full_name on a 40-million-row table taking 900 writes per second. Their first attempt is one revision with alter_column; 40 seconds into the deploy it holds an exclusive lock and checkout starts timing out. They split it. Revision one adds full_name as nullable and the ORM dual-writes. A separate job backfills 5,000 rows per batch with a sleep between batches and logs progress. Revision two, two releases later, sets NOT NULL after a gap query returns zero and drops name. Reads move behind a feature flag. Downtime is zero and the work finishes across four 14-minute windows.
steps: Create the revision with alembic revision --autogenerate, then read every line of the generated diff.
Rewrite operations to be compatible with running code: nullable first, batched backfill, constraints later.
Run upgrade head against a restored production snapshot and record duration and lock waits.
Deploy the migration before the code, verify both versions serve traffic, then switch the readers.
Test the downgrade locally, but plan a forward fix for production and document that rule.

code.title: An expand-phase revision: nullable column, bounded backfill batches, and a concurrent index build.
code.code:
from alembic import op
import sqlalchemy as sa

revision = "20261026_01"
down_revision = "20261019_04"
BACKFILL = (
  "UPDATE customers SET full_name = name WHERE id IN "
  "(SELECT id FROM customers WHERE full_name IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000)"
)

def upgrade() -> None:
  op.add_column("customers", sa.Column("full_name", sa.Text(), nullable=True))
  for _ in range(8):
    op.execute(BACKFILL)
  with op.get_context().autocommit_block():
    op.create_index("ix_customers_full_name", "customers", ["full_name"],
              postgresql_concurrently=True)

def downgrade() -> None:
  op.drop_column("customers", "full_name")
what_to_notice: The loop caps at eight batches so the revision lasts seconds; a 40-million-row backfill belongs in a separate job with progress metrics.
The index is built inside autocommit_block, because CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction and would otherwise hold writes.

Both columns exist after this revision, so the previous application version keeps reading name without error. Three pages per lesson Page 118 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Editing a migration that already ran in staging or production, so environments disagree about the schema.
Letting autogenerate decide the plan, then discovering it dropped an index or ignored a data backfill.
Adding a NOT NULL column with a default to a large table in one step and locking writes for minutes.
production_notes: Run migrations as an explicit deploy step with a single runner; replica startups applying head concurrently cause races and duplicate work.
Log revision, duration, and lock wait for every migration, and alert when deploy time exceeds the previous baseline.
Take a verified snapshot before destructive steps and rehearse the restore, not just the upgrade, in a staging environment.
checklist: Every migration has a reviewed diff and either a tested downgrade or a documented forward fix.
Schema changes stay compatible with the previous application version during rollout.
Large backfills run in batches with progress logs, outside the migration transaction.
I measured migration duration and lock impact on production-sized data.
Destructive steps ship at least one release after the code stops using the old shape.

Which PostgreSQL operations take an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, and how do you avoid them on a hot table?
What does alembic_version store, and what happens when two deploys run upgrade head at once?
Why must CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY run outside a transaction block?
How would you verify a backfill is complete before adding a NOT NULL constraint?
When is a downgrade the wrong answer to a failed migration in production?

lessons.title: Redis
lessons.subtitle: Use Redis as a fast, disposable side-store for counters, locks, sessions, and streams, never as the only copy of a fact.
lessons.meta: Backend Engineering · Lesson 17 of 21 · study guide
why_it_matters: Redis answers in under a millisecond because everything lives in memory, and that is exactly why it must be treated as expendable. Teams lose sessions, rate limits, and locks when an instance restarts without persistence, or when a missing TTL fills memory and the eviction policy deletes keys nobody expected. Using it well means knowing which command is atomic and what happens when a key is absent.
outcomes: Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.
Make compound operations atomic with single commands, transactions, or Lua scripts.
Set TTLs and an eviction policy so memory stays bounded and misses degrade predictably.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Keys, structures, and TTL Everything is a key mapped to a typed value: string for counters and cached blobs, hash for objects whose fields change individually, sorted set for leaderboards and time-ordered work, stream for an append-only log with consumer groups. Namespace keys as service:entity:id:version, because SCAN output is unreadable otherwise. Set a TTL on every key that is not a lock, and prefer SET key value EX 300 NX over separate SET and EXPIRE calls. Atomicity is per command One Redis command is atomic; two commands from your client are not, because another connection can interleave between them. INCR is a safe counter and SET NX EX is a safe lock acquisition. For multi-step logic use a Lua script or MULTI/EXEC, which runs without interruption. A read-modify-write in Python is a race: two workers both read 9 and both write 10, and your rate limit silently allows double the traffic. Test the race with concurrent clients. Memory, eviction, and durability Redis executes commands on one thread, so an O(N) command such as KEYS * or a 100,000-member SMEMBERS blocks every other client. Set maxmemory and choose an eviction policy deliberately: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, noeviction for queues and locks where silent loss breaks correctness. Enable AOF with everysec if a restart may cost a minute of data, because RDB snapshots alone can lose more. A replica is failover, not a backup.

key_terms.definition: A per-key expiry in seconds or milliseconds after which Redis deletes the key and later reads report a miss.
The rule Redis applies at maxmemory, such as allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, or noeviction, which rejects writes.

A script executed atomically inside Redis, combining reads and writes that must not interleave with other clients. MENTAL MODEL Redis is the whiteboard beside the filing cabinet: fast, shared, and wiped without warning, so anything that must survive belongs in the cabinet.
Page 120 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: An API gateway limits 4,000 tenants to 60 requests per minute. The first version calls INCR then EXPIRE as two commands; when a worker dies between them the key never expires and the tenant stays blocked. During an incident an engineer runs KEYS ratelimit:* and stalls all traffic for 900 ms. The team moves to one Lua script that increments and sets the window expiry only when the counter is 1, keeps a 90-second TTL, and scans with SCAN in batches of 200. Memory falls from 3.1 GB to 640 MB after tenant configs gain a 120-second TTL, and p99 latency holds at 0.4 ms.

Set maxmemory and an eviction policy per workload; separate cache keys from queue keys.
Load-test with redis-benchmark at realistic key counts, then watch used_memory, evicted_keys, and latency.
Stop the instance and verify the API degrades to a database path rather than returning 500.

code.title: A fixed-window rate limiter that increments and expires atomically inside Redis.
code.code:
from time import time
from redis.asyncio import Redis

RATE_LIMIT = """
local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
if n > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 end
return 1
"""

async def allow(redis: Redis, tenant: str, per_minute: int = 60) -> bool:
  window = int(time()) // 60
  args = (90, per_minute)
  result = await redis.eval(RATE_LIMIT, 1, f"rl:{tenant}:{window}", *args)
  return bool(result)
what_to_notice: The script expires the key only when the counter is 1, so the window is fixed and a late burst cannot extend a block.
The minute is embedded in the key, so old counters age out on their own and no cleanup job is needed.

eval ships the whole script per call; production registers it once and invokes the cached SHA to save bandwidth. YOUR WORKING NOTES Three pages per lesson Page 121 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

production_notes: Run a replica with sentinel or managed failover, set client timeouts, and treat a connection error as a cache miss.
Separate cache and queue workloads onto different instances or logical databases, so eviction cannot delete jobs that no worker acknowledged.
Track used_memory, evicted_keys, connected_clients, and latency percentiles; a rising eviction rate predicts user-visible misses within minutes.

maxmemory and the eviction policy match the workload, and queues never share a cache-only instance.

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Redis answers in under a millisecond because everything lives in memory, and that is exactly why it must be treated as
expendable. Teams lose sessions, rate limits, and locks when an instance restarts without persistence, or when a missing
TTL fills memory and the eviction policy deletes keys nobody expected. Using it well means knowing which command is
atomic and what happens when a key is absent.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Choose a Redis data structure and key naming scheme for a concrete access pattern.
 • Make compound operations atomic with single commands, transactions, or Lua scripts.
 • Set TTLs and an eviction policy so memory stays bounded and misses degrade predictably.
CORE CONCEPTS
Keys, structures, and TTL
Everything is a key mapped to a typed value: string for counters and cached blobs, hash for objects whose fields change
individually, sorted set for leaderboards and time-ordered work, stream for an append-only log with consumer groups.
Namespace keys as service:entity:id:version, because SCAN output is unreadable otherwise. Set a TTL on every key that is
not a lock, and prefer SET key value EX 300 NX over separate SET and EXPIRE calls.
Atomicity is per command
One Redis command is atomic; two commands from your client are not, because another connection can interleave
between them. INCR is a safe counter and SET NX EX is a safe lock acquisition. For multi-step logic use a Lua script or
MULTI/EXEC, which runs without interruption. A read-modify-write in Python is a race: two workers both read 9 and both
write 10, and your rate limit silently allows double the traffic. Test the race with concurrent clients.
Memory, eviction, and durability
Redis executes commands on one thread, so an O(N) command such as KEYS * or a 100,000-member SMEMBERS blocks
every other client. Set maxmemory and choose an eviction policy deliberately: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, noeviction for
queues and locks where silent loss breaks correctness. Enable AOF with everysec if a restart may cost a minute of data,
because RDB snapshots alone can lose more. A replica is failover, not a backup.
KEY TERMS
 TTL                              A per-key expiry in seconds or milliseconds after which Redis deletes the key and later reads report a miss.
 Eviction policy                  The rule Redis applies at maxmemory, such as allkeys-lru, volatile-ttl, or noeviction, which rejects writes.
 Lua script                       A script executed atomically inside Redis, combining reads and writes that must not interleave with other
                                  clients.

  MENTAL MODEL Redis is the whiteboard beside the filing cabinet: fast, shared, and wiped without warning, so anything that must
  survive belongs in the cabinet.

An API gateway limits 4,000 tenants to 60 requests per minute. The first version calls INCR then EXPIRE as two commands;

1.    List every value Redis will hold, its structure, key pattern, TTL, and what a miss must do.
2.    Replace read-modify-write sequences with INCR, SET NX EX, a Lua script, or a single pipelined round trip.
3.    Set maxmemory and an eviction policy per workload; separate cache keys from queue keys.

CODE
A fixed-window rate limiter that increments and expires atomically inside Redis.
  from time import time
  from redis.asyncio import Redis

  RATE_LIMIT = """
  local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
  if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end
  if n > tonumber(ARGV[2]) then return 0 end
  return 1
  """

  async def allow(redis: Redis, tenant: str, per_minute: int = 60) -> bool:
    window = int(time()) // 60
    args = (90, per_minute)
    result = await redis.eval(RATE_LIMIT, 1, f"rl:{tenant}:{window}", *args)
    return bool(result)
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The script expires the key only when the counter is 1, so the window is fixed and a late burst cannot extend a block.
 → The minute is embedded in the key, so old counters age out on their own and no cleanup job is needed.
 → eval ships the whole script per call; production registers it once and invokes the cached SHA to save bandwidth.
