Median latency fell to 2.9 seconds and the timeout rate from 7% to 0.4%.

STEP BY STEP

2.    Assign each step an input schema, an output schema, a p95 target in milliseconds, and a named failure mode.
3.    Compute the request deadline from the product SLO, then divide it so the stage budgets fit with 20% headroom.
4.    Mark each stage optional or required, and write the exact degraded response for every optional failure.
5.    Add a trace span per stage and replay the slowest ten production traces against the new budgets.
CODE
A budget-aware executor: each stage receives only the time that is left, and late stages are skipped rather than allowed to overrun the request.
  from dataclasses import dataclass
  from time import monotonic
  from typing import Callable

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Stage:
    name: str
    run: Callable[[float], dict]

  def execute(stages: list[Stage], total_s: float = 4.0) -> list[dict]:
    started, log = monotonic(), []
    for stage in stages:
       left = total_s - (monotonic() - started)
       if left < 0.2:
          log.append({"stage": stage.name, "status": "skipped"})
       else:
          log.append({"stage": stage.name,
                  "result": stage.run(round(left * 0.6, 2))})
    return log
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → Stages receive the remaining budget, not their own timeout, so one slow dependency cannot consume the whole request.
 → Skipped stages are logged with a status, which makes degraded responses countable and alertable instead of invisible.
 → The 0.6 multiplier reserves 40% of remaining time for later stages; tune it from trace data, not intuition.

lessons.title: Prompt Templates
lessons.subtitle: Treat prompts as versioned, validated templates: one source of truth, explicit variables, and a rendered artefact you can
why_it_matters: A prompt embedded in an f-string is invisible until it breaks. When three services copy the same instruction, a fix in one leaves the others wrong. Templates give prompts a name, a version, an owner, and a test surface. That costs an hour of setup and repays it the first time a variable rename, a locale, or a model migration touches a prompt in production.
outcomes: Extract prompts from application code into a registry with names, versions, and typed input variables.
Render a template that fails loudly on missing variables and keeps untrusted text inside delimiters.
Ship a prompt change behind an evaluation gate and a version identifier visible in every trace.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Template, not concatenation A template is a text asset with named placeholders, a declared schema, and a renderer. The caller supplies values; the renderer checks that every placeholder has one and that no supplied value is ignored. Keep stable instructions first and variable data last, because providers cache prompt prefixes and because a diff on the data section is easier to review than a change buried mid-sentence. Version the rendered contract Version the pair of template text and input schema, not the file path. Record a short id such as classify@3:a1b2c3d4 in logs, traces, and evaluation results. When accuracy moves you can tell whether the prompt, the model, or the data changed. Keep old versions renderable for replay; deleting them destroys your ability to reproduce last week's incident. A prompt rollback should be a config change, never a redeploy. Untrusted values stay data User text, retrieved chunks, and tool output can contain instructions. Label and delimit them to make provenance clear, but do not treat delimiters or prompt instructions as a security boundary; enforce permissions and tool limits in application code. Validate length and encoding before rendering, and enforce a byte cap per variable; a 200 KB pasted document silently consumes the context you reserved for instructions and output.

key_terms.definition: A versioned store of templates, schemas, and owners that application code references by name instead of pasting text.
The deterministic step that substitutes validated variables into a template and returns the final prompt string.

Silent divergence between copies of the same instructions in different services, producing inconsistent behaviour and unreproducible results. MENTAL MODEL A prompt template is a function signature for language: named arguments in, one deterministic string out, and a version number so you know which function produced a result.

worked_example: TalentLoop, a recruitment marketplace, had 23 prompts spread across four services and two notebooks. A rename of job_title to role_title broke the screening prompt in the worker but not in the API, so 3% of candidates were scored against an empty role for six hours. The team moved every prompt into a registry addressed by name and version, added a schema listing required variables, and made the renderer raise on missing keys. They replay 500 stored requests before each prompt release. The fix took four days; the next rename was caught in CI in ninety seconds.

leaves the others wrong. Templates give prompts a name, a version, an owner, and a test surface. That costs an hour of
setup and repays it the first time a variable rename, a locale, or a model migration touches a prompt in production.

CORE CONCEPTS
Template, not concatenation

logs, traces, and evaluation results. When accuracy moves you can tell whether the prompt, the model, or the data
changed. Keep old versions renderable for replay; deleting them destroys your ability to reproduce last week's incident. A
prompt rollback should be a config change, never a redeploy.

<ticket> or fenced blocks, and state in the system section that content inside those tags is data. Validate length and
encoding before rendering, and enforce a byte cap per variable; a 200 KB pasted document silently consumes the context
you reserved for instructions and output.

Prompt Templates
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
TalentLoop, a recruitment marketplace, had 23 prompts spread across four services and two notebooks. A rename of
job_title to role_title broke the screening prompt in the worker but not in the API, so 3% of candidates were scored
against an empty role for six hours. The team moved every prompt into a registry addressed by name and version, added
a schema listing required variables, and made the renderer raise on missing keys. They replay 500 stored requests before
each prompt release. The fix took four days; the next rename was caught in CI in ninety seconds.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Inventory every prompt string, noting its owner, call site, model, and the variables it expects.
2.    Move each prompt into a named asset with a version, a required-variable schema, and a one-line purpose.
3.    Replace string concatenation with a renderer that raises on missing variables and returns a version id.
4.    Log template id, version, and rendered token count with every request so traces identify the prompt.
5.    Add a replay test over 200 recorded inputs and block the release if schema or output checks regress.
CODE
A minimal template registry: the rendered id pins text and version, and a missing variable fails before the model sees the prompt.
  from hashlib import sha256
  from string import Template

  class PromptTemplate:
    def __init__(self, name: str, version: str, body: str) -> None:
       self.name, self.version, self.body = name, version, body
       self.id = f"{name}@{version}:{sha256(body.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]}"

     def render(self, **values: str) -> str:
       missing = set(Template(self.body).get_identifiers()) - set(values)
       if missing:
          raise ValueError(f"{self.id} missing {sorted(missing)}")
       return Template(self.body).substitute(values)

  classify = PromptTemplate("classify", "3", "Ticket: $ticket\nLabels: $labels\n")
  print(classify.render(ticket="Refund not received", labels="billing,shipping"))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The id combines name, version, and a content hash, so editing the text without bumping the version still changes the trace.
 → Only declared identifiers are checked; extra values are ignored by substitute, so keep the schema authoritative.
 → The template body stays data, which means it can be loaded from a file or database without changing the renderer.

  from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

  class LineItem(BaseModel):
    description: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=200)
    amount: float = Field(ge=0, le=1_000_000)
    page: int = Field(ge=1)
    quote: str = Field(min_length=3, description="verbatim source text")

  class Invoice(BaseModel):
    number: str = Field(pattern=r"^INV-[0-9]{6}$")
    currency: str = Field(pattern=r"^(GBP|EUR|USD)$")
    items: list[LineItem] = Field(min_length=1)

  def parse(raw: str) -> Invoice | None:
    try:
      return Invoice.model_validate_json(raw)
    except ValidationError as exc:
      print("review", [e["loc"] for e in exc.errors()])
      return None

lessons.title: Function Calling
lessons.subtitle: Function calling is a typed loop: the model proposes JSON arguments, your code validates and executes them, and results
why_it_matters: Function calling is the mechanism that turns a chat model into an actor. The model does not run code; it emits a structured request that your process decides whether to honour. Understanding the wire loop prevents two common failures: treating model-supplied arguments as trusted, and letting a tool error crash the request instead of letting the model recover with a valid alternative.
outcomes: Describe the request, tool_calls, tool-result, and second-completion sequence in one model turn.
Validate model-supplied arguments before execution and return errors as tool results instead of exceptions.
Bound the loop with an iteration cap and decide when to stop, answer partially, or escalate to a human.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The loop, precisely A request carries tools, each with a name, a description, and JSON Schema parameters. The model may respond with finish_reason tool_calls and one or more calls, each with an id and JSON-encoded arguments. Your code validates and executes them, appends one tool message per call with the matching id, and sends the conversation back. The model then calls another tool or answers. Every iteration is a new billed completion. Arguments are untrusted input The schema constrains shape, not truth. An order_id can be syntactically valid and belong to another tenant. Validate with the same Pydantic model the schema was generated from, enforce authorisation against the caller's scope, and clamp limits. Treat unknown tool names, extra keys, and wrong types as recoverable errors returned to the model, because a clear error message often produces a correct second call. Cap the loop Set a maximum of three to five tool iterations and a token budget for the whole conversation. Track cumulative tool latency against the request deadline. When the cap or budget is hit, stop calling tools and return a partial answer naming what could not be completed, or escalate. Without a cap, a model that keeps retrying a failing tool will happily spend your entire margin.

  import json

  ORDERS = {1042: "shipped", 1043: "refunded"}

code.title: An executor that checks scope, derives an idempotency key from the tool call id, and reports a timeout as unknown state rather than failure.
code.code:
import asyncio

async def issue_refund(order_id: int, idempotency_key: str) -> str:
  return f"refund {order_id} queued with key {idempotency_key}"

TOOLS = {"refund_order": {"scope": "billing:write", "timeout_s": 6,
             "impl": issue_refund}}

async def call_tool(name: str, call_id: str, grants: set[str], args: dict) -> str:
  spec = TOOLS.get(name)
  if spec is None or spec["scope"] not in grants:
     return f"DENIED {name}: unknown tool or missing scope"
  try:
     out = await asyncio.wait_for(
       spec["impl"](**args, idempotency_key=call_id), spec["timeout_s"])
  except asyncio.TimeoutError:
     return f"{name} timed out; state unknown, reconcile before retry"
  return out[:2000]
what_to_notice: The guard runs before the implementation, so an invented tool name or a missing scope returns a denial without reaching the supplier API.
The call id doubles as the idempotency key, which means a retried call is safe but a re-planned call is a new operation.

lessons.title: Model Routing
lessons.subtitle: Route each request to the cheapest model that provably clears the quality bar, with calibrated thresholds and a safe
why_it_matters: A single model for all traffic either overspends on easy requests or underperforms on hard ones. Routing turns model selection into a per-request decision, but a router that is not measured is just a second source of randomness. The discipline is to find features that predict difficulty, set thresholds from evaluation data, and keep a strong default for cases the router cannot classify.
outcomes: Define routing dimensions from measured request features rather than guessed categories.
Calibrate an escalation threshold on a labelled evaluation set and record its error cost.
Version the routing policy and monitor escalation rate, quality, latency, and spend per route.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Route on evidence, not vibes Good routing signals are observable before the call: prompt length, document type, schema complexity, tenant tier, language, retrieval score, and a cheap classifier's confidence. Bad signals include the model's own claim about difficulty, which costs a call and correlates weakly with correctness. Start with two or three features, measure their separation on labelled data, and add more only when the confusion matrix justifies them. Thresholds come from the cost matrix Pick the threshold where a false escalation costs less than a missed error. If a small model is wrong on 9% of a slice and a bad answer costs GBP 4 while escalation costs GBP 0.02, escalate aggressively. Plot quality and cost against the threshold, choose a point, then verify it on a held-out slice. Recalibrate whenever the model version, prompt, or input distribution changes. A router is versioned policy Store routing rules as configuration with a version id, log the chosen route and reason on every request, and replay a sample through shadow routes to compare outcomes. Keep a fallback to the strongest model when features are missing or the classifier is unavailable. Route ids belong in traces and dashboards, because a report that quality dropped is unanswerable without knowing which route served the traffic.

key_terms.definition: The share of requests routed from a cheaper model to a stronger one, used to monitor router behaviour and cost.
The confidence or feature cutoff at which a request is sent to a stronger model instead of the default.

A routing decision evaluated in parallel and logged without affecting the user's response, used to compare policies. MENTAL MODEL Routing is triage at a hospital: a quick, cheap assessment sends most patients to the right department, and anything ambiguous goes to the senior clinician by default.

  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)

why_it_matters: Every model provider has bad minutes: a 429 spike, a 503 during a regional rollover, or a model that starts returning empty completions after a silent deploy. Without a fallback plan the user sees an error; with a careless plan they see a slower, worse answer that nobody notices. A fallback strategy names the ladder, the trigger for each rung, and the quality you are willing to lose.
outcomes: Rank fallback options by quality, latency, and cost, and write the degradation contract each one must honour.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The fallback ladder Order responses from best to acceptable: primary model, same model on a second provider, smaller sibling model, cached or retrieval-only answer, then clear human escalation. Each rung must satisfy the request contract, so define which fields may degrade and which are mandatory. A ladder of four rungs that all return the same schema beats a clever chain of prompts. Record the rung used on every response so quality dashboards can separate primary traffic from degraded traffic. Triggers, not vibes Fallback fires on measured signals: HTTP 429 after retries, 5xx above a threshold, a timeout at 80% of the request deadline, an empty or schema-invalid completion, or a safety refusal that policy allows you to re-route. Do not fall back on a single transient blip; randomise and cap retries first. Each trigger has an owner and a counter. If you cannot name the metric that opens the rung, the fallback will either never fire or fire constantly. Degradation contract A fallback changes quality, latency, or both, so state the trade explicitly. The degraded answer may be shorter, older, or ungrounded, but it must never be silently wrong. Attach a `degraded` flag, a reason code, and a user-visible note when the contract changes, such as 'answer from cache, 12 minutes old'. For machine consumers, keep the response schema stable and put the difference in metadata, so downstream parsers do not break when the ladder moves.

key_terms.definition: An ordered list of substitute paths, from best-quality to last-resort, used when the primary model call fails or misses its contract.
The explicit statement of which answer properties may worsen during fallback and which must stay invariant.

The total time a request may spend across retries and fallbacks before the caller gives up. MENTAL MODEL A fallback ladder is an emergency staircase: every step is inspected, load-rated, and signed, and you always know which floor you exited on.

CODE
A deadline-aware ladder: each rung gets only the time that remains, and only transient errors advance it.
  import time

  class TransientError(Exception): ...
  class FallbackExhausted(Exception): ...

  def run_ladder(rungs, payload, deadline=8.0):
    """rungs: [(name, call, timeout_s)] ordered best to last resort."""
    start, errors = time.monotonic(), []
    for name, call, timeout in rungs:
       left = deadline - (time.monotonic() - start)
       if left < 1.0:
          break
       try:
          return call(payload, min(timeout, left)), name
       except TransientError as exc:
          errors.append(f"{name}:{exc}")
    raise FallbackExhausted(errors) from None

lessons.title: Streaming Architecture
lessons.subtitle: Design a streaming path that gets the first token out fast, survives disconnects, and still validates what the user finally
why_it_matters: Users judge a slow answer as broken long before it finishes. Streaming converts a six-second wait into a 400 ms first token and a readable trickle, which changes perceived latency without changing model speed. It also changes failure handling: once bytes are sent, you cannot return a 500, so the stream must carry its own errors, heartbeat, and completion signal. Design the protocol before the UI.
outcomes: Separate time-to-first-token from total latency and choose where each budget is enforced.
Deliver model output as typed server-sent events that a browser, CLI, and proxy all handle correctly.
Handle disconnects, mid-stream failures, and final validation without leaving half-written state.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Time to first token vs completion Measure two numbers: time to first token (TTFT) and time to last token (TTLT). A large model may take 900 ms to prefill a long prompt but stream at 45 tokens per second; a smaller model starts in 300 ms and finishes the same answer later. Route interactive requests by TTFT and batch jobs by TTLT and cost. Report percentiles separately, because averaging the two hides the queueing that users actually feel. Events, not raw text Server-sent events give you a named envelope: `start`, `delta`, `usage`, `error`, `done`. Each event carries a request id and a monotonic sequence number so reconnects can detect gaps. Send a comment heartbeat every 15 seconds to keep proxies from closing an idle connection. Reserve the final `done` event for validated output and token usage, so a client can tell a complete answer from a truncated one. Newlines inside deltas must be JSON-escaped, never raw SSE separators. Disconnects and backpressure When the client disconnects, cancel the upstream model call; otherwise you pay for tokens nobody reads. In FastAPI, watch `request.is_disconnected()` or catch `asyncio.CancelledError` and close the provider stream in a `finally` block. Apply backpressure by bounding the queue between provider and socket, and drop or coalesce deltas when the consumer is slow. A generation that outruns a slow mobile client is a memory leak with extra steps.

key_terms.definition: The interval from request start to the first content token, the dominant driver of perceived responsiveness in chat interfaces.
A one-way HTTP response of text/event-stream frames that browsers consume through EventSource, well suited to token streams.

The mechanism that slows or buffers a fast producer when the consumer cannot keep up, preventing unbounded memory growth. MENTAL MODEL Streaming is a live broadcast, not a printed report: the show starts early, the signal needs keep-alives, and you need an explicit sign-off before anyone trusts the ending.

worked_example: A support-assistant team shipped streaming and celebrated a 380 ms TTFT, then saw complaints about answers that stopped mid-sentence. Logs showed nginx buffering the response for 30 seconds and a mobile client reconnecting after 60 seconds idle. The fix was three changes: send `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, emit a heartbeat comment every 15 seconds, and add a final `done` event carrying `finish_reason` and token usage. Streaming Architecture
Design a streaming path that gets the first token out fast, survives disconnects, and still validates what the user finally
sees.
LLM Application Engineering · Lesson 9 of 14 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Users judge a slow answer as broken long before it finishes. Streaming converts a six-second wait into a 400 ms first token
and a readable trickle, which changes perceived latency without changing model speed. It also changes failure handling:
once bytes are sent, you cannot return a 500, so the stream must carry its own errors, heartbeat, and completion signal.
Design the protocol before the UI.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Separate time-to-first-token from total latency and choose where each budget is enforced.
 • Deliver model output as typed server-sent events that a browser, CLI, and proxy all handle correctly.
 • Handle disconnects, mid-stream failures, and final validation without leaving half-written state.
CORE CONCEPTS
Time to first token vs completion
Measure two numbers: time to first token (TTFT) and time to last token (TTLT). A large model may take 900 ms to prefill a
long prompt but stream at 45 tokens per second; a smaller model starts in 300 ms and finishes the same answer later.
Route interactive requests by TTFT and batch jobs by TTLT and cost. Report percentiles separately, because averaging the
two hides the queueing that users actually feel.
Events, not raw text
Server-sent events give you a named envelope: `start`, `delta`, `usage`, `error`, `done`. Each event carries a request id and
a monotonic sequence number so reconnects can detect gaps. Send a comment heartbeat every 15 seconds to keep
proxies from closing an idle connection. Reserve the final `done` event for validated output and token usage, so a client
can tell a complete answer from a truncated one. Newlines inside deltas must be JSON-escaped, never raw SSE
separators.
Disconnects and backpressure
When the client disconnects, cancel the upstream model call; otherwise you pay for tokens nobody reads. In FastAPI,
watch `request.is_disconnected()` or catch `asyncio.CancelledError` and close the provider stream in a `finally` block.
Apply backpressure by bounding the queue between provider and socket, and drop or coalesce deltas when the
consumer is slow. A generation that outruns a slow mobile client is a memory leak with extra steps.
KEY TERMS
 Time to first token              The interval from request start to the first content token, the dominant driver of perceived responsiveness in
                                  chat interfaces.
 Server-sent events               A one-way HTTP response of text/event-stream frames that browsers consume through EventSource, well
                                  suited to token streams.
 Backpressure                     The mechanism that slows or buffers a fast producer when the consumer cannot keep up, preventing
                                  unbounded memory growth.

  MENTAL MODEL Streaming is a live broadcast, not a printed report: the show starts early, the signal needs keep-alives, and you need an
  explicit sign-off before anyone trusts the ending.

Streaming Architecture
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A support-assistant team shipped streaming and celebrated a 380 ms TTFT, then saw complaints about answers that
stopped mid-sentence. Logs showed nginx buffering the response for 30 seconds and a mobile client reconnecting after
60 seconds idle. The fix was three changes: send `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, emit a heartbeat comment every 15 seconds, and
add a final `done` event carrying `finish_reason` and token usage. They also cancelled the provider call on disconnect,
which cut spend by 11% because abandoned tabs had been generating full answers. The design review rejected client-side
retry on a partial stream: resuming needs sequence numbers and server state they did not have.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define the event schema with start, delta, usage, error, and done events, each carrying a request id and sequence.
2.    Configure the proxy and framework to disable response buffering and compression on the event stream.
3.    Emit a heartbeat every 15 seconds and cancel the provider call when the client disconnects.
4.    Validate the assembled text before the done event, and send an error event if validation fails.
5.    Measure time to first token, time to last token, disconnect rate, and completion rate per model.
CODE
A FastAPI SSE endpoint that stops generating on disconnect, disables proxy buffering, and ends with an explicit done event.
  import json
  from fastapi import FastAPI, Request
  from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

  app = FastAPI()

  @app.get("/stream")
  async def stream(request: Request, q: str) -> StreamingResponse:
    async def events():
      try:
        async for token in call_model(q):
           if await request.is_disconnected():
              return
           data = json.dumps({"delta": token})
           yield f"event: delta\ndata: {data}\n\n"
        yield 'event: done\ndata: {"finish_reason": "stop"}\n\n'
      except Exception as exc:
        yield f'event: error\ndata: {json.dumps({"message": str(exc)})}\n\n'
    headers = {"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"}
    return StreamingResponse(events(), media_type="text/event-stream", headers=headers)
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The endpoint never buffers the full answer: the first delta leaves as soon as the provider yields a token, which is the entire
   point.
 → The done event is emitted only after generation completes, so clients can distinguish a finished answer from a dropped
   connection.
 → Disconnect detection runs per token; without it the provider continues burning tokens after the browser tab closes.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Three token counts Track input tokens, reserved output tokens, and the model's hard limit separately. Your request must satisfy `input + max_tokens <= context_limit`, and your wallet cares about actual output, not the reservation. Tokenisers differ: `cl100k_base` is not the tokenizer for every model, and a 4% miscount on a 30,000-token prompt is 1,200 tokens. Count with the provider's own tokenizer or its count-tokens endpoint, and re-count after any template change. Budget by section Give each prompt section a cap: system 1,000, retrieved documents 6,000, conversation history 3,000, user turn 500, output 1,500. When the total exceeds the window, trim in a declared order, usually oldest history first, then lowest- scoring retrieved chunks, then verbose few-shot examples. Never trim the system policy or the current user question. Publish the caps in configuration so a retrieval change cannot silently starve the output budget. Quality cost of trimming Dropping tokens is not free: a truncated policy section causes invented refund rules, and a summarised history loses the order number the user gave three turns ago. Evaluate each trimming strategy on a fixed set of long conversations, measuring task success and citation accuracy against the full-context baseline. Prefer structured compression, such as extracting decisions and entity state, over naive head truncation. Reserve five to ten percent headroom for tokeniser drift and tool schemas.

Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A contract-review assistant sent the entire 60-page agreement on every question. At 78,000 input tokens per call, p95
latency was 14 seconds and monthly spend reached USD 4,100. The team introduced a section budget: 1,000 tokens for

STEP BY STEP
1.    Measure the current input and output token distribution by endpoint, not by average alone.
2.    Set caps per prompt section and reserve output tokens before any trimming happens.
3.    Implement section-aware trimming with a fixed priority order and a log of what was dropped.
4.    Add a pre-flight check that rejects or reroutes requests that still exceed the model limit.

CODE
A section-budget assembler that reserves output tokens, keeps history newest-first, and refuses a prompt that cannot fit.
  import tiktoken

  ENC = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
  CAPS = {"system": 1_000, "context": 8_000, "history": 2_000, "output": 1_500}

  def count(text: str) -> int:
    return len(ENC.encode(text))

  def fit(system: str, context: str, history: list[str], limit: int) -> dict:
    budget = limit - CAPS["output"]
    used = count(system) + count(context)
    kept: list[str] = []
    for turn in reversed(history):
       cost = count(turn)
       if used + cost > budget:
          break
       used += cost
       kept.append(turn)
    if used > budget: raise ValueError("prompt exceeds budget after assembly")
    return {"system": system, "context": context, "history": kept[::-1]}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The output reservation is subtracted before history is considered, so the model always has room to finish.
 → History is trimmed oldest-first while the system prompt and current context stay intact, preserving the task definition.
 → The final check raises instead of silently truncating, which surfaces a retrieval configuration error early.

lessons.title: Cost Management
lessons.subtitle: Turn token prices into unit economics you can forecast, attribute, and defend before the invoice surprises you.
lessons.meta: LLM Application Engineering · Lesson 11 of 14 · study guide
why_it_matters: Model spend is variable, usage-driven, and easy to grow accidentally: a retry storm, a prompt that includes a whole document, or a new feature that fans out five calls per request. Finance sees one invoice; engineering needs cost per request, per tenant, and per successful outcome. Without that unit economics you cannot price a plan, defend an architecture choice, or notice that a caching regression doubled the bill.
outcomes: Build a cost model per request, per tenant, and per feature from token usage and provider price tiers.
Choose caching, batching, routing, and output limits based on measured cost per successful task.
Set budgets and anomaly alerts that catch a runaway prompt or retry loop within hours, not at month end.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Unit economics The useful unit is cost per successful task, not cost per token. Divide monthly model spend by completed tasks, then break it into input, output, cache-read, and retry components. A support answer that costs USD 0.004 but resolves only 60% of tickets costs USD 0.0067 per resolution, which changes the comparison with a cheaper model. Track the same unit per tenant and per feature so one customer's 200-page uploads do not hide inside a healthy average. Levers that move the bill Output tokens usually cost three to five times input tokens, so cap max_tokens and shorten answers before shopping for a cheaper model. Prompt caching cuts repeated system and document prefixes, often 50 to 90% of input, but only when the prefix is stable and ordered first. Batch APIs trade latency for roughly half price on non-interactive jobs. Routing sends easy requests to a small model. Measure each lever against quality, not in isolation. Budgets and anomalies Tag every call with tenant, feature, prompt version, and model, then aggregate usage daily. Set soft budgets per tenant and hard caps per environment; a cap that returns 429 to an internal batch job is better than a five-figure surprise. Alert on cost per request deviating more than 30% from a seven-day baseline, and on retry rate, which often signals a silent failure loop. Reconcile your ledger against the provider invoice monthly, because rounding and cached-token rules will differ.

key_terms.definition: Total model spend for a feature divided by the number of tasks it completed, including retries and failed attempts.
A provider feature that bills a repeated prefix at a lower rate when it matches a previously cached prompt.

Metadata attached to each model call, such as tenant, feature, and prompt version, used to allocate spend. MENTAL MODEL Model spend is a taxi meter with several rates: distance, waiting time, and luggage. You cannot lower the fare by complaining at the end; you change the route before you start.

worked_example: A B2B analytics product launched a 'summarise this dashboard' button. Usage grew 8% week over week, but the bill grew 60% because each click sent the full 40,000-token schema and sample rows. The team added a stable system prefix and enabled prompt caching, moved the schema to a compressed representation, capped output at 400 tokens, and routed simple 'what changed' questions to a small model. Cost per summary fell from USD 0.031 to USD 0.009 while the evaluation score stayed within one point. They also found a retry loop triggered by a 400 error on long dashboards; fixing it removed 18% of calls. The product kept the button and set a per-tenant monthly cap.

code.title: A usage ledger that prices fresh input, cached input, and output separately, then returns dollars per call.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

PRICES = { # USD per million tokens
  "small": {"in": 0.15, "cached": 0.075, "out": 0.60},
  "large": {"in": 2.50, "cached": 1.25, "out": 10.00},
}

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Usage:
  model: str
  input_tokens: int
  cached_tokens: int
  output_tokens: int

def cost(u: Usage) -> float:
  p = PRICES[u.model]
  fresh = u.input_tokens - u.cached_tokens
  return (fresh * p["in"] + u.cached_tokens * p["cached"]
       + u.output_tokens * p["out"]) / 1_000_000
what_to_notice: Cached tokens are subtracted from input before pricing, so the discount is visible rather than applied twice.
Prices are per million tokens, matching provider sheets; mixing per-thousand and per-million rates is a common tenfold error.

The ledger prices observed usage from the response, not estimated tokens, so it reconciles against the invoice. Three pages per lesson Page 213 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Cost Management
Turn token prices into unit economics you can forecast, attribute, and defend before the invoice surprises you.
LLM Application Engineering · Lesson 11 of 14 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Model spend is variable, usage-driven, and easy to grow accidentally: a retry storm, a prompt that includes a whole
document, or a new feature that fans out five calls per request. Finance sees one invoice; engineering needs cost per
request, per tenant, and per successful outcome. Without that unit economics you cannot price a plan, defend an
architecture choice, or notice that a caching regression doubled the bill.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Build a cost model per request, per tenant, and per feature from token usage and provider price tiers.
 • Choose caching, batching, routing, and output limits based on measured cost per successful task.
 • Set budgets and anomaly alerts that catch a runaway prompt or retry loop within hours, not at month end.
CORE CONCEPTS
Unit economics
The useful unit is cost per successful task, not cost per token. Divide monthly model spend by completed tasks, then break
it into input, output, cache-read, and retry components. A support answer that costs USD 0.004 but resolves only 60% of
tickets costs USD 0.0067 per resolution, which changes the comparison with a cheaper model. Track the same unit per
tenant and per feature so one customer's 200-page uploads do not hide inside a healthy average.
Levers that move the bill
Output tokens usually cost three to five times input tokens, so cap max_tokens and shorten answers before shopping for
a cheaper model. Prompt caching cuts repeated system and document prefixes, often 50 to 90% of input, but only when
the prefix is stable and ordered first. Batch APIs trade latency for roughly half price on non-interactive jobs. Routing sends
easy requests to a small model. Measure each lever against quality, not in isolation.
Budgets and anomalies
Tag every call with tenant, feature, prompt version, and model, then aggregate usage daily. Set soft budgets per tenant
and hard caps per environment; a cap that returns 429 to an internal batch job is better than a five-figure surprise. Alert
on cost per request deviating more than 30% from a seven-day baseline, and on retry rate, which often signals a silent
failure loop. Reconcile your ledger against the provider invoice monthly, because rounding and cached-token rules will
differ.
KEY TERMS
 Cost per successful task         Total model spend for a feature divided by the number of tasks it completed, including retries and failed
                                  attempts.
 Prompt caching                   A provider feature that bills a repeated prefix at a lower rate when it matches a previously cached prompt.
 Attribution tag                  Metadata attached to each model call, such as tenant, feature, and prompt version, used to allocate spend.

  MENTAL MODEL Model spend is a taxi meter with several rates: distance, waiting time, and luggage. You cannot lower the fare by
  complaining at the end; you change the route before you start.

A B2B analytics product launched a 'summarise this dashboard' button. Usage grew 8% week over week, but the bill grew
60% because each click sent the full 40,000-token schema and sample rows. The team added a stable system prefix and

evaluation score stayed within one point. They also found a retry loop triggered by a 400 error on long dashboards; fixing
it removed 18% of calls. The product kept the button and set a per-tenant monthly cap.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Instrument calls with tenant, feature, model, prompt version, and token counts before optimising anything.
2.    Compute cost per successful task for the top three features and compare it with their revenue or value.
3.    Rank levers by measured saving: output cap, prefix caching, context trimming, batch, then routing.
4.    Apply one lever at a time and re-run the quality evaluation to catch regressions.
5.    Set per-tenant budgets, anomaly alerts, and a monthly invoice reconciliation in the finance calendar.
CODE
A usage ledger that prices fresh input, cached input, and output separately, then returns dollars per call.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  PRICES = { # USD per million tokens
    "small": {"in": 0.15, "cached": 0.075, "out": 0.60},
    "large": {"in": 2.50, "cached": 1.25, "out": 10.00},
  }

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Usage:
    model: str
    input_tokens: int
    cached_tokens: int
    output_tokens: int

  def cost(u: Usage) -> float:
    p = PRICES[u.model]
    fresh = u.input_tokens - u.cached_tokens
    return (fresh * p["in"] + u.cached_tokens * p["cached"]
         + u.output_tokens * p["out"]) / 1_000_000
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → Cached tokens are subtracted from input before pricing, so the discount is visible rather than applied twice.
 → Prices are per million tokens, matching provider sheets; mixing per-thousand and per-million rates is a common tenfold
   error.
 → The ledger prices observed usage from the response, not estimated tokens, so it reconciles against the invoice.

code.title: A tiered assembler that always keeps pinned items, ranks candidates by authority and date, and stops at the token budget.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Item:
  source: str
  text: str
  tokens: int
  rank: tuple[int, str] # authority, effective_date

def assemble(pinned: list[Item], candidates: list[Item], budget: int) -> list[Item]:
  pack, seen = list(pinned), set()
  used = sum(i.tokens for i in pack)
  for item in sorted(candidates, key=lambda i: i.rank, reverse=True):
     key = item.text.strip().lower()
     if key in seen or used + item.tokens > budget:
        continue
     seen.add(key)
     pack.append(item)
     used += item.tokens
  return pack
what_to_notice: Pinned items bypass ranking and budget admission, which is correct for policy but dangerous if a caller can pin arbitrary text.
Sorting by authority then effective date puts the current policy ahead of a better lexical match from an archived document.

The dedupe key is normalised text, so whitespace and case changes do not smuggle a second copy into the pack. Three pages per lesson Page 216 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Ranking purely by similarity score, letting an outdated document outrank the current policy because its wording matches.
Filtering by tenant after retrieval, so a revoked or foreign document has already entered the prompt.
Concatenating every retrieved chunk until the window is full, burying the decisive evidence in the middle.
production_notes: Store the assembled pack, its item ids, and the prompt version with each request trace, so a wrong answer can be reconstructed exactly.
Test conflicting-source questions in CI; if the current policy does not win, the ranking or the metadata is wrong.
Expire documents by review interval in the retrieval filter, and alert when an answer cites a superseded version.

Authorisation filters run inside the retrieval query, not after ranking.
Pinned policy and the current user turn are never trimmed.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.subtitle: Classify every failure before you retry it, then return an error envelope callers can act on and operators can trace.
lessons.meta: LLM Application Engineering · Lesson 13 of 14 · study guide
why_it_matters: An LLM call can fail in more ways than a normal HTTP dependency: rate limits, overloaded capacity, timeouts, content filters, context overflow, malformed JSON, and tool errors. Retrying all of them wastes money and worsens overload; retrying none turns a transient blip into a user-visible outage. Error handling starts with classification, then applies a policy per class and reports the result in a form the caller can act on.
outcomes: Map provider and application failures into retriable, terminal, and policy categories.
Implement jittered retries, timeouts, and a circuit breaker that respect the request deadline.
Return a structured error envelope with a stable code, request id, and safe retry guidance.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Classify before retrying Retry 429 and 5xx responses, connection resets, and timeouts, but only within the deadline; honour `Retry-After` when present. Never blindly retry 400, 401, 403, 404, or 422: they mean the request, key, or schema is wrong, and repetition cannot fix it. Treat content-filter refusals and context-length errors as policy or input problems that need a different prompt, model, or trimming. Mark every exception with one of three classes and one stable code before it reaches the retry layer. Backoff, deadlines, breakers Use exponential backoff with full jitter: sleep a random duration between zero and the capped delay, so a thousand clients do not retry in lockstep. Give the whole operation one deadline and pass the remaining time to each attempt; a retry that cannot finish before the deadline is just a slower failure. Add a circuit breaker per provider and model, opening after a sustained error rate and probing with a single request. Retries without jitter and breakers turn a provider wobble into a self-inflicted outage. An envelope callers can use Return a JSON body with `code`, `message`, `request_id`, `retriable`, and `retry_after_ms`; map it to the right HTTP status, such as 429 for rate limit, 503 for provider unavailable, 504 for deadline exceeded, and 422 for invalid output. Never leak provider stack traces, keys, or raw model output into the message. Log provider, model, attempt count, latency, and error class against the same request id. Clients should branch on code, not on prose or status alone.

key_terms.definition: A transient failure, such as a 429, 503, or timeout, where a later identical attempt may succeed.
A state machine that stops calling a failing dependency after a threshold and probes it cautiously before restoring traffic.

A stable JSON response shape carrying a machine-readable code, request id, and retry guidance. MENTAL MODEL Errors are triage, not a shrug: sort each failure into try again, fix the request, or stop and escalate, then treat it accordingly.
Page 218 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: During a load test, a FastAPI service returned 500 for 22% of requests after a provider began sending 529 'overloaded'. The existing retry loop caught every exception and retried three times without jitter, so 400 concurrent users produced 1,600 immediate calls. p99 reached 41 seconds and the provider escalated the rate limit. The fix classified errors, retried only 429/5xx with full jitter and a 6-second deadline, added a breaker that opened after 20 failures in 30 seconds, and returned 503 with retry_after_ms instead of 500. Error rate fell to 0.4% and p99 to 4.1 seconds. The review also removed a retry on validation errors, which had been tripling cost on a broken prompt.

what_to_notice: The retry cap is small and the remaining deadline shrinks each attempt, so the loop cannot outlive the caller's patience.
Retry-After overrides computed jitter, which keeps the client compliant when the provider asks for a longer pause.

Error Handling
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
During a load test, a FastAPI service returned 500 for 22% of requests after a provider began sending 529 'overloaded'.
The existing retry loop caught every exception and retried three times without jitter, so 400 concurrent users produced
1,600 immediate calls. p99 reached 41 seconds and the provider escalated the rate limit. The fix classified errors, retried
only 429/5xx with full jitter and a 6-second deadline, added a breaker that opened after 20 failures in 30 seconds, and
returned 503 with retry_after_ms instead of 500. Error rate fell to 0.4% and p99 to 4.1 seconds. The review also removed
a retry on validation errors, which had been tripling cost on a broken prompt.
STEP BY STEP
1.    List every exception the service can raise and assign a class: retriable, input, policy, or internal.
2.    Set one request deadline and derive per-attempt timeouts and a retry cap from it.
3.    Implement full-jitter backoff that honours Retry-After, plus a breaker per provider and model.
4.    Map each class to an HTTP status and an envelope with code, request id, and retriable flag.
5.    Test with injected 429s, 503s, timeouts, and malformed outputs, and assert the envelope and latency.
CODE
A jittered retry loop that retries only known-transient statuses, honours Retry-After, and stops when the deadline is spent.
  import asyncio
  import random

  RETRIABLE = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 529}

  async def call_with_retry(call, deadline_s: float = 8.0, max_attempts: int = 3):
    loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
    start = loop.time()
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
      left = deadline_s - (loop.time() - start)
      if left <= 0.2:
         raise TimeoutError("deadline exhausted")
      try:
         return await asyncio.wait_for(call(), timeout=left)
      except ProviderError as exc:
         if exc.status not in RETRIABLE or attempt == max_attempts:
            raise
         delay = min(2 ** (attempt - 1) * 0.5, left / 2)
         await asyncio.sleep(exc.retry_after or random.uniform(0, delay))
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The retry cap is small and the remaining deadline shrinks each attempt, so the loop cannot outlive the caller's patience.
 → Retry-After overrides computed jitter, which keeps the client compliant when the provider asks for a longer pause.
 → ProviderError carries the status; a validation or authentication error is not wrapped as ProviderError and therefore never
   retried.

Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Catching every exception and retrying three times, turning a permanent 400 into three billable failures.
2.     Retrying without jitter across a fleet, so recovery traffic arrives in a synchronised wave that re-triggers the outage.

    ◆ Keep breakers per provider and model rather than one global breaker, so a single bad model does not disable every route.
    ◆ Store the request id in logs, traces, and the response envelope so support can join a user complaint to a provider attempt.

□      Every raised exception carries a class and a stable error code.
□      Only 429, 5xx, timeouts, and connection failures are retried; validation errors surface immediately.
□      All retries share one deadline and use full jitter, honouring Retry-After.

code.code:
import asyncio
from dataclasses import dataclass
from fastapi import HTTPException

@dataclass
class Budget:
  deadline_s: float = 9.0
  max_tokens: int = 8_000

async def handle(req, deps) -> dict:
  budget = Budget()
  try:
    async with asyncio.timeout(budget.deadline_s):
       context, used = deps.assemble(req, budget.max_tokens)
       answer, rung = await deps.ladder(context, budget)
       parsed = deps.schema.model_validate_json(answer)
       deps.metrics.observe(rung=rung, tokens=used, request_id=req.id)
       return {"data": parsed.model_dump(), "degraded": rung != "primary"}
  except TimeoutError:
    raise HTTPException(504, {"code": "deadline_exceeded", "retriable": True})
what_to_notice: The timeout wraps retrieval, generation, and fallback together, so no stage can spend the budget twice.
Validation happens before the response is shaped, and a schema failure is not caught by the timeout handler.

lessons.title: Why LLMs Hallucinate
lessons.subtitle: Understand why a next-token predictor invents facts, and separate knowledge gaps from retrieval and formatting failures.
why_it_matters: A hallucination is not a bug that a better prompt eliminates; it is the predictable behaviour of a model optimised to produce plausible continuations. Engineers who treat every wrong answer as a prompt problem burn weeks. Engineers who classify the failure spend that time on the right fix: retrieval for missing facts, verification for unchecked claims, and abstention when evidence is absent.
outcomes: Explain how next-token prediction produces fluent text without any lookup step or built-in check on factual truth.
Classify a wrong answer as knowledge gap, stale memory, entity confusion, prompt pressure, or decoding noise.
Choose a mitigation per failure class: abstention, retrieval, verification, prompt change, or lower-variance decoding.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Prediction is not lookup A model encodes statistical patterns from training text into weights, then generates one token at a time by scoring likely continuations. There is no row to read, no source to cite, and no flag that says 'I do not know'. A policy number, a citation, or an API field appears because that shape of string usually follows the question. Fluent grammar and confident tone are properties of the generator, not evidence of correctness. Five failure classes Knowledge gaps cover facts never in training or too rare to memorise. Stale memory covers facts that changed after the training cutoff. Entity confusion merges similar names, products, or versions. Prompt pressure covers leading questions and instructions that reward agreement. Decoding noise covers the same prompt producing different answers above temperature zero. Each class has a different fix, so label the class before changing anything. Confidence is not calibrated Models are trained and tuned to answer, so refusal is rare unless you ask for it explicitly and give it somewhere to go. Token probabilities measure fluency, not truth: a fabricated citation can be generated with higher confidence than a correct one. That is why grounded systems check claims against retrieved text, require citations that resolve to real chunk IDs, and offer a visible not-found path instead of trusting the model's self-report.

key_terms.definition: A fluent model output that is unsupported by evidence or contradicted by the source of truth.
Facts compressed into model weights during training, with no provenance and no update path between retraining runs.

Supplying authoritative text at inference time and requiring the answer to stay within it. MENTAL MODEL A model is an improviser with a vast memory of how sentences usually go: brilliant at shape, unreliable at facts, and unable to tell you which is which.
Page 225 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: At a UK bank, the internal policy assistant answers 4,000 staff questions a week. A staff member asks whether a bereavement refund is allowed after 60 days. The model replies that Policy 14.3 permits it within 90 days. No such policy exists: the number and the window were invented, and the answer reads more confidently than the correct one beside it. The team replays 200 logged questions. Forty-one percent are knowledge gaps, 22% cite superseded 2023 guidance, and 15% merge two similar products. The decision: retrieve policy clauses with effective dates, require a resolvable clause ID, and return 'not found in current policy' when retrieval scores fall below threshold. Fabricated citations fall from 19% to 2%.
steps: Collect 100 to 200 real questions with the correct answer and the authoritative source that settles each one.
Replay them and label every wrong answer as gap, stale, confusion, pressure, or decoding noise.
Measure the class mix; if gaps and stale facts dominate, retrieval is the fix rather than prompt wording.
Add a refusal path and test whether the model uses it when the source is deliberately removed.
Re-run after each change and report citation validity and abstention rate beside accuracy.

code.title: Self-consistency sampling exposes unstable answers before they reach a user.
code.code:
from collections import Counter

def stable_answer(ask, question, samples=5):
  """ask(question, temperature) returns one answer string."""
  answers = [ask(question, temperature=0.7) for _ in range(samples)]
  top, count = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0]
  agreement = count / samples
  if agreement < 0.6:
     return 'I cannot answer that reliably from the available evidence.', agreement
  return top, agreement
what_to_notice: Agreement is a proxy, not proof: five samples can agree on the same invented policy number, so pair it with citation checks.
Temperature 0.7 makes disagreement visible; running at 0 makes the test useless because sampling variation disappears.

Five samples multiply cost and latency by five, so reserve this check for high-risk answers or offline evaluation. YOUR WORKING NOTES Three pages per lesson Page 226 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

production_notes: Log claim-level support: which chunk IDs were cited, whether each resolved, and whether the answer abstained.
Track hallucination rate per document collection, because a stale index fails differently from a weak model.
Alert on abstention spikes; a sudden rise often means ingestion lag or an embedding model change, not model regression.

Why LLMs Hallucinate
Understand why a next-token predictor invents facts, and separate knowledge gaps from retrieval and formatting failures.
RAG · Lesson 1 of 19 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A hallucination is not a bug that a better prompt eliminates; it is the predictable behaviour of a model optimised to
produce plausible continuations. Engineers who treat every wrong answer as a prompt problem burn weeks. Engineers
who classify the failure spend that time on the right fix: retrieval for missing facts, verification for unchecked claims, and
abstention when evidence is absent.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Explain how next-token prediction produces fluent text without any lookup step or built-in check on factual truth.
 • Classify a wrong answer as knowledge gap, stale memory, entity confusion, prompt pressure, or decoding noise.
 • Choose a mitigation per failure class: abstention, retrieval, verification, prompt change, or lower-variance decoding.
CORE CONCEPTS
Prediction is not lookup
A model encodes statistical patterns from training text into weights, then generates one token at a time by scoring likely
continuations. There is no row to read, no source to cite, and no flag that says 'I do not know'. A policy number, a citation,
or an API field appears because that shape of string usually follows the question. Fluent grammar and confident tone are
properties of the generator, not evidence of correctness.
Five failure classes
Knowledge gaps cover facts never in training or too rare to memorise. Stale memory covers facts that changed after the
training cutoff. Entity confusion merges similar names, products, or versions. Prompt pressure covers leading questions
and instructions that reward agreement. Decoding noise covers the same prompt producing different answers above
temperature zero. Each class has a different fix, so label the class before changing anything.
Confidence is not calibrated
Models are trained and tuned to answer, so refusal is rare unless you ask for it explicitly and give it somewhere to go.
Token probabilities measure fluency, not truth: a fabricated citation can be generated with higher confidence than a
correct one. That is why grounded systems check claims against retrieved text, require citations that resolve to real chunk
IDs, and offer a visible not-found path instead of trusting the model's self-report.
KEY TERMS
 Hallucination                    A fluent model output that is unsupported by evidence or contradicted by the source of truth.
 Parametric knowledge             Facts compressed into model weights during training, with no provenance and no update path between
                                  retraining runs.
 Grounding                        Supplying authoritative text at inference time and requiring the answer to stay within it.

  MENTAL MODEL A model is an improviser with a vast memory of how sentences usually go: brilliant at shape, unreliable at facts, and
  unable to tell you which is which.

Why LLMs Hallucinate
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
At a UK bank, the internal policy assistant answers 4,000 staff questions a week. A staff member asks whether a
bereavement refund is allowed after 60 days. The model replies that Policy 14.3 permits it within 90 days. No such policy
exists: the number and the window were invented, and the answer reads more confidently than the correct one beside it.
The team replays 200 logged questions. Forty-one percent are knowledge gaps, 22% cite superseded 2023 guidance, and
15% merge two similar products. The decision: retrieve policy clauses with effective dates, require a resolvable clause ID,
and return 'not found in current policy' when retrieval scores fall below threshold. Fabricated citations fall from 19% to
2%.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Collect 100 to 200 real questions with the correct answer and the authoritative source that settles each one.
2.    Replay them and label every wrong answer as gap, stale, confusion, pressure, or decoding noise.
3.    Measure the class mix; if gaps and stale facts dominate, retrieval is the fix rather than prompt wording.
4.    Add a refusal path and test whether the model uses it when the source is deliberately removed.
5.    Re-run after each change and report citation validity and abstention rate beside accuracy.
CODE
Self-consistency sampling exposes unstable answers before they reach a user.
  from collections import Counter

  def stable_answer(ask, question, samples=5):
    """ask(question, temperature) returns one answer string."""
    answers = [ask(question, temperature=0.7) for _ in range(samples)]
    top, count = Counter(answers).most_common(1)[0]
    agreement = count / samples
    if agreement < 0.6:
       return 'I cannot answer that reliably from the available evidence.', agreement
    return top, agreement
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → Agreement is a proxy, not proof: five samples can agree on the same invented policy number, so pair it with citation checks.
 → Temperature 0.7 makes disagreement visible; running at 0 makes the test useless because sampling variation disappears.
 → Five samples multiply cost and latency by five, so reserve this check for high-risk answers or offline evaluation.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Retrieve, then generate A RAG request has two stages. Retrieval embeds the question, searches an index for the k most similar passages, optionally filters by tenant or date, and returns text with IDs. Generation receives those passages as numbered context and is instructed to answer only from them, citing IDs. What Is RAG?
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A hospital's clinical-guidance assistant serves 700 nurses. The first version pastes the full 40-page formulary into every
prompt: 52,000 input tokens, 18-second p95, and wrong doses pulled from the wrong section. The team builds a RAG
path over 1,900 guidance sections with section-level metadata. Retrieval returns four passages; the prompt requires a
section ID per claim. On a 120-question set, answer accuracy rises from 61% to 88%, but 9% of answers cite a section that
was never retrieved. Adding citation validation catches those, and answers with a top similarity below 0.72 now abstain.
Cost per question falls from USD 0.14 to USD 0.006.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Write 100 questions whose answers exist in your documents and record the authoritative section for each.
2.    Build a retriever that returns five passages with stable IDs; measure recall at five before touching the prompt.
3.    Construct a prompt that numbers each passage, forbids outside knowledge, and requires an ID per claim.
4.    Add a similarity threshold and validate that every cited ID was actually retrieved.
5.    Compare accuracy, citation validity, latency, and cost against the no-retrieval baseline.
CODE
A retrieve-then-verify function that abstains on weak evidence and rejects unretrieved citation IDs.
  def answer(question, retrieve, generate, min_score=0.72):
    hits = [h for h in retrieve(question, k=5) if h["score"] >= min_score]
    if not hits:
       return {"answer": "Not found in the indexed documents.", "citations": []}
    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{i}] {h['text']}" for i, h in enumerate(hits, 1))
    draft = generate(question, context)
    cited = [i for i in draft["citations"] if 1 <= i <= len(hits)]
    if not cited:
       return {"answer": "Not found in the indexed documents.", "citations": []}
    return {"answer": draft["answer"], "citations": cited}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The threshold is applied before generation; without it, an empty or weak context becomes an invitation to invent.
 → Numbering starts at 1 and citation IDs are checked against the returned hits, so a plausible but unretrieved ID fails.
 → This function trusts the retriever's scores; production must also record which index version produced them.

lessons.title: RAG Architecture
lessons.subtitle: Separate the ingestion pipeline from the query pipeline, and version every artefact that can silently change an answer.
why_it_matters: Most RAG incidents are pipeline incidents: a parser upgrade drops table text, a chunker change invalidates the index, or the query path embeds with a different model than the index used. A clear architecture makes those couplings visible and testable before a customer sees a wrong answer. It also tells you where to spend latency, because retrieval and generation compete for the same budget.
outcomes: Draw the ingestion and query pipelines with their queues, stores, and failure boundaries.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Two pipelines, one contract Ingestion runs offline: fetch, parse, clean, chunk, embed, and upsert into the index with metadata and provenance. Query runs per request: authenticate, rewrite or embed the question, retrieve, filter, rerank, build context, generate, validate, and log. The contract between them is the document schema: chunk ID, text, source URI, page, ACL, timestamps, and embedding version. Break that schema and retrieval fails quietly rather than loudly. Versions that must agree The embedding model that built the index must be the one that embeds the query; mixing two spaces produces near- random neighbours. Chunk size, overlap, parser version, and normalisation rules also shape what can be retrieved. Store all of them in an index manifest and stamp every chunk with the manifest ID. When any changes, build a new index, evaluate it, then switch traffic atomically instead of updating in place. Where the latency goes Budgets are easier to defend when each stage has a number: authentication 20 ms, query embedding 40 ms, ANN search 30 ms, metadata filter 20 ms, rerank 120 ms, generation 1,500 ms, validation 20 ms. Ingestion work such as OCR, summarisation, and parent-document expansion belongs offline or in a cache. Anything that must run online should have a timeout and a defined degradation, not a retry loop that doubles the budget.

key_terms.definition: A record of parser, chunker, embedding model, and index settings that produced a given index.
The offline process that fetches, parses, chunks, embeds, and stores documents with provenance metadata.

Transforming a user question into one or more retrieval queries, for example by resolving pronouns or expanding acronyms. MENTAL MODEL RAG is a supply chain: documents are manufactured into chunks, stored in a warehouse, and picked per order. Version the factory before you blame the chef.

  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class IndexManifest:
    index_id: str
    embedding_model: str
    dimensions: int
    chunker: str
    parser: str

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Meaning as geometry An embedding model maps text to a vector, typically 384 to 3,072 floats, positioned so texts used in similar ways land near each other. Similarity is usually cosine, which compares direction rather than length. Related phrases such as 'cancel my subscription' and 'stop the plan renewing' score higher than unrelated ones, even with no shared keywords. The model learned this from co-occurrence, not from a dictionary, so it captures paraphrase and domain jargon present in training. Choosing a model Compare candidates on your own 100 to 300 question set: recall at k, latency, dimensions, maximum input tokens, multilingual coverage, and price per million tokens. Hosted options include OpenAI's text-embedding-3 family and Cohere's embed models; open options include BGE, E5, and GTE variants you can run locally. Larger dimensions often help slightly and cost more storage and search time; Matryoshka models let you truncate dimensions with a measurable quality loss. Scores are not probabilities A cosine score of 0.81 means the two vectors point in a similar direction. It does not mean 81% relevant, and thresholds do not transfer between models: 0.72 may be a good cut-off for one model and useless for another. Distributions also shift with document length and language. Calibrate thresholds empirically on labelled pairs, then monitor the score distribution per collection rather than hard-coding a number from a blog post.

lessons.title: Vector Databases
lessons.subtitle: Pick an index that returns the right neighbours fast enough, with filters that enforce tenancy before similarity is computed.
why_it_matters: Similarity search is easy at 10,000 vectors and hard at 10 million with per-tenant filters and hourly updates. The index you choose determines recall, memory, and how much operational work your team inherits. Getting this wrong shows up as slow queries, missing results, or a second database that nobody knows how to back up.
outcomes: Explain what a vector database adds beyond storing floats: ANN indexes, filtering, updates, and snapshots.
Tune HNSW parameters against a recall and latency target rather than accepting defaults.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: What the database actually does A vector database stores vectors plus payload metadata and builds an approximate nearest-neighbour index. HNSW layers a navigable graph for fast search; IVF-PQ clusters vectors and compresses them to fit memory. Approximate means recall is below 100% by design, traded for latency. The database also owns upserts, deletes, filtering, namespaces, and snapshots. Those operational features, not the distance function, are what you are really choosing. Filtering changes everything Post-filtering searches the whole index and discards non-matching rows, so a tenant with 1% of the corpus may return three results instead of ten. Pre-filtering restricts the search to eligible vectors, which is correct but can defeat the index if the filter is too selective. Qdrant, Weaviate, and pgvector support filtered search with different strategies. For multi- tenant systems, partition by tenant or index tenant_id and test recall with a small tenant. Choosing a store pgvector keeps vectors beside relational data, transactions, and existing backups, and handles millions of rows with HNSW. A dedicated database such as Qdrant, Milvus, or Weaviate earns its place when you need billions of vectors, specialised quantisation, or independent scaling of search. Managed services remove operational work at a price and add a network hop. Decide with measured numbers: rows, QPS, p95 latency, recall target, and the team's on-call capacity.

key_terms.definition: A hierarchical graph index that connects nearby vectors, giving fast approximate search controlled by M and ef parameters.
The fraction of queries whose truly relevant passages appear in the top k returned results.

A metadata condition applied during search so only vectors matching tenant, date, or ACL are considered. MENTAL MODEL A vector index is a library catalogue built for approximate lookup: fast shelves, imperfect filing, and a filter that must be applied before you walk the aisles.

The team starts with pgvector and a single HNSW index. p95 search is 40 ms at 200 QPS, but the largest tenant, with 2.1 million chunks, sees recall drop to 0.62 when a date filter is applied. Raising ef_search from 40 to 120 restores recall to 0.91 at 85 ms p95, still inside the 150 ms budget. They add a composite index on tenant_id and created_at, partition the three largest tenants into their own tables, and keep pgvector rather than adding a second system. The decision is revisited if p95 passes 120 ms or vector count triples.

A pgvector table with an HNSW index and a tenant-scoped query that returns cosine scores.

  CREATE TABLE chunks (

     tenant_id uuid NOT NULL,
     created_at timestamptz NOT NULL,
     content text NOT NULL,
     embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL
  );
  CREATE INDEX chunks_embedding_idx ON chunks
     USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);
  CREATE INDEX chunks_tenant_idx ON chunks (tenant_id, created_at);

  SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 120;

  SELECT id, content, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS score
  FROM chunks
  WHERE tenant_id = $2 AND created_at >= $3
  ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
  LIMIT 10;

code.title: A hash-guarded upsert that makes re-running the ingestion job cheap and safe.
code.code:
import hashlib
import sqlite3

def sync_document(conn, doc_id, body, acl):
  digest = hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest()
  cur = conn.execute('SELECT digest FROM documents WHERE id = ?', (doc_id,))
  row = cur.fetchone()
  if row and row[0] == digest:
     return 'unchanged'
  conn.execute(
     'INSERT INTO documents (id, digest, acl, body) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?) '
     'ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET digest = excluded.digest, '
     'acl = excluded.acl, body = excluded.body',
     (doc_id, digest, acl, body.decode('utf-8')),
  )
  conn.commit()
  return 'indexed'
what_to_notice: The hash check skips unchanged documents entirely, so a nightly run costs only the changed set.
ON CONFLICT makes retries safe, but the ACL column is replaced wholesale, so an empty ACL means public unless the code rejects it.

why_it_matters: Retrieval cannot return text that extraction never captured. Most 'the model missed it' tickets end with a PDF whose table was flattened, a scan with no text layer, or a page of navigation menus. Processing is where document structure becomes metadata, and where a cheap quality gate prevents thousands of useless chunks from entering the index.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Parsing is structure recovery Raw bytes become text, but the valuable output is structure: page numbers, headings, tables, lists, and reading order. PDFs store glyph positions rather than paragraphs, so two-column layouts and footers scramble naive extraction. Use a layout-aware parser for complex documents and keep a page-mapped fallback for simple ones. Preserve the page number and section path on every chunk; without them a citation points at a 200-page file instead of a paragraph. Route by quality, not extension A .pdf may be a text document, a scan, or a mix of both. Measure extracted characters per page and compare with the page area; a page with fewer than about 50 to 100 characters per 1,000 square points is probably an image. Send those pages to OCR, keep the original page image reference, and record which engine produced the text. OCR is slower and less accurate, so route only what needs it and review the error rate on a sample. Normalise without rewriting Strip repeated headers, footers, and navigation, collapse whitespace, repair hyphenated line breaks, and convert curly quotes only if your embedding model is sensitive to them. Do not summarise, translate, or improve text at this stage: retrieval and citation depend on the original wording. Deduplicate near-identical documents by hash of normalised text, keeping the copy with the best permissions and the newest timestamp.

key_terms.definition: Optical character recognition, which converts text in page images into machine-readable characters, with measurable error rates.
The sequence in which a human would read a page, which must be recovered for multi-column layouts to make sense.

Holding extracted documents out of the index until a quality check passes or a human reviews them. MENTAL MODEL Processing is a translation layer: the goal is to move the document's meaning and structure into text without adding, losing, or rearranging it.

CODE
Page-level extraction that keeps citation numbers and marks weak pages for OCR instead of indexing them.
  from pypdf import PdfReader

  MIN_CHARS_PER_PAGE = 80

  def extract_pages(path):
    reader = PdfReader(path)
    pages = []
    for number, page in enumerate(reader.pages, start=1):
       text = " ".join((page.extract_text() or "").split())
       pages.append(
         {
            "page": number,
            "text": text,
            "route": "ocr" if len(text) < MIN_CHARS_PER_PAGE else "index",
         }
       )
    return pages

lessons.title: Chunking
lessons.subtitle: Choose chunk boundaries that preserve meaning, keep citations precise, and give retrieval a fair chance to find the right
why_it_matters: Chunking decides what retrieval can possibly return. Cut a table in half and the answer becomes unprovable; make chunks enormous and the embedding blurs several topics into one vector. No reranker or prompt can recover a passage that was never indexed as a coherent unit. Treat chunking as an evaluation variable: measure recall on real questions, then change one boundary rule at a time.
outcomes: Explain how chunk size, overlap, and boundaries trade retrieval precision against enough surrounding context for the model.
Split documents on structural boundaries such as headings, tables, and lists instead of fixed character counts alone.
Attach stable identifiers and parent metadata so every chunk can be cited, filtered, and re-embedded safely.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Size sets the precision-context trade-off Small chunks, around 150 to 300 tokens, produce sharp embeddings and precise citations, but they often omit the sentence that explains a pronoun or a condition. Large chunks, around 800 to 1,200 tokens, carry context yet average several topics into one vector, so similarity search matches weakly. Start near 300 to 500 tokens for prose and tune against labelled questions. Measure recall@k, not the visual tidiness of the split. Split on structure, not character count Headings, clauses, tables, and code blocks are natural boundaries because the author already marked a change of meaning. Parse Markdown, HTML, or PDF layout first, then pack whole sentences or rows up to a limit. Add 10 to 15 percent overlap only where a sentence can straddle a boundary. Prepend the document title and section path to each chunk so the embedding sees the context the reader will see. Chunks are citation and version units Every chunk needs a stable identifier derived from document, version, and ordinal, plus metadata for section, page, and access scope. Parent-child schemes index small children for matching but return the surrounding parent section to the prompt. When the source or embedding model changes, write new identifiers rather than mutating old rows. This makes citations checkable, deletions auditable, and re-embedding a background job instead of a rebuild.

key_terms.definition: A retrievable unit of text with a stable identifier, stored alongside its embedding and metadata.
Text repeated at the start of the next chunk so a sentence crossing a boundary remains readable.

Indexing small child chunks for precise matching while returning the larger parent section for context. MENTAL MODEL A chunk is a paragraph-sized promise: it must be small enough to match one question and complete enough to answer it without its neighbours.
