Letting retrieved memory outrank the current request, so a stale preference overrides what the user just said.
production_notes: Scope every query by tenant and user at the database layer, and add a test that proves a forged user ID returns no memories.
Keep a provenance link to the conversation and message for each memory so corrections, deletions, and audits have a traceable path.
Run scheduled expiry and contradiction-resolution jobs, and alert when a user's memory count or retrieval volume grows abnormally.

lessons.title: Short-Term Memory
lessons.subtitle: Spend the context window like a budget: pin the facts that matter, summarise the history, and drop the rest before quality
why_it_matters: Every turn resends the conversation, tool results, and instructions, so a long agent session costs more per step and eventually exceeds the window. Naive truncation removes the original goal; naive summarisation loses the exact error message needed two steps later. Short-term memory design decides what stays verbatim, what becomes a summary, and what becomes a reference. Getting it right lowers cost and latency while keeping the agent coherent past turn fifty.
outcomes: Explain why the context window is the agent's short-term memory and how token pressure degrades instruction following.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The window is a working set The model has no memory between calls; it sees exactly what you send. That makes the context window the whole of short-term memory, and every token competes with instructions and evidence. Long transcripts crowd out the current question, and models attend less reliably to material in the middle. WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Every turn resends the conversation, tool results, and instructions, so a long agent session costs more per step and
eventually exceeds the window. Naive truncation removes the original goal; naive summarisation loses the exact error
message needed two steps later. Short-term memory design decides what stays verbatim, what becomes a summary, and
what becomes a reference. Getting it right lowers cost and latency while keeping the agent coherent past turn fifty.

CORE CONCEPTS
The window is a working set

short-term memory, and every token competes with instructions and evidence. Long transcripts crowd out the current

current plan, recent turns, and selected tool output, then rebuild it each step from state rather than appending forever.

exact values may pass a chat test and fail a reconciliation task. Log token counts by section and compaction events, and
alert when summarisation runs on more than a set share of requests.

CODE
A budgeted context builder that keeps pinned facts and recent turns, stopping before 70 percent of the window is consumed.
  def build_context(pinned: list[str], turns: list[str], scratch: str,
            budget: int = 12_000) -> list[str]:
    def cost(text: str) -> int:
      return int(len(text.split()) * 1.3)

     kept, used = [], cost(scratch) + sum(cost(p) for p in pinned)
     for turn in reversed(turns):
       size = cost(turn)
       if used + size > budget * 0.7:
          break
       kept.append(turn)
       used += size
     return pinned + [scratch] + list(reversed(kept))

   into scratch first.

   budget checks.

lessons.title: Long-Term Memory
lessons.subtitle: Persist what should outlive a session, then retrieve it with scope, provenance, and an expiry date you can defend.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 12 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Long-term memory is where an agent becomes useful across weeks instead of minutes. It is also where mistakes become permanent and leaks become legal problems. A record written once may be retrieved a thousand times, in front of the wrong user, long after it stopped being true. The engineering work is mostly not the vector search: it is extraction quality, identity, scoping, contradiction handling, and deletion that actually removes data from every index.
outcomes: Design a durable memory schema with namespaces, provenance, confidence, and retention for each record.
Build an extraction and deduplication pipeline that writes facts instead of raw conversation logs.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Write facts, not transcripts Raw conversation archives are expensive to search and full of noise. Extract structured records instead: a subject, a predicate, a value, a source message, a confidence, and a timestamp. Ask the model for candidate memories only at defined moments, such as an explicit preference, a completed task, or a correction, and validate the output against a schema. Deduplicate by normalised subject and predicate so 'prefers email' updates one row rather than creating forty. Identity decides everything Every memory needs a namespace: tenant, user, agent, and often project. The query must constrain all of them from authenticated context, never from model output. Store provenance so a fact can be traced to a conversation and corrected, and keep confidence and expiry so stale records lose weight and disappear. A shared organisation memory should be written only through an explicit review path, because one user's note should not silently become another user's policy. Maintain, don't accumulate Long-term memory needs a maintenance loop: contradiction detection, merges, expiry, deletion requests, and index rebuilds. When a new value conflicts with an old one, supersede it and keep the history rather than overwriting silently. Run retrieval evaluation with questions that require memory, and measure hit rate, wrong-memory rate, and stale- memory rate. Delete from the primary store, vector index, cache, and backups on a documented schedule. An unmaintained memory store becomes a liability with a search box.

key_terms.definition: An isolation boundary such as tenant, user, or project that every memory read and write must constrain.
The recorded origin of a memory, linking it to the conversation, message, or document that justified it.

Replacing an outdated memory with a newer value while retaining the earlier record and the reason for the change. MENTAL MODEL Long-term memory is a land registry: every entry has an owner, a source deed, a date, and a procedure for transfer and deletion, so a later dispute can be settled.

worked_example: A health-coaching assistant adds long-term memory for 12,000 users. A penetration test finds that retrieval filters on a user ID supplied by the model, so a crafted prompt asks for another patient's medication note; the API returns it because the query never binds the authenticated subject. A follow-up test of 300 forged identifiers returns zero rows. The team also adds a nightly job that deletes expired records from Postgres, the vector index, and the cache, and records each deletion.

code.title: A scoped upsert keyed by tenant, user, subject, and predicate, so a corrected fact replaces the old value instead of duplicating it.
code.code:
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone

DDL = '''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS memory (
 tenant TEXT, user TEXT, subject TEXT, predicate TEXT, value TEXT,
 source TEXT, confidence REAL, created TEXT,
 PRIMARY KEY (tenant, user, subject, predicate))'''

def remember(conn, tenant, user, subject, predicate, value, source, confidence):
  sql = '''INSERT INTO memory VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT (tenant, user, subject, predicate) DO UPDATE SET
value = excluded.value, source = excluded.source,
confidence = excluded.confidence, created = excluded.created'''
  now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
  conn.execute(DDL)
  conn.execute(sql, (tenant, user, subject, predicate, value, source,
              confidence, now))
what_to_notice: The primary key enforces one value per subject and predicate, so a new fact supersedes the old without a separate read.
The table has no expiry or provenance columns in this snippet; add expires_at and a source message ID before storing anything personal.

lessons.title: Planning
lessons.subtitle: Make the agent's plan an explicit, inspectable artefact so decomposition, dependencies, and replanning stay under your
why_it_matters: Planning is where an agent's cost and failure modes are decided. A plan implicit in the message history is hard to inspect, resume, or evaluate. Making it explicit lets you validate dependencies before spending tokens, show the intended path to a reviewer, and compare executed work against it. The plan is also the unit you re-run when a tool or model changes.
outcomes: Choose between a static plan-then-execute graph and an interleaved ReAct loop for a given task shape.
Represent a plan as typed steps with dependencies, an owning tool, and a completion check.
Set replan triggers and a replan budget so a failed step does not become an unbounded retry loop.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A plan is data, not prose When the model returns a plan, parse it into steps: identifier, tool, arguments, dependencies, and a success check. Validate the graph before execution: every dependency exists, no cycles, every step names a registered tool. Store the plan beside the run so a reviewer can see intended versus executed work. A prose plan cannot be validated, resumed, or diffed after a prompt change, and it tempts the model to skip steps silently. Plan-and-execute versus ReAct Use plan-and-execute when subtasks are knowable up front, parallelisable, or need approval before spending money; the plan is reviewed once and executed with a scheduler. Use an interleaved reason-act-observe loop when each result changes what to do next, such as debugging or open-ended search. Many production agents combine them: a short plan for the first two levels, then ReAct inside each step. Choosing wrongly yields brittle scripts or runaway loops. Replanning needs a trigger and a budget Replan only on named events: a permanent tool error, a failed success check, new evidence that invalidates an assumption, or a human rejection. Cap replans at two and carry the failed step and its error into the new plan, otherwise the model repeats it. Keep completed steps, mark invalidated ones, and log the reason. Every replan costs a model call and can widen scope, so treat it as an exception with an owner.

key_terms.definition: An agent pattern that produces a complete multi-step plan first, then executes it with a scheduler and replans only on failure.
A directed acyclic graph of steps in which an edge means the target step needs the source step's output.

The maximum number of times an agent may rebuild its plan during one run before stopping or escalating. MENTAL MODEL A plan is a flight itinerary, not a promise: check the legs and dependencies before take-off, and rebook only when a named disruption makes the original route impossible.

worked_example: A research agent at a market-intelligence firm must produce a competitor brief from ten sources. Its first version used ReAct with a 40-step cap; traces showed repeated searches and a cost of USD 1.80 per brief. The team rewrote it as a five- step plan: resolve the company, fetch filings, extract three metrics, cross-check dates, write the brief. Steps two and three run in parallel, and the plan is rejected before execution if a source is missing. Median cost fell to USD 0.55 and p95 latency from 71 to 34 seconds. Planning
Make the agent's plan an explicit, inspectable artefact so decomposition, dependencies, and replanning stay under your
control.
AI Agents · Lesson 13 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Planning is where an agent's cost and failure modes are decided. A plan implicit in the message history is hard to inspect,
resume, or evaluate. Making it explicit lets you validate dependencies before spending tokens, show the intended path to
a reviewer, and compare executed work against it. The plan is also the unit you re-run when a tool or model changes.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Choose between a static plan-then-execute graph and an interleaved ReAct loop for a given task shape.
 • Represent a plan as typed steps with dependencies, an owning tool, and a completion check.
 • Set replan triggers and a replan budget so a failed step does not become an unbounded retry loop.
CORE CONCEPTS
A plan is data, not prose
When the model returns a plan, parse it into steps: identifier, tool, arguments, dependencies, and a success check.
Validate the graph before execution: every dependency exists, no cycles, every step names a registered tool. Store the
plan beside the run so a reviewer can see intended versus executed work. A prose plan cannot be validated, resumed, or
diffed after a prompt change, and it tempts the model to skip steps silently.
Plan-and-execute versus ReAct
Use plan-and-execute when subtasks are knowable up front, parallelisable, or need approval before spending money; the
plan is reviewed once and executed with a scheduler. Use an interleaved reason-act-observe loop when each result
changes what to do next, such as debugging or open-ended search. Many production agents combine them: a short plan
for the first two levels, then ReAct inside each step. Choosing wrongly yields brittle scripts or runaway loops.
Replanning needs a trigger and a budget
Replan only on named events: a permanent tool error, a failed success check, new evidence that invalidates an
assumption, or a human rejection. Cap replans at two and carry the failed step and its error into the new plan, otherwise
the model repeats it. Keep completed steps, mark invalidated ones, and log the reason. Every replan costs a model call
and can widen scope, so treat it as an exception with an owner.
KEY TERMS
 Plan-and-execute                 An agent pattern that produces a complete multi-step plan first, then executes it with a scheduler and
                                  replans only on failure.
 Dependency graph                 A directed acyclic graph of steps in which an edge means the target step needs the source step's output.
 Replan budget                    The maximum number of times an agent may rebuild its plan during one run before stopping or escalating.

  MENTAL MODEL A plan is a flight itinerary, not a promise: check the legs and dependencies before take-off, and rebook only when a
  named disruption makes the original route impossible.

lessons.title: Human-in-the-Loop
lessons.subtitle: Put a person at the decision points that carry irreversible risk, and make the pause durable, scoped, and fast to review.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 14 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Human review is not a fallback for a weak model; it is a control for decisions where a wrong action cannot be undone. Refunds, deletions, outbound emails, and infrastructure changes need a person who sees what will happen and can stop it. The engineering work is making that pause reliable: the run must survive a restart, the approval must bind to exact arguments, and the queue must not become the bottleneck.
outcomes: Classify agent actions into auto-approve, notify, require-approval, and blocked tiers using reversibility and blast radius.
Suspend a run at an approval gate, persist its state, and resume idempotently after a decision or expiry.
Design an approval card that shows the exact tool arguments, evidence, and consequences an approver needs.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Tier actions by reversibility Sort every tool by what a mistake costs. Read-only searches auto-approve. Reversible writes, such as creating a draft, notify afterwards. Irreversible or externally visible actions, such as sending an email, issuing a refund, or deleting a record, require approval before execution. Anything outside the allowlist is blocked and escalated to engineering. The tier belongs to the tool and its argument range, not to the model's confidence, because a confident model can still be wrong. Pause durably, resume idempotently An approval gate ends the current process; it does not hold a thread open for an hour. Persist the run state, the pending call, and an idempotency key, then return a ticket to the user or queue. When a decision arrives, reload state, re-check policy and expiry, and execute at most once. Use compare-and-set on the approval record so two clicks or two workers cannot both execute the refund. Test the resume path like the happy path. Make the approval card sufficient An approver cannot judge a JSON blob. Show the proposed action in one sentence, the exact tool and arguments, the evidence used, the expected effect, and what happens on rejection. Include a diff where possible: the email body, the amount before and after. Set a short expiry, a default of deny, and a reason field. Log who approved what and when. If reviewers routinely approve without reading, the gate is decorative.

key_terms.definition: A control point where an agent run pauses until a named human explicitly allows or denies a specific action.
A stable identifier attached to an action so retries and duplicate approvals execute it at most once.

The set of records, users, or external systems a failed action can affect before it is detected and reversed. MENTAL MODEL An approval gate is a railway signal, not a comment box: the train stops, a named person clears the route, and the signal fails closed if nobody answers.

worked_example: A payables agent at a construction firm processes 6,200 invoices a month. Payments under GBP 500 auto-approve when the purchase order matches; anything above runs through an approval queue. The team rebuilt the card around supplier, amount, PO match, and bank-detail change, with a 24-hour expiry that denies. Median decision time fell to 92 seconds, reversals to 0.4%, and only 3.1% of invoices needed a human. A bank-detail change always requires two approvers.

CODE
An approval ticket bound to the exact call arguments and an expiry, so a swapped amount or a late click cannot execute.
  import hashlib, time

  def digest(action: str, args: dict[str, object]) -> str:
    payload = f"{action}:{sorted(args.items())}".encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()[:16]

  def approved(action: str, args: dict, ticket: dict, now: float) -> bool:
    if not ticket or action != ticket["action"] or now >= ticket["expires_at"]:
       return False
    return digest(action, args) == ticket["digest"]

  ARGS = {"invoice": "INV-1042", "amount": 740}
  ticket = {"action": "issue_refund", "expires_at": time.time() + 86400,
        "digest": digest("issue_refund", ARGS)}
  print(approved("issue_refund", ARGS, ticket, time.time()))
  print(approved("issue_refund", {**ARGS, "amount": 9000}, ticket, time.time()))

 → The digest sorts argument items, so reordered dictionaries still match, but a changed amount produces a different ticket
   hash.
 → Expiry is checked before the digest, and both failures return False; the caller must treat False as deny, never as permission
   to retry.
 → The ticket stores only a digest, not the arguments, so the execution path must reload the original call from persisted run
   state.

lessons.title: Agent Error Handling
lessons.subtitle: Separate transient, permanent, semantic, and budget failures, then answer each with the cheapest recovery that keeps
why_it_matters: Agents fail in layers: the tool times out, the model emits invalid arguments, the plan no longer makes sense, or the budget runs out. A single try/except treats all four the same and usually makes things worse by retrying a permanent error. Dependable agents classify the failure, choose one recovery, record why, and stop with useful partial work when recovery is impossible.
outcomes: Classify tool and model failures by whether retrying, repairing, replanning, or stopping is the correct response.
Return structured, sanitised errors to the model so it can correct arguments without learning internal details.
Bound retries, steps, and spend, and emit partial results with an explicit account of what failed.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Four failure classes Transient failures, such as a 429, 503, or socket timeout, may succeed on retry. Permanent failures, such as a 404, invalid credentials, or a schema violation, will not. Semantic failures return a valid but wrong result, detected only by a check or a reviewer. Budget failures mean steps, tokens, or wall-clock time are exhausted. Each needs a different response: bounded retry, repair or replan, verification, or a clean stop. Misclassifying permanent as transient is the expensive mistake. Errors are prompts, sanitised A tool error is model input, not just a log line. Return a short structured object with the error class, a stable code, the offending field, and one corrective hint, for example invalid_arguments on amount: expected a positive number. Do not paste stack traces, SQL, secrets, or full upstream responses; they waste context and leak internals. Cap repair attempts at two, because a model that cannot fix the arguments after two hints needs a different tool or a human. Stop well, keep partial work Every loop needs a hard step cap, a token budget, and a deadline, checked before the next model call rather than after. When one is hit, stop and return what is verified: completed steps, sources fetched, unresolved questions. Mark the run as partial, not successful, and emit a machine-readable reason. A research brief with three confirmed findings beats a fabricated fourth paragraph. Route repeated failures to a dead-letter queue with the trace identifier.

key_terms.definition: A failure expected to succeed if repeated later, such as a rate limit, timeout, or unavailable upstream service.
A guard that stops calling a failing dependency for a cooldown period after a threshold of consecutive failures.

A store for runs that exhausted recovery so engineers can inspect and replay them without blocking users. MENTAL MODEL Error handling is triage, not optimism: sort the injury, apply the one treatment that fits, and stop before the patient loses more blood.
Page 325 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: During a launch, a support agent's order-lookup tool returned 503 for 22% of calls. The first release retried every exception three times, which tripled load and pushed p95 latency to 19 seconds without improving success. The team split errors by class: 503 and timeouts retried twice with jitter; 404 returned a not-found answer immediately; invalid arguments triggered one repair call. A circuit breaker opened after ten consecutive failures and served cached order status. Successful runs rose from 61% to 94%, and partial answers told users which fields could not be checked. Full upstream errors went to the dead-letter queue, not the prompt.

code.title: Retry only transient failures, with an absolute deadline and jitter; permanent errors surface immediately to the caller.
what_to_notice: The deadline is absolute, so retries cannot silently extend a request beyond the caller's timeout; compute it once at entry.
Only TransientError is caught. A permanent 404 or schema error reaches the caller immediately instead of consuming three attempts.

Agent Error Handling
Separate transient, permanent, semantic, and budget failures, then answer each with the cheapest recovery that keeps
the run explainable.
AI Agents · Lesson 15 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Agents fail in layers: the tool times out, the model emits invalid arguments, the plan no longer makes sense, or the budget
runs out. A single try/except treats all four the same and usually makes things worse by retrying a permanent error.
Dependable agents classify the failure, choose one recovery, record why, and stop with useful partial work when recovery
is impossible.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Classify tool and model failures by whether retrying, repairing, replanning, or stopping is the correct response.
 • Return structured, sanitised errors to the model so it can correct arguments without learning internal details.
 • Bound retries, steps, and spend, and emit partial results with an explicit account of what failed.
CORE CONCEPTS
Four failure classes
Transient failures, such as a 429, 503, or socket timeout, may succeed on retry. Permanent failures, such as a 404, invalid
credentials, or a schema violation, will not. Semantic failures return a valid but wrong result, detected only by a check or a
reviewer. Budget failures mean steps, tokens, or wall-clock time are exhausted. Each needs a different response: bounded
retry, repair or replan, verification, or a clean stop. Misclassifying permanent as transient is the expensive mistake.
Errors are prompts, sanitised
A tool error is model input, not just a log line. Return a short structured object with the error class, a stable code, the
offending field, and one corrective hint, for example invalid_arguments on amount: expected a positive number. Do not
paste stack traces, SQL, secrets, or full upstream responses; they waste context and leak internals. Cap repair attempts at
two, because a model that cannot fix the arguments after two hints needs a different tool or a human.
Stop well, keep partial work
Every loop needs a hard step cap, a token budget, and a deadline, checked before the next model call rather than after.
When one is hit, stop and return what is verified: completed steps, sources fetched, unresolved questions. Mark the run
as partial, not successful, and emit a machine-readable reason. A research brief with three confirmed findings beats a
fabricated fourth paragraph. Route repeated failures to a dead-letter queue with the trace identifier.
KEY TERMS
 Transient error                  A failure expected to succeed if repeated later, such as a rate limit, timeout, or unavailable upstream service.
 Circuit breaker                  A guard that stops calling a failing dependency for a cooldown period after a threshold of consecutive
                                  failures.
 Dead-letter queue                A store for runs that exhausted recovery so engineers can inspect and replay them without blocking users.

  MENTAL MODEL Error handling is triage, not optimism: sort the injury, apply the one treatment that fits, and stop before the patient
  loses more blood.

Agent Error Handling
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
During a launch, a support agent's order-lookup tool returned 503 for 22% of calls. The first release retried every
exception three times, which tripled load and pushed p95 latency to 19 seconds without improving success. The team
split errors by class: 503 and timeouts retried twice with jitter; 404 returned a not-found answer immediately; invalid
arguments triggered one repair call. A circuit breaker opened after ten consecutive failures and served cached order
status. Successful runs rose from 61% to 94%, and partial answers told users which fields could not be checked. Full
upstream errors went to the dead-letter queue, not the prompt.
STEP BY STEP
1.    List every failure the agent can see and assign it a class, a code, and one recovery.
2.    Wrap tool calls with a deadline, a transient-only retry policy, and a circuit breaker.
3.    Convert exceptions into a compact error object with a corrective hint and no internals.
4.    Cap repair attempts and loop steps at fixed limits, then define the partial-result format.
5.    Replay ten recorded failures and confirm each takes the intended path without duplicate side effects.
CODE
Retry only transient failures, with an absolute deadline and jitter; permanent errors surface immediately to the caller.
  import random, time

  class TransientError(Exception):
    pass

  class PermanentError(Exception):
    pass

  def call_with_retry(fn, *args, attempts: int = 3, deadline: float):
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
       try:
         return fn(*args)
       except TransientError:
         if attempt == attempts or time.monotonic() > deadline:
            raise
         delay = min(4.0, 0.5 * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
         time.sleep(delay * (0.5 + random.random()))
    raise AssertionError("unreachable")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The deadline is absolute, so retries cannot silently extend a request beyond the caller's timeout; compute it once at entry.
 → Only TransientError is caught. A permanent 404 or schema error reaches the caller immediately instead of consuming three
   attempts.
 → Jitter is multiplied into an exponential base, so concurrent clients do not retry in lockstep and re-create the spike.

lessons.subtitle: Treat retrieved text and tool output as hostile input, and give the agent only the permissions its current task can justify.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 16 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: An agent with tools is a program that takes instructions from untrusted text. A retrieved page, an email, or a tool response can contain instructions the model may follow, and the resulting action runs with your service's credentials. Security therefore cannot live in the prompt alone. It lives in permissions, network policy, argument validation, and review gates, so a successful injection gains little. Assume the model will be fooled sometimes.
outcomes: Model the agent threat surface: prompt injection, excessive agency, data exfiltration, and confused-deputy tool use.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Untrusted content is data Every document, web page, email, and tool result is untrusted input. It may contain text designed to redirect the agent, such as instructions to ignore prior rules, call a tool, or send data to an external address. Delimit and label untrusted content, keep it out of the system prompt, and never let retrieved text alter tool permissions. Tell the model to treat embedded instructions as content to report, but assume that advice will fail sometimes; enforcement belongs in code. Least privilege per task Give each run a capability set, not the union of every tool. A research task gets search and read; it does not get email or payment. Scope credentials per tool, prefer read-only OAuth scopes, and constrain arguments: an HTTP tool resolves only allowlisted hosts, a file tool only one directory. Split broad tools into narrow ones so policy can distinguish read from send. The most dangerous capability is an over-scoped token that outlives the task. Contain and audit the blast radius Run tool code in a sandbox with no ambient credentials, a filesystem allowlist, and deny-by-default egress through a proxy. Strip or quarantine active content from retrieved files. Require human approval for writes, and bind that approval to exact arguments. Log every model decision, tool call, argument digest, and result to an append-only store with the run identifier. Alert on unusual hosts, volumes, or first-time tool combinations, because a clean audit trail is also an incident tool.

2.    List each tool's worst possible action and cut its scope, arguments, and credentials to the minimum.

CODE
A runtime capability check: unknown tools are denied, writes need approval, and HTTP egress is limited to named hosts.
  from urllib.parse import urlparse

  ALLOWED_HOSTS = {"api.github.com", "docs.python.org"}

  class PolicyError(Exception):
    pass

  def check_tool(name: str, args: dict, approved: bool) -> None:
    if name in {"read_file", "search"}:
       return
    if name not in {"http_get", "create_issue"}:
       raise PolicyError(f"tool {name} is not permitted")
    if name == "create_issue" and not approved:
       raise PolicyError("create_issue requires human approval")
    if name == "http_get":
       host = urlparse(str(args["url"])).hostname or ""
       if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS:
          raise PolicyError(f"egress blocked: {host}")

 → The tool allowlist is checked before argument inspection, so an unknown tool cannot reach a permissive branch by accident.
 → Approval is required for the write tool, but reads still validate the destination host; least privilege applies to both.

why_it_matters: Frameworks hide the loop, and hiding is useful only when you know what is hidden. Building a small agent yourself shows where state lives, how tool arguments are validated, what a step costs, and which failure ends the run. The result is not a framework competitor; it is a reference implementation and a debugging skill. When you later adopt LangGraph, you will recognise the graph, checkpointer, and retry policy.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A loop with explicit states Model the run as a state machine: receive goal, build context, call model, parse action, authorise, execute, observe, then continue or stop. Each transition appends an event. Terminal states are answer, refusal, budget exhausted, policy denied, and fatal error. Writing the states down prevents the tangle where a loop, retries, and tool dispatch all mutate one message list. It also gives you one place to enforce limits before the next call. Four seams worth isolating Keep four interfaces narrow: a model adapter taking messages and returning a structured action, a tool registry validating arguments and returning typed results, a state store persisting messages and step count, and a policy gate approving or denying the action. Each seam can then be tested with a fake: scripted model, stub tool, in-memory store, deny-all policy. Swapping providers or adding tracing touches one seam. Deterministic replay before intelligence Start with a scripted fake model that returns a fixed sequence of tool calls and a final answer. That proves dispatch, error paths, and termination without spending tokens or depending on a provider. Record every event, then replay it to reproduce a bug. Add the real model only after the mechanics pass. Keep the budget checks and the event log in production: they are the difference between an agent you can debug and one you can only re-prompt.

key_terms.definition: A thin interface that converts between your agent's messages and a provider's request and response format.
A validated mapping from tool names to implementations, schemas, and permission requirements.

An ordered, append-only record of model calls, tool calls, results, and state transitions for a run. MENTAL MODEL Building the agent by hand is building a clock once: after you have placed the gears, a purchased clock is a convenience rather than a mystery.

denying the action. Each seam can then be tested with a fake: scripted model, stub tool, in-memory store, deny-all policy.
Swapping providers or adding tracing touches one seam.
Deterministic replay before intelligence
Start with a scripted fake model that returns a fixed sequence of tool calls and a final answer. That proves dispatch, error
paths, and termination without spending tokens or depending on a provider. Record every event, then replay it to
reproduce a bug. Add the real model only after the mechanics pass. Keep the budget checks and the event log in
production: they are the difference between an agent you can debug and one you can only re-prompt.
KEY TERMS
 Model adapter                    A thin interface that converts between your agent's messages and a provider's request and response format.
 Tool registry                    A validated mapping from tool names to implementations, schemas, and permission requirements.
 Event log                        An ordered, append-only record of model calls, tool calls, results, and state transitions for a run.

  MENTAL MODEL Building the agent by hand is building a clock once: after you have placed the gears, a purchased clock is a convenience
  rather than a mystery.

Build an Agent From Scratch
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A platform team needed a research agent but could not justify a framework on day one. One engineer built a 210-line
implementation: four tools, a 12-step cap, a JSON event log, and a scripted model for tests. It ran for two weeks behind an
internal flag and exposed two bugs: a tool returned a string where the loop expected a dict, and a retry duplicated a
search. With the seams proven, the team replaced the scripted model with a provider adapter and the in-memory store
with Postgres checkpoints. The move to LangGraph later took two days because those seams existed.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define the state object, terminal states, and the hard step, token, and time budgets.
2.    Write the model adapter and a scripted fake that returns recorded actions for tests.
3.    Implement the tool registry with schema validation, typed results, and a policy check per call.
4.    Run the loop against the fake until dispatch, errors, and every terminal state are covered by tests.
5.    Swap in a real provider and durable store, then replay one recorded trace to verify parity.
CODE
A minimal loop with a tool registry, step budget, structured tool errors, and a scripted model for deterministic tests.
  TOOLS = {"add": lambda a, b: a + b, "done": lambda answer: answer}

  def run(goal: str, model, max_steps: int = 6) -> str:
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
       action = model(history)
       name, args = action["tool"], action["args"]
       try:
          result = TOOLS[name](**args)
       except (KeyError, TypeError) as exc:
          history.append({"role": "tool", "error": repr(exc)})
          continue
       if name == "done":
          return f"{result} after {step} steps"
       history.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})
    return "stopped: step budget exhausted"

  script = [{"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": 3}},
        {"tool": "done", "args": {"answer": "5"}}]
  print(run("2+3", lambda history: script.pop(0)))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The scripted model makes the run deterministic: dispatch, the step counter, and the terminal answer can be asserted
   without a provider.
 → A KeyError or TypeError becomes a tool message the model can read, but the loop still owns the step budget and stop
   condition.
 → The loop returns after the done tool rather than continuing, so a chatty model cannot spend the remaining budget on prose.

Orchestration frameworks exist to manage what ad-hoc agent code struggles with: state, routing, persistence, streaming,
and human review. They are useful when the graph is real; they are overhead when a single prompt would do.

why_it_matters: Every agent framework promises to simplify agents. What they actually provide is an execution model: typed state, deterministic routing, durable checkpoints, streaming events, and a place to pause for human approval. If your loop is fifty lines and loses nothing when the process restarts, a framework adds a dependency without removing work. If a run must survive deploys, resume after a crash, and show every step to an auditor, you are already building a worse version of one.
outcomes: Identify the state, resumption, and audit requirements that push an ad-hoc agent loop past its limit.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The requirements arrive quietly An agent starts as a while loop over messages. Then the product asks for conversation history after a restart, a retry when a tool times out, a branch on the tool result, a progress indicator, a reviewer approval step, and a replay of the run that produced a bad answer. Each request is twenty lines of code. Together they are a runtime with a state model, a scheduler, a persistence layer, and an event stream. Frameworks exist because those pieces must be designed together. What is actually standardised A serious framework defines a state schema, a node contract, an edge or routing function, a checkpoint store, and an event stream. Evaluate it on those five things, not on the demo. Ask how often it checkpoints, whether a node can resume mid-execution, what exactly is serialised, how a paused run is resumed, and whether routing can be tested without calling a model. If the answers are vague, the framework is a prompt wrapper with a marketing site rather than an execution model. The adoption tax Frameworks bring vocabulary, version churn, and a debugging layer between you and the HTTP request. LangChain's 0.1 to 0.3 transition broke imports across partner packages; LangGraph's checkpoint schema has changed with releases. A three-node, ten-minute pipeline rarely repays that tax. Adopt when state or durability is a real requirement, and write the requirement down. The decision record should name the failure it prevents, the weekly maintenance cost you accept, and the signal that would make you remove it.

key_terms.definition: A library that runs agent steps as a graph or pipeline, owning state, routing, retries, persistence, and event emission.
A serialised snapshot of graph state at a step boundary, used to resume, replay, or inspect a run.

A runtime property where a process crash resumes from the last recorded step instead of restarting the work. MENTAL MODEL A framework is scaffolding, not foundation: invaluable while the building goes up, expensive to leave inside the walls of a small house.

CODE
The checkpoint code teams write by hand at 2am, which is the moment an orchestration framework starts to earn its dependency.
  import json
  from pathlib import Path
  STORE = Path("runs")

  def resume(run_id: str) -> dict:
    path = STORE / f"{run_id}.json"
    if path.exists():
       return json.loads(path.read_text())
    return {"step": 0, "done": False}

  def save(run_id: str, state: dict) -> None:
    STORE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (STORE / f"{run_id}.json").write_text(json.dumps(state))

  state = resume("run-8841")
  while not state["done"] and state["step"] < 8:
    state["step"] += 1
    state["done"] = state["step"] >= 3
    save("run-8841", state)
  print(state)
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The write is not atomic, so a crash mid-save leaves a truncated JSON file that resume cannot parse.
 → Two workers using the same run id overwrite each other, because this hand-rolled store has no locking or lease.
 → The loop cap of eight is a budget, not a guarantee: it stops runaway steps but says nothing about cost or time.

  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Invoice:
    layout: str
    pages: int
    confidence: float
    total_eur: float

  def route(inv: Invoice) -> str:
    if inv.layout not in {"acme_v2", "nordic_v1", "scan_std"}:
       return "agent"
    if inv.confidence < 0.80 or inv.pages > 12:
       return "agent"
    if inv.total_eur > 25_000:
       return "human"
    return "workflow"

  print(route(Invoice("acme_v2", 3, 0.94, 1_240.0)))
  print(route(Invoice("scan_std", 2, 0.71, 880.0)))

    "plan": ["search", "answer"],
    "search": ["extract"],
    "extract": ["synthesise"],
    "synthesise": ["search", "cite"],
    "cite": ["answer"],
    "answer": [],
  }

  def reachable(graph: dict[str, list[str]], entry: str = "plan") -> set[str]:
    seen, queue = {entry}, deque([entry])
    while queue:
       for node in graph[queue.popleft()]:

lessons.subtitle: A node is one job with a typed input, a partial output, and a failure path; every guarantee in the graph rests on that
why_it_matters: Most graph bugs are node bugs: a function that mutates shared state, does two unrelated things, or repeats a side effect on retry. Because a checkpointer can re-run a node after a crash, a node is never called exactly once by design. Treating each node as a small, idempotent, observable function is what makes the rest of the architecture safe to reason about and safe to resume.
outcomes: Write a node that reads state, performs one bounded operation, and returns only the keys it changed.

core_concepts.title: Concept

A node is one job with a typed input, a partial output, and a failure path; every guarantee in the graph rests on that

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most graph bugs are node bugs: a function that mutates shared state, does two unrelated things, or repeats a side effect
on retry. Because a checkpointer can re-run a node after a crash, a node is never called exactly once by design. Treating
each node as a small, idempotent, observable function is what makes the rest of the architecture safe to reason about
and safe to resume.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write a node that reads state, performs one bounded operation, and returns only the keys it changed.
 • Make every side-effecting node idempotent and prove it with a double-invocation test.
 • Separate recoverable errors recorded in state from unrecoverable errors that must raise.
CORE CONCEPTS
The node contract
A node reads current state and returns a partial update. It must not mutate the input dictionary, must not return the full
state, and must name only the keys it owns. Pure transformations are trivial to test: build a state literal, call the function,
assert the returned dictionary. Side effects belong at the graph's edges, wrapped so a duplicate call is harmless. Keep
conditional logic out of nodes where a routing function can express it, because hidden branches are invisible in the
diagram.
Retries make idempotency mandatory
A crash between a side effect and the checkpoint means the node runs again. Pass an idempotency key derived from
stable state, such as an order id, to the downstream API, or check a dedupe table first. For writes you cannot repeat, split
the node: record intent in state, execute once, then record the receipt. Tests should invoke the node twice with the same
state and assert exactly one external effect. Without that test, replay safety is an assumption rather than a property.
One job, one failure mode
Nodes named extract_policy, score_draft, or fetch_source tell a reviewer what changed and what can break. A node that
plans, retrieves, and writes has three failure modes and no useful retry policy. Capture errors into a declared state key
when the graph can recover, and raise when it cannot; never swallow an exception into an empty string. Put a timeout
around every I/O call, and keep it shorter than the node budget so the failure surfaces before the graph deadline.

 Node                             A function in a graph that reads state and returns a partial update, optionally performing one bounded side
                                  effect.
 Idempotency key                  A stable identifier sent with a write so a retried request produces one effect rather than duplicates.

A side-effecting node that appends to state without mutating it and reuses one idempotency key across retries.
  import operator
  from typing import Annotated, TypedDict

  class ReceiptState(TypedDict):
    order_id: str
    sent: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]
    errors: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]

  def send_receipt(state: ReceiptState) -> dict:
    key = f"receipt:{state['order_id']}"
    try:
       mailer.send(order_id=state["order_id"], idempotency_key=key, timeout=8)
    except TimeoutError:
       return {"errors": [f"{key} timed out; safe to retry"]}
    return {"sent": [key]}

  state = {"order_id": "ord_5512", "sent": [], "errors": []}
  print(send_receipt(state))
  print(state["sent"]) # unchanged: the node did not mutate its input

lessons.title: Edges
lessons.subtitle: Wire nodes into a fixed topology, learn what fan-out and fan-in really execute, and know when an edge should stay static.
lessons.meta: Agent Orchestration · Lesson 7 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Most agent bugs are topology bugs: a branch that never runs, a join that fires twice, or a cycle with no exit. Edges are the graph's control flow, and unlike prompt text they are deterministic and reviewable. Reading the diagram before running it turns a class of silent failures into a design conversation, and keeps the model's freedom inside nodes rather than in the wiring.
outcomes: Draw a graph topology with START and END, then read LangGraph's superstep order from the edges alone.
Explain how fan-out branches run in parallel and why a fan-in node waits for every incoming edge.
Choose static edges over conditional routing when the sequence never depends on runtime state.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Static edges are a contract An edge says the target runs after the source completes, always. START marks entry, END stops the run, and every other static edge is unconditional. Because nothing in state can skip or repeat an edge, you can review the sequence in a diff. Use static edges for pipelines whose steps are fixed: load history, retrieve, draft, validate. Push choice into a conditional edge or a node, never into an edge that quietly returns nothing. Fan-out, fan-in and supersteps Two edges from one node run both targets in the same superstep, so they execute concurrently and each sees state as it was when the step began. A node with several incoming edges waits for all of them, then runs once. Ordering between branches is not guaranteed, so never rely on which finishes first. Fan-in is your barrier: merge results there rather than inside either branch. Cycles need a bound An edge can point backwards, which is how LangGraph implements retry and tool loops. Every cycle needs an exit in graph code: a counter in state, a maximum-attempt check in the routing function, or LangGraph's recursion_limit, which defaults to 25 supersteps and raises GraphRecursionError. Document the limit beside the edge, and emit a metric so a graph that keeps looping appears before the invoice does.

key_terms.definition: One round of graph execution in which every node scheduled by the previous step's edges runs, potentially in parallel.

A node with multiple incoming edges that acts as a barrier, running once after all upstream branches complete. recursion_limit LangGraph's cap on supersteps per invocation, raising GraphRecursionError when a cycle fails to terminate. MENTAL MODEL Edges are the rails, nodes are the stations, and supersteps are the timetable: a train only moves along laid track, and two trains on separate rails do not wait for each other.

worked_example: At a legal-tech company, Nadia reviews the retrieval graph for a 40,000-contract assistant. The beta chains dense search into sparse search: 1.4 seconds plus 1.9 seconds, so users wait 3.3 seconds before the model even starts, against a 5- second target. In the review she draws the edges on a whiteboard and finds no dependency between the branches, only habit. She rewires the topology as fan-out from START to both retrievers and a join node with two incoming edges, cutting retrieval to about 2.0 seconds. The same review finds an unbounded retry cycle around citation checking; she caps it at three attempts with a counter in state. The recorded decision is that every cycle must show its exit on the graph diagram.
steps: List every step the request performs and mark which steps genuinely depend on another step's output.
Create the nodes, then wire START, the fan-out branches, a fan-in join, and END with plain add_edge calls.
Print the topology with get_graph().draw_mermaid() and compare the picture against your dependency list.
Put a counter in state and enforce an exit on every back edge; set recursion_limit explicitly in the run config.

code.title: Parallel retrieval as explicit topology: two branches from START, one join, and END.
code.code:
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class State(TypedDict):
  dense: list[str]
  sparse: list[str]
  merged: list[str]

def dense(state: State) -> dict:
  return {"dense": ["d1", "d2"]}

def sparse(state: State) -> dict:
  return {"sparse": ["s1"]}
g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("dense", dense); g.add_node("sparse", sparse)
g.add_node("join", lambda s: {"merged": s["dense"] + s["sparse"]})
g.add_edge(START, "dense"); g.add_edge(START, "sparse")
g.add_edge("dense", "join"); g.add_edge("sparse", "join")
g.add_edge("join", END)
print(g.compile().get_graph().draw_mermaid())
what_to_notice: Both retrievers start from START, so they receive identical input state; anything dense writes is invisible to sparse in that superstep.
The join node has two incoming edges from one superstep, so LangGraph runs it once after both complete rather than twice.

No cycle appears here deliberately; a back edge would need a state counter and an explicit recursion_limit, which is the next lesson's work. Three pages per lesson Page 354 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Chaining independent branches to force ordering, paying the sum of their latencies instead of the maximum.
Relying on which parallel branch finishes first to populate state that the other branch reads.
Adding a retry edge back to a node without a counter, then meeting the loop at recursion_limit in production.
production_notes: Render the compiled graph in CI and diff the Mermaid output, so an accidental edge change appears in review rather than in an incident.
Give every node a timeout and log its duration per superstep; a slow join usually means one branch is the real bottleneck.
Set recursion_limit from the product's tolerance, alert on GraphRecursionError, and treat that error as a bug report rather than user input.

Independent steps share a superstep instead of being chained end to end.

lessons.title: Conditional Routing
lessons.subtitle: Turn a state value into a labelled decision, keep the router pure, and make every unresolved label a visible failure rather
why_it_matters: Routing is where an agent's judgement becomes control flow, so it deserves the same treatment as any branch in production code. A router that returns a label nobody mapped silently ends the run, and a threshold guessed inside a prompt cannot be reviewed or tuned. Explicit bands, total mappings, and tests make expensive decisions predictable before a user sees them.
outcomes: Write a router function that reads state and returns a key present in the edge mapping.
Design confidence bands with explicit fallback branches, including a refusal path that is counted.
Test every routing outcome, including an unmapped key, without calling a live model.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A router is a pure function add_conditional_edges takes a source node, a function, and a mapping from returned labels to destinations. The function should read state and return a label or a list of labels for fan-out, and nothing else: no model call, no database write, no exception for ordinary input. Keeping it pure means a unit test can drive every branch from a hand-built state dictionary, and a reviewer can read all thresholds in one place. Bands, not vibes Thresholds belong in configuration with a stated owner. For a support assistant, confidence at or above 0.80 answers directly, 0.45 to 0.80 queues for review, and below 0.45 refuses with a handoff. Each band carries a metric: answer accuracy, reviewer override rate, refusal rate. Tune one band at a time against a labelled set, because a change that lifts automation usually raises the override rate. Put the numbers in graph code, not in the prompt. Every label must resolve The mapping is the contract between router and topology. If the function returns an unknown label, the run fails or ends without an answer, depending on version. Add a test asserting that the label set the router can produce equals the mapping keys. Route unhappy paths into nodes, not straight to END, so refusals and failures are recorded, counted, and visible in traces. A default branch hides bugs; prefer an explicit catch-all with its own metric.

key_terms.definition: A graph edge whose destination is chosen at runtime by a function that maps state to one or more destination labels.
The string a router returns, which must appear as a key in the edge mapping for the run to continue.

An explicit destination that receives unmatched or low-confidence cases so they are handled and counted rather than dropped. MENTAL MODEL A router is a signal box, not a road: it decides which track the train takes, but the points must already exist and every point must lead somewhere.

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Routing is where an agent's judgement becomes control flow, so it deserves the same treatment as any branch in
production code. A router that returns a label nobody mapped silently ends the run, and a threshold guessed inside a
prompt cannot be reviewed or tuned. Explicit bands, total mappings, and tests make expensive decisions predictable
before a user sees them.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write a router function that reads state and returns a key present in the edge mapping.
 • Design confidence bands with explicit fallback branches, including a refusal path that is counted.
 • Test every routing outcome, including an unmapped key, without calling a live model.
CORE CONCEPTS
A router is a pure function
add_conditional_edges takes a source node, a function, and a mapping from returned labels to destinations. The function
should read state and return a label or a list of labels for fan-out, and nothing else: no model call, no database write, no
exception for ordinary input. Keeping it pure means a unit test can drive every branch from a hand-built state dictionary,
and a reviewer can read all thresholds in one place.
Bands, not vibes
Thresholds belong in configuration with a stated owner. For a support assistant, confidence at or above 0.80 answers
directly, 0.45 to 0.80 queues for review, and below 0.45 refuses with a handoff. Each band carries a metric: answer
accuracy, reviewer override rate, refusal rate. Tune one band at a time against a labelled set, because a change that lifts
automation usually raises the override rate. Put the numbers in graph code, not in the prompt.
Every label must resolve
The mapping is the contract between router and topology. If the function returns an unknown label, the run fails or ends
without an answer, depending on version. Add a test asserting that the label set the router can produce equals the
mapping keys. Route unhappy paths into nodes, not straight to END, so refusals and failures are recorded, counted, and
visible in traces. A default branch hides bugs; prefer an explicit catch-all with its own metric.

 Conditional edge                 A graph edge whose destination is chosen at runtime by a function that maps state to one or more

 Routing key                      The string a router returns, which must appear as a key in the edge mapping for the run to continue.
 Catch-all branch                 An explicit destination that receives unmatched or low-confidence cases so they are handled and counted
                                  rather than dropped.

lessons.subtitle: Design the graph's state as a versioned schema with explicit reducers, so parallel branches merge instead of overwriting
why_it_matters: State is the only thing that survives between nodes, so every design mistake in it is durable. A missing reducer turns two parallel findings into one, and an oversized state turns every checkpoint into a slow, expensive write. Treating state as a schema with owners and merge rules makes agent behaviour inspectable and makes persistence affordable.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: State is a schema, not a bag LangGraph passes a TypedDict or Pydantic model between nodes; a node returns a partial update and the graph merges it into state. Declare every key you rely on and keep the shape flat: messages, query, findings, answer, attempt. Separate what the caller supplies from what the graph accumulates and what the API returns. A flat schema with named owners is easier to validate and to migrate than nested dictionaries that gain a key every sprint. Reducers decide conflicts By default a returned key replaces the previous value. For keys that accumulate, wrap the type in Annotated with a reducer such as operator.add or add_messages, which appends and de-duplicates by message ID. Parallel branches then merge deterministically as LangGraph applies updates, instead of the last write winning. Choose a reducer for every list key on purpose; an unannotated list is a bug waiting for the second branch to finish. Test the collision case. Serialisable and small A checkpointer serialises state on every superstep, so state must survive JSON encoding unless you register a serialiser. Keep model clients, database connections, and API keys out of state; pass them through config or closures. Store large documents by ID or object-store key, never as full text. A 500 KB message history written at every step turns a cheap graph into a storage bill and a slow resume, so trim history with a summarising node.

key_terms.definition: A function attached to a state key that combines the current value with a node's update instead of replacing it.

The dictionary a node returns containing only the keys it changed; untouched keys keep their previous values. add_messages LangGraph's built-in reducer for message lists that appends new messages and replaces existing entries by ID. MENTAL MODEL State is a shared spreadsheet with column rules: anyone may add a row, but each column decides whether a new entry replaces the old cell or is appended below it.

lessons.title: Persistence
lessons.subtitle: Give each conversation a durable thread, choose a checkpoint store you can operate, and isolate tenants before the first
why_it_matters: Without persistence every request starts from nothing: no follow-up questions, no resume after a crash, no audit trail. A checkpointer turns a graph run into a resumable record, but it also creates a database you must secure, back up, and prune. The engineering decision is which store, which key, and how long to keep what.
outcomes: Attach a checkpointer and address runs by thread_id so a conversation survives a process restart.
Compare in-memory, SQLite, and Postgres checkpoint stores on durability, concurrency, and operating cost.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Threads are the unit of memory A checkpointer saves state after each superstep under a thread_id supplied in config. The same thread continues a conversation; a new thread starts clean. Thread identifiers are an application concern: use a server-generated UUID combined with tenant and user identifiers, never a raw client-supplied string you trust. One thread equals one conversation rather than one user, so a person with three chats gets three threads and no history bleeds between them. Pick a store you can operate MemorySaver is for tests; it dies with the process. SqliteSaver suits a single-instance tool and local development, with file locking as its concurrency limit. PostgresSaver is the production default when you already run Postgres: transactions, backups, connection pooling, and concurrent writers across replicas. Run its schema setup command once and pin the package version, because checkpointer tables change between releases. A Redis-backed community store trades durability for speed and fits poorly when audits matter. Persistence has a privacy surface Checkpoints hold the full message history, retrieved context, and intermediate drafts, which means customer text and possibly personal data. Encrypt the volume, restrict access with the same rules as the application database, and run a retention job that deletes threads older than policy allows. A user deletion request must remove checkpoints, not just rows in your conversations table. Log thread identifiers, never checkpoint contents, and treat support read access as a privileged action.

key_terms.definition: A LangGraph component that serialises graph state after each superstep and restores it when a run resumes. thread_id The configurable identifier that selects which saved state a run loads and appends to.

The guarantee that committed state survives a process crash, redeploy, or host failure. MENTAL MODEL A checkpointer is a save file and thread_id is the slot name: the game resumes exactly where it stopped, so choose slot names users cannot guess or overwrite.

Every deploy dropped live conversations, and support measured 22% of chats restarting mid-booking during the Thursday release window. The team moves to PostgresSaver on the database they already run, applies the library's schema setup, and schedules a 90-day retention job. Thread keys become tenant, user, and a server-generated UUID, after a pen test shows that a client-supplied thread_id could read another tenant's transcript. Resume after a forced pod kill works on the first attempt. The decision recorded is that checkpoint storage inherits the application database's backup, encryption, and access policy instead of adding a second store.

code.code:
import os
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class State(TypedDict):
  messages: list

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("reply", lambda s: {"messages": s["messages"] + [("ai", "ok")]})
g.add_edge(START, "reply")
g.add_edge("reply", END)

with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as saver:

Give each conversation a durable thread, choose a checkpoint store you can operate, and isolate tenants before the first
customer arrives.
Agent Orchestration · Lesson 10 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Without persistence every request starts from nothing: no follow-up questions, no resume after a crash, no audit trail. A
checkpointer turns a graph run into a resumable record, but it also creates a database you must secure, back up, and
prune. The engineering decision is which store, which key, and how long to keep what.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Attach a checkpointer and address runs by thread_id so a conversation survives a process restart.
 • Compare in-memory, SQLite, and Postgres checkpoint stores on durability, concurrency, and operating cost.
 • Design thread keys, retention, and tenant isolation for a multi-user agent.
CORE CONCEPTS
Threads are the unit of memory
A checkpointer saves state after each superstep under a thread_id supplied in config. The same thread continues a
conversation; a new thread starts clean. Thread identifiers are an application concern: use a server-generated UUID
combined with tenant and user identifiers, never a raw client-supplied string you trust. One thread equals one
conversation rather than one user, so a person with three chats gets three threads and no history bleeds between them.
Pick a store you can operate
MemorySaver is for tests; it dies with the process. SqliteSaver suits a single-instance tool and local development, with file
locking as its concurrency limit. PostgresSaver is the production default when you already run Postgres: transactions,
backups, connection pooling, and concurrent writers across replicas. Run its schema setup command once and pin the
package version, because checkpointer tables change between releases. A Redis-backed community store trades
durability for speed and fits poorly when audits matter.
Persistence has a privacy surface
Checkpoints hold the full message history, retrieved context, and intermediate drafts, which means customer text and
possibly personal data. Encrypt the volume, restrict access with the same rules as the application database, and run a
retention job that deletes threads older than policy allows. A user deletion request must remove checkpoints, not just
rows in your conversations table. Log thread identifiers, never checkpoint contents, and treat support read access as a
privileged action.
KEY TERMS
 Checkpointer                     A LangGraph component that serialises graph state after each superstep and restores it when a run resumes.
 thread_id                        The configurable identifier that selects which saved state a run loads and appends to.
 Durability                       The guarantee that committed state survives a process crash, redeploy, or host failure.

  MENTAL MODEL A checkpointer is a save file and thread_id is the slot name: the game resumes exactly where it stopped, so choose slot
  names users cannot guess or overwrite.

A travel platform's booking assistant kept state in MemorySaver. Every deploy dropped live conversations, and support

2.    Run the checkpointer's schema setup, pin the package version, and include its tables in backup and restore drills.
3.    Generate thread_id on the server from tenant, user, and a UUID, and reject client attempts to set it directly.

A Postgres-backed graph addressed by a server-composed thread key, resumed in a later process.
  import os
  from typing import TypedDict
  from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver
  from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

  class State(TypedDict):
    messages: list

  g = StateGraph(State)
  g.add_node("reply", lambda s: {"messages": s["messages"] + [("ai", "ok")]})
  g.add_edge(START, "reply")
  g.add_edge("reply", END)

  with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as saver:
    saver.setup()
    graph = g.compile(checkpointer=saver)
    cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1:u9:6f2a"}}
    graph.invoke({"messages": [("human", "hello")]}, cfg)
    print(graph.get_state(cfg).values["messages"])

why_it_matters: A checkpoint is more than a save point: it is the record of how the graph reached its answer. That record lets you resume after a provider outage, replay a disputed decision for review, and try a corrected prompt from step three without paying for steps one and two. It only works if side effects are idempotent, because replay repeats nodes.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Every superstep is a version With a checkpointer attached, LangGraph writes a snapshot after each superstep carrying an ID, step number, the next nodes, and state values. get_state returns the latest; get_state_history returns the lineage newest first. That lineage is the audit trail for an agent decision: you can see which node produced a value and what state it read. Snapshots are immutable, so time travel means selecting an earlier ID rather than editing history. Keep history long enough for disputes, then prune. Resume, replay, fork Invoking with a null input on an existing thread resumes from the last checkpoint, which is how a crashed run continues after a provider recovers. Passing the checkpoint_id of an older snapshot replays from that point and re-runs downstream nodes with current code. update_state writes a corrected value as if a named node produced it, the mechanism behind human editing before approval. Forking replays into a new thread_id so the original stays intact as evidence while you experiment. Replay makes side effects dangerous A node that sends an email, charges a card, or opens a ticket will do it again on replay, because the graph cannot know the effect already happened. Give every external write an idempotency key derived from thread_id, node name, and a version, and make the downstream service honour it. Record the returned external ID in state so a later node checks instead of duplicating. Read-only tools replay safely; anything with a cost or a customer-visible effect needs this discipline.

lessons.title: Streaming
lessons.subtitle: Stream the right granularity to the right client, keep the persisted turn consistent with what the user saw, and cancel work
why_it_matters: Users judge latency by the first useful token, not by total run time, and a six-second silent wait feels broken. Streaming also changes your failure model: output is already on screen when validation fails, the client may disconnect mid-run, and the final state must match what was rendered. Consistency requires deliberate choices about granularity, transport, and cancellation.
outcomes: Choose between values, updates, messages, and custom stream modes for a specific interface need.
Expose a graph as server-sent events with a stable event schema and trace identifiers.
Handle disconnect, partial output, and post-stream validation without losing the turn.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Granularity is a product decision values emits the full state after each superstep, updates emits only each node's returned delta, messages emits token chunks plus metadata from inside model calls, and debug adds task metadata. A chat UI needs messages for token feel and updates to show which tool is running. An internal dashboard may need only updates. Custom mode lets a node emit domain events such as retrieved four chunks through a stream writer. Pick the smallest set the interface actually renders; every extra mode costs bandwidth and parsing. Transport and event schema Server-sent events suit one-way token flow over HTTP and reconnect natively, while WebSockets are worth it only when the client also sends mid-stream. Define the envelope once: event type, request ID, sequence number, and payload. Emit a heartbeat every 15 seconds so proxies do not close an idle connection during a slow model call. End with a terminal event carrying the validated answer and citation IDs, and let the UI replace speculative text with that final value. Disconnect, cancel, consistency When the client disconnects, stop the graph rather than paying for an answer nobody reads; in FastAPI check request.is_disconnected, cancel the task, and rely on a checkpointer so a reconnect can resume the thread. Assemble the text server-side and persist only after validation, marking the turn incomplete if the stream breaks. Never let streamed tokens bypass output checks: stream a draft, then confirm citations and schema before the terminal event. Log first-token latency and stream duration separately.

key_terms.definition: A one-way HTTP stream of text/event-stream messages that browsers consume through EventSource and reconnect automatically. stream_mode The LangGraph option selecting what each streamed chunk contains: values, updates, messages, custom, or debug.

The time from request start to the first content chunk reaching the client, which users experience as responsiveness. MENTAL MODEL Streaming is a live broadcast with a published transcript: viewers may tune out at any moment, so the recording must stand alone and the station must stop transmitting to an empty room.

worked_example: A 30-person SaaS company benchmarks its chat assistant at 5.8 seconds p95 to first visible text. The team had streamed values, so the browser received one large chunk after the answer node finished and nothing during a slower validator. Switching to messages gives token-level output, while updates drives a status chip for each tool call. First token drops to 900 milliseconds at p95, though total completion stays at 4.2 seconds, confirming the change is perceptual rather than faster. A reconnect test shows duplicated sentences because the client replayed from sequence zero; a request ID and last-seen sequence fix it. The decision is to stream tokens only from the answer node and keep critic and validator nodes silent until their verdict.

code.title: An SSE endpoint that streams node updates and answer tokens from one compiled graph.
code.code:
import json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()
graph = build_graph() # compiled at startup with a Postgres checkpointer

async def events(payload: dict, config: dict):
  async for mode, chunk in graph.astream(
       payload, config, stream_mode=["updates", "messages"]):
    if mode == "messages":
       token, _ = chunk
       yield f"event: token\ndata: {json.dumps({'t': token.content})}\n\n"
    else:
       yield f"event: node\ndata: {json.dumps(list(chunk))}\n\n"

@app.post("/threads/{thread_id}/messages")
async def send(thread_id: str, body: dict):
  config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}
  return StreamingResponse(events(body, config), media_type="text/event-stream")
what_to_notice: The client sees nothing until the answer node emits tokens, so earlier tool activity must travel through the updates mode as separate events.
Each chunk arrives tagged with its mode; a client assuming every chunk is a token will render a dictionary into the chat window.

Streaming
Stream the right granularity to the right client, keep the persisted turn consistent with what the user saw, and cancel work
when they leave.
Agent Orchestration · Lesson 12 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Users judge latency by the first useful token, not by total run time, and a six-second silent wait feels broken. Streaming
also changes your failure model: output is already on screen when validation fails, the client may disconnect mid-run, and
the final state must match what was rendered. Consistency requires deliberate choices about granularity, transport, and
cancellation.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Choose between values, updates, messages, and custom stream modes for a specific interface need.
 • Expose a graph as server-sent events with a stable event schema and trace identifiers.
 • Handle disconnect, partial output, and post-stream validation without losing the turn.
CORE CONCEPTS
Granularity is a product decision
values emits the full state after each superstep, updates emits only each node's returned delta, messages emits token
chunks plus metadata from inside model calls, and debug adds task metadata. A chat UI needs messages for token feel
and updates to show which tool is running. An internal dashboard may need only updates. Custom mode lets a node emit
domain events such as retrieved four chunks through a stream writer. Pick the smallest set the interface actually renders;
every extra mode costs bandwidth and parsing.
Transport and event schema
Server-sent events suit one-way token flow over HTTP and reconnect natively, while WebSockets are worth it only when
the client also sends mid-stream. Define the envelope once: event type, request ID, sequence number, and payload. Emit
a heartbeat every 15 seconds so proxies do not close an idle connection during a slow model call. End with a terminal
event carrying the validated answer and citation IDs, and let the UI replace speculative text with that final value.
Disconnect, cancel, consistency
When the client disconnects, stop the graph rather than paying for an answer nobody reads; in FastAPI check
request.is_disconnected, cancel the task, and rely on a checkpointer so a reconnect can resume the thread. Assemble the
text server-side and persist only after validation, marking the turn incomplete if the stream breaks. Never let streamed
tokens bypass output checks: stream a draft, then confirm citations and schema before the terminal event. Log first-token
latency and stream duration separately.
KEY TERMS
 Server-sent events               A one-way HTTP stream of text/event-stream messages that browsers consume through EventSource and
                                  reconnect automatically.
 stream_mode                      The LangGraph option selecting what each streamed chunk contains: values, updates, messages, custom, or
                                  debug.
 First-token latency              The time from request start to the first content chunk reaching the client, which users experience as
                                  responsiveness.

  MENTAL MODEL Streaming is a live broadcast with a published transcript: viewers may tune out at any moment, so the recording must
  stand alone and the station must stop transmitting to an empty room.
