code.title: A digest and lifecycle probe: what you pin, how many layers you pull, and whether the process is still running.
code.code:
import json
import subprocess

def docker(*args: str) -> str:
  cmd = ["docker", *args]
  return subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout

ref = "python:3.12-slim"
repo = docker("image", "inspect", "--format", "{{index .RepoDigests 0}}", ref)
layers = json.loads(docker("image", "inspect", "--format", "{{json .RootFS.Layers}}", ref))
print("pin:", repo.strip(), f"({len(layers)} layers)", sep="\n")

docker("run", "--detach", "--name", "probe", ref, "sleep", "30")
print(docker("ps", "--filter", "name=probe", "--format", "{{.Status}}").strip())
docker("rm", "--force", "probe")
what_to_notice: The file disappeared because removal, not restart, discards the writable layer; a restart of the same container would have kept it.
The 1.9 GB image was mostly build context, so the fix was a .dockerignore rather than a smaller base image.
Pull time matters in CI and autoscaling; dropping 1.7 GB saves 41 seconds on every cold node. Three pages per lesson Page 507 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Storing user uploads or database files inside the container filesystem and losing them on the next deploy.
Treating a mutable tag as a version pin, then wondering why a rebuild produced different behaviour.
Running a shell as PID 1, so the process ignores SIGTERM and every stop waits for the timeout.
production_notes: Pin every base image by digest, label the resulting image with its source commit, and deploy that digest to every environment.
Set CPU and memory limits from measured usage, and alert when a container is killed for exceeding them.
Mount state on volumes or object storage, and include the volume in the service's tested recovery plan.

I know which command shows layers, mounts, and limits for a running container.
Every stateful path in my service is backed by a volume or an external store.
My deployment references an image digest, not only a tag.
I can read an exit code and a log stream to locate a start-up failure.

What does the writable layer contain, and when is it destroyed?
How can a mutable tag cause two CI builds to produce different runtime behaviour?
Which process becomes PID 1 in a container, and why does that matter for shutdown?
Why is a named volume a better home for Postgres data than a bind mount in production?

lessons.title: Dockerfile
lessons.subtitle: Order instructions for cache hits, split build from runtime, and end with a small non-root image that handles signals.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 3 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: A Dockerfile is a build program, and its instruction order decides both rebuild time and image size. Copying the whole repository before installing dependencies invalidates the dependency cache on every commit. Shipping a compiler and build headers into production adds hundreds of megabytes and attack surface. The difference between a four-minute rebuild and a fifteen-second one is usually ordering, not hardware or network speed.
outcomes: Order Dockerfile instructions so dependency layers survive source changes and rebuilds stay under a minute.
Use a multi-stage build to keep compilers and build caches out of the runtime image.
Run the service as a non-root user with an exec-form entrypoint that receives SIGTERM.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Cache order: dependencies before source Each layer is keyed by its parent, the instruction, and the content it copies. Put COPY requirements.txt and the install step before COPY . so editing a Python file reuses installed dependencies. A wildcard copy of the repository also drags in .git, tests, and datasets unless .dockerignore excludes them, changing the cache key for reasons unrelated to the build. Measure rebuild time after a one-line source change; that is the number developers feel every day. Multi-stage separates build from run A builder stage can install compilers, headers, and build tools, produce wheels or a virtual environment, then disappear. The runtime stage copies only the artefacts and the interpreter it needs. This keeps the final image small, reduces CVE surface, and shortens pulls on cold nodes. Copy the virtual environment to the same absolute path in both stages, or its shebangs and compiled paths will point at a directory that no longer exists. Non-root, exec form, signal handling By default a container runs as root, so a compromised process has more room to move. Create a user with a fixed UID, chown only the files it needs, and switch with USER before CMD. Use exec form so the application is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly; shell form hides it behind /bin/sh. Then handle SIGTERM in the application, stop accepting connections, and finish in-flight requests within the platform grace period.

key_terms.definition: The files sent to the Docker daemon at build time, filtered by .dockerignore and hashed for COPY instructions.
A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where later stages copy only selected artefacts from earlier ones.

A JSON-array ENTRYPOINT or CMD that runs the binary directly as PID 1 instead of through a shell. MENTAL MODEL A Dockerfile is a cooking plan: prep that rarely changes goes first, the plate holds only what is served, and the waiter carries the signal to stop.

worked_example: A team of five ships a FastAPI service whose CI build takes 6 minutes 40 seconds and whose image is 1.4 GB. # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
  pip wheel --no-cache-dir -w /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels
COPY --chown=app:app app ./app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

Dockerfile
Order instructions for cache hits, split build from runtime, and end with a small non-root image that handles signals.
Docker & Deployment · Lesson 3 of 12 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A Dockerfile is a build program, and its instruction order decides both rebuild time and image size. Copying the whole
repository before installing dependencies invalidates the dependency cache on every commit. Shipping a compiler and
build headers into production adds hundreds of megabytes and attack surface. The difference between a four-minute
rebuild and a fifteen-second one is usually ordering, not hardware or network speed.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Order Dockerfile instructions so dependency layers survive source changes and rebuilds stay under a minute.
 • Use a multi-stage build to keep compilers and build caches out of the runtime image.
 • Run the service as a non-root user with an exec-form entrypoint that receives SIGTERM.
CORE CONCEPTS
Cache order: dependencies before source
Each layer is keyed by its parent, the instruction, and the content it copies. Put COPY requirements.txt and the install step
before COPY . so editing a Python file reuses installed dependencies. A wildcard copy of the repository also drags in .git,
tests, and datasets unless .dockerignore excludes them, changing the cache key for reasons unrelated to the build.
Measure rebuild time after a one-line source change; that is the number developers feel every day.
Multi-stage separates build from run
A builder stage can install compilers, headers, and build tools, produce wheels or a virtual environment, then disappear.
The runtime stage copies only the artefacts and the interpreter it needs. This keeps the final image small, reduces CVE
surface, and shortens pulls on cold nodes. Copy the virtual environment to the same absolute path in both stages, or its
shebangs and compiled paths will point at a directory that no longer exists.
Non-root, exec form, signal handling
By default a container runs as root, so a compromised process has more room to move. Create a user with a fixed UID,
chown only the files it needs, and switch with USER before CMD. Use exec form so the application is PID 1 and receives
SIGTERM directly; shell form hides it behind /bin/sh. Then handle SIGTERM in the application, stop accepting connections,
and finish in-flight requests within the platform grace period.
KEY TERMS
 Build context                    The files sent to the Docker daemon at build time, filtered by .dockerignore and hashed for COPY
                                  instructions.
 Multi-stage build                A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where later stages copy only selected artefacts from earlier ones.
 Exec form                        A JSON-array ENTRYPOINT or CMD that runs the binary directly as PID 1 instead of through a shell.

  MENTAL MODEL A Dockerfile is a cooking plan: prep that rarely changes goes first, the plate holds only what is served, and the waiter
  carries the signal to stop.

lessons.title: Containerizing FastAPI
lessons.subtitle: Make the API container start quickly, report liveness and readiness honestly, and shut down without dropping requests.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 4 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: A FastAPI container that boots is not the same as one that is ready. Model loading, database pools, and Redis connections take seconds, and a liveness probe that checks them will restart a healthy process during a dependency outage. Getting readiness, worker count, and shutdown right prevents crash loops, connection exhaustion, and requests cut off mid- stream during a rollout.
outcomes: Separate build-time packaging from run-time configuration so one image serves every environment.
Design liveness and readiness endpoints that distinguish a dead process from a degraded dependency.
Choose worker count, connection pool size, and shutdown grace from measured concurrency.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One image, configuration at run time Bake code, dependencies, and the interpreter into the image; inject endpoints, credentials, log level, and feature flags as environment variables at start. A settings object built with pydantic-settings validates them once and fails fast with a clear message. Never rebuild for staging, because then the artefact you tested is not the artefact you ship. Use the same digest in every environment and vary only configuration and secrets from the platform secret store. Liveness, readiness, start-up Liveness answers whether the process is wedged; it should check almost nothing and never call Postgres. Readiness answers whether this instance should receive traffic; it can check the connection pool and cache with a 500 ms timeout. Start-up probes cover slow model loading so liveness does not kill the pod first. A failing readiness removes an instance from the load balancer without restarting it, which is what you want during a database failover. Workers, pools, graceful shutdown Each Uvicorn worker is a process with its own memory and connection pool, so four workers multiply connections by four. For async endpoints, one worker with a high concurrency limit often beats four workers competing for CPU. Size the pool from Postgres max_connections divided by total replicas, leaving headroom for migrations and admin sessions. On SIGTERM, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close pools, and exit before the grace period expires.

key_terms.definition: A platform check that restarts the container when the process is unresponsive, deliberately avoiding dependency calls.
A check that controls whether the instance receives traffic, allowed to fail while dependencies recover.

The sequence of refusing new work, finishing in-flight requests, and closing resources after SIGTERM. MENTAL MODEL A container is a new employee: the build is the interview, start-up is the first day, readiness is permission to serve customers, and liveness is whether they are still conscious.

CODE
Dependency-aware readiness beside a liveness check that stays green, plus pool cleanup on shutdown.
  from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
  from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
  from redis.asyncio import Redis
  @asynccontextmanager
  async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.redis = Redis.from_url("redis://cache:6379/0", socket_timeout=0.5)
    yield
    await app.state.redis.aclose()
  app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
  @app.get("/healthz")
  async def healthz() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"status": "ok"}
  @app.get("/readyz")
  async def readyz(response: Response) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:
      await app.state.redis.ping()
    except Exception:
      response.status_code = 503
      return {"status": "degraded"}
    return {"status": "ready"}

 → Liveness returns 200 even when Redis is down, so the platform does not restart a process that is merely waiting.
 → Readiness times out after 500 ms and removes the instance from the load balancer without killing it.
 → The lifespan hook closes the Redis client, which prevents connection leaks across repeated rollouts.

lessons.title: PostgreSQL + Redis + API
lessons.subtitle: Connect the API to Postgres and Redis with bounded pools, explicit timeouts, and a start-up sequence that survives
why_it_matters: Postgres and Redis fail differently. Postgres refuses connections when max_connections is reached and holds locks during migrations; Redis loses data on eviction and restart unless persistence is configured. An API that opens pools lazily, retries forever, or runs migrations in every replica turns a routine deploy into an outage. These three services need explicit budgets, timeouts, and ownership.
outcomes: Size database and Redis connection pools from server limits and the number of API replicas.
Separate durable state in Postgres from disposable cache and queue data in Redis.
Run migrations once per deploy and gate traffic on dependency readiness.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Postgres is the system of record Put durable entities, constraints, and transactions in Postgres. Use a migration tool such as Alembic, run migrations as a single job before the new API version, and keep them backward compatible for one release so old and new pods coexist. Set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a stuck query cannot hold a connection forever. Keep analytical scans off the primary, and index the columns your filters actually use. Redis is a cache with an eviction policy Redis holds values you can rebuild: rendered answers, embeddings, rate-limit counters, and job locks. Every key needs a namespace, a TTL, and a documented rebuild path. Choose maxmemory and maxmemory-policy deliberately; allkeys-lru is fine for pure cache, but noeviction is safer when Redis also holds queue state. Do not treat a cache hit as proof of correctness, and never store the only copy of a user record in Redis. Pools, retries, start-up order Each API replica opens a pool; total connections equal replicas multiplied by pool size, and Postgres has a hard ceiling. Use a small pool per replica, a short acquire timeout, and PgBouncer when replica counts grow. At start-up, retry with capped exponential backoff and jitter, then fail readiness rather than crashing. Migrations belong in a separate job, not in application start-up, because concurrent replicas will race on the same schema change.

key_terms.definition: A bounded set of reusable database connections shared by requests, with acquire timeouts and a maximum size.
The rule Redis applies when memory is full, such as dropping least-recently-used keys or refusing writes.

A versioned, ordered schema change applied once by a dedicated job before application code depends on it. MENTAL MODEL Postgres is the ledger, Redis is the whiteboard, and the API is the clerk: write facts in the ledger, scribble guesses on the board, and never let the board become the only record.
Page 515 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: A retail API runs six replicas, each with a 20-connection asyncpg pool, against Postgres with max_connections 100. During a flash sale the seventh autoscaled replica fails and the others log 'remaining connection slots are reserved', pushing the error rate to 28%. The team also stores password-reset tokens only in Redis with no persistence, losing 40 tokens in a restart. They move tokens to a Postgres table with an expiry index, set pools to five, add PgBouncer in transaction mode, and cap replicas at ten. Redis keeps only rendered search results with a 300-second TTL and a 2 GB allkeys-lru limit. Connections peak at 52, the error rate returns to 0.4%, and the cache hit rate is 63%.
steps: Write the connection budget: replicas times pool size, plus migration and admin headroom, against max_connections.
Classify every Redis key as cache, counter, lock, or queue, and give each a namespace, TTL, and rebuild path.
Run schema migrations as a single pre-deploy job and keep each change backward compatible for one release.
Add connect, acquire, command, and statement timeouts, then retry only transient errors with jittered backoff.
Start the stack cold and confirm readiness waits for both dependencies without crash-looping.

code.title: A bounded start-up that retries transient connection failures, then fails loudly instead of hanging.
code.code:
import asyncio

import asyncpg
from redis.asyncio import Redis

async def connect(url: str, redis_url: str):
  for delay in (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8):
    try:
       pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(url, min_size=2, max_size=5, timeout=3)
       redis = Redis.from_url(redis_url, socket_timeout=0.5)
       await redis.ping()
       return pool, redis
    except (OSError, asyncpg.PostgresError):
       await asyncio.sleep(delay)
  raise RuntimeError("database unavailable after 5 attempts")
what_to_notice: The budget includes autoscaling headroom, so the pool is sized for ten replicas even when six are usually running.
Password-reset tokens moved to Postgres because Redis eviction or restart made them irrecoverable.

PgBouncer in transaction mode lets 50 clients share 20 server connections, but breaks session-level features. YOUR WORKING NOTES Three pages per lesson Page 516 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Caching the only copy of a record in Redis and discovering the gap during an eviction or restart.

PostgreSQL + Redis + API
Connect the API to Postgres and Redis with bounded pools, explicit timeouts, and a start-up sequence that survives
restarts.
Docker & Deployment · Lesson 5 of 12 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Postgres and Redis fail differently. Postgres refuses connections when max_connections is reached and holds locks during
migrations; Redis loses data on eviction and restart unless persistence is configured. An API that opens pools lazily, retries
forever, or runs migrations in every replica turns a routine deploy into an outage. These three services need explicit
budgets, timeouts, and ownership.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Size database and Redis connection pools from server limits and the number of API replicas.
 • Separate durable state in Postgres from disposable cache and queue data in Redis.
 • Run migrations once per deploy and gate traffic on dependency readiness.
CORE CONCEPTS
Postgres is the system of record
Put durable entities, constraints, and transactions in Postgres. Use a migration tool such as Alembic, run migrations as a
single job before the new API version, and keep them backward compatible for one release so old and new pods coexist.
Set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a stuck query cannot hold a connection forever. Keep
analytical scans off the primary, and index the columns your filters actually use.
Redis is a cache with an eviction policy
Redis holds values you can rebuild: rendered answers, embeddings, rate-limit counters, and job locks. Every key needs a
namespace, a TTL, and a documented rebuild path. Choose maxmemory and maxmemory-policy deliberately; allkeys-lru
is fine for pure cache, but noeviction is safer when Redis also holds queue state. Do not treat a cache hit as proof of
correctness, and never store the only copy of a user record in Redis.
Pools, retries, start-up order
Each API replica opens a pool; total connections equal replicas multiplied by pool size, and Postgres has a hard ceiling. Use
a small pool per replica, a short acquire timeout, and PgBouncer when replica counts grow. At start-up, retry with capped
exponential backoff and jitter, then fail readiness rather than crashing. Migrations belong in a separate job, not in
application start-up, because concurrent replicas will race on the same schema change.
KEY TERMS
 Connection pool                  A bounded set of reusable database connections shared by requests, with acquire timeouts and a maximum
                                  size.
 Eviction policy                  The rule Redis applies when memory is full, such as dropping least-recently-used keys or refusing writes.
 Migration                        A versioned, ordered schema change applied once by a dedicated job before application code depends on it.

  board, and never let the board become the only record.

Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A retail API runs six replicas, each with a 20-connection asyncpg pool, against Postgres with max_connections 100. During
a flash sale the seventh autoscaled replica fails and the others log 'remaining connection slots are reserved', pushing the
error rate to 28%. The team also stores password-reset tokens only in Redis with no persistence, losing 40 tokens in a
restart. They move tokens to a Postgres table with an expiry index, set pools to five, add PgBouncer in transaction mode,
and cap replicas at ten. Redis keeps only rendered search results with a 300-second TTL and a 2 GB allkeys-lru limit.
Connections peak at 52, the error rate returns to 0.4%, and the cache hit rate is 63%.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Write the connection budget: replicas times pool size, plus migration and admin headroom, against max_connections.
2.    Classify every Redis key as cache, counter, lock, or queue, and give each a namespace, TTL, and rebuild path.
3.    Run schema migrations as a single pre-deploy job and keep each change backward compatible for one release.
4.    Add connect, acquire, command, and statement timeouts, then retry only transient errors with jittered backoff.
5.    Start the stack cold and confirm readiness waits for both dependencies without crash-looping.
CODE
A bounded start-up that retries transient connection failures, then fails loudly instead of hanging.
  import asyncio

  import asyncpg
  from redis.asyncio import Redis

  async def connect(url: str, redis_url: str):
    for delay in (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8):
      try:
         pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(url, min_size=2, max_size=5, timeout=3)
         redis = Redis.from_url(redis_url, socket_timeout=0.5)
         await redis.ping()
         return pool, redis
      except (OSError, asyncpg.PostgresError):
         await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("database unavailable after 5 attempts")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The budget includes autoscaling headroom, so the pool is sized for ten replicas even when six are usually running.
 → Password-reset tokens moved to Postgres because Redis eviction or restart made them irrecoverable.
 → PgBouncer in transaction mode lets 50 clients share 20 server connections, but breaks session-level features.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Compose is a development and CI tool Compose runs several containers on one host with a shared network and project namespace. It is excellent for local development, integration tests, and small demos because the file is versioned and the stack starts in one command. It is not a production orchestrator: it has no rolling deploys, multi-node scheduling, or self-healing beyond restart policies. Use it to reproduce the production topology, then deploy the same images with a platform that provides those guarantees. Health gates beat sleep loops depends_on controls start order only unless you request condition: service_healthy. Pair it with a real health check that proves the dependency accepts queries, and set interval, timeout, retries, and start_period from measured start-up time. Even then, application-level retries remain necessary: a dependency can fail after the gate passes, and Compose restarts do not coordinate with your process. Health gates remove the common cold-start race, not every race. Volumes, bind mounts, configuration Named volumes are managed by Docker and persist until explicitly removed; bind mounts map a host path and are useful for live code during development. Mount source in development but never in production, where the image must be the source of truth. Put non-secret defaults in .env, require secrets with ${VAR:?message}, and use separate project names so two branches do not share a database. Seed data belongs in an idempotent script, not a manual step.

STEP BY STEP
1.    List the services, images, ports, environment variables, and volumes the stack needs to run one request.
2.    Write the Compose file with pinned image tags and a health check per stateful dependency.
3.    Gate the API on service_healthy and keep its own retry loop for failures after start-up.
4.    Put database data in a named volume, mount source only in a development profile, and seed idempotently.
5.    Run the full stack from a clean checkout in CI, execute integration tests, and tear it down.
CODE
A health-gated stack with pinned database images, persistent Postgres data, and a required password.
  services:
   api:
    build: .
    env_file: .env
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
     db: {condition: service_healthy}
     cache: {condition: service_healthy}
   db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set in .env}"}
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    healthcheck: {test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"], interval: 5s, retries: 10}
   cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "256mb"]
    healthcheck: {test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"], interval: 5s}
  volumes: {pgdata: {}}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The API waits for service_healthy rather than a fixed sleep, so a slow first Postgres start does not break the run.
 → Source is bind-mounted only in the dev profile, so CI tests the image that will be deployed.
 → Secrets are required with ${VAR:?}, which fails with a readable message instead of booting with an empty password.

lessons.title: Production Containers
lessons.subtitle: Turn a working image into one that is small, non-root, pinned, and safe to terminate under load.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 7 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: A container that runs on your laptop can still be unfit for production: 1.4 GB of compilers, a root process, an unpinned base, and a shell that swallows SIGTERM. Those choices widen the attack surface, slow cold starts, and drop in-flight requests during every deploy. Production containers are boring on purpose: small, reproducible, least-privilege, and quick to stop.
outcomes: Convert a single-stage build into a multi-stage image that ships no compilers, caches, or test fixtures.
Harden the runtime with a non-root user, read-only filesystem, pinned base, and explicit signal handling.
Verify image size, vulnerability count, and shutdown behaviour before the image reaches a registry.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Build with tools, run without them A multi-stage Dockerfile separates the build environment from the runtime. The builder installs compilers and headers, resolves wheels, and exports them; the final stage copies only the wheels and the application. Pin the runtime base by digest, not by a floating tag, so a rebuild cannot silently adopt a new libc. Keep .dockerignore strict: .git, tests, notebooks, and local data inflate the context and can leak into layers. Least privilege at runtime Create an unprivileged user with a fixed UID and GID, copy files with ownership, and set USER in the final stage. Run with a read-only root filesystem and mount only the writable paths you need, such as /tmp. Drop Linux capabilities and set no- new-privileges. These controls matter more for AI services because they often carry provider keys and fetch user documents. A root process turns a small dependency vulnerability into host-level risk. Stop cleanly, start quickly Use exec-form ENTRYPOINT so the server receives SIGTERM directly; a shell wrapper may ignore it. Set the orchestrator grace period above the server's shutdown timeout, and stop accepting new work before exiting. Health checks should test readiness, not just liveness, and never call a paid model endpoint. Smaller images pull faster, which shortens scale-out and recovery; model weights belong in a mounted volume or object store, not baked into every layer.

key_terms.definition: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where artefacts are copied from a builder into a smaller runtime image.
A minimal base image containing the language runtime and application but no shell, package manager, or general-purpose utilities.

A check that tells the orchestrator whether an instance should receive traffic, separate from whether the process is alive. MENTAL MODEL A production image is a sealed shipping container: built with heavy tools in the yard, loaded only with cargo, locked, labelled, and easy to unload.
Page 521 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: The document-ingestion service at a nine-person legal-tech company ships as a 1.6 GB image built from python:3.12 with build-essential, git, and the test suite inside. A scan finds 143 CVEs, mostly in compilers the runtime never uses, and cold starts take 38 seconds. During a rolling deploy, 4% of uploads fail because uvicorn receives SIGTERM through a shell and exits before finishing requests. The platform engineer rebuilds with a wheel-building stage, copies the wheels into python:3.12-slim, runs as UID 10001, and pins the base digest in CI. The image drops to 210 MB, CVEs to 9, cold start to 6 seconds, and failed uploads to zero after adding a 25-second grace period. The decision: weights stay in object storage, mounted at boot.
steps: Separate dependency installation into a builder stage and copy only the wheels into the runtime stage.
Pin the runtime base by digest, pass it through a build argument, and add a strict .dockerignore file.
Create UID 10001, copy files with --chown, set USER, and test with a read-only root filesystem.
Switch to exec-form ENTRYPOINT, set a shutdown timeout, and confirm SIGTERM reaches uvicorn mid-request.
Measure image size, scan findings, cold-start time, and shutdown behaviour, then record them beside the Dockerfile.
common_mistakes: Copying the entire build context before installing dependencies, so every source edit invalidates the dependency cache.
Using floating latest tags in production and discovering that a new base image changed glibc during a redeploy.
Baking model weights into the image and multiplying registry size by every replica that scales out.
production_notes: Scan every image in CI, fail on critical fixable CVEs, and publish an SBOM so responders can answer 'are we affected' in minutes.
Tag images with the Git commit SHA and promote the digest between environments; never rebuild the same commit twice.
Set CPU and memory requests from measured usage, because a pod without requests is the first to be evicted under pressure.

The runtime base is pinned and the container runs as a non-root UID.
SIGTERM reaches the server directly and in-flight requests finish within the grace period.
Readiness, liveness, CPU, and memory are defined and measured under load.

Production Containers
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
The document-ingestion service at a nine-person legal-tech company ships as a 1.6 GB image built from python:3.12 with
build-essential, git, and the test suite inside. A scan finds 143 CVEs, mostly in compilers the runtime never uses, and cold
starts take 38 seconds. During a rolling deploy, 4% of uploads fail because uvicorn receives SIGTERM through a shell and
exits before finishing requests. The platform engineer rebuilds with a wheel-building stage, copies the wheels into
python:3.12-slim, runs as UID 10001, and pins the base digest in CI. The image drops to 210 MB, CVEs to 9, cold start to 6
seconds, and failed uploads to zero after adding a 25-second grace period. The decision: weights stay in object storage,
mounted at boot.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Separate dependency installation into a builder stage and copy only the wheels into the runtime stage.
2.    Pin the runtime base by digest, pass it through a build argument, and add a strict .dockerignore file.
3.    Create UID 10001, copy files with --chown, set USER, and test with a read-only root filesystem.
4.    Switch to exec-form ENTRYPOINT, set a shutdown timeout, and confirm SIGTERM reaches uvicorn mid-request.
5.    Measure image size, scan findings, cold-start time, and shutdown behaviour, then record them beside the Dockerfile.
CODE
A two-stage build that ships only wheels, runs unprivileged, and sends SIGTERM straight to uvicorn.
  ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
  FROM ${BASE} AS builder
  WORKDIR /build
  COPY requirements.txt .
  RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

  FROM ${BASE} AS runtime
  ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
  RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/*.whl \
    && rm -rf /wheels
  COPY --chown=10001:10001 app ./app
  USER 10001:10001
  EXPOSE 8000
  HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s \
   CMD python -c "import urllib.request as u;u.urlopen('http://0.0.0.0:8000/ready')"
  ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The builder stage keeps compilers out of the runtime, but only because the final COPY selects wheels rather than the whole
   filesystem.
 → The health check calls a local readiness route with a three-second timeout; it never spends tokens or depends on a provider.
 → USER and exec-form ENTRYPOINT are the two lines most often missing; without them the container runs as root and may
   ignore SIGTERM.

Production Containers
Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Copying the entire build context before installing dependencies, so every source edit invalidates the dependency cache.
2.     Using floating latest tags in production and discovering that a new base image changed glibc during a redeploy.
3.     Baking model weights into the image and multiplying registry size by every replica that scales out.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Scan every image in CI, fail on critical fixable CVEs, and publish an SBOM so responders can answer 'are we affected' in
      minutes.
    ◆ Tag images with the Git commit SHA and promote the digest between environments; never rebuild the same commit twice.
    ◆ Set CPU and memory requests from measured usage, because a pod without requests is the first to be evicted under
      pressure.

□      The final image contains no compilers, test fixtures, Git history, or local data.
□      The runtime base is pinned and the container runs as a non-root UID.
□      SIGTERM reaches the server directly and in-flight requests finish within the grace period.
□      Readiness, liveness, CPU, and memory are defined and measured under load.
□      Image size, scan findings, and cold-start time are recorded for each release.

1.     Why does a multi-stage build reduce attack surface even when the application code is identical?

2.     What happens to in-flight requests when ENTRYPOINT uses shell form and the orchestrator sends SIGTERM?

3.     Why should a container health check avoid calling a paid model endpoint?

4.     How would you prove that a read-only root filesystem does not break your application?

5.     What is the risk of tagging production images with latest instead of a commit SHA?

CODE
A pipeline that tests against real services, builds one image, gates on evaluation, and deploys by digest.
  name: release
  on:
   push: { branches: [main] }
  permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }
  concurrency: { group: release, cancel-in-progress: true }
  jobs:
   verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres: { image: postgres:16, env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test } }
      redis: { image: redis:7 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest -q
      - run: |
         docker buildx build --push --iidfile digest.txt \
          -t ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }} .
      - run: python scripts/evaluate.py --gate 0.85 --dataset eval/rag_v7.jsonl
      - run: python scripts/deploy.py --digest "$(cat digest.txt)" --canary 10

lessons.title: Environment Management
lessons.subtitle: Make configuration explicit, typed, and environment-specific so production cannot silently inherit a staging value.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 9 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: Most 'it works in staging' incidents are configuration incidents: a missing variable, a copied bucket name, a default timeout that only matters at production volume. Containers sharpen this because the same image runs everywhere, so behaviour is decided entirely by injected configuration. Treating that configuration as typed, validated, versioned input is cheaper than debugging a silent fallback at 02:00.
outcomes: Separate build-time constants from deploy-time configuration and secrets, and explain why the boundary matters.
Load configuration through one typed settings object that validates at startup and fails fast with a useful message.
Design promotion so staging and production differ only in values, never in code paths or hidden defaults.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Same artefact, different values Twelve-factor configuration lives in environment variables, not in the image, so one digest can run in every environment. Build-time values are limited to things that never vary: the Python version, compiled extensions, and static assets. Everything else, including database URLs, provider keys, bucket names, feature flags, and log levels, arrives at runtime. A .env file is a developer convenience, not a production mechanism; production injects values from the platform or a secret manager. One typed settings object Define settings once with pydantic-settings: field types, required fields, allowed ranges, and explicit aliases. Validate on import, print every invalid key without printing its value, and exit non-zero so a bad deploy fails immediately instead of serving errors. Avoid scattered os.environ lookups with defaults, because a default that is convenient locally becomes a silent production misconfiguration. Tests can construct Settings directly, which removes environment dependence from the suite. Secrets and drift Keep secrets in a managed store, inject them at runtime, and reference them by name rather than value. Rotate on a schedule and after any exposure; a secret in an image layer or CI log is compromised even if it was later deleted. Record the resolved configuration for each deploy, with secret values redacted, so you can answer which values were live during an incident. Alert on drift between the declared configuration and the running service.

key_terms.definition: The practice of storing deploy-varying configuration in environment variables so one build runs unchanged in every environment.
A difference between the declared configuration and the values actually running in an environment.

A service that stores, controls access to, and audits credentials, injecting them at runtime instead of baking them into artefacts. MENTAL MODEL Configuration is the difference between the same machine in two factories: identical equipment, different raw material, and a checklist that refuses to start with the wrong input.
Page 527 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: A media company runs one image in staging and production. During a cost review, an engineer copies staging's .env into the production task definition to fix a missing key. The copy includes STORAGE_BUCKET=acme-staging-media, so for six hours production writes new uploads into the staging bucket, where a lifecycle rule deletes them after 24 hours. The restore takes two days. The team replaces .env parsing with a Settings class, marks storage_bucket as required with an environment prefix, and adds a startup assertion that production bucket names begin with acme-prod-. Terraform now owns the task definition, secrets come from AWS Secrets Manager, and each deploy logs a redacted configuration fingerprint. The decision: no defaults for anything that names an external resource.
steps: Inventory every environment variable the service reads and mark each as build-time, deploy-time config, or secret.
Replace scattered lookups with one Settings class that declares types, required fields, and validation ranges.
Store secrets in a managed service and inject them by reference; remove .env from the production path.
Add a startup check that compares critical values against the environment name and refuses obvious crossovers.
Log a redacted configuration fingerprint per deploy and diff it against the previous release during incidents.

code.title: One typed settings object validates required values at startup and refuses a staging bucket in production.
code.code:
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import AnyUrl, Field, model_validator
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
  model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="APP_", extra="forbid")
  env: Literal["dev", "staging", "prod"]
  database_url: AnyUrl
  storage_bucket: str = Field(min_length=3)
  model_timeout_s: float = Field(gt=0, le=60)

   @model_validator(mode="after")
   def guard_prod(self):
     prod_bucket = self.storage_bucket.startswith("acme-prod-")
     if self.env == "prod" and not prod_bucket:
        raise ValueError("prod bucket must start with acme-prod-")
     return self

settings = Settings()
what_to_notice: extra='forbid' turns a typo such as APP_MODEL_TIMOUT into a startup error instead of a silently ignored setting.
The production bucket assertion catches the exact copy-paste failure in the example before the service accepts traffic.

Secrets are not fields here; keys come from platform injection, so this object never logs a credential. Three pages per lesson Page 528 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Giving every setting a convenient default, so a missing production value silently becomes localhost or a staging bucket.
Committing a real .env to fix a teammate's setup, then discovering it in the image layer two years later.
Treating a feature flag as code and requiring a full deploy to disable an expensive model path.
production_notes: Validate configuration at startup and exit non-zero; a container that starts with bad settings is harder to diagnose than one that crashes.
Own production configuration in infrastructure code with review, not in a console where changes leave no diff and no owner.
Rotate secrets on a schedule and after exposure, and keep a redacted configuration fingerprint for each deploy.

Secrets come from a managed store, never from the image, repository, or CI logs.

Each deploy records a redacted configuration fingerprint that can be compared later.

    env: Literal["dev", "staging", "prod"]
    database_url: AnyUrl
    storage_bucket: str = Field(min_length=3)
    model_timeout_s: float = Field(gt=0, le=60)

     @model_validator(mode="after")
     def guard_prod(self):
       prod_bucket = self.storage_bucket.startswith("acme-prod-")

Environment Management
Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Giving every setting a convenient default, so a missing production value silently becomes localhost or a staging bucket.
2.     Committing a real .env to fix a teammate's setup, then discovering it in the image layer two years later.
3.     Treating a feature flag as code and requiring a full deploy to disable an expensive model path.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Validate configuration at startup and exit non-zero; a container that starts with bad settings is harder to diagnose than one
      that crashes.
    ◆ Own production configuration in infrastructure code with review, not in a console where changes leave no diff and no
      owner.
    ◆ Rotate secrets on a schedule and after exposure, and keep a redacted configuration fingerprint for each deploy.
CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□      One image runs in every environment and differs only by injected configuration.
□      All settings are declared in one typed object with explicit required fields.
□      Secrets come from a managed store, never from the image, repository, or CI logs.
□      Startup validation fails fast and names the bad key without revealing its value.
□      Each deploy records a redacted configuration fingerprint that can be compared later.
SHORT QUESTIONS
1.     Which values belong at build time, and why do database URLs and bucket names not qualify?

2.     Why is a default value more dangerous in production than a required field that is missing?

3.     How does extra='forbid' change the failure mode of a misspelled environment variable?

4.     What would you compare to detect drift between declared and running configuration?

5.     Why is a .env file acceptable locally but unsuitable as a production injection mechanism?

6.     How would you investigate an incident where production wrote to the wrong bucket for six hours?

TASKS
□      Inventory your service's environment variables, classify each as build-time, config, or secret, and delete unused entries.
□      Implement a Settings class with validation and a startup test that asserts a non-zero exit on a missing required value.
□      Write a promotion checklist that lists every value differing between staging and production, with an owner for each.

  metadata: { name: support-api }

   template:
    spec:
     containerConcurrency: 20
     timeoutSeconds: 60

lessons.subtitle: Scale the queue and the concurrency limit, not the CPU graph, because model latency and provider quotas set your real
why_it_matters: A model call takes seconds and varies in cost, so an AI service rarely saturates CPU the way a CRUD API does. Scaling on CPU therefore reacts late, after users already wait. The real constraints are in-flight provider requests, tokens per minute, connection pools, and memory per stream. Scaling well means measuring those, limiting admission, and moving long work to queues that absorb bursts.
outcomes: Distinguish stateless API scaling from model-bound scaling and identify the actual bottleneck under load.
Apply admission control, queueing, and backpressure so overload degrades predictably instead of collapsing.
Choose autoscaling signals from observed concurrency and queue depth rather than CPU utilisation alone.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Find the constrained resource Load a single instance until latency breaks, recording concurrency, provider latency, tokens per second, CPU, and memory. A streaming endpoint often hits a connection or memory limit first; a batch extraction job hits the provider's tokens-per-minute quota; a retrieval-heavy path hits the database connection pool. The bottleneck determines the fix: more replicas, a queue, smaller payloads, or a cache. Adding replicas to a provider-quota problem increases 429s and cost without improving throughput. Admission control and backpressure A semaphore around provider calls bounds concurrent work per instance and keeps memory predictable. When the semaphore is full, wait with a deadline, return 429 with Retry-After, or push the job to a queue. Unbounded asyncio.gather looks efficient and then exhausts file descriptors and provider quota. Propagate deadlines so a request abandoned by the client cancels its model call; otherwise you pay for tokens nobody reads. Shed load early rather than degrade every request. Scale on the right signal Autoscaling on CPU is a lagging proxy for a system waiting on the network. Use concurrency, queue depth, or tokens per minute, exported as custom metrics, and set a target from the per-instance load test. Keep a minimum replica count for latency-sensitive traffic and a maximum that matches provider quota across all replicas. Scale in slowly, because a replica that exits mid-stream drops a response; finish in-flight work before termination.

key_terms.definition: A gate that limits how many requests enter a service or provider call at once, protecting memory and quotas.
A signal that tells callers to slow down, through a queue, a 429, or a deadline, before the system collapses.

The number of jobs waiting for a worker, a leading indicator of saturation when processing time is variable. MENTAL MODEL Scaling an AI service is managing a queue at a popular counter: add staff when the line grows, but also cap how many orders each cook can hold.

worked_example: A research assistant serves 12,000 queries a day with a p95 target of eight seconds. On a launch day traffic triples; CPU stays at 35% while p95 reaches 41 seconds and 9% of calls return 429 from the provider. The team had autoscaled on CPU at 70%, so no new replicas appeared. They add a per-instance semaphore of 16 concurrent model calls, export that gauge, and autoscale at 70% of the limit. Long reports move to a queue with a visible position, and the synchronous endpoint returns 429 with Retry-After when the wait exceeds five seconds. The next spike holds p95 at 7.4 seconds, provider 429s fall below 0.4%, and cost per query rises 6%.

CODE
A per-instance admission limit that rejects fast instead of letting a traffic spike exhaust memory and provider quota.
  import asyncio
  from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
  class Admission:
    def __init__(self, limit: int) -> None:
       self._slots = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)
       self.in_flight = 0
       self.rejected = 0
    @asynccontextmanager
    async def slot(self, wait_s: float = 5.0):
       try:
          await asyncio.wait_for(self._slots.acquire(), timeout=wait_s)
       except TimeoutError:
          self.rejected += 1
          raise OverflowError("queue_full") from None
       self.in_flight += 1
       try:
          yield
       finally:
          self.in_flight -= 1
          self._slots.release()

   consistent.

code.title: A serial availability calculation that turns an architecture diagram into a monthly downtime budget.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Hop:
  name: str
  availability: float
  fallback: float = 0.0

def path(hops: list[Hop]) -> tuple[float, float]:
  total = 1.0
  for hop in hops:
    total *= 1 - (1 - hop.availability) * (1 - hop.fallback)
  return total, (1 - total) * 30 * 24 * 60

stack = [Hop("api", 0.999), Hop("postgres", 0.9995), Hop("model", 0.999, 0.95)]
availability, downtime = path(stack)
print(f"{availability:.3%} available, {downtime:.0f} min of downtime/month")
what_to_notice: The model hop improves from 99.9% to 99.995% because a 95% fallback covers most failures; without it the product is 99.5%.
Downtime is computed for a 30-day month, so the number maps to an error budget rather than an abstract percentage.

The calculation assumes independent failures; a shared network or region outage fails several hops together and is worse. Three pages per lesson Page 537 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

The model is a variable, expensive dependency; the durable parts are contracts, data ownership, state, and failure paths. A design that names those boundaries can swap models without a rewrite. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Constraints before components Start with the user decision, the acceptable error, the p95 latency, the cost ceiling, and the data classification. Those constraints eliminate most architectures before a vendor enters the conversation. A contract review that must cite clauses needs retrieval and provenance; a classification task with 40 fixed labels may need no generation at all. Write the constraints as numbers, because fast and cheap cannot be tested or defended in a review. Three flows, one diagram Draw requests, data, and state separately. Requests show synchronous hops and timeouts; data shows ingestion, ownership, retention, and deletion; state shows where conversation, jobs, and approvals live. Overlay trust boundaries: browser to API, API to provider, worker to tenant data. Most design defects appear as a line crossing a boundary without authentication, or as state stored in a process that can restart. One diagram, reviewed by an operator, exposes more than a fifty-page document. Design the failure, then the feature For every dependency, state what happens when it is slow, wrong, or gone. Provider timeout: serve a cached answer, queue the job, or return 503 with a retry hint. Vector store outage: fall back to keyword search with a visible quality warning. Write these paths as part of the design, not as tickets after launch. Also assign a cost and latency budget per stage so a regression in retrieval cannot quietly consume the generation budget.

key_terms.definition: A point where data or control crosses between components with different privileges, requiring authentication, authorisation, and validation.
The acceptable rate and duration of a dependency failure before the system degrades, queues, or refuses work.

A short, versioned note recording a design choice, its context, alternatives, and consequences. MENTAL MODEL A system design is a flight plan: the aircraft matters, but fuel reserves, alternate airports, and diversion rules decide whether the trip ends safely.

worked_example: At a 60-person legal-tech firm, the contract-review assistant is three weeks from launch. The first design puts retrieval, model call, and citation rendering inside the HTTP request, with a 90-second provider timeout. In review, the platform lead redraws the flows: a 45-second edge timeout, no state store for review sessions, and one shared database role for all tenants. The team moves extraction to a queue, stores drafts with tenant_id and row-level security, and puts the provider call behind a circuit breaker. They keep synchronous only the six-second clause lookup. The decision: launch with asynchronous full review, synchronous clause search, and a written fallback to keyword results when embeddings are unavailable.

code.title: A per-stage design budget that fails the build when latency or cost crosses the agreed ceiling.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Stage:
  name: str
  p95_ms: int
  usd_per_call: float
STAGES = [
  Stage("auth", 8, 0.0),
  Stage("retrieve", 120, 0.0004),
  Stage("rerank", 90, 0.0008),
  Stage("generate", 2600, 0.0180),
  Stage("validate", 25, 0.0),
]
budget_ms, budget_usd = 4000, 0.025
total_ms = sum(s.p95_ms for s in STAGES)
total_usd = sum(s.usd_per_call for s in STAGES)
assert total_ms <= budget_ms, f"latency {total_ms}ms over {budget_ms}ms"
assert total_usd <= budget_usd, f"cost ${total_usd:.4f} over ${budget_usd}"
print(f"p95 {total_ms}ms, ${total_usd:.4f} per request")
what_to_notice: The budget sums p95 values, which is optimistic for independent stages; measure the end-to-end distribution under load.
Cost excludes retries, failed calls, and embedding refresh; a 5% retry rate adds roughly 5% to the model line.

The assertion fails the build rather than warning, because a design budget that nobody enforces is a comment. Three pages per lesson Page 541 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Storing conversation state in the API process, so a restart or a second replica loses the session.
Assuming a provider timeout equals a failed request, then charging and duplicating side effects on retry.
production_notes: Keep a one-page current-state diagram with owners, dependencies, data classifications, and the last review date; stale diagrams mislead more than none.
Put every model call behind a named client with timeout, retry, circuit breaker, and cost metrics, so the design boundary is also an operational boundary.
Review the design against a real incident: pick a provider outage and trace which requests fail, which queue, and who is paged.

What three flows belong on the design diagram, and what does each one expose?
How would the system behave if the vector store were unavailable for ten minutes?

What evidence would justify moving a synchronous step into a queue?

code.title: A capacity check that compares worker concurrency and token quota before a launch.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Capacity:
  rps: float
  seconds: float
  workers: int
  tokens_per_min: int
  avg_tokens: float

def utilisation(c: Capacity) -> tuple[float, float]:
  in_flight = c.rps * c.seconds
  token_rps = c.tokens_per_min / 60 / c.avg_tokens
  return in_flight / c.workers, token_rps / c.rps

plan = Capacity(40, 2.5, 20, 400_000, 1_200)
workers, quota = utilisation(plan)
print(f"workers {workers:.0%} used, quota {quota:.0%} used")
if max(workers, quota) > 0.7:
   raise SystemExit("resize before launch: keep both ratios at or below 0.7")
what_to_notice: The calculation uses average token length; a few long-context requests can consume the minute's quota and starve everyone else.
Little's law measures concurrency, not queue length; a pool at 100% utilisation has unbounded wait, not stable throughput.

The 0.7 threshold is a starting point for variable service times, not a law; measure your own queue growth under load. Three pages per lesson Page 544 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous AI
lessons.subtitle: Match the request pattern to the work: answer inside the user's patience window, or acknowledge with a durable job and
why_it_matters: A model call can take 300 milliseconds or three minutes, and the difference is architectural. Holding an HTTP connection open past the edge timeout produces 504s, duplicate work, and users who retry. Moving everything to a queue adds latency and state to simple questions. The design question is not which pattern is modern; it is how long the user will wait and what must survive a restart.
outcomes: Decide between synchronous, streaming, and queued execution using edge timeouts, work duration, and user expectations.
Design a job contract with 202 Accepted, a status resource, idempotency, and a terminal failure state.
Choose the notification path of polling, webhook, or stream to fit the client and the failure model.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Synchronous has a hard ceiling A synchronous request is bounded by the client, the load balancer, the gateway, and the provider timeout. A typical edge allows 30-60 seconds, so a chain of model calls, retries, and tool use must fit inside roughly half of that. Synchronous is right for a single fast completion, a short retrieval pass, or a streaming answer where the first token arrives quickly. It is wrong when work includes batch retrieval, multiple agents, or human approval. Async is a contract, not a queue Asynchronous work needs a submission endpoint that returns 202 Accepted with a job identifier and a Location header, a status resource with queued, running, succeeded, and failed states, and a result that survives worker restarts. Store the request payload, the owner, the idempotency key, and the attempt count. The client needs a defined way to collect the result: polling with backoff, a webhook with signature verification, or a server-sent event stream. Without that contract, a queue is just delayed failure. Hybrid: acknowledge fast, stream progress Many products need both: a fast acknowledgement and visible progress. Start the job, return the identifier immediately, then stream status or partial output over SSE or WebSocket while the worker writes durable checkpoints. If the connection drops, the client reconnects by job id and resumes from the last checkpoint. Keep the synchronous path for lightweight status reads, and never make the worker depend on the client staying connected. This pattern protects the user experience without pretending a long job is a short request.

key_terms.definition: A client-supplied identifier that lets the server return the same job or result when a request is retried.

A client request that waits briefly for a state change before returning, reducing empty status checks. MENTAL MODEL Synchronous is a phone call; asynchronous is a ticket with a reference number. Use the phone for a quick question and a ticket for work that outlives the conversation.

The prototype runs it inside one FastAPI request; the load balancer cuts the connection at 60 seconds, the client retries, and each retry starts another model job. Weekly spend triples and analysts see duplicate briefings. A worker writes progress and the final artefact to storage; GET /briefings/{id} returns state and a download URL. The UI polls every two to five seconds. Decision: synchronous validation and status reads, asynchronous generation, no webhook because the client is a browser.

  from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, Response
  from pydantic import BaseModel

  app, JOBS = FastAPI(), {}
  class Briefing(BaseModel):
    topic: str

  @app.post("/briefings", status_code=202)
  def submit(
     body: Briefing, response: Response, key: str = Header(alias="Idempotency-Key")
  ) -> dict:
     job = JOBS.setdefault(key, {"state": "queued", "topic": body.topic})
     response.headers["Location"] = f"/briefings/{key}"
     return job

  @app.get("/briefings/{key}")
  def status(key: str) -> dict:
    if key not in JOBS:
       raise HTTPException(404, "unknown job")
    return JOBS[key]

code.title: A leased claim with full-jitter retry, dead-letter routing, and an acknowledgement marker.
code.code:
import random
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

def claim() -> str | None:
  return r.brpoplpush("embed", "embed:working", timeout=5)

def settle(raw: str, status: int, attempt: int) -> str:
  if status in {429, 500, 502, 503, 504} and attempt < 5:
     r.rpush("embed", raw)
     r.lrem("embed:working", 1, raw)
     return f"retry in {random.uniform(0, 2 ** attempt):.1f}s"
  if status >= 400:
     r.rpush("embed:dlq", raw)
     r.lrem("embed:working", 1, raw)
     return "dead_letter"
  r.set(f"done:{raw}", 1, ex=604800)
  r.lrem("embed:working", 1, raw)
  return "ack"
what_to_notice: The claim moves the message to a working list, so a crashed worker leaves it there until a reaper returns it; the lease is not self-healing.
Full jitter reduces thundering herds but makes retry order non-deterministic; use a FIFO queue only where ordering is a product requirement.

lessons.subtitle: Cache the deterministic, expensive parts of the AI path, not the whole answer, and make every key depend on the model,
why_it_matters: AI calls are expensive, slow, and often repeated. Caching can cut cost by 30-60% on real support traffic, but a cache that ignores model version or tenant scope becomes a data-leak and correctness bug. The engineering decision is which layer to cache, how to key it, and how to invalidate it when prompts, documents, or permissions change. A high hit rate is only good if the hits are correct.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Cache the narrowest expensive object A final-answer cache has the highest hit value and the highest risk: it can leak another tenant's data or serve a policy that changed this morning. An embedding cache keyed by text hash is deterministic and safe to share across tenants. A retrieval cache keyed by query and index version saves vector search but still needs permission filtering. A prompt-prefix cache works only when the provider supports it and the prefix is byte-stable. Start narrow: embeddings, then retrieval, then whole answers for public content. Keys encode every dependency A cache key must include the model and version, prompt template version, normalised input, tenant or permission scope, and index or document version. Hash the full canonical payload rather than concatenating unchecked strings. If any dependency changes and the key does not, you serve a wrong answer that looks like a hit. Normalise before hashing: trim whitespace, lowercase where the domain allows it, and sort tool arguments. Never include raw personal data in the key or in cache logs. Invalidation, TTL, and stampedes TTL is a blunt but honest invalidation tool: 24 hours for public FAQs, five minutes for account balances, and zero for anything that must reflect a just-completed write. For document updates, bump an index version so old keys become unreachable and expire naturally. Protect the origin with single-flight: when a key misses, one worker computes while others wait or receive a stale value. Add jitter to expiry so a popular key does not expire for every request at once.

A surge of concurrent recomputation when a popular key expires or is invalidated. MENTAL MODEL A cache is a photocopy on the wall: fast to read, but useless and dangerous once the original changes and nobody replaces the copy.

CODE
A tenant-scoped response cache with a versioned key and a per-key lock against stampedes.
  import hashlib, json, redis

  r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

  def key(tenant: str, question: str, prompt_v: str) -> str:
    parts = [tenant, " ".join(question.lower().split()), prompt_v, "gpt-4.1-mini"]
    return "ans:" + hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(parts).encode()).hexdigest()

  def answer(tenant: str, question: str, compute) -> str:
    k = key(tenant, question, "v7")
    if (cached := r.get(k)) is not None:
       return cached
    with r.lock(k + ":lock", timeout=30, blocking_timeout=5):
       if (cached := r.get(k)) is not None:
          return cached
       value = compute(question)
       r.set(k, value, ex=600)
       return value

lessons.title: Vector Database Architecture
lessons.subtitle: Treat the vector index as a product with recall, latency, memory, and tenancy budgets, not as a library you install and
why_it_matters: A vector index is approximate. It trades recall for speed and memory, and those trade-offs change as the corpus grows. The failure modes are quiet: recall drops after a bulk insert, a filter is applied after the search so the top ten are empty, or a re-embedding leaves half the corpus on an old model. Vector architecture is the discipline of measuring recall against a labelled set and making index changes reversible.
outcomes: Choose HNSW, IVF, or flat search from corpus size, recall target, latency budget, and memory cost.
Design tenant-safe filtered search and keep embedding versions aligned with index builds.
Plan ingestion, compaction, snapshots, and rebuilds so index maintenance does not take retrieval offline.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Approximate means measurable HNSW builds a graph with a configurable M and ef_construction; higher values improve recall and cost memory and build time. IVF clusters vectors and searches a subset, so recall depends on nprobe. Flat search is exact but linear. Choose by corpus size and recall target, then measure recall@10 against exact search on 500-1,000 labelled queries. A 1536- dimension float32 vector costs about 6 KB before index overhead; 20 million chunks is 120 GB of raw vectors, so memory is usually the first constraint. Filter before or beside the search A metadata filter applied after top-k retrieval can return fewer results than requested, or none, when the filter is selective. Use a store that supports filtered search natively, and keep tenant_id in the filter on every query. Pre-filtering can hurt recall if the index is built across tenants; partitioning by tenant or by a coarse key keeps the search space small. Test a rare tenant with 200 chunks, not only the largest tenant, and assert the result count before sending context to the model. Ingestion and rebuilds are part of the design Embedding model versions change. Store the model name and dimension beside every vector, and never mix versions in one index. New documents should be written to a staging index, validated for count, dimension, and recall, then promoted by alias swap. Keep the raw text and metadata in object storage so a rebuild does not depend on the old index. Budget for compaction and snapshot time: a 20-million-vector snapshot can take minutes and consume IOPS that retrieval also needs.

key_terms.definition: A graph-based approximate index that links nearby vectors across layers to trade memory and build time for fast search.

A stable name that points to a physical index, allowing a rebuild to be promoted by switching the alias atomically. MENTAL MODEL A vector index is a library catalogue built for speed: it usually finds the right shelf, but you must test how often it misses and rebuild it when the books are reclassified.

lessons.title: Model Routing
lessons.subtitle: Send each request to the cheapest model that passes its own evaluation slice, and keep the routing decision logged and
why_it_matters: One model cannot be simultaneously the cheapest, fastest, and most capable choice for every request. Routing turns that trade-off into an explicit policy: classify the request, pick the model that clears the quality bar for that class, and record why. Teams that skip routing either overpay for trivial work or under-serve the hard 5% that carries most of the risk. The router is ordinary software, so it can be tested, versioned, and rolled back.
outcomes: Define route classes from task type, input size, risk tier, and tool needs rather than from model fashion.
Build a two-stage router with deterministic rules first and a measured classifier for ambiguous requests.
Evaluate every route as its own slice with a quality floor, a latency target, and a cost ceiling.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Routing is a costed classification Routing is a classification problem with a cost function, not a preference. Start by listing the request classes your evaluation already distinguishes: short extraction, long-context summarisation, tool-using agent steps, policy-sensitive answers. For each class, measure pass rate and p95 latency on at least 100 labelled cases for two or three candidate models. The router then encodes the cheapest model that clears the class floor, with the frontier model reserved for classes where the gap is real. Rules first, classifier second Most traffic does not need a model to route it. Deterministic rules cover input length, language, tenant plan, endpoint, attachment presence, and risk tier, and they are cheap, explainable, and easy to audit. Send only the ambiguous remainder to a small classifier or embedding nearest-neighbour lookup trained on labelled route decisions. Keep the rule table and classifier version in configuration, log the chosen route and reason on every request, and shadow new policies before they take traffic. Model Routing
Send each request to the cheapest model that passes its own evaluation slice, and keep the routing decision logged and

AI System Design · Lesson 8 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
One model cannot be simultaneously the cheapest, fastest, and most capable choice for every request. Routing turns that
trade-off into an explicit policy: classify the request, pick the model that clears the quality bar for that class, and record
why. Teams that skip routing either overpay for trivial work or under-serve the hard 5% that carries most of the risk. The
router is ordinary software, so it can be tested, versioned, and rolled back.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Define route classes from task type, input size, risk tier, and tool needs rather than from model fashion.
 • Build a two-stage router with deterministic rules first and a measured classifier for ambiguous requests.
 • Evaluate every route as its own slice with a quality floor, a latency target, and a cost ceiling.
CORE CONCEPTS
Routing is a costed classification
Routing is a classification problem with a cost function, not a preference. Start by listing the request classes your
evaluation already distinguishes: short extraction, long-context summarisation, tool-using agent steps, policy-sensitive
answers. For each class, measure pass rate and p95 latency on at least 100 labelled cases for two or three candidate
models. The router then encodes the cheapest model that clears the class floor, with the frontier model reserved for
classes where the gap is real.
Rules first, classifier second
Most traffic does not need a model to route it. Deterministic rules cover input length, language, tenant plan, endpoint,
attachment presence, and risk tier, and they are cheap, explainable, and easy to audit. Send only the ambiguous
remainder to a small classifier or embedding nearest-neighbour lookup trained on labelled route decisions. Keep the rule
table and classifier version in configuration, log the chosen route and reason on every request, and shadow new policies
before they take traffic.
Every route is a separate product
Split the evaluation set by route and score each slice independently; an aggregate 94% hides a route that fails 30% of
billing disputes. Give each route its own quality floor, p95 target, and monthly cost ceiling, then alert when a slice drifts.
Escalate to a stronger model when validation fails, confidence is low, or the request matches a risky intent. Canary a
changed policy on 5% of traffic for a day, compare cost and quality, and roll back by flipping the table version.

  specialist before harm is done.

CODE
A versioned routing table with an explicit risk check, returning the reason alongside the model.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  TIERS = {"small": "gpt-4.1-mini", "large": "gpt-4.1"}

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Request:
    tokens: int
    risk: str    # "low" or "high"
    needs_tools: bool

  def route(r: Request) -> tuple[str, str]:
    if r.risk == "high" or r.tokens > 12_000:
       return TIERS["large"], "risk_or_length"
    if r.needs_tools:
       return TIERS["large"], "tool_use"
    return TIERS["small"], "default_low_risk"

  for req in (Request(800, "low", False), Request(900, "high", False)):
    print(route(req))

why_it_matters: Any serious platform ends up with several models: a frontier reasoner, a cheap bulk extractor, an embedding model, a guard classifier, and a fallback from a second provider. Each has different token limits, JSON behaviour, tool semantics, pricing, and outage patterns. Without a common contract, every new model means edits across the codebase and a fresh round of surprises. Portfolio thinking makes model choice a configuration decision while keeping evaluation, cost, and failure handling in one place.
outcomes: Assign each model in the system a role, an interface, and an owner instead of duplicating provider SDK calls.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A portfolio with roles Write down every model role before choosing vendors: reasoning and planning, high-volume extraction, embeddings, moderation or policy classification, and emergency fallback. Give each role an interface describing inputs, output schema, maximum tokens, and timeout. Pin an exact snapshot per environment so an upstream upgrade cannot change behaviour during a release. The portfolio is healthy when no single provider outage removes a capability, and when every role has a measured quality floor and a named cost owner. Adapters absorb the differences Providers disagree about message roles, tool-call formatting, stop reasons, JSON modes, and how they report token usage. Put those differences behind a thin adapter that converts to your internal request and response types, validates the output schema, and records usage. Normalise finish reasons into completed, length, tool_call, and refused so retry logic stays provider-neutral. Keep the adapter small and tested with recorded fixtures, because provider schema drift appears as a parsing bug at 2am, not as a release note. Cascades and cross-checks A cascade runs the cheap model first and escalates when validation fails or confidence is below a threshold, so most traffic stays cheap. A cross-check runs a second model on high-risk output and compares structured fields; disagreement routes to a human. Both add cost, so measure the escalation rate and the false-accept rate before enabling them broadly. A second provider is also a failover path: exercise it on a schedule, because an untested fallback is a design document rather than a capability.

A confidence cascade that escalates to the larger model and refuses to auto-accept disagreement on critical fields.
  def agree(a: dict, b: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...]) -> float:
    hits = sum(a[f] == b[f] for f in fields)
    return hits / len(fields)

  def cascade(text, schema, small, large, critical=()):
    first = small.extract(text, schema)
    if first.ok and first.confidence >= 0.82 and not critical:
       return first.value, small.name
    second = large.extract(text, schema)
    if not second.ok:
       raise ValueError(f"both models failed for {schema.__name__}")
    if critical and agree(first.value, second.value, critical) < 0.9:
       raise NeedsHumanReview(text_id=text.id)
    return second.value, large.name

  value, model = cascade(form_text, Claim, SMALL, LARGE)
  print(model, value["claim_id"])
