lessons.title: Reliability
lessons.subtitle: Reliability is a measured promise: define the service level, give every dependency a share of the budget, and prove it under
why_it_matters: Users do not care that the model is probabilistic; they care that the answer arrives correctly and on time. Reliability engineering turns that expectation into numbers: a success definition, a latency target, an error budget, and the dependency budgets that add up to it. Without those numbers, every incident debate becomes an argument about opinion, retries grow without limit, and nobody can say whether the last release made the service better or merely luckier.
outcomes: Write user-centred SLIs and a 99.5% availability target with an error budget and burn-rate alerts.
Decompose the latency budget across edge, retrieval, model, and storage, with deadlines propagated end to end.
Run load tests, game days, and canaries that prove fallbacks work before users discover them.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The promise comes first An SLI is a ratio you can compute from telemetry, such as successful answers under eight seconds divided by all requests. Define it at the user boundary, not at the model call, so a fast 500 still counts as a failure. A 99.5% monthly target allows about 3.6 hours of full outage, and the error budget is the currency for releases and experiments. Decompose the latency target across edge, auth, retrieval, generation, and validation; if generation gets 3.5 seconds, a 4-second p95 is impossible. Deadlines and retries share one budget Every request carries a deadline that is passed to each dependency, and each layer subtracts its own slice rather than starting a fresh timeout. Retries consume the same budget: two attempts at a 2-second timeout cannot fit inside three seconds. Cap attempts at two or three, retry only 429, 5xx, timeouts, and connection errors, with jittered exponential backoff. Hedge only when the tail matters and you can pay for duplicate tokens; otherwise a hedge doubles spend to protect a few requests. Prove it with deliberate failure Load tests at 1.5 times peak reveal queue growth and quota exhaustion before customers do. Game days inject provider 429s, 30-second latency, a dead replica, and a corrupt cache entry, then check that fallbacks and alerts fire. Canary releases move 5% of traffic for thirty minutes and roll back automatically on error rate, p95 latency, or evaluation score. Record each exercise with detection time, mitigation time, and a follow-up owner; an untested rollback is a hope, not a control.

key_terms.definition: A measured ratio of good events to valid events, such as successful answers under eight seconds.
The amount of unreliability a target permits in a period, spent on releases, experiments, and incidents.

How fast the error budget is consumed relative to the period, used to trigger alerts early. MENTAL MODEL Reliability is a service-level contract with a fuel gauge: the error budget shows how much risk you can spend this month before the promise breaks.

worked_example: Support platform Relay serves 6 million answers a month with a 99.5% target: at most 30,000 failed requests. Its p95 latency target is four seconds, split into 150 ms edge, 300 ms retrieval, 3,200 ms generation, and 150 ms validation. In February a provider slowdown pushes generation p95 to 9.4 seconds, and the retry loop triples traffic, exhausting the monthly budget in nine days. The team removes the second retry, propagates a 4-second deadline, adds a circuit breaker, and reruns the game day. Detection falls from 22 minutes to 4, and the service degrades to cached answers instead of timing out. The decision is recorded: no release ships while the seven-day burn rate exceeds 2.

Reliability
Reliability is a measured promise: define the service level, give every dependency a share of the budget, and prove it under
injected failure.
AI System Design · Lesson 10 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Users do not care that the model is probabilistic; they care that the answer arrives correctly and on time. Reliability
engineering turns that expectation into numbers: a success definition, a latency target, an error budget, and the
dependency budgets that add up to it. Without those numbers, every incident debate becomes an argument about
opinion, retries grow without limit, and nobody can say whether the last release made the service better or merely
luckier.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write user-centred SLIs and a 99.5% availability target with an error budget and burn-rate alerts.
 • Decompose the latency budget across edge, retrieval, model, and storage, with deadlines propagated end to end.
 • Run load tests, game days, and canaries that prove fallbacks work before users discover them.
CORE CONCEPTS
The promise comes first
An SLI is a ratio you can compute from telemetry, such as successful answers under eight seconds divided by all requests.
Define it at the user boundary, not at the model call, so a fast 500 still counts as a failure. A 99.5% monthly target allows
about 3.6 hours of full outage, and the error budget is the currency for releases and experiments. Decompose the latency
target across edge, auth, retrieval, generation, and validation; if generation gets 3.5 seconds, a 4-second p95 is
impossible.
Deadlines and retries share one budget
Every request carries a deadline that is passed to each dependency, and each layer subtracts its own slice rather than
starting a fresh timeout. Retries consume the same budget: two attempts at a 2-second timeout cannot fit inside three
seconds. Cap attempts at two or three, retry only 429, 5xx, timeouts, and connection errors, with jittered exponential
backoff. Hedge only when the tail matters and you can pay for duplicate tokens; otherwise a hedge doubles spend to
protect a few requests.
Prove it with deliberate failure
Load tests at 1.5 times peak reveal queue growth and quota exhaustion before customers do. Game days inject provider
429s, 30-second latency, a dead replica, and a corrupt cache entry, then check that fallbacks and alerts fire. Canary
releases move 5% of traffic for thirty minutes and roll back automatically on error rate, p95 latency, or evaluation score.
Record each exercise with detection time, mitigation time, and a follow-up owner; an untested rollback is a hope, not a
control.
KEY TERMS
 SLI                              A measured ratio of good events to valid events, such as successful answers under eight seconds.
 Error budget                     The amount of unreliability a target permits in a period, spent on releases, experiments, and incidents.
 Burn rate                        How fast the error budget is consumed relative to the period, used to trigger alerts early.

  MENTAL MODEL Reliability is a service-level contract with a fuel gauge: the error budget shows how much risk you can spend this
  month before the promise breaks.

Reliability
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
Support platform Relay serves 6 million answers a month with a 99.5% target: at most 30,000 failed requests. Its p95
latency target is four seconds, split into 150 ms edge, 300 ms retrieval, 3,200 ms generation, and 150 ms validation. In
February a provider slowdown pushes generation p95 to 9.4 seconds, and the retry loop triples traffic, exhausting the
monthly budget in nine days. The team removes the second retry, propagates a 4-second deadline, adds a circuit breaker,
and reruns the game day. Detection falls from 22 minutes to 4, and the service degrades to cached answers instead of
timing out. The decision is recorded: no release ships while the seven-day burn rate exceeds 2.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define the user-facing success event and compute the SLI from traces, not from infrastructure metrics.
2.    Set an availability target and split the p95 latency budget across edge, retrieval, model, and validation.
3.    Propagate one deadline through every call and cap retries so attempts cannot exceed it.
4.    Load test at 1.5 times peak and run a game day that injects 429s, latency, and a dead dependency.
5.    Canary at 5% with automatic rollback on errors, p95, and evaluation score; record the outcome.
CODE
One absolute deadline shared by every attempt, with jittered backoff that cannot sleep past the budget.
  import asyncio
  import random

  async def call_with_budget(fn, budget_s: float, attempts: int = 3):
    end = asyncio.get_running_loop().time() + budget_s
    for attempt in range(attempts):
      left = end - asyncio.get_running_loop().time()
      if left <= 0:
         raise TimeoutError(f"budget of {budget_s}s exhausted")
      try:
         return await asyncio.wait_for(fn(), timeout=left)
      except (asyncio.TimeoutError, ConnectionError):
         if attempt == attempts - 1:
            raise
         backoff = 0.25 * 2**attempt + random.random() * 0.1
         remaining = max(0.0, end - asyncio.get_running_loop().time())
         await asyncio.sleep(min(backoff, remaining))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The deadline is absolute, so every retry and backoff is subtracted from the same budget instead of resetting the clock.
 → Only transient exceptions are caught; validation and authentication failures fail fast rather than burning the budget.
 → The backoff wait is capped by the remaining time, so the function cannot sleep past its own deadline.

lessons.title: Fault Tolerance
lessons.subtitle: Assume every dependency will fail: isolate the blast radius, break failing circuits, and recover without duplicating side
why_it_matters: Retries alone turn a slow dependency into a queue of doomed requests. Fault tolerance is the set of mechanisms that keep a partial failure partial: separate pools so one tenant cannot exhaust capacity, breakers that stop calling a failing provider, fallbacks that return something honest, and idempotent writes so recovery does not bill a customer twice. These are ordinary distributed-systems patterns; the AI twist is that a degraded answer may still be useful if it is labelled as degraded.
outcomes: Isolate model, retrieval, and database calls with bulkheads and concurrency limits per dependency and tenant.
Implement circuit breakers with explicit thresholds, half-open probes, and user-visible degraded modes.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Isolate the blast radius Give each dependency its own connection pool, semaphore, and worker pool, and consider a per-tenant concurrency cap on expensive routes. A bulkhead means a provider returning 429s saturates only its own pool while retrieval and cached answers continue. Set queue wait limits, not just execution timeouts, so rejected work fails fast instead of ageing for a minute. Measure saturation per pool; a pool above 80% for five minutes is a capacity signal, not a reason to raise the timeout. Break the circuit, choose the mode A breaker moves from closed to open after a threshold, for example 50% errors across at least 20 requests in 20 seconds, then rejects calls immediately. After a cool-off it enters half-open and admits a few probes; success closes it, failure reopens it for longer. While open, the system must choose a degraded mode: cached answer with a timestamp, a smaller model, a queued job, or a clear apology. Name that mode in the response and the trace so support can explain what the user received. Recover without duplicating effects Failover and retries repeat work, so any write needs an idempotency key derived from the request, stored with the result and reused on retry. Prefer upserts and unique constraints over read-then-write sequences. On shutdown, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight messages inside the visibility timeout, and return the rest to the queue. Send permanently failing messages to a dead-letter queue with payload and error, and alert on depth rather than waiting for a customer to report a missing document.

key_terms.definition: A separate pool or concurrency limit per dependency so one failing resource cannot exhaust shared capacity.
A stateful guard that stops calls to a failing dependency and probes recovery with limited requests.

A defined, labelled response served when a dependency is unavailable, such as a cached answer. MENTAL MODEL Fault tolerance is a ship's watertight compartments: a breach floods one section, the crew seals it, and the vessel keeps moving at reduced speed.

worked_example: A travel assistant handles 18,000 itinerary requests an hour across three providers. During a regional provider outage, every request retried twice, worker pools filled with waiting calls, and the whole service returned 504s for eleven minutes even though retrieval and cache were healthy. The redesign gives each provider its own pool of 40 connections, opens a breaker after 50% errors across 20 requests, and serves a cached itinerary with a visible timestamp while open. Booking writes now carry an idempotency key stored in Postgres, and shutdown drains for 25 seconds before requeueing. The next provider incident produced 3.1% degraded responses and zero duplicate bookings, with p95 at 1.8 seconds.

CODE
A per-dependency circuit breaker with a failure threshold, cool-off, and a limited half-open probe.
  import time

  class Breaker:
    def __init__(self, threshold: int = 5, reset_after: float = 20.0) -> None:
       self.threshold, self.reset_after = threshold, reset_after
       self.failures, self.opened_at = 0, 0.0

     def allow(self) -> bool:
       if self.failures < self.threshold:
          return True
       if time.monotonic() - self.opened_at >= self.reset_after:
          self.failures = self.threshold - 1 # half-open probe
          return True
       return False

     def record(self, ok: bool) -> None:
       self.failures = 0 if ok else self.failures + 1
       if self.failures >= self.threshold:
          self.opened_at = time.monotonic()
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The breaker counts failures but not slow successes; pair it with a latency rule so a 30-second provider also trips it.
 → The half-open probe lowers the count by one rather than resetting it, so a still-broken provider reopens quickly.
 → The breaker is per provider and per operation, not global, so a failing image endpoint does not block text generation.

lessons.title: Cost vs Performance
lessons.subtitle: Optimise cost per successful task, not cost per token, and spend the latency budget where users actually notice the
why_it_matters: Model prices vary by more than an order of magnitude, and the expensive choice is not always the better product. A support answer that costs four times more but improves resolution by one point may still lose money. Cost engineering means measuring the full unit cost of a successful task, understanding which latency users feel, and buying quality only on routes where it changes the outcome. That discipline keeps a growing product from becoming a subsidy.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Cost per successful task Price per million tokens is an input, not a result. Add input and output tokens per call, retry rate, cache hit rate, retrieval and embedding work, evaluation, observability, and human review. Divide by the task success rate to get cost per successful task, then compare candidates on that number. A cheap model that fails 12% of the time and triggers a second call plus a human review can cost more than the frontier model it replaced. Track the figure weekly by route and tenant. Latency is three numbers Users experience time to first token, total completion time, and the tail. Streaming improves perceived speed without reducing total work; shortening context or retrieval improves all three. Prompt caching cuts prefill cost and time-to-first- token when the prefix is stable. For interactive answers, optimise p95 total latency under the four-second budget; for batch enrichment, optimise cost and ignore the tail. Never quote an average that hides a two-second p50 behind a twelve-second p99. Buy quality where it changes outcomes Rank routes by business value and by how much model quality moves the metric. Regulatory answers and billing disputes justify the frontier model; FAQ reformatting and tag extraction rarely do. Set a per-tenant budget, alert at 80%, and degrade non-critical routes to smaller models before failing requests. Re-run the route's evaluation after every downgrade, and keep the previous model configuration one flag away so a regression becomes a rollback rather than a rewrite.

key_terms.definition: Total spend divided by tasks meeting the quality bar, including retries, retrieval, and human review.
The delay before the first streamed output appears, which dominates perceived responsiveness in chat.

The configurations where no cheaper option matches the quality and no better option lowers cost. MENTAL MODEL Think of a delivery fleet: bicycles for nearby parcels, vans for bulk, and couriers only when the promise genuinely requires speed.

Analysis shows 68% of traffic is FAQ and order-status work that passes on a small model, 9% is billing disputes where the frontier model wins by 14 points, and 23% is RAG summarisation with a 2,400-token prompt that repeats the same policy prefix. The team moves FAQ traffic to the small model, adds prompt caching for the stable prefix, trims retrieved chunks from eight to five, and keeps the frontier model for disputes. code.title: Ranking two plans by cost per accepted answer, where retries, cache hits, and the pass rate all affect the result.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Plan:
  name: str
  in_price: float # USD per million input tokens
  out_price: float # USD per million output tokens
  quality: float    # pass rate on the route evaluation
  retry_rate: float = 0.06
  cache_hit: float = 0.20

def cost_per_accepted(p: Plan, in_tok: int = 1800, out_tok: int = 220) -> float:
  call = (in_tok * p.in_price + out_tok * p.out_price) / 1_000_000
  per_request = call * (1 + p.retry_rate) * (1 - p.cache_hit)
  return per_request / p.quality

PLANS = [Plan("small", 0.40, 1.60, 0.918), Plan("frontier", 2.00, 8.00, 0.941)]
for plan in PLANS:
  print(plan.name, f"${cost_per_accepted(plan):.5f} per accepted answer")
what_to_notice: The formula divides by quality, so a cheaper model with a lower pass rate can lose on cost per accepted answer.
Retry and cache rates are measured inputs, not assumptions; both change materially after a routing or prompt change.

Cost vs Performance
Optimise cost per successful task, not cost per token, and spend the latency budget where users actually notice the
difference.
AI System Design · Lesson 12 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Model prices vary by more than an order of magnitude, and the expensive choice is not always the better product. A
support answer that costs four times more but improves resolution by one point may still lose money. Cost engineering
means measuring the full unit cost of a successful task, understanding which latency users feel, and buying quality only on
routes where it changes the outcome. That discipline keeps a growing product from becoming a subsidy.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Calculate cost per successful request including retries, retrieval, embeddings, and human review.
 • Separate time-to-first-token, total latency, and tail latency, then choose the right lever for each.
 • Build a cost-quality frontier per route and defend each downgrade with evaluation evidence.
CORE CONCEPTS
Cost per successful task
Price per million tokens is an input, not a result. Add input and output tokens per call, retry rate, cache hit rate, retrieval
and embedding work, evaluation, observability, and human review. Divide by the task success rate to get cost per
successful task, then compare candidates on that number. A cheap model that fails 12% of the time and triggers a second
call plus a human review can cost more than the frontier model it replaced. Track the figure weekly by route and tenant.
Latency is three numbers
Users experience time to first token, total completion time, and the tail. Streaming improves perceived speed without
reducing total work; shortening context or retrieval improves all three. Prompt caching cuts prefill cost and time-to-first-
token when the prefix is stable. For interactive answers, optimise p95 total latency under the four-second budget; for
batch enrichment, optimise cost and ignore the tail. Never quote an average that hides a two-second p50 behind a
twelve-second p99.
Buy quality where it changes outcomes
Rank routes by business value and by how much model quality moves the metric. Regulatory answers and billing disputes
justify the frontier model; FAQ reformatting and tag extraction rarely do. Set a per-tenant budget, alert at 80%, and
degrade non-critical routes to smaller models before failing requests. Re-run the route's evaluation after every
downgrade, and keep the previous model configuration one flag away so a regression becomes a rollback rather than a
rewrite.
KEY TERMS
 Cost per successful task         Total spend divided by tasks meeting the quality bar, including retries, retrieval, and human review.
 Time to first token              The delay before the first streamed output appears, which dominates perceived responsiveness in chat.
 Cost-quality frontier            The configurations where no cheaper option matches the quality and no better option lowers cost.

  MENTAL MODEL Think of a delivery fleet: bicycles for nearby parcels, vans for bulk, and couriers only when the promise genuinely
  requires speed.

Cost vs Performance
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A support platform spends USD 61,000 a month on 2.1 million answers, up from 24,000 two quarters earlier. Analysis
shows 68% of traffic is FAQ and order-status work that passes on a small model, 9% is billing disputes where the frontier
model wins by 14 points, and 23% is RAG summarisation with a 2,400-token prompt that repeats the same policy prefix.
The team moves FAQ traffic to the small model, adds prompt caching for the stable prefix, trims retrieved chunks from
eight to five, and keeps the frontier model for disputes. Spend falls to USD 27,400, p95 latency drops from 6.2 to 4.1
seconds, and dispute accuracy is unchanged. The saving funds a second evaluation run per release.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Instrument tokens, retries, cache hits, and human escalations per route before changing any model.
2.    Compute cost per successful task for each route and rank the gaps by monthly spend.
3.    Measure time-to-first-token, p50, and p95 separately, then attribute cost and delay to the largest segment.
4.    Test cheaper configurations on each route's evaluation set and record quality deltas with confidence.
5.    Roll out behind a flag with a per-tenant budget alert and a one-step rollback path.
CODE
Ranking two plans by cost per accepted answer, where retries, cache hits, and the pass rate all affect the result.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Plan:
    name: str
    in_price: float # USD per million input tokens
    out_price: float # USD per million output tokens
    quality: float    # pass rate on the route evaluation
    retry_rate: float = 0.06
    cache_hit: float = 0.20

  def cost_per_accepted(p: Plan, in_tok: int = 1800, out_tok: int = 220) -> float:
    call = (in_tok * p.in_price + out_tok * p.out_price) / 1_000_000
    per_request = call * (1 + p.retry_rate) * (1 - p.cache_hit)
    return per_request / p.quality

  PLANS = [Plan("small", 0.40, 1.60, 0.918), Plan("frontier", 2.00, 8.00, 0.941)]
  for plan in PLANS:
    print(plan.name, f"${cost_per_accepted(plan):.5f} per accepted answer")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The formula divides by quality, so a cheaper model with a lower pass rate can lose on cost per accepted answer.
 → Retry and cache rates are measured inputs, not assumptions; both change materially after a routing or prompt change.
 → The comparison excludes retrieval and review cost, so it ranks model choice but does not replace a full unit-cost model.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Constraints before components Begin with the decisions the platform supports and the cost of being wrong, then quantify volume, concurrency, latency, quality floor, budget, data residency, and retention. Name the non-goals explicitly, because scope creep usually arrives as a reasonable feature request. A claims assistant that must cite policy and survive audit has a different architecture from a marketing copy generator, even if both call the same model. One page of constraints eliminates most component debates before they start. Five planes and their contracts Draw the request plane (edge, auth, rate limits), the orchestration plane (workflow, agents, prompt versions), the model gateway (routing, fallbacks, quotas), the data plane (Postgres, object store, vector index, ingestion), and the operations plane (traces, evaluation, alerts, cost). For each boundary, name the request and response contract, the system of record, and the owner. Move ingestion and evaluation outside the synchronous path, and make every asynchronous handoff idempotent. A box with no owner or metric is a diagram, not a design. Design failure, money, and sequence For each plane write the degraded behaviour, the detection signal, and the recovery action. Budget latency and cost per component so the totals fit the brief, then define the unit metric, such as cost per resolved claim. Sequence delivery in phases that each produce a reviewable artefact: ingestion and evaluation first, then retrieval, generation, agents and MCP, then hardening. Each phase has an exit gate with numbers. Record decisions and rejected alternatives, because the next engineer inherits the reasoning.

code.title: A component budget table that turns the architecture's latency and cost targets into a startup assertion.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Budget:
  component: str
  p95_ms: int
  usd_per_1k: float

PLAN = [Budget("auth + edge", 40, 0.00), Budget("retrieval", 220, 0.31),
   Budget("gateway", 60, 0.02), Budget("generation", 2_100, 41.50),
   Budget("validation", 80, 0.07)]

def check(plan, latency_ms: int = 3_000, spend_usd: float = 90.0) -> tuple[int, float]:
  p95 = sum(b.p95_ms for b in plan)
  spend = sum(b.usd_per_1k for b in plan)
  assert p95 <= latency_ms and spend <= spend_usd, (p95, spend)
  return p95, spend

print(check(PLAN))

lessons.title: Phase 1 — Requirements
lessons.subtitle: Turn a platform idea into testable requirements with named actors, numeric budgets, non-goals, and a test for every
why_it_matters: Most failed AI projects did not fail at the model; they failed because nobody agreed what correct meant. A requirement such as "helpful answers" cannot be tested, budgeted, or refused. Phase 1 converts a stakeholder wish list into a small set of observable claims, each with a threshold, a test, and an owner. That contract protects the team from scope creep and gives every later phase a definition of done.
outcomes: Write requirements as actor, trigger, observable outcome, and threshold, so each one can pass or fail in a test.
Set quality, latency, cost, and safety budgets from the decision the platform supports, not from vendor claims.
Build a traceability matrix that links every requirement to an evaluation case, a dashboard metric, and an owner.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Requirements as testable claims A usable requirement names the actor, the trigger, the observable outcome, and the threshold. "Claims handlers can find the current policy clause in under two minutes with a citation" is testable; "fast, accurate answers" is not. Write each requirement as one sentence plus acceptance criteria a test can evaluate. If you cannot imagine the failing output, the requirement is still a preference. Non-goals and hard constraints Non-goals are requirements with the opposite sign: no autonomous payments, no voice input, no cross-tenant search in v1. Hard constraints come from outside the product: data residency, retention, accessibility, procurement rules, and the classification of the documents being indexed. Naming them early removes architectures that cannot pass a security review, however well they demo. Revisit non-goals at each phase gate rather than silently expanding scope. Traceability from clause to test A traceability matrix maps each requirement to an evaluation case, a metric, an owner, and the phase that delivers it. Orphans are visible in both directions: a requirement without a test will not be checked, and a test without a requirement measures something nobody asked for. Nine requirements with nine tests beat sixty requirements with a demo. Keep the matrix in the repository and make it part of the phase gate.

key_terms.definition: An observable condition, with a threshold, that a test can evaluate to decide whether a requirement is met.
A capability deliberately excluded from the current release, recorded so later scope requests start from an explicit decision.

A table linking each requirement to its test, metric, owner, and delivery phase so gaps are visible. MENTAL MODEL A requirements document is a contract, not a wish list: every clause needs an observable test, a number, and a person who signs it.

worked_example: Halden Facilities runs 1,900 maintenance jobs a week and wants an operations assistant. A two-week discovery with dispatchers, engineers, and compliance produces 63 wishes. Turn a platform idea into testable requirements with named actors, numeric budgets, non-goals, and a test for every

Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 1 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most failed AI projects did not fail at the model; they failed because nobody agreed what correct meant. A requirement
such as "helpful answers" cannot be tested, budgeted, or refused. Phase 1 converts a stakeholder wish list into a small set
of observable claims, each with a threshold, a test, and an owner. That contract protects the team from scope creep and
gives every later phase a definition of done.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write requirements as actor, trigger, observable outcome, and threshold, so each one can pass or fail in a test.
 • Set quality, latency, cost, and safety budgets from the decision the platform supports, not from vendor claims.
 • Build a traceability matrix that links every requirement to an evaluation case, a dashboard metric, and an owner.
CORE CONCEPTS
Requirements as testable claims
A usable requirement names the actor, the trigger, the observable outcome, and the threshold. "Claims handlers can find
the current policy clause in under two minutes with a citation" is testable; "fast, accurate answers" is not. Write each
requirement as one sentence plus acceptance criteria a test can evaluate. If you cannot imagine the failing output, the
requirement is still a preference.
Non-goals and hard constraints
Non-goals are requirements with the opposite sign: no autonomous payments, no voice input, no cross-tenant search in
v1. Hard constraints come from outside the product: data residency, retention, accessibility, procurement rules, and the
classification of the documents being indexed. Naming them early removes architectures that cannot pass a security
review, however well they demo. Revisit non-goals at each phase gate rather than silently expanding scope.
Traceability from clause to test
A traceability matrix maps each requirement to an evaluation case, a metric, an owner, and the phase that delivers it.
Orphans are visible in both directions: a requirement without a test will not be checked, and a test without a requirement
measures something nobody asked for. Nine requirements with nine tests beat sixty requirements with a demo. Keep the
matrix in the repository and make it part of the phase gate.
KEY TERMS
 Acceptance criterion              An observable condition, with a threshold, that a test can evaluate to decide whether a requirement is met.
 Non-goal                          A capability deliberately excluded from the current release, recorded so later scope requests start from an
                                   explicit decision.
 Traceability matrix               A table linking each requirement to its test, metric, owner, and delivery phase so gaps are visible.

  MENTAL MODEL A requirements document is a contract, not a wish list: every clause needs an observable test, a number, and a person
  who signs it.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Boundaries outlive models Put the model behind a gateway interface, retrieval behind a retriever interface, and tools behind a registry with schemas. The API layer calls services, services call interfaces, and only adapters know provider names. This is not abstraction for its own sake: it allows a model swap, a second vector store, or a staged migration without editing every route. Enforce the rule with an import test in CI, because diagrams drift. Three paths, three budgets Interactive answers are synchronous and must fit a 6-second p95, so retrieval and generation get 4.5 seconds with 1.5 seconds of headroom. Document ingestion is queued, idempotent, and measured in documents per minute. Streaming improves perceived latency but does not relax the total budget, and validation must still run before the answer is persisted. Assign every path a timeout, a retry policy, and a terminal state. Design the degraded mode For each dependency, write what users see when it is slow, wrong, or absent. Provider timeout: return a cached answer with its timestamp or 503 with Retry-After. Vector store outage: fall back to keyword search and label the result as reduced quality. Queue backlog: accept the job, show its position, and alert at fifteen minutes. Degraded modes are product decisions, so they belong in the ADR, not in a runbook written later.

CODE
A dependency test that fails the build when a route imports a provider or retrieval adapter directly.
  import ast
  from pathlib import Path

  FORBIDDEN = ("app.providers", "app.retrieval")

  def check(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    tree = ast.parse(path.read_text())
    hits = []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
       if isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom) and node.module:
          if node.module.startswith(FORBIDDEN):
             hits.append(f"{path}:{node.lineno} imports {node.module}")
    return hits

  hits = [h for p in Path("app/api").rglob("*.py") for h in check(p)]
  if hits:
     raise SystemExit("boundary violations:\n" + "\n".join(hits))
  print("api layer uses services only")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The scan catches direct imports only; dynamic imports and framework dependency injection can still cross the boundary.
 → Set the rule at the layer that matters: routes may import services, services may import interfaces, adapters may import
   SDKs.
 → Run the test on every pull request; a boundary check that runs weekly will be bypassed within a month.

lessons.title: Phase 3 — Repository
lessons.subtitle: Make the repository the single source of truth: reproducible setup, enforced layout, fast CI, and decisions stored beside the
why_it_matters: A prototype survives on one engineer's laptop; a platform must be reproducible for reviewers, CI, and containers. Repository decisions are cheap now and expensive later: a flat folder of scripts becomes impossible to secure, and an unpinned dependency turns a green build red without a code change. Phase 3 makes setup a command, review automatic, and the layout an expression of the architecture. It is also the first artefact a hiring panel or security reviewer will read.
outcomes: Create a src-layout package with separate API, service, provider, retrieval, and evaluation modules.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Layout encodes the architecture Use src/app with api, services, providers, retrieval, tools, and domain packages, plus tests/unit, tests/integration, tests/eval, infra, and docs/adr. Keep route modules thin, put orchestration in services, and let only providers import vendor SDKs. Name modules after responsibilities rather than technologies. Avoid a utils package; it becomes the place where boundaries go to die. The tree should let a reader predict where a change belongs before opening a file. Automate the review you would do by hand The pull-request gate runs ruff format and lint, mypy on domain and services, pytest with unit and integration markers, pip-audit, and gitleaks. Target under five minutes so nobody bypasses it. Run the slower evaluation suite nightly and on release branches. A gate that fails on formatting but not on a leaked key has the priorities backwards. Make the same commands available locally through make check so CI and laptop agree. Reproducibility is a build artefact Pin the Python version in .python-version, dependencies in uv.lock, and the base image by digest. A new engineer should reach a passing test run in fifteen minutes from a clean machine. Commit .env.example, never .env, and document every required variable with its type and default. Treat the lockfile as reviewed code: an unexplained dependency upgrade is a supply-chain change, not housekeeping.

key_terms.definition: A generated record of exact dependency versions and hashes so every environment installs the same packages.
A package structure placing importable code under src/ so tests run against the installed package, not the working directory.

Automated detection of credentials and keys in commits and pull requests, usually blocking the merge and requiring rotation. MENTAL MODEL The repository is the building's service corridor: unseen during a demo, but every cable, valve, and label determines whether maintenance is routine or a demolition.

code.title: A repository contract check that fails when required artefacts are missing or a secret is tracked.
code.code:
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

REQUIRED = ["pyproject.toml", "uv.lock", ".python-version", "src/app/main.py",
        "tests", "docs/adr", "eval"]
missing = [p for p in REQUIRED if not Path(p).exists()]
tracked = subprocess.run(["git", "ls-files"], capture_output=True,
                 text=True, check=True).stdout.splitlines()
leaks = [f for f in tracked if f == ".env" or f.endswith(".pem")]
if missing or leaks:
   raise SystemExit(f"missing={missing} tracked_secrets={leaks}")
print(f"repository contract satisfied: {len(REQUIRED)} paths, no secrets")
what_to_notice: Git tracks history, so removing .env in a later commit does not remove the key; rotate it and scan the full history.
The check asserts presence, not quality; a tests directory can exist and contain nothing, so pair it with coverage.

Phase 3 — Repository
Make the repository the single source of truth: reproducible setup, enforced layout, fast CI, and decisions stored beside the
code.
Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 3 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A prototype survives on one engineer's laptop; a platform must be reproducible for reviewers, CI, and containers.
Repository decisions are cheap now and expensive later: a flat folder of scripts becomes impossible to secure, and an
unpinned dependency turns a green build red without a code change. Phase 3 makes setup a command, review
automatic, and the layout an expression of the architecture. It is also the first artefact a hiring panel or security reviewer
will read.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Create a src-layout package with separate API, service, provider, retrieval, and evaluation modules.
 • Enforce formatting, typing, tests, dependency audit, and secret scanning in a CI job under five minutes.
 • Pin the interpreter and dependencies so local, CI, and container builds install identical versions.
CORE CONCEPTS
Layout encodes the architecture
Use src/app with api, services, providers, retrieval, tools, and domain packages, plus tests/unit, tests/integration,
tests/eval, infra, and docs/adr. Keep route modules thin, put orchestration in services, and let only providers import
vendor SDKs. Name modules after responsibilities rather than technologies. Avoid a utils package; it becomes the place
where boundaries go to die. The tree should let a reader predict where a change belongs before opening a file.
Automate the review you would do by hand
The pull-request gate runs ruff format and lint, mypy on domain and services, pytest with unit and integration markers,
pip-audit, and gitleaks. Target under five minutes so nobody bypasses it. Run the slower evaluation suite nightly and on
release branches. A gate that fails on formatting but not on a leaked key has the priorities backwards. Make the same
commands available locally through make check so CI and laptop agree.
Reproducibility is a build artefact
Pin the Python version in .python-version, dependencies in uv.lock, and the base image by digest. A new engineer should
reach a passing test run in fifteen minutes from a clean machine. Commit .env.example, never .env, and document every
required variable with its type and default. Treat the lockfile as reviewed code: an unexplained dependency upgrade is a
supply-chain change, not housekeeping.
KEY TERMS
 Lockfile                          A generated record of exact dependency versions and hashes so every environment installs the same
                                   packages.
 Src layout                        A package structure placing importable code under src/ so tests run against the installed package, not the
                                   working directory.
 Secret scanning                   Automated detection of credentials and keys in commits and pull requests, usually blocking the merge and
                                   requiring rotation.

  MENTAL MODEL The repository is the building's service corridor: unseen during a demo, but every cable, valve, and label determines
  whether maintenance is routine or a demolition.

WORKED EXAMPLE
A five-person team has a working RAG prototype in a notebook and a folder called scripts. Onboarding takes 40 minutes
and fails on three undocumented system packages. Before the first sprint they migrate to src/app with api, services,

version, and make setup. CI runs ruff, mypy, 118 unit tests, pip-audit, and gitleaks in 3 minutes 40 seconds. gitleaks finds a
provider key in the second commit; they rotate it, rewrite nothing, and add a pre-commit hook. The decision: no merge
without the gate, and no vendor SDK import outside app/providers.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Create src/app packages for api, services, providers, retrieval, tools, and domain, plus tests, eval, infra, and docs/adr.
2.    Add pyproject.toml, .python-version, uv.lock, .env.example, and a Makefile with setup, check, and test targets.
3.    Configure ruff, mypy, pytest markers, coverage on changed lines, pip-audit, and gitleaks in the pull-request workflow.
4.    Run the repository contract check below and fix every missing path before inviting reviewers.
5.    Time a clean clone through make setup and make check; record the result in the README.
CODE
A repository contract check that fails when required artefacts are missing or a secret is tracked.
  import subprocess
  from pathlib import Path

  REQUIRED = ["pyproject.toml", "uv.lock", ".python-version", "src/app/main.py",
          "tests", "docs/adr", "eval"]
  missing = [p for p in REQUIRED if not Path(p).exists()]
  tracked = subprocess.run(["git", "ls-files"], capture_output=True,
                   text=True, check=True).stdout.splitlines()
  leaks = [f for f in tracked if f == ".env" or f.endswith(".pem")]
  if missing or leaks:
     raise SystemExit(f"missing={missing} tracked_secrets={leaks}")
  print(f"repository contract satisfied: {len(REQUIRED)} paths, no secrets")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → Git tracks history, so removing .env in a later commit does not remove the key; rotate it and scan the full history.
 → The check asserts presence, not quality; a tests directory can exist and contain nothing, so pair it with coverage.
 → Import order and line length are enforced by ruff, which keeps review comments about substance rather than style.

lessons.subtitle: Build the authenticated, tenant-scoped, idempotent request path that every model call, job, and tool will depend on.
lessons.meta: Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 4 of 13 · study guide
why_it_matters: The backend is where the platform becomes a product: it authenticates, authorises, validates, durably records, and admits or rejects work. Model quality cannot compensate for a duplicate charge, a cross-tenant read, or a request that times out after the answer was generated. Phase 4 builds the contract and the safety rails first, then lets the AI layer plug into a path that already behaves correctly under retries, quota limits, and restarts.
outcomes: Implement tenant-scoped authentication, request IDs, and idempotency on every state-changing endpoint.
Define request and response schemas with stable error codes and correct HTTP status mapping.
Move slow work to a queue and expose job status without leaking another tenant's data.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The backend owns the contract Define request models, response envelopes, and a closed set of error codes before the model layer exists. A successful answer returns content, citations, usage, and a request ID; a failure returns a code such as unauthenticated, forbidden, conflict, rate_limited, or unavailable. Never pass raw provider errors to clients. Version the path and keep additive changes compatible. Contract tests for 401, 403, 409, 429, and 503 catch the failures that demos never show. Tenancy at the data edge Derive tenant_id from the verified token, never from a request body, and set it on the database session so row-level security applies to every query. Use separate roles for migrations, application reads, and workers. Check tool permissions against the same tenant and role, because a model can be persuaded to request another customer's record. Log tenant and request IDs, never document contents. A missing WHERE clause is a breach, not a bug. Slow work leaves the request path Any operation that can exceed two seconds becomes a job: validate, persist, enqueue, return 202 with a job ID, and let the client poll or subscribe. Store an idempotency key per tenant for 24 hours so a retried POST returns the original job rather than a second charge. Workers update job state transactionally and expose queued, running, succeeded, and failed. The request path stays fast while expensive work is retried on its own schedule.

key_terms.definition: A client-supplied identifier stored with a write so retries return the original result instead of creating a duplicate.
A database policy filtering rows by the current session's tenant, enforcing isolation even when application code forgets a filter.

Rejecting or delaying new work with 429 or 503 when capacity or quota is exhausted, rather than queueing without bound. MENTAL MODEL The backend is the building's front desk: it checks identity, records the request, gives a ticket, and refuses to let two people claim the same room.

worked_example: Lantern, a 30-person ticketing SaaS, launches an assistant that summarises threads and drafts replies. During a provider slowdown, clients retry POST /v1/answers; the endpoint creates a new job each time. In 40 minutes, 1,400 duplicate jobs consume 2.6 million tokens and GBP 62, and some users see two drafts. The team adds a tenant-scoped idempotency table with a 24-hour TTL, returns 202 with a job ID, and maps provider quota exhaustion to 429 with Retry-After: 30 instead of 503. They also find that a support role could read another tenant's job by guessing the ID, so job lookups gain a tenant predicate. The decision: no synchronous model call on any write path.

Phase 4 — Backend
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
Lantern, a 30-person ticketing SaaS, launches an assistant that summarises threads and drafts replies. During a provider
slowdown, clients retry POST /v1/answers; the endpoint creates a new job each time. In 40 minutes, 1,400 duplicate jobs
consume 2.6 million tokens and GBP 62, and some users see two drafts. The team adds a tenant-scoped idempotency
table with a 24-hour TTL, returns 202 with a job ID, and maps provider quota exhaustion to 429 with Retry-After: 30
instead of 503. They also find that a support role could read another tenant's job by guessing the ID, so job lookups gain a
tenant predicate. The decision: no synchronous model call on any write path.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define Pydantic request models, a response envelope, and a closed error catalogue with HTTP mappings.
2.    Implement token verification that resolves tenant_id and role, then set both on the database session.
3.    Add an idempotency table keyed by tenant and key, and return the stored job for duplicate writes.
4.    Move model work to a worker, expose job status, and return 202 with a polling or streaming URL.
5.    Write contract tests for 401, 403, 409, 429, and 503, including a cross-tenant lookup attempt.
CODE
A 202 write path that resolves the tenant from the token and collapses retries onto one job.
  from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
  from pydantic import BaseModel
  app = FastAPI()
  JOBS: dict[tuple[str, str], str] = {}

  def tenant_from(token: str = Header(...)) -> str:
    if token != "demo-token":
       raise HTTPException(401, "invalid token")
    return "tenant-a"

  class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str

  @app.post("/v1/answers", status_code=202)
  def ask(body: Ask, idem: str = Header(...), tenant: str = Depends(tenant_from)):
    key = (tenant, idem)
    if key in JOBS:
       return {"job_id": JOBS[key], "duplicate": True}
    JOBS[key] = f"job-{len(JOBS) + 1}"
    return {"job_id": JOBS[key], "duplicate": False}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The dependency rejects any token except the demo value; production must verify signature, issuer, audience, and expiry.
 → The idempotency store is in memory here, so it disappears on restart; use Postgres with a unique constraint on tenant and
   key.
 → Returning 202 means the client must poll; include a Location header and a status endpoint that also enforces tenancy.

lessons.title: Phase 5 — AI Layer
lessons.subtitle: Put every model call behind one gateway with typed output, bounded retries, token budgets, and per-tenant cost
why_it_matters: The AI layer is where a probabilistic dependency meets a deterministic contract. Without a gateway, provider SDKs spread through the codebase, retries multiply cost, and a malformed JSON response becomes a 500. Phase 5 concentrates model access in one place so timeouts, routing, usage, validation, and fallbacks can be tested once and observed everywhere. It is also the only layer allowed to know a model name, which keeps the rest of the platform swappable.
outcomes: Build a provider-neutral gateway that normalises messages, usage, errors, and streaming events.
Validate structured output against a schema, allow one repair attempt, then fail to a known fallback.
Enforce input, output, and per-tenant cost budgets before the call rather than after the invoice.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One gateway, many providers The gateway accepts a normalised request (system, messages, max tokens, response schema) and returns content, usage, model, latency, and retry count. Adapters translate to each provider. Retry only 429 and 5xx, with jittered exponential backoff and an overall deadline; never retry 400 or 401. Give each attempt a connect timeout and a total timeout. Normalise error classes so the service layer can choose between fallback, queueing, and user-visible failure without importing a vendor SDK. Structured output is a contract Ask for JSON that matches a schema, parse it with Pydantic, and treat validation failure as a first-class outcome. Allow one repair attempt that includes the validation errors, then return a typed failure rather than guessing. Never extract JSON with a regular expression or strip fences by hand. Log the schema version and validator errors, not the full prompt. A model that cannot satisfy the schema should trigger a stronger model or a deterministic fallback, and the decision should be visible in metrics. Budgets before, accounting after Estimate prompt tokens before sending, reserve the output maximum, and reject requests that exceed the task or tenant budget. Track actual usage from the provider response, including cached and reasoning tokens where billed. Set a monthly tenant cap and a per-request ceiling, then alert at 80%. Summarise older context instead of silently truncating it. Cost per successful request, not cost per token, is the number to review with the product owner.

key_terms.definition: A single internal service normalising requests, retries, usage, and errors across providers so callers stay provider-neutral.
A response constrained to a schema and validated before use, with failure handled as an explicit outcome rather than parsed by hope.

The maximum input, output, and monetary allowance reserved for a request or tenant before a model call is permitted. MENTAL MODEL The gateway is a customs post: every model call declares its goods, passes inspection, pays duty, and leaves a record, whichever border it crosses.
Page 592 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: Vantage, a 200-person insurer, runs 90,000 policy questions a month. A benchmark shows the strong model answers 94% correctly at USD 0.031 per question; the fast model reaches 88% at USD 0.004. But 12% of fast-model responses fail the citation schema, and retries push the blended cost to USD 0.007. The team routes extraction and classification to the fast model, answer synthesis to the strong model, and adds a schema-repair attempt capped at 600 tokens. With prompt caching on the 3,100-token policy preamble, the strong path falls to USD 0.024. The decision: quality-critical answers use the strong model; summarisation falls back to the fast model with a visible label.

code.title: A pre-call budget reservation that rejects a request before it can exceed the tenant's ceiling.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Budget:
  max_input_tokens: int = 8_000
  max_output_tokens: int = 700
  max_usd: float = 0.045

PRICES = {"fast": (0.15, 0.60), "strong": (3.00, 15.00)} # USD per 1M tokens

def reserve(model: str, prompt: str, budget: Budget) -> int:
  input_tokens = len(prompt) // 4 + 1
  if input_tokens > budget.max_input_tokens:
     raise ValueError(f"input {input_tokens} over {budget.max_input_tokens}")
  price_in, price_out = PRICES[model]
  worst = (input_tokens * price_in + budget.max_output_tokens * price_out) / 1e6
  if worst > budget.max_usd:
     raise ValueError(f"worst case ${worst:.4f} over ${budget.max_usd}")
  return input_tokens

print(reserve("strong", "policy preamble " * 700, Budget()))
what_to_notice: The token estimate uses a four-characters-per-token heuristic; production should use the provider tokenizer and include tool schemas.
Prices change and differ by region; load them from configuration and record the price version with each usage event.

Reserving the output maximum is conservative, so a request may be refused even when the actual answer would be cheap. Three pages per lesson Page 593 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Emit usage and latency per attempt and per request; a retry that succeeds still costs money and time.

accounting.
Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 5 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
The AI layer is where a probabilistic dependency meets a deterministic contract. Without a gateway, provider SDKs spread
through the codebase, retries multiply cost, and a malformed JSON response becomes a 500. Phase 5 concentrates model
access in one place so timeouts, routing, usage, validation, and fallbacks can be tested once and observed everywhere. It
is also the only layer allowed to know a model name, which keeps the rest of the platform swappable.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Build a provider-neutral gateway that normalises messages, usage, errors, and streaming events.
 • Validate structured output against a schema, allow one repair attempt, then fail to a known fallback.
 • Enforce input, output, and per-tenant cost budgets before the call rather than after the invoice.
CORE CONCEPTS
One gateway, many providers
The gateway accepts a normalised request (system, messages, max tokens, response schema) and returns content, usage,
model, latency, and retry count. Adapters translate to each provider. Retry only 429 and 5xx, with jittered exponential
backoff and an overall deadline; never retry 400 or 401. Give each attempt a connect timeout and a total timeout.
Normalise error classes so the service layer can choose between fallback, queueing, and user-visible failure without
importing a vendor SDK.
Structured output is a contract
Ask for JSON that matches a schema, parse it with Pydantic, and treat validation failure as a first-class outcome. Allow one
repair attempt that includes the validation errors, then return a typed failure rather than guessing. Never extract JSON
with a regular expression or strip fences by hand. Log the schema version and validator errors, not the full prompt. A
model that cannot satisfy the schema should trigger a stronger model or a deterministic fallback, and the decision should
be visible in metrics.
Budgets before, accounting after
Estimate prompt tokens before sending, reserve the output maximum, and reject requests that exceed the task or tenant
budget. Track actual usage from the provider response, including cached and reasoning tokens where billed. Set a
monthly tenant cap and a per-request ceiling, then alert at 80%. Summarise older context instead of silently truncating it.
Cost per successful request, not cost per token, is the number to review with the product owner.
KEY TERMS
 Model gateway                     A single internal service normalising requests, retries, usage, and errors across providers so callers stay
                                   provider-neutral.
 Structured output                 A response constrained to a schema and validated before use, with failure handled as an explicit outcome
                                   rather than parsed by hope.
 Token budget                      The maximum input, output, and monetary allowance reserved for a request or tenant before a model call is
                                   permitted.

  MENTAL MODEL The gateway is a customs post: every model call declares its goods, passes inspection, pays duty, and leaves a record,
  whichever border it crosses.

Phase 5 — AI Layer
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
Vantage, a 200-person insurer, runs 90,000 policy questions a month. A benchmark shows the strong model answers 94%
correctly at USD 0.031 per question; the fast model reaches 88% at USD 0.004. But 12% of fast-model responses fail the
citation schema, and retries push the blended cost to USD 0.007. The team routes extraction and classification to the fast
model, answer synthesis to the strong model, and adds a schema-repair attempt capped at 600 tokens. With prompt
caching on the 3,100-token policy preamble, the strong path falls to USD 0.024. The decision: quality-critical answers use
the strong model; summarisation falls back to the fast model with a visible label.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define a normalised request and response type, then write adapters for two providers and one fake.
2.    Add per-attempt timeouts, overall deadlines, and retries limited to 429 and 5xx with jitter.
3.    Validate JSON against a Pydantic schema, allow one repair with errors, then return a typed failure.
4.    Estimate input tokens, reserve output, and reject calls above the request or tenant budget.
5.    Record usage, model, latency, retry count, and cost per successful request in metrics and traces.
CODE
A pre-call budget reservation that rejects a request before it can exceed the tenant's ceiling.
  from dataclasses import dataclass
  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Budget:
    max_input_tokens: int = 8_000
    max_output_tokens: int = 700
    max_usd: float = 0.045

  PRICES = {"fast": (0.15, 0.60), "strong": (3.00, 15.00)} # USD per 1M tokens

  def reserve(model: str, prompt: str, budget: Budget) -> int:
    input_tokens = len(prompt) // 4 + 1
    if input_tokens > budget.max_input_tokens:
       raise ValueError(f"input {input_tokens} over {budget.max_input_tokens}")
    price_in, price_out = PRICES[model]
    worst = (input_tokens * price_in + budget.max_output_tokens * price_out) / 1e6
    if worst > budget.max_usd:
       raise ValueError(f"worst case ${worst:.4f} over ${budget.max_usd}")
    return input_tokens

  print(reserve("strong", "policy preamble " * 700, Budget()))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The token estimate uses a four-characters-per-token heuristic; production should use the provider tokenizer and include
   tool schemas.
 → Prices change and differ by region; load them from configuration and record the price version with each usage event.
 → Reserving the output maximum is conservative, so a request may be refused even when the actual answer would be cheap.

Phase 5 — AI Layer
Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Calling provider SDKs directly from route handlers, so a timeout or schema change requires edits in a dozen places.
2.     Retrying every error, including 400 and 401, which multiplies cost and hides the configuration bug causing the failure.
3.     Parsing JSON with a regular expression after the model wraps it in prose, instead of validating and repairing explicitly.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Pin model identifiers and prompt versions, and record both with every request so quality and cost regressions are
      attributable.
    ◆ Emit usage and latency per attempt and per request; a retry that succeeds still costs money and time.
    ◆ Keep one fake provider that returns malformed output, rate limits, and timeouts, and run it in CI.
CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□      All model calls pass through one gateway with a provider-neutral interface.
□      Retries cover only 429 and 5xx, with jitter and an overall deadline.
□      Structured output is schema-validated, with one repair attempt and a typed failure.
□      Input, output, and cost budgets are enforced before the call.
□      Usage, model, prompt version, and cost per success are observable.
SHORT QUESTIONS
1.     Why should a gateway normalise errors before the service layer sees them?

2.     When is one repair attempt better than an automatic second model call?

3.     Why is reserving the maximum output tokens safer than estimating the actual answer length?

4.     What does cost per successful request reveal that cost per million tokens hides?

5.     Which failures should trigger a fallback model, and which should fail immediately?

6.     How does prompt caching change the routing decision between two models?

TASKS
□      Build the gateway with two real adapters and a fake that can return malformed JSON and 429.
□      Benchmark 50 representative prompts on two models and record accuracy, p95 latency, and cost per success.
□      Add a per-tenant monthly cap and prove a request is rejected before the provider is called.
    CAPSTONE CONNECTION This phase delivers the capstone AI layer: one gateway, two adapters, schema validation with repair, enforced
    budgets, and a measured cost per success.

lessons.subtitle: Use traces and evaluation evidence to choose a deterministic workflow, one agent, or multiple agents; multi-agent design is an optional branch.
lessons.meta: Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · study guide · reviewed 2026
why_it_matters: Adding agents adds calls, latency, cost, and failure paths. A capstone should demonstrate sound architecture judgment, including the ability to reject a multi-agent design when one bounded agent or a deterministic workflow meets the requirements.

core_concepts.title: Start with the simplest adequate control flow
core_concepts.content: Use deterministic code for known sequences, validation, permissions, and transactions. Use one agent when model-led tool choice adds value. Use multiple agents only when distinct context, permissions, ownership, or independently measurable work justify coordination.

core_concepts.title: A split needs a measurable hypothesis
core_concepts.content: Name the failure a specialist is meant to reduce and define a baseline. Compare the split against the same task set and include handoff errors, duplicate work, extra model calls, latency, and spend. More workers do not imply more correctness.

core_concepts.title: Preserve one accountable result
core_concepts.content: Whether the workflow has one model or several, the application owns authorization, budgets, state validation, and the final response contract. Each delegated step receives only the required data and capabilities.

key_terms.definition: The routing agent that selects the next specialist and decides when the evidence is sufficient to answer.
An explicit transfer of task, constraints, and expected output from one agent to another through shared state.

A hard cap on graph steps that stops a runaway loop even when routing logic misbehaves. MENTAL MODEL A multi-agent system is a case conference: one consultant routes the case, specialists report into the same chart, and someone must sign the discharge summary.

Phase 9 — Choose the Right Orchestration Shape
Use traces and evaluation evidence to choose a deterministic workflow, one agent, or multiple agents; multi-agent design is an optional branch.
Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 12.09 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Adding agents adds calls, latency, cost, and failure paths. A capstone should demonstrate sound architecture judgment, including the ability to reject a multi-agent design when one bounded agent or a deterministic workflow meets the requirements.

WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
• Compare a deterministic workflow, a single bounded agent, and a multi-agent design against stated requirements.
• Use trace and evaluation evidence to justify any orchestration split.
• Measure routing, handoff, quality, latency, cost, and failure propagation when multiple agents are warranted.

CORE CONCEPTS
Start with the simplest adequate control flow
Use deterministic code for known sequences, validation, permissions, and transactions. Use one agent when model-led tool choice adds value. Use multiple agents only when distinct context, permissions, ownership, or independently measurable work justify coordination.

A split needs a measurable hypothesis
Name the failure a specialist is meant to reduce and define a baseline. Compare the split against the same task set and include handoff errors, duplicate work, extra model calls, latency, and spend. More workers do not imply more correctness.

Preserve one accountable result
Whether the workflow has one model or several, the application owns authorization, budgets, state validation, and the final response contract. Each delegated step receives only the required data and capabilities.

Phase 9 — Choose the Right Orchestration Shape
Build it

WORKED EXAMPLE
The capstone’s document assistant has a fixed retrieve, rank, answer pipeline. Its team first evaluates a single agent for ambiguous queries. Only if traces show repeated tool-selection failures that a specialized retriever can measurably reduce does the team prototype a second agent.

STEP BY STEP
1. Write the task requirements and baseline success, safety, latency, and cost metrics.
2. Implement the simplest plausible workflow and collect representative traces.
3. Identify a specific failure that added orchestration could address.
4. Prototype the alternative behind a feature flag using the same evaluation set.
5. Keep the split only if it improves the target without violating safety or budgets; record the decision either way.

Phase 9 — Choose the Right Orchestration Shape
Operate it

COMMON MISTAKES
1. Adding agents because the capstone checklist expects them.
2. Comparing a tuned multi-agent system with an untuned single-agent baseline.
3. Scoring only the final answer and ignoring tool permissions or trajectory.
4. Sharing unrestricted state and credentials across specialists.

PRODUCTION NOTES
◆ Set hard per-run model, step, wall-clock, and tool-call budgets.
◆ Persist only validated state and give each worker minimum necessary data and permissions.
◆ Keep the no-split decision as valid architecture evidence when measurements do not justify extra agents.

CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□ The baseline architecture is implemented and evaluated.
□ Any proposed split has a named failure hypothesis.
□ Results compare quality, safety, latency, and cost on the same cases.
□ The final design has explicit budgets and ownership.
□ The ADR records why a split was accepted or rejected.

SHORT QUESTIONS
1. When is a deterministic workflow preferable to an agent?
2. What evidence would justify a specialist agent?
3. How can handoffs create a new security boundary?
4. What metrics can worsen while answer quality improves?
5. Why is rejecting multi-agent architecture a valid capstone result?

TASKS
□ Write an ADR comparing workflow, single-agent, and multi-agent options.
□ Evaluate at least 30 representative runs and report quality, trajectory, latency, and cost.
□ If multi-agent is not justified, document the evidence and improve the simplest design instead.

CAPSTONE CONNECTION
Replaces the mandatory supervisor-plus-three-specialists build with an evidence-based architecture decision and optional implementation.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: SLOs for a probabilistic service Availability and latency are necessary but not sufficient. Set a quality SLO on a rolling sample, for example groundedness at or above 0.90 over 500 traces, alongside p95 latency under 3.5 seconds and cost under USD 0.06 per request. Define the window, the sampling method, and the action when the budget burns. A single evaluation score is a release gate; a rolling SLO is how you operate. Resilience at every seam Each model and tool call gets a timeout, a bounded retry, and a breaker. Retry only 429 and 5xx with jittered exponential backoff; never retry validation errors. After ten consecutive failures, open the breaker, serve a cached or extractive answer, and probe recovery with a single request. Cap total attempts per user request so an outage cannot be amplified into three times the traffic. Release gates, not launch day A deploy is an experiment with a rollback plan. CI evaluates the exact image on a 300-case golden set and blocks if groundedness falls more than two points, p95 exceeds 3.8 seconds, or cost exceeds USD 0.08. The canary takes 5% of traffic for ten minutes and compares against a baseline window. Automate rollback on error-rate or quality breach; require a human for judgement calls.

key_terms.definition: A measurable target for service behaviour over a defined window, with an error budget attached.
The allowed shortfall against an SLO, used to decide whether to ship features or fix reliability.

A guard that stops calls to a failing dependency after a threshold and fails fast until recovery. MENTAL MODEL Production is a flight envelope, not a finish line: the aircraft may fly in turbulence, but the crew knows the limits, watches the gauges, and has a diversion plan.

worked_example: Meridian's first load test at 30 requests per second shows p95 at 9.4 seconds and 8% provider 429s. The client retried every failure, tripling load and turning a throttle into an outage. A second run at 45 requests per second holds p95 at 2.8 seconds and USD 0.041 per request. Groundedness is 0.91 on the 300-case set, so the release gate passes, but the team delays launch nine days to run an outage drill and finish the runbook.

Meridian's first load test at 30 requests per second shows p95 at 9.4 seconds and 8% provider 429s. The client retried

STEP BY STEP
1.    Write the service contract with availability, p95 latency, groundedness, and cost, each with a window and owner.
2.    Instrument every model, tool, and database call with a span, token counts, tenant, and outcome.
3.    Add timeouts, one jittered retry, circuit breakers, a short-lived cache, and per-tenant rate limits.
4.    Build a 300-case release evaluation and make CI fail on the agreed thresholds.
5.    Run a 60-minute load test at twice peak, inject a provider outage, and write the runbook from the evidence.
CODE
A CI release gate that blocks deployment when groundedness, latency, or cost breach the service contract.
  import json
  import sys
  LIMITS = {"groundedness": 0.90, "p95_ms": 3500.0, "cost_usd": 0.06}
  def gate(report: dict) -> list[str]:
     failures = []
     if report["cases"] < 300:
        failures.append("fewer than 300 evaluation cases")
     for key, limit in LIMITS.items():
        value = report[key]
        breached = value < limit if key == "groundedness" else value > limit
        if breached:
           failures.append(f"{key}={value} breaches {limit}")
     return failures
  failures = gate(json.load(open(sys.argv[1])))
  if failures:
     raise SystemExit("; ".join(failures))
  print("release gate passed")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The gate reads a fresh report for the same image digest; a cached evaluation can pass after the prompt changed twice.
 → Groundedness is a sample estimate, so state the confidence interval and the minimum case count.
 → Retries amplify load during an outage; cap attempts per request and retry only 429 and 5xx.
