lessons.title: Phase 11 — Infrastructure
lessons.subtitle: Define the platform's network, data stores, secrets, and scaling rules as reviewable infrastructure code with reproducible
why_it_matters: Infrastructure decisions are architecture decisions. Whether the vector store is public, where backups live, and how a subnet is routed determine what an incident can reach. Treating infrastructure as reviewable code makes those choices visible, reproducible, and testable before any production traffic depends on them, and it shortens the next audit.
outcomes: Model the platform as infrastructure code with separate dev, staging, and production stacks.
Place Postgres, pgvector, Redis, object storage, and the API inside a private network with controlled egress.
Prove recovery with backups, restore drills, and autoscaling rules tied to measured load.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Environments are copies, not cousins One module should produce dev, staging, and production. Differences are explicit variables: instance size, replica count, retention, and deletion protection. Apply the same commit through the same pipeline, with remote state locking and a plan reviewed before merge. Manual console changes create drift, and drift turns an incident fix into a surprise during the next apply. If production needs a unique resource, encode it and review it. Network and data boundaries Postgres, pgvector, Redis, and object storage belong in private subnets with no public endpoint. The API reaches them through security groups; outbound model and tool traffic leaves through a controlled egress path. Encrypt volumes and backups with customer-managed keys, issue the workload an IAM role, and fetch secrets at runtime. A public vector database is a data breach with a query interface. Capacity and recovery by measurement Autoscale on the signal that saturates first: queue depth for ingestion, CPU or concurrent requests for the API, and memory for pgvector indexes. Set a cost ceiling so scaling has a limit. Choose an RPO and RTO from business impact, then configure point-in-time recovery and test a restore into an isolated account. An untested backup is a hope, not a recovery plan.

key_terms.definition: A declarative, version-controlled definition of cloud resources applied through a reviewed pipeline.
A difference between declared and actual infrastructure, usually caused by manual console changes.

The maximum tolerable data loss and recovery time, which set backup and failover design. MENTAL MODEL Infrastructure code is a building plan with an inspection schedule: the drawing must match the building, and the fire drill proves the exits work.
Page 610 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

worked_example: Meridian's staging environment was cloned from production sizing and cost USD 4,800 a month for a platform used by six engineers. A review finds the pgvector instance at 4% CPU and an idle read replica. The team parameterises the stack, drops staging to a smaller instance and one replica, and adds scale-to-zero for workers outside office hours, cutting spend to USD 1,150. Budget alerts fire at 80% and 100% of the monthly forecast. The same review tests recovery and discovers the stated 15-minute RPO was actually six hours because point-in-time recovery was disabled. PITR is enabled, a restore drill passes at 11 minutes, and the production apply is blocked until the drill evidence is attached.
steps: Draw trust boundaries and list every resource with its data classification, owner, and monthly cost.
Write one reusable stack module and parameterise dev, staging, and production from reviewed config.
Move data stores to private subnets, attach customer-managed keys, and replace static credentials with IAM roles.
Configure point-in-time recovery and run a restore into an isolated account, measuring actual RPO and RTO.
Apply to staging, review the plan diff, then promote the same commit to production through the same CI pipeline.

code.title: A Pulumi stack that creates an encrypted, backed-up Postgres instance in private subnets and exports only its endpoint.
code.code:
import pulumi
import pulumi_aws as aws
cfg = pulumi.Config("atlas")
subnets = aws.ec2.get_subnets(filters=[{"name": "tag:tier", "values": ["private"]}])
group = aws.rds.SubnetGroup("atlas", subnet_ids=subnets.ids)
db = aws.rds.Instance(
  "atlas-pg",
  engine="postgres",
  engine_version="16.4",
  instance_class="db.r6g.large",
  allocated_storage=100,
  storage_encrypted=True,
  backup_retention_period=14,
  deletion_protection=cfg.require_bool("prod"),
  db_subnet_group_name=group.name,
  performance_insights_enabled=True,
  skip_final_snapshot=False,
)
pulumi.export("db_endpoint", db.endpoint)
what_to_notice: Deletion protection is false in dev by design; the production stack must read the flag from reviewed config.
The snippet exports an endpoint, not a password; runtime credentials come from Secrets Manager after workload authentication.
A subnet tag is a weak selector; confirm the plan shows private routes, not the default VPC. Three pages per lesson Page 611 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Fixing production in the console during an incident and leaving drift for the next apply to reverse.
Sizing staging like production, then paying for idle memory and replicas every month.
Backing up the database without restoring it, so RPO and RTO stay theoretical.
production_notes: Apply infrastructure only through CI with remote state locking and a named production approver who reviews the plan.
Pin engine versions and test the extension list after every upgrade; pgvector failures should surface in staging, not startup.
Tag every resource with environment, owner, and cost centre; untagged spend is the first signal of shadow infrastructure.
checklist: One module produces dev, staging, and production with enumerated differences.
No data store accepts public connections and egress paths are documented.
Keys, secrets, and IAM roles are managed outside application code.
A restore drill has met the stated RPO and RTO within the last quarter.
Autoscaling uses a measured signal and has a documented cost ceiling.
questions: Why should the production stack use the same reviewed module as staging rather than a separate configuration?
Which resources need private networking, and what breaks if the vector database is publicly reachable?
How does point-in-time recovery change the way you plan a schema migration?
What evidence from a restore drill would convince a reviewer that the stated RTO is real rather than theoretical?
Why is CPU a poor autoscaling signal for a RAG service, and what metric would you use instead?
What does an untagged cloud resource usually indicate about a team's operating discipline and ownership?
tasks: Draw the VPC and data-flow diagram for the platform, marking public, private, and egress paths with the data each carries.
Write an infrastructure module for Postgres and Redis, run a preview for staging, and record the cost delta.

Run a restore drill into an isolated account and measure actual RPO and RTO against the stated targets. WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Deployment is a control system, not a command. Most rollback failures come from rebuilding artefacts, destructive

migrations compatible, and rolls back on a measured signal turns release from a ceremony into a repeatable operation.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Build one immutable image per commit and promote the same digest across environments.
 • Run migrations, smoke tests, and a 5% canary with automatic rollback on SLO breach.
 • Document the release, rollback, and incident handoff so another engineer can repeat them.
CORE CONCEPTS
Build once, promote the digest
CI builds one image per commit, signs it, generates an SBOM, and records the digest. Staging and production receive that
digest; nothing is rebuilt. Configuration arrives through environment variables and secrets, not a new image. A migration
job runs before the new pods start, and the release record names the digest, migration version, and flag state. Rebuilding
per environment invalidates every test you ran on the artefact.
Progressive delivery
Send 5% of traffic to the new version for ten minutes and compare error rate, p95 latency, groundedness, and cost
against a baseline window from the same hour. Promote automatically when the canary is inside tolerance; roll back
automatically when it is not. Feature flags separate deploy from release, so a risky behaviour can be disabled without
rebuilding. A canary without a baseline is just a smaller outage.
Migrations that can go back
Use expand and contract. Add a nullable column, dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads, then drop the old column in
a later release. Never ship a destructive migration in the same release as the code that stops using it, because old pods
still serve traffic during the canary. Every migration must be safe for both versions and resumable if the job dies halfway.

2.    Run unit, integration, and 300-case evaluation tests against that exact image digest.
3.    Apply expand-only migrations as a separate job while old and new versions can both serve traffic.

CODE
A release workflow that builds one image, pushes it once, then runs migration, evaluation, and canary scripts that deploy that artefact.
  name: release
  on:
   push:
    branches: [main]
  jobs:
   ship:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    services:
      postgres:
        image: pgvector/pgvector:pg16
        env:
         POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker build -t ghcr.io/meridian/atlas:${{ github.sha }} .
      - run: docker push ghcr.io/meridian/atlas:${{ github.sha }}
      - run: ./ci/migrate.sh && ./ci/evaluate.sh && ./ci/canary.sh

 → Deploy the digest, not the tag; latest can be overwritten between the staging and production steps.
 → The migration job runs before the canary and must stay compatible with old pods still serving traffic.
 → Automatic rollback needs a baseline from the same hour; comparing with last week creates false alarms.

lessons.meta: Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 13 of 13 · study guide
why_it_matters: A final review is not a demo. Reviewers are looking for ownership, evidence, failure behaviour, and honest gaps. A platform that cannot explain why it chose a vector store, what happens when a provider fails, or who owns a critical finding is not ready to hand over, regardless of how well the demo answers questions.
outcomes: Run a structured review against requirements, security, reliability, cost, and operability.
Defend each major decision with an ADR, a measurement, and the alternative you rejected.
Produce a prioritised risk register and a 90-day roadmap that a new owner could execute.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Review the system, not the slides Start with one real request and follow it: authentication, tenant resolution, retrieval, prompt assembly, model call, tool invocation, persistence, and billing. Name the owner and the failure behaviour at each seam. Reviewers learn more from one trace with timings and token counts than from a deck of component diagrams, because the seams are where the platform actually fails under load, partial failure, or a bad deploy. Evidence over assertion Every claim needs a dated artefact: an evaluation report for quality, a load test for latency, a cost dashboard for spend, a restore drill for recovery, a threat model and pen-test note for security. Link the commit, dataset version, and trace IDs. If the evidence is stale, say so and schedule the re-run; an unsupported claim damages trust more than a known gap. Name the gaps A review that reports no material risks is not credible. Maintain a register with likelihood, impact, owner, mitigation, review date, and status. Separate blockers from accepted risks, and state what would change the decision. 'Future work' is not a mitigation; a monitored signal with a threshold is. The output is a decision plus a short, owned roadmap, not a numeric score.

key_terms.definition: A short document capturing context, decision, alternatives, and consequences for one architectural choice.
An ordered list of risks with likelihood, impact, owner, mitigation, and next review date.

An automated check that keeps an architectural property true as the system changes. MENTAL MODEL An architecture review is a pre-flight inspection: the reviewer walks the route a passenger will take and checks every hatch, gauge, and exit.

worked_example: Meridian's review board gives the platform a conditional approval after two hours and nine reviewers. One request walk- through exposes a shared API key used by all MCP clients, scored critical; the restore drill has never been run, high; 38% of traces lack the retrieval index version, medium; and model spend is 22% over the approved forecast. The board sets a 30- day window for the three blockers, assigns owners, and schedules a follow-up. The team fixes the key with per-client OAuth scopes, runs a restore in 11 minutes, and adds index version to trace metadata. The cost overrun is accepted with a monthly review because usage grew 40%.

Record findings with severity, owner, mitigation, and due date; separate blockers from accepted risks.
Publish the decision, the 90-day roadmap, and the date of the follow-up review.

code.title: A small review scorecard that turns findings into a verdict: critical issues block approval, lower severities stay tracked with owners and dates.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Finding:
  area: str
  severity: str
  owner: str
  due: str
FINDINGS = [
  Finding("mcp-auth", "critical", "security", "2026-11-08"),
  Finding("restore-drill", "high", "platform", "2026-11-22"),
  Finding("trace-versioning", "medium", "ai", "2026-12-06"),
]
def verdict(findings: list[Finding]) -> str:
  blockers = [f for f in findings if f.severity == "critical"]
  if blockers:
     return f"conditional: {len(blockers)} blocker(s) due {blockers[0].due}"
  return "approved with tracked risks"
print(verdict(FINDINGS))
what_to_notice: Conditional approval only works when each blocker has an owner and a date; otherwise it is approval with extra words.
Follow one request through auth, retrieval, model, tool, and storage; slide-only reviews miss the seams.

Cost and operability findings belong in the same register as security findings, with equal severity discipline. Three pages per lesson Page 617 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Presenting only the happy path and calling hard questions out of scope; reviewers read that as hidden risk.
Listing every improvement as future work, which hides the three risks that actually threaten the service.
Closing a finding without a regression check, so the same authentication gap returns next release.
production_notes: Re-run the review after any material trust-boundary, data-classification, or model-provider change; unexamined architecture drifts silently between scheduled reviews.
Turn every accepted risk into a monitored signal with a threshold, so a known weakness becomes an alert rather than a surprise.
Keep the evidence pack reproducible by linking the commit, dataset version, and trace IDs used in every review.
checklist: A reviewer can follow one real request through every component and data store.
Each major decision has an ADR with alternatives and consequences.
Every quality, latency, and cost claim links to a dated report.
The risk register has owners, severities, mitigations, and review dates.
The 90-day roadmap names the first three actions and their measures.
questions: Why is a conditional approval with dated blockers stronger than an unconditional approval with verbal caveats?
Which artefacts would you bring to prove that the platform's groundedness claim is current?
How do you distinguish an accepted risk from an unowned defect in the register?
What does a review of one end-to-end request typically reveal that a component-by-component review misses?
When should an architecture review be repeated after launch, and what triggers it?
How would you present a 22% cost overrun without losing the review board's confidence in the platform?

lessons.title: Welcome to the Course
lessons.subtitle: Start from zero: understand how this course works and build the right habits to become an AI engineer.
lessons.meta: AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 1 of 5 · study guide
why_it_matters: Becoming an AI engineer isn't about memorizing every AI tool or chasing the latest chatbot. It's about learning to build reliable, useful AI systems step by step. This first lesson shows you the map of the journey ahead, sets you up with the right tools, and teaches you how to learn effectively - so you can go from complete beginner to building real AI products with confidence.
outcomes: Understand what an AI engineer does and how it's different from other roles (like data scientist or ML engineer)
Know the 13-module journey you'll take and see how each piece fits together into one big project
Set up your coding workspace (Git, Python, virtual environment) the right way from day one
Learn a simple, repeatable study routine that actually works for busy people
Create your first plan and know exactly what 'done' means for your learning

core_concepts.title: What is AI Engineering?
core_concepts.content: Think of building with AI like building a house. A foundation model (like GPT, Claude, or LLaMA) is like a very talented builder - incredibly skilled at many things, but not reliable on its own for your specific needs. AI engineering is about everything around that builder: the blueprint (your app design), the plumbing and electricity (APIs and connections), the safety checks (testing and guardrails), the permits and maintenance (deployment and monitoring), and making sure it all works together reliably for real users. You're not just asking an AI to write something - you're building a complete system that uses AI to solve real problems.

core_concepts.title: This Course Builds ONE Project, Step by Step
core_concepts.content: Instead of jumping between random tutorials, you'll build the same project throughout all 13 modules. You start with the basics (Python, project setup), add a web backend, connect to AI models, add search and memory (RAG), give it tools to take actions (agents), add safety checks and testing, and finally deploy it for the world to use. Each new lesson adds one more piece to this same project. By the end, you'll have built a reviewable AI application whose optional components fit the product brief - not 13 separate toys.

core_concepts.title: How to Learn: Build > Watch
core_concepts.content: The most common mistake is watching videos and reading without coding. Your brain learns by doing. For every lesson: (1) Understand the 'why' - read why it matters, (2) Learn the concept - go through each idea one by one and explain it out loud in your own words, (3) Follow the worked example - type it yourself, don't copy-paste blindly, (4) Do the hands-on tasks - this is the most important part, (5) Check yourself with the questions. Aim for 'I can build this' not just 'I understand this'.

key_terms.definition: Someone who builds complete applications using AI models. They focus on making AI reliable, useful, and ready for real people to use.
A large, pre-trained AI model (like GPT-4, Claude, or LLaMA) that can do many different tasks. Think of it as a general-purpose brain you can build on top of.
An AI application that's built to actually be used by real people - with proper error handling, security, testing, and monitoring, not just a demo.
A way for different programs to talk to each other. When you call an AI model through its API, you're asking another computer to run the AI and send back the answer.
A folder that tracks all your code changes using Git. It's like a time machine for your project - you can save snapshots and go back if something breaks.

lessons.mental_model: Building an AI product is like opening a restaurant. The foundation model (ChatGPT, Claude) is a brilliant chef - amazing at cooking, but you can't just let them loose in a busy restaurant. You need a kitchen (your backend code), a menu (your API design), recipes (prompts and logic), quality control (testing), suppliers (data), health inspections (security), and a way to serve customers reliably (deployment). AI engineering is learning to run that whole restaurant, not just hire the chef.
worked_example: Meet Alex - someone who's never built an AI app before, but wants to become an AI engineer. Instead of starting with 'build a chatbot', Alex picks a real problem: helping small business owners write product descriptions. Welcome to the Course
Learn how the course works, what you will build, and how to study so the skills survive contact with a real product.
AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 1 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI engineering is learned by building and operating systems, not by collecting explanations. A clear workspace and a habit
of producing evidence will matter more than watching every video. This lesson sets those expectations before the
technical work begins.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Describe the three-page lesson pattern and the artefact each module expects you to produce.
 • Set up a course workspace with Python 3.11+, Git, a virtual environment, and an organised notes folder.
 • Write a one-sentence definition of done for your first AI feature that covers quality, latency, cost, and safety.
CORE CONCEPTS
A course built around a system
Each module teaches a component or architecture decision that you can apply to one product brief. You will begin
with Python and backend engineering, then add models, retrieval, tools, agents, evaluation, deployment, and operations.
By the final module you will have a reviewable AI system, and your architecture record will explain which optional components you included or rejected. A prompt is one line inside that system, not the system itself.
How each lesson works
Page one gives you the mental model: objectives, concepts, terms, and a rule of thumb. Page two makes it concrete with
a worked example, an ordered procedure, and code where code is useful. Page three moves to production concerns, self-
checks, questions, and hands-on tasks. Read with a terminal and notebook open; answer the questions before checking
the material again.
Your learning contract
Plan for five to seven focused hours each week and protect two of them for building. Keep one repository, write short
decision records, and record the measurements behind each claim. Completion means you can explain a choice,
reproduce a result, and name its failure modes. Finishing a lesson without producing an artefact is only reading.
KEY TERMS
 Foundation model                 A large pre-trained model, usually accessed through an API or as open weights, that can be adapted to many
                                  tasks without training from scratch.
 Evaluation harness               A repeatable script and dataset that scores system outputs against explicit criteria so changes can be
                                  compared fairly.
 Capstone                         The final integrated project in which you design, build, test, and deploy the production AI platform.

  MENTAL MODEL Building an AI product is like running a restaurant: the model is a talented but unpredictable chef, while the kitchen
  workflow, suppliers, health checks, and complaints process make service dependable. Learn the kitchen, not only the chef.

why_it_matters: Before diving into code, it's important to understand the role you're training for. Many people think AI engineering is just using ChatGPT or building chatbots, but it's much more. Knowing what AI engineers actually do will help you focus on the right skills and understand why this course is structured the way it is.

core_concepts.title: AI Engineer vs Other Roles
core_concepts.content: A Data Scientist mostly analyzes data and finds insights. An ML Engineer focuses on training and optimizing machine learning models. An AI Engineer takes existing models (like GPT) and builds products with them - connecting them to apps, adding features, making them reliable and useful. Think of it as: ML engineers build the engines, AI engineers build the cars people actually drive.

core_concepts.title: From Model to Product
core_concepts.content: Having access to an AI model is just the beginning. To make a real product, you need to handle user input, call the model correctly, process its response, handle errors, add safety checks, store data, authenticate users, and more. AI engineering is 80% building the 'plumbing' around the model and 20% working with the model itself. That's why this course spends a lot of time on APIs, databases, and backend development.

core_concepts.title: The Build-Measure-Improve Loop
core_concepts.content: AI engineering is iterative. You build a simple version, test it with real use cases, see what breaks or could be better, then improve it. You don't need perfection on day one. You need to ship something small, learn from it, and make it better. This is how real products are built.

key_terms.definition: Finds patterns and insights in data using statistics and analysis.
Trains, tests, and deploys machine learning models from scratch or fine-tunes them.
Builds applications using pre-trained AI models to solve real user problems.
The instructions you give to an AI model to get the response you want.
Planning how all the pieces of your app fit together before coding.

lessons.mental_model: If AI models are like powerful engines, AI engineers are the ones who design the whole vehicle - steering wheel, seats, safety features, fuel system - so anyone can drive it safely to their destination.

code.title: An order-of-magnitude cost model that makes model choice a measurable decision rather than a preference.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Usage:
  requests_per_month: int
  input_tokens: int
  output_tokens: int

def monthly_cost(u: Usage, in_price: float, out_price: float) -> float:
  input_cost = u.requests_per_month * u.input_tokens / 1_000_000 * in_price
  output_cost = u.requests_per_month * u.output_tokens / 1_000_000 * out_price
  return input_cost + output_cost

triage = Usage(requests_per_month=8_000, input_tokens=1_200, output_tokens=120)
print(f"USD {monthly_cost(triage, 0.50, 1.50):,.2f} per month")
what_to_notice: The estimate is driven by volume multiplied by tokens; a 20% retry rate adds 20% to the bill even when the prompt is unchanged.
Input tokens dominate here because 1,200 tokens of instructions and policy accompany every 120-token answer.

The model excludes embedding, retrieval, observability, and human-review costs, so it is a floor rather than the full unit economics. Three pages per lesson Page 8 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

What Is an AI Engineer?
Separate the AI engineer's responsibilities from adjacent roles and learn the loop that turns a model into a dependable
product.
AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 2 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most AI failures are integration and ownership failures rather than insufficient model intelligence. Someone must connect
the model to real data, constrain its output, measure quality, and answer the pager. The AI engineer owns that seam
between a probabilistic model and a dependable service.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Classify project tasks as model work, application engineering, evaluation, or operations.
 • Explain the trade-offs between a hosted API, an open-weight model, and fine-tuning to a non-technical stakeholder.
 • Produce a one-page role map for a chosen feature, naming the owner and metric for each component.
CORE CONCEPTS
Integration plus ownership
An ML engineer commonly trains models, builds feature pipelines, and studies model quality. A researcher invents
methods, while an AI engineer composes existing foundation models into a running product. The deliverable is a service
with clear contracts: authenticated requests, grounded context, validated output, fallbacks, and observed cost. That
engineer may fine-tune, but only when evaluation shows that prompting, retrieval, or a smaller model cannot meet the
requirement.
The five-part working loop
Specify the user decision and the cost of being wrong; ground the model in trusted data and tools; constrain it with
schemas, timeouts, and permissions; evaluate it on a representative dataset; then operate it with traces, cost limits, and
incident paths. The loop repeats as evidence changes, not as a one-off launch checklist. For example, a schema failure
might send you back to prompt or model choice, while a new data source may require retrieval and evaluation changes.
Engineering judgement is knowing which part of the loop the evidence implicates.
Judgement over model worship
Start with the simplest architecture that can pass the evaluation. A rules engine, a classifier, or a fixed workflow may beat
an agent on accuracy, latency, and cost for narrowly defined tasks. Add model complexity only when a measured failure
justifies it, and record the trade-off. Choosing a cheaper model is an engineering decision only after quality has been
tested, not before.
KEY TERMS
 Inference                        A single model call that produces output from an input, typically billed by input and output tokens and
                                  measured for latency.
 Orchestration                    The application code that assembles context, calls models and tools, validates results, and decides the next
                                  step.
 Evaluation set                   A versioned collection of representative inputs with expected properties or labels, used to score changes
                                  consistently.

  MENTAL MODEL The AI engineer is the ship's engineer, not the engine designer: the engine matters, but someone must wire the fuel,
  alarms, steering, and maintenance so the voyage completes.

lessons.subtitle: See the big picture of how modern AI apps are built, piece by piece.

why_it_matters: Understanding the pieces before building makes everything less confusing. You'll see how user interface, backend, AI model, data, and monitoring all work together.

core_concepts.title: The Five Layers of an AI App
core_concepts.content: Every modern AI app has layers: (1) User Interface - what people see and click, (2) Backend/API - the brain that coordinates everything, (3) AI Model - the intelligence that generates responses, (4) Data Layer - stores user data, past conversations, etc., (5) Infrastructure/Operations - keeps it running, secure, and fast.

core_concepts.title: How a Request Flows
core_concepts.content: When a user asks a question: it goes from UI → Backend (which adds context, checks permissions) → AI Model (generates answer) → Backend (processes answer, saves it) → UI (shows to user). Understanding this flow helps you debug when things go wrong.

core_concepts.title: Building This Course's App
core_concepts.content: Throughout this course, you'll build all these layers for your own AI app. You'll start simple and add pieces each module until you have a complete, production-ready system.

key_terms.definition: The part users interact with - forms, buttons, chat interface
Server code that handles logic, talks to databases and AI models
Where your app stores information permanently
Making your app available on the internet for others to use
How long it takes for your app to respond (measured in milliseconds/seconds)

lessons.mental_model: An AI app is like a restaurant: UI = dining room (customers see this), Backend = kitchen (does the work), AI Model = special chef, Database = pantry/storage, Deployment/Operations = keeping doors open 24/7.
worked_example: A customer asks a retail assistant, 'Where is order 4821, and can I still change the address?' The browser sends the message to a FastAPI service, which authenticates the session and loads six recent turns. The orchestrator retrieves two shipping-policy chunks and calls the order service, which responds in 340 ms with status packed and address_editable false. The model must return an answer plus source IDs; validation confirms both citations exist. The order service then exceeds its 800 ms deadline on a second attempt, so the assistant reports the known policy, says the live status is temporarily unavailable, and offers a callback. The trace records 3.2 seconds total, 1,180 input tokens, 96 output tokens, and the degraded path; no order status is invented.
steps: Open a chat AI product in your browser, use the network panel to capture one request, and list every visible hand-off and payload.
Draw the six layers and place each hand-off in the layer that owns it, including data stores and background jobs.
For each external call, write a timeout, retry policy, validation rule, and user-visible fallback.
Mark which facts must come from a system of record and which may come from retrieved documents.
Implement a trace ID that survives success, validation failure, and fallback, then verify it appears in every log line.

code.title: A boundary-focused request handler that validates citations, records a trace, and degrades safely when generation fails.
what_to_notice: The trust layer rejects a plausible answer with zero valid citations instead of showing it to the user.
The trace ID is created before retrieval, so a failure still produces a searchable record.

Authentication, quotas, persistence, and streaming are deliberately outside this function; those belong to other layers and must not be forgotten. Three pages per lesson Page 11 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Treating the model as a database and asking it for facts that live in an order or account system.
Putting all conversation state into one ever-growing prompt instead of loading and trimming the relevant history.

Anatomy of a Modern AI Application
Trace one request through six layers and learn where reliability is won or lost before a framework hides the details.
AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 3 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A model call is only one dependency in a distributed system that also includes authentication, databases, retrieval, tools,
and networks. Real incidents often come from a missing timeout, a malformed response, or a stale index rather than a
weak model. Seeing the whole request path makes those failures visible before users find them.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Draw the six layers of an AI application and state the responsibility of each.
 • Follow a streamed request from client to persisted trace and name the artefacts produced.
 • Assign a timeout, validation rule, and fallback to every external dependency on the request path.
CORE CONCEPTS
Six layers, six contracts
The interface accepts input and explains progress; the backend authenticates, authorises, limits, and persists;
orchestration assembles context and controls the model loop; model access selects a provider and accounts for usage; the
data layer holds records, caches, files, and vectors; and the trust layer validates outputs, traces behaviour, and enforces
policy. Each boundary should have an explicit input, output, timeout, and failure behaviour. Frameworks may collapse
several boxes into one file, but the contracts still exist.
One request, many hand-offs
A chat turn begins with HTTPS, authentication, quota checks, and conversation history. The orchestrator retrieves two to
six relevant chunks, builds a prompt, and calls a model through a gateway. Tokens stream back while the backend
assembles the full response, validates schema and citations, and persists the turn with token counts, latency, model
version, and a trace ID. Background work updates analytics, memory, and evaluation samples. If the client disconnects,
the server should cancel downstream work rather than paying for an answer nobody receives.
Failure is designed, not discovered
Every remote call needs a deadline, and the total deadline must fit inside the user-facing latency target. A retrieval
timeout might degrade to a plain answer with a warning; an order-service timeout must not become an invented order
status. Validate model output against a schema and check that cited sources actually exist. A fallback is only useful if it has
been exercised, so test it deliberately and record which path served each request.
KEY TERMS
 Orchestrator                     The code that builds context, invokes models and tools, validates results, and controls the sequence of a
                                  request.
 Trace ID                         A unique identifier attached to every log, span, and record produced by one request so the path can be
                                  reconstructed.
 System of record                 The authoritative source for a fact, such as the order database, which must be queried rather than guessed.

  MENTAL MODEL An AI feature is a normal distributed system with one probabilistic dependency. Treat the model like a remote service
  that is slow, expensive, occasionally wrong, and can change without notice.

Anatomy of a Modern AI Application
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A customer asks a retail assistant, 'Where is order 4821, and can I still change the address?' The browser sends the
message to a FastAPI service, which authenticates the session and loads six recent turns. The orchestrator retrieves two
shipping-policy chunks and calls the order service, which responds in 340 ms with status packed and address_editable
false. The model must return an answer plus source IDs; validation confirms both citations exist. The order service then
exceeds its 800 ms deadline on a second attempt, so the assistant reports the known policy, says the live status is
temporarily unavailable, and offers a callback. The trace records 3.2 seconds total, 1,180 input tokens, 96 output tokens,
and the degraded path; no order status is invented.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Open a chat AI product in your browser, use the network panel to capture one request, and list every visible hand-off and
      payload.
2.    Draw the six layers and place each hand-off in the layer that owns it, including data stores and background jobs.
3.    For each external call, write a timeout, retry policy, validation rule, and user-visible fallback.
4.    Mark which facts must come from a system of record and which may come from retrieved documents.
5.    Implement a trace ID that survives success, validation failure, and fallback, then verify it appears in every log line.
CODE
A boundary-focused request handler that validates citations, records a trace, and degrades safely when generation fails.
  from dataclasses import dataclass
  from uuid import uuid4
  from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError
  class Draft(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    cited_chunk_ids: list[int]
  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Turn:
    trace_id: str
    answer: str
    source_ids: list[int]
  def handle(question, retrieve, generate) -> Turn:
    tid, chunks = uuid4().hex, retrieve(question, limit=4)
    try:
       draft = Draft.model_validate(generate(question, chunks, timeout_s=8))
       ids = [i for i in draft.cited_chunk_ids if 0 <= i < len(chunks)]
       if not ids:
          raise ValueError("no valid citation")
       return Turn(tid, draft.answer, ids)
    except (ValidationError, ValueError, TimeoutError):
       return Turn(tid, "I cannot verify that answer right now.", [])
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The trust layer rejects a plausible answer with zero valid citations instead of showing it to the user.
 → The trace ID is created before retrieval, so a failure still produces a searchable record.
 → Authentication, quotas, persistence, and streaming are deliberately outside this function; those belong to other layers and
   must not be forgotten.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Boring infrastructure and data Start with a container runtime, a relational database, object storage, and a cache or queue only when a workload requires one. PostgreSQL with pgvector can hold millions of chunks and, more importantly, keeps metadata filtering, permissions, and transactions beside your application data. A dedicated vector database earns its place when scale, indexing features, or isolation justify another service to operate. The same logic applies to Kubernetes: three engineers serving 12,000 documents a month rarely need it. Model access through a stable boundary A gateway gives the application one interface for providers while centralising keys, quotas, retries, fallbacks, caching, and usage accounting. It also lets you switch models without editing every service. Keep the gateway thin: validate the request, enforce a timeout, route to a provider, normalise the response, and record cost. If the gateway becomes a second application with its own agent framework and business rules, it has stopped reducing complexity. Evaluation and operations are stack layers A stack is incomplete without a versioned evaluation set, a way to run it in CI, structured logs, traces, and cost dashboards. These tools answer different questions: evaluations ask whether quality changed, traces ask where a request spent time, and dashboards ask whether the service is healthy and affordable. Instrument the request path before launch, because reconstructing it after an incident is expensive. Keep prompt, model, and dataset versions linked in every result.

code.title: A provider-neutral gateway call with explicit timeouts and token accounting from the response.
code.code:
import os
import httpx
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Completion(BaseModel):
  text: str
  input_tokens: int
  output_tokens: int
async def complete(prompt: str, model: str = "small") -> Completion:
  base = os.environ["MODEL_GATEWAY_URL"].rstrip("/")
  headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['GATEWAY_TOKEN']}"}
  payload = {"model": model, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]}
  timeout = httpx.Timeout(20.0, connect=2.0)
  async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=timeout) as client:
     r = await client.post(f"{base}/v1/chat", json=payload, headers=headers)
     r.raise_for_status()
     data = r.json()
  usage = data.get("usage", {})
  return Completion(
     text=data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"],
     input_tokens=usage.get("prompt_tokens", 0),
     output_tokens=usage.get("completion_tokens", 0),
  )
what_to_notice: The connect timeout is two seconds while the read timeout is twenty, so a dead gateway fails quickly without cutting off a legitimate long generation.
Retries are intentionally absent; retrying a 401 makes an auth problem worse, and a retry policy belongs in the gateway or a wrapper that handles 429 and 5xx only.

Missing usage fields default to zero, which keeps the call working but can silently under-report cost; production should alert on absent accounting. Three pages per lesson Page 14 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Hard-coding one provider's request schema throughout the application, then discovering that a fallback needs a second schema.
Logging full prompts and responses that contain customer data, secrets, or personal information.
production_notes: Apply per-tenant quotas, budget alarms, and rate limits at the gateway; unbounded model access is an availability and finance risk.
Pin model and dependency versions, but rehearse upgrades against the evaluation set because hosted models can change behaviour.
Test backup restoration and provider failover, not just their configuration; a documented fallback that has never run is an assumption.
checklist: I can name each stack layer and the smallest tool that satisfies its contract.
Every managed service has a stated reason, owner, cost estimate, and exit or revisit condition.
The model is reached through a boundary with timeouts, quotas, and usage accounting.
Traces, logs, evaluation reports, and cost data are designed before launch.
The stack fits the team's operating capacity, not just the architecture diagram.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The dependency spine Modules 1 and 2 build Python and backend foundations, because every later feature needs a request, validation, storage, and tests. Modules 3 and 4 add model behaviour, prompting, structured output, streaming, and reliability. Module 5 adds retrieval; Modules 6 to 8 add agents, orchestration, and MCP; Modules 9 to 11 cover production, deployment, and system design; Module 12 integrates them. Skipping the backend or production modules does not save time, because their gaps reappear as incident work during the capstone. One product through-line Choose a capstone domain by Module 2 and keep using the same repository. Each module then adds a capability to one product: extraction to the intake path, RAG to the knowledge path, tools to actions, MCP to integration, evaluation to the release gate, and deployment to the delivery path. Reuse is not laziness; it exposes the integration problems that isolated demos hide. Write down the scope boundary so the capstone stays achievable alongside the lessons. Cadence, gates, and evidence A workable pace is five to seven hours a week for roughly twenty weeks, with at least half the time spent building. Each module ends with a small artefact, a passing self-check, an evaluation number, and a short decision record. Gate progress on demonstrated capability, not on finishing a page count: if you cannot explain and reproduce the artefact, repeat the relevant task. Two buffer weeks are part of the plan, not evidence of failure.

AI Engineering Foundations · Lesson 5 of 5 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A broad curriculum fails when it becomes an unordered playlist. Dependencies matter: agents assume HTTP, tool calling,
and state, while production work assumes a working application to observe. A plan protects the scarce resource, your
attention, and turns each module into evidence rather than another unfinished tutorial.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Sequence the modules and explain which prerequisites each later module assumes.
 • Map module artefacts to capstone capabilities so work is reused rather than discarded.
 • Create a dated study plan with module gates, buffer time, and a measurable definition of progress.
CORE CONCEPTS
The dependency spine
Modules 1 and 2 build Python and backend foundations, because every later feature needs a request, validation, storage,
and tests. Modules 3 and 4 add model behaviour, prompting, structured output, streaming, and reliability. Module 5 adds
retrieval; Modules 6 to 8 add agents, orchestration, and MCP; Modules 9 to 11 cover production, deployment, and system
design; Module 12 integrates them. Skipping the backend or production modules does not save time, because their gaps
reappear as incident work during the capstone.
One product through-line
Choose a capstone domain by Module 2 and keep using the same repository. Each module then adds a capability to one
product: extraction to the intake path, RAG to the knowledge path, tools to actions, MCP to integration, evaluation to the
release gate, and deployment to the delivery path. Reuse is not laziness; it exposes the integration problems that isolated
demos hide. Write down the scope boundary so the capstone stays achievable alongside the lessons.
Cadence, gates, and evidence
A workable pace is five to seven hours a week for roughly twenty weeks, with at least half the time spent building. Each
module ends with a small artefact, a passing self-check, an evaluation number, and a short decision record. Gate progress
on demonstrated capability, not on finishing a page count: if you cannot explain and reproduce the artefact, repeat the
relevant task. Two buffer weeks are part of the plan, not evidence of failure.
KEY TERMS
 Prerequisite                     A skill or artefact that later material assumes you can already use without instruction.
 Artefact                         A concrete output such as a service, evaluation report, diagram, or decision record that demonstrates a
                                  capability.
 Capstone phase                   One of the thirteen stages in Module 12, each producing a reviewed part of the final platform.

  MENTAL MODEL A curriculum is a dependency graph, not a playlist: do not play a module until the modules it imports are working.

lessons.title: Python prerequisites
lessons.subtitle: Learn the Python basics you'll actually use when building AI apps - data, loops, and reading errors.
why_it_matters: When working with AI APIs, you'll constantly deal with data in the form of lists and dictionaries (JSON). You'll need to loop through results, extract what you need, and handle errors when things go wrong. This lesson teaches just enough Python to get you comfortable with these patterns - no need to become a Python expert, just learn what AI engineers use every day.
outcomes: Understand Python's basic data types (strings, numbers, lists, dictionaries)

core_concepts.title: Data Types You'll Use Every Day
core_concepts.content: Think of data types like different kinds of containers. Strings hold text (like messages). Numbers hold values (like costs or counts). Lists hold ordered collections (like a list of search results). Dictionaries hold key-value pairs (like a person's info - name, email). When you get data from an AI API, it almost always comes as a dictionary with lists inside it. Learning to navigate these is like learning to read a map.

core_concepts.title: Loops and Making Decisions
core_concepts.content: Loops let you do the same thing many times without repeating code. If you get 10 results from an API, a loop can process each one. If/else statements let your code make decisions - like 'if the answer is too long, shorten it' or 'if there's an error, try again'. These are the building blocks of smart, flexible code.

core_concepts.title: Reading Errors (Your Superpower)
core_concepts.content: Every programmer sees errors constantly - even experts! The difference is knowing how to read them. A Python traceback tells you exactly what went wrong and where. The most important line is usually at the bottom - it tells you the error type and message. The lines above show the path your code took to get there. Learning to read tracebacks will save you hours of frustration.

key_terms.definition: An ordered collection of items in square brackets [ ]. Like a shopping list - order matters.
A collection of key-value pairs in curly braces { }. Like a contact card - look up by name to find info.
Code that repeats - does something for each item in a list or until a condition is met.
Python's way of showing you where and why an error happened, with the full chain of calls.
Python's way of saying 'nothing here' or 'no value'. Different from zero or empty string!

lessons.mental_model: Working with API data is like unpacking a delivery box. The outer box might be a dictionary with labels (keys) pointing to what's inside. Some things might be single items, others might be lists of items. Your job is to open it up and grab exactly what you need.

Python prerequisites
Get your Python to the level AI code demands: correct data shapes, predictable iteration, and tracebacks you can actually
read.
Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 1 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Almost every AI task starts as data wrangling: parse a response, filter records, compute a cost, print a result. If list, dict,
string, and loop behaviour is shaky, every later lesson becomes a debugging session about Python rather than about
models. This lesson closes those gaps quickly, with the subset of the language that appears in production clients, loaders,
and evaluation scripts.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Run a script, a module, and a REPL session, and explain which one you are using when a bug appears.
 • Manipulate the list-of-dicts structures that arrive from every model and data API without mutating them by accident.
 • Read a traceback to the failing line and fix the three errors that account for most beginner scripts.
CORE CONCEPTS
The data shapes you will meet
Model APIs return nested dictionaries: a response with choices, usage, and finish_reason. Catalogues are lists of
dictionaries. Your job is to move between those shapes, keep types honest, and avoid silent coercion. Know the difference
between rebinding a name and mutating an object, because appending to a list while looping over that same list is how
scripts double their data. Treat None as a distinct value, never as zero or an empty string.
Comprehensions and lazy iteration
Use a list comprehension when you need every result; use a generator when you need one pass over a large file.
dict.get(key, default) beats a KeyError; enumerate and zip remove index bookkeeping. Unpacking a row into named
variables documents its shape at the point of use. Sorting a list of dicts with key=lambda r: r["cost"] is stable, so equal
costs keep their original order, which matters for reproducible reports.
Tracebacks and the run loop
Run scripts as modules (python -m package.module) so imports resolve the same way in development and CI. Read a
traceback bottom-up: the last frame is where the exception surfaced, but the cause is often the line that passed a string
where an integer was expected. python -c and the REPL are for one-line experiments only; anything you want to keep
belongs in a file under version control.
KEY TERMS
 Truthiness                       The rule that empty containers, 0, None, and the empty string evaluate as false, while any non-empty
                                  container or non-zero number is true.
 Comprehension                    A one-expression loop that builds a list, dictionary, or generator from an iterable, optionally filtered by a
                                  condition.
 Traceback                        The report Python prints when an exception escapes, listing each frame from the outermost call to the failing
                                  line.

  MENTAL MODEL Python is a data-plumbing language: names point at objects, and most bugs are a wrong shape, a wrong type, or an
  object mutated by a function you did not suspect.

On her first day, Tomas inherits a 60-line script that reports average model prices. It prints GBP 0.00 for every provider.

guards the fix. The decision: convert types once, at ingestion, never in formatting code.
STEP BY STEP

2.    Open a REPL and test list slicing, dict.get, and an f-string until results match your predictions.
3.    Write a ten-line script that aggregates a hard-coded list of five model dictionaries by provider.

CODE
One-pass aggregation with the type conversion kept at the edge, and a formatted report a reviewer can check.
  from collections import defaultdict

  models = [
    {"name": "Atlas-S", "provider": "Northwind", "price": "0.50"},
    {"name": "Atlas-L", "provider": "Northwind", "price": "3.00"},
    {"name": "Kestrel-8", "provider": "Cobalt", "price": "1.20"},
  ]

  def provider_average(rows: list[dict[str, str]]) -> dict[str, float]:
    totals: dict[str, list[float]] = defaultdict(list)
    for row in rows:
      totals[row["provider"]].append(float(row["price"]))
    return {name: round(sum(v) / len(v), 3) for name, v in sorted(totals.items())}

  if __name__ == "__main__":
     for provider, avg in provider_average(models).items():
       print(f"{provider:<10} USD {avg:.2f} per million tokens")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The float() conversion happens once at the edge; formatting later cannot repair a price that arrived as "0.50 USD" and
   raised ValueError.
 → defaultdict never raises KeyError, so a misspelled provider silently becomes a new bucket instead of a visible failure.
 → The average hides outliers: one model at USD 15 per million drags the mean far above what most requests pay.

lessons.title: Python project structure
lessons.subtitle: Lay out a Python package so imports resolve the same way on your laptop, in tests, and in the container that runs your API
why_it_matters: AI clients grow from one script into a package with schemas, an HTTP layer, retries, and tests. Without a layout, imports work only from the directory you happen to be in, and the first CI run or container build fails. A deliberate structure keeps the dependency graph acyclic, makes the public surface obvious, and lets you move a module without editing every caller.
outcomes: Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
Draw the dependency direction between schemas, I/O, domain logic, and the command-line entry point.
Explain why python -m package avoids the import failures caused by running a file inside the package.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: src layout, not script soup Place the importable package under src/, for example src/model_catalog/, and keep tests, data, and configuration beside it at the repository root. The extra directory prevents Python from importing the working directory by accident, so a test can only pass by importing the installed package. pyproject.toml declares the package name, version, and dependencies; one editable install then serves your shell, editor, and CI. Boundaries follow change Group code by the reason it changes, not by technical type. schemas.py holds data shapes, loader.py owns file and network I/O, catalog.py holds pure business rules, and main.py wires them together. Dependencies point one way: main imports catalog, catalog imports schemas, and schemas import nothing from the project. When loader needs catalog you have a cycle, and the fix is usually a new module or an injected function. Entry points and import-time calm Expose one main() and guard it with if __name__ == "__main__":. Add __main__.py so python -m model_catalog works, and use absolute imports such as from model_catalog.loader import load_models everywhere inside the package. Importing a module must not read files, call an API, or start a server; those belong in main(), where tests can choose not to run them. Keep one public function per module and import helpers from their own module, not through a package re- export.

key_terms.definition: The single function or module Python runs to start the program, kept separate from the library code it calls.

A failure where two modules import each other, usually revealing that responsibilities or dependency direction are wrong. MENTAL MODEL A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb through a window to reach the database.

lessons.mental_model: Think of python project structure as a building block - once you understand it, you'll use it again and again as you build your AI app.
worked_example: At a four-person team building a model-catalogue client, loader.py starts importing catalog.py to reuse a price formatter, while catalog.py already imports loader.py to read files. Tests pass on one laptop because the modules were imported in a lucky order, then fail in CI with ImportError: partially initialized module. In the review, the team moves the formatter into formatting.py, points both modules at it, and adds __main__.py. They also replace sys.path.append("..") in the tests with an editable install. The CI run drops from four minutes to ninety seconds because tests no longer resolve three copies of the package. The decision: no module may import a module that imports it, and shared helpers get their own home.
steps: Create src/model_catalog/ with __init__.py plus schemas, loader, catalog, main, and __main__ modules.
Declare the package in pyproject.toml, then install it editable so import model_catalog resolves from any directory.
Move one function at a time into its module and run the entry point after each move to catch import errors early.
Delete every sys.path modification and make the tests import the package by its installed name.
Draw the import graph on paper; if it contains a cycle, extract the shared helper before adding another feature.

code.title: A package entry point that keeps import-time free of I/O and supports python -m model_catalog.
code.code:
# src/model_catalog/__main__.py
from model_catalog.catalog import summarise
from model_catalog.loader import load_models

def main(path: str = "data/models.json") -> int:
  rows = load_models(path)
  summary = summarise(rows)
  print(f"{summary['count']} models across {summary['providers']} providers")
  return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
   raise SystemExit(main())
what_to_notice: __main__.py exists so python -m model_catalog runs the package; without it, users must know a file path inside src.
The guard means importing main in a test does not read data/models.json or print anything, keeping tests fast.

Absolute imports inside the package survive renames of the working directory; relative imports break when a module moves levels. YOUR WORKING NOTES Three pages per lesson Page 24 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Adding sys.path.append in tests instead of installing the package, so CI and containers keep failing.
Putting HTTP calls, file reads, and argument parsing in __init__.py, where every import pays for them.
Creating one utils.py that everything imports, which becomes a second, unnamed package with no owner.
production_notes: Build the wheel and install it in a clean container as part of CI; this catches missing package data before deployment does.
Keep the import graph acyclic and shallow so cold-start time and test collection stay predictable as the client grows.

Lay out a Python package so imports resolve the same way on your laptop, in tests, and in the container that runs your API
client.
Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 2 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI clients grow from one script into a package with schemas, an HTTP layer, retries, and tests. Without a layout, imports
work only from the directory you happen to be in, and the first CI run or container build fails. A deliberate structure keeps
the dependency graph acyclic, makes the public surface obvious, and lets you move a module without editing every caller.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Create a src layout with a package, an entry point, and a tests directory that imports the package without path hacks.
 • Draw the dependency direction between schemas, I/O, domain logic, and the command-line entry point.
 • Explain why python -m package avoids the import failures caused by running a file inside the package.
CORE CONCEPTS
src layout, not script soup
Place the importable package under src/, for example src/model_catalog/, and keep tests, data, and configuration beside
it at the repository root. The extra directory prevents Python from importing the working directory by accident, so a test
can only pass by importing the installed package. pyproject.toml declares the package name, version, and dependencies;
one editable install then serves your shell, editor, and CI.
Boundaries follow change
Group code by the reason it changes, not by technical type. schemas.py holds data shapes, loader.py owns file and
network I/O, catalog.py holds pure business rules, and main.py wires them together. Dependencies point one way: main
imports catalog, catalog imports schemas, and schemas import nothing from the project. When loader needs catalog you
have a cycle, and the fix is usually a new module or an injected function.
Entry points and import-time calm
Expose one main() and guard it with if __name__ == "__main__":. Add __main__.py so python -m model_catalog works,
and use absolute imports such as from model_catalog.loader import load_models everywhere inside the package.
Importing a module must not read files, call an API, or start a server; those belong in main(), where tests can choose not
to run them. Keep one public function per module and import helpers from their own module, not through a package re-
export.
KEY TERMS
 src layout                       A repository convention where the importable package lives under src/, so tests import the installed package
                                  rather than loose files.
 Entry point                      The single function or module Python runs to start the program, kept separate from the library code it calls.
 Circular import                  A failure where two modules import each other, usually revealing that responsibilities or dependency
                                  direction are wrong.

  MENTAL MODEL A package is a building with labelled rooms: the corridor is short, the doors face one direction, and you never climb
  through a window to reach the database.

1.    Create src/model_catalog/ with __init__.py plus schemas, loader, catalog, main, and __main__ modules.
2.    Declare the package in pyproject.toml, then install it editable so import model_catalog resolves from any directory.
3.    Move one function at a time into its module and run the entry point after each move to catch import errors early.
4.    Delete every sys.path modification and make the tests import the package by its installed name.
5.    Draw the import graph on paper; if it contains a cycle, extract the shared helper before adding another feature.
CODE
A package entry point that keeps import-time free of I/O and supports python -m model_catalog.
  # src/model_catalog/__main__.py
  from model_catalog.catalog import summarise
  from model_catalog.loader import load_models

  def main(path: str = "data/models.json") -> int:
    rows = load_models(path)
    summary = summarise(rows)
    print(f"{summary['count']} models across {summary['providers']} providers")
    return 0

  if __name__ == "__main__":
     raise SystemExit(main())

 → __main__.py exists so python -m model_catalog runs the package; without it, users must know a file path inside src.
 → The guard means importing main in a test does not read data/models.json or print anything, keeping tests fast.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A function is a contract The signature states what goes in; the return statement states what comes out; the docstring states what can go wrong. Callers should not need to read the body to use it. Name the unit in the function name: parse_usage(response) returns a Usage or raises ValueError, and it never prints, retries, or writes a file. When a function needs a paragraph explaining its order of operations, it is probably two functions. Keep printing, network calls, and file writes at the edges; a pure function that takes data and returns data can be tested with literals. Inject collaborators such as a fetch callable instead of importing a module-level client, so a test can pass a fake. Composition over cleverness Build behaviour by calling small functions, not by adding flags. A retry parameter that changes the return type, or a mode string that selects three code paths, is a sign the caller should choose a different function. Keyword-only arguments such as *, timeout_s: float = 10.0 make call sites readable and let you add parameters without breaking positional callers. Return early on errors; keep the happy path unindented.

CODE
Per-case error isolation with an injected fetch callable, so the batch survives one bad response and tests run offline.
  from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable

  def score_case(case: dict[str, str], fetch: Callable[[str], str]) -> dict[str, object]:
    try:
       score = float(fetch(case["prompt"]))
       return {"id": case["id"], "score": score, "error": None}
    except (KeyError, ValueError) as exc:
       return {"id": case.get("id", "?"), "score": None, "error": type(exc).__name__}

  def run(
     cases: Iterable[dict[str, str]], fetch: Callable[[str], str]
  ) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
     return [score_case(case, fetch) for case in cases]

  def fake_fetch(prompt: str) -> str:
    return "0.8" if "safe" in prompt else "not-a-number"

  print(run([{"id": "c1", "prompt": "safe?"}, {"id": "c2", "prompt": "bad"}], fake_fetch))

lessons.title: Type hints
lessons.subtitle: Annotate the boundaries of your client so editors, mypy, and reviewers catch wrong shapes before a request reaches the
why_it_matters: Type hints are executable documentation that a checker verifies. In AI code they are especially valuable because the data is loosely typed JSON: a response may have usage or not, a finish reason is one of four strings, and a missing field becomes None three calls later. Annotations move those failures from production logs into your editor and CI, at the cost of a few minutes per function.
outcomes: Annotate functions and data shapes with builtin generics, unions, TypedDict, and Literal without resorting to Any.
Run mypy in strict mode on a package and triage errors by boundary, narrowing, and missing annotations.
Decide where runtime validation is still required despite a clean static check.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Types describe values, not variables An annotation says what a name may hold at that point, and mypy tracks it through assignments and branches. list[dict[str, float]] is a list of dictionaries with string keys and float values; dict[str, list[float]] is a different shape. Use X | None for values that may be absent and narrow with an early if value is None: return. Avoid Any, which silently disables checking for everything it touches. Model JSON with TypedDict and Literal TypedDict describes a dictionary with fixed keys and per-key types, which matches API payloads better than a wide dict[str, object]. Mark optional keys with NotRequired, or use total=False on a separate class. Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"] turns a magic string into a checked set of values. These are static shapes only: they do not validate a response at runtime, so a cast from json.loads is a promise you have not verified. Gradual typing and the checker loop Start with public functions and the data that crosses a module boundary; private helpers can stay unannotated until they are stable. Run mypy with strict = true in pyproject.toml, then fix errors by adding a missing annotation, narrowing a union, or correcting the shape. reveal_type(value) prints what the checker inferred, which is faster than guessing. Keep the checker in CI so a new Any cannot quietly spread.

key_terms.definition: An approach where some functions are fully annotated and checked while unannotated code is treated as compatible, allowing adoption over time.
The process where a type checker uses a runtime check, such as if x is not None, to prove a union has one specific member.

A typing construct describing a dictionary with known string keys and a distinct value type for each key. MENTAL MODEL Type hints are a contract sketch: cheap to draw, checked by a machine, and never a substitute for checking the parcel that actually arrived.

response at runtime, so a cast from json.loads is a promise you have not verified.

union, or correcting the shape. reveal_type(value) prints what the checker inferred, which is faster than guessing. Keep
the checker in CI so a new Any cannot quietly spread.

Type hints
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
During a migration to a second model provider, a client starts failing with TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +:
'NoneType' and 'int' in the cost report. The cause: the new provider omits completion_tokens for cached responses, and
the code summed usage.get("completion_tokens") unchecked. The team adds a Usage TypedDict with NotRequired keys,
annotates extract_usage(payload: dict[str, object]) -> Usage, and runs mypy strict, which surfaces 23 errors in four
modules. They fix the boundary first: parse into Usage with a default of zero and a warning log, then let the rest of the
code use plain integers. The decision: absent fields are normalised once, where the payload enters.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Add a [tool.mypy] section with strict = true and run it on the package to capture a baseline error count.
2.    Annotate the module boundaries first: loaders, HTTP calls, and anything that builds a prompt or parses a response.
3.    Replace bare dict and Any with TypedDict, Literal, and concrete generics, then re-run the checker.
4.    Use reveal_type on three confusing values and record what mypy inferred before changing the annotation.
5.    Add mypy to CI and reject new errors, keeping a short list of ignored modules with an owner and a date.
CODE
A TypedDict that reflects the provider contract, with optional usage and a Literal finish reason checked by mypy.
  from typing import Literal, NotRequired, TypedDict

  class Usage(TypedDict):
    prompt_tokens: int
    completion_tokens: NotRequired[int]

  class Response(TypedDict):
    finish_reason: Literal["stop", "length", "tool_calls"]
    usage: NotRequired[Usage]

  def output_tokens(response: Response) -> int:
    usage = response.get("usage")
    if usage is None:
       return 0
    return usage.get("completion_tokens", 0)

  print(output_tokens({"finish_reason": "stop"}))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → NotRequired reflects the API contract honestly; a required completion_tokens would force every test to invent a value.
 → The None check is what lets the checker narrow usage; indexing without it fails strict mode and would fail on a real cached
   response.
 → The annotation did not validate the JSON: a payload with prompt_tokens as the string "12" type-checks here and still breaks
   at runtime.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: State plus invariants A class earns its place when several functions share state that must remain valid together. A ModelClient owns base_url, timeout_s, and a usage counter; every method can assume the URL has no trailing slash because __init__ normalised it once. If your class has no state, or the state is a bag of unrelated settings, functions with parameters will be simpler. The test is whether an invariant needs protecting, not whether the domain sounds like a noun. Encapsulation is a convention Python has no private fields, only names with a leading underscore that signal intent. Build it

A client class grows to 780 lines covering chat, embeddings, uploads, retries, and CSV export. Every new endpoint copies

STEP BY STEP
1.    List the state a candidate class would own and write the invariant each field must satisfy after construction.
2.    If the list is empty or fields share no rule, keep functions; otherwise write __init__ that validates and normalises.
3.    Add __repr__, one classmethod factory, and underscore-prefixed attributes that callers must not touch.
4.    Replace any subclass with an injected collaborator, then write a fake that records calls for tests.

CODE
A small client that enforces its URL invariant, injects transport, and exposes usage state without leaking secrets.
  class ModelClient:
    def __init__(self, base_url: str, transport, *, timeout_s=10.0) -> None:
       if not base_url.startswith("https://"):
          raise ValueError("base_url must use https")
       self.base_url = base_url.rstrip("/")
       self.timeout_s = timeout_s
       self._transport = transport
       self._requests = 0

     @classmethod
     def from_env(cls, env, transport):
       return cls(env["MODEL_BASE_URL"], transport, timeout_s=float(env["TIMEOUT_S"]))

     def request(self, path: str, payload: dict) -> dict:
       self._requests += 1
       return self._transport(f"{self.base_url}{path}", payload, self.timeout_s)

     def __repr__(self) -> str:
       return f"ModelClient({self.base_url!r}, requests={self._requests})"

 → The constructor rejects a non-HTTPS base URL and strips a trailing slash, so every later method can trust the invariant.

 → __repr__ exposes the host and request count but not headers or keys, which is what you want in logs.

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.subtitle: Replace hand-written record classes with dataclasses, and choose frozen fields, factories, and validation deliberately.
lessons.meta: Python for AI Engineers · Lesson 6 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: AI pipelines are full of small records: a usage report, a scored case, a retrieved chunk, a cost summary. Writing __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ by hand for each is noise that hides bugs. Dataclasses generate those methods from the field list, so the shape of the data is visible in one place. The decisions that remain, defaults, mutability, and invariants, are where the real engineering sits.
outcomes: Define record types with the dataclass decorator, including defaults, field(default_factory=...), and computed properties.
Choose between mutable and frozen dataclasses based on whether identity or value semantics fit the data.
Explain why a dataclass is not a validation layer and where a schema model must take over.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Generated methods, visible shape The dataclass decorator reads the class annotations and generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__. Two instances with the same field values compare equal, which is what you want for records and what you rarely want for clients holding sockets. field(default_factory=list) supplies a new list per instance; a bare class-level list raises at definition because dataclasses reject the shared-default bug outright. asdict() converts nested dataclasses to dictionaries for JSON, at the cost of a deep copy. Frozen records and invariants dataclass(frozen=True) blocks attribute assignment and makes instances hashable, so a record can key a dictionary or live in a set. Use it for values that represent a fact at a point in time: a usage report does not change, a new report replaces it. Add __post_init__ to validate combinations the type system cannot express, such as a non-negative token count. Raise ValueError there; a record that exists should already be valid. Dataclass or schema model A dataclass describes data your code already trusts. It does not coerce the string "12" into 12, reject an unknown field, or explain a validation error to an API caller. Put a Pydantic model at the trust boundary, where JSON from a provider or a request body arrives, then convert to a dataclass for internal use if you want immutability and cheap construction. Using Pydantic everywhere is also defensible; mixing them without a rule creates confusion.

key_terms.definition: A dataclass whose attributes cannot be assigned after construction, making instances immutable and hashable by field value. post_init hook A method that runs after the generated initialiser, used to validate or derive fields that depend on each other. MENTAL MODEL A dataclass is a labelled parts tray: the fields are visible at a glance, each slot gets its own contents, and nothing enters the tray unvalidated.

The rewrite uses a frozen dataclass for CaseResult and a mutable dataclass with field(default_factory=list) for the summary, plus a post-init check that rejects a score outside 0 to 1. A property computes pass_rate from counts instead of storing it. The decision: records are frozen, aggregates are mutable, and invalid scores fail at construction rather than in a dashboard.

2.    Declare a BaseModel with typed fields, Field bounds, and extra='forbid'; add a cross-field validator where rules span fields.
