lessons.title: Agent vs Workflow
lessons.subtitle: Choose a workflow when the path is known and an agent only when the path must be discovered; most reliable systems
why_it_matters: Agents are attractive because they promise to handle anything, and that is exactly why they are hard to operate. A workflow encodes what the organisation already knows about a process: order, owners, retries, and approval points. An agent is justified when the steps cannot be enumerated in advance, such as investigating an unfamiliar incident. Choosing correctly decides whether a failure appears as a failing step with a clear owner or as an open-ended loop with an unexplained bill.
outcomes: Compare workflows and agents on predictability, cost, latency, and how easily each can be evaluated.
Decompose a task into fixed stages and isolate the one or two decisions that genuinely need model judgement.
Design a hybrid where a deterministic workflow owns the path and a bounded agent handles exceptions.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Known path versus discovered path A workflow executes a defined sequence: validate, enrich, classify, route, notify. Each step has an input contract, a timeout, and a retry rule, and the same input follows the same path. An agent decides the next step from the current observation, so the path can differ between runs. Neither is superior. Use a workflow when the process is stable and auditable; use an agent when the space of situations is too varied to enumerate and the cost of a wrong turn is bounded. Evaluate what you can reproduce A workflow can be tested step by step, with unit tests for each branch and a regression suite for the whole path. An agent is evaluated at the level of trajectories: did it choose useful tools, avoid unsafe actions, and stop in time? That evaluation is expensive and probabilistic. If a task has one correct sequence, a workflow gives you a deterministic test and a clear incident boundary. If it has many acceptable sequences, you need trajectory scoring and a step budget, not a brittle script. Hybrid is the normal answer Production systems usually run a workflow around a small agent. The workflow handles authentication, document parsing, schema validation, routing, retries, and persistence. It invokes an agent only for the exception: reconcile these three conflicting invoices, or find why this customer's delivery failed. The agent gets a narrow goal, three tools, a six-step budget, and a typed result the workflow can validate. Agent vs Workflow
Choose a workflow when the path is known and an agent only when the path must be discovered; most reliable systems
use both.
AI Agents · Lesson 3 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Agents are attractive because they promise to handle anything, and that is exactly why they are hard to operate. A
workflow encodes what the organisation already knows about a process: order, owners, retries, and approval points. An
agent is justified when the steps cannot be enumerated in advance, such as investigating an unfamiliar incident. Choosing
correctly decides whether a failure appears as a failing step with a clear owner or as an open-ended loop with an
unexplained bill.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Compare workflows and agents on predictability, cost, latency, and how easily each can be evaluated.
 • Decompose a task into fixed stages and isolate the one or two decisions that genuinely need model judgement.
 • Design a hybrid where a deterministic workflow owns the path and a bounded agent handles exceptions.
CORE CONCEPTS
Known path versus discovered path
A workflow executes a defined sequence: validate, enrich, classify, route, notify. Each step has an input contract, a
timeout, and a retry rule, and the same input follows the same path. An agent decides the next step from the current
observation, so the path can differ between runs. Neither is superior. Use a workflow when the process is stable and
auditable; use an agent when the space of situations is too varied to enumerate and the cost of a wrong turn is bounded.
Evaluate what you can reproduce
A workflow can be tested step by step, with unit tests for each branch and a regression suite for the whole path. An agent
is evaluated at the level of trajectories: did it choose useful tools, avoid unsafe actions, and stop in time? That evaluation
is expensive and probabilistic. If a task has one correct sequence, a workflow gives you a deterministic test and a clear
incident boundary. If it has many acceptable sequences, you need trajectory scoring and a step budget, not a brittle script.
Hybrid is the normal answer
Production systems usually run a workflow around a small agent. The workflow handles authentication, document
parsing, schema validation, routing, retries, and persistence. It invokes an agent only for the exception: reconcile these
three conflicting invoices, or find why this customer's delivery failed. The agent gets a narrow goal, three tools, a six-step
budget, and a typed result the workflow can validate. That keeps the predictable majority cheap and auditable while
preserving judgement where the path is genuinely unknown.

 Workflow                         A deterministic sequence of steps with explicit inputs, outputs, retries, and branch conditions, usually
                                  expressed as code or a graph.
 Trajectory                       The ordered record of an agent's model calls, tool calls, and observations during one task.
 Exception path                   The branch that handles cases the standard process cannot complete, often requiring judgement or human
                                  review.

  map, and a destination.

lessons.title: Anatomy of an Agent
lessons.subtitle: Name the seven parts of an agent: goal, policy, tools, runtime, state, guardrails, and trace, each with a written contract.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 4 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Agent tutorials collapse everything into a while loop with a prompt, which works until the tool returns an error, the model repeats itself, or a reviewer asks who approved the action. Naming the parts forces explicit contracts: what the goal contains, what the model may choose, what the runtime enforces, and what the trace preserves. That structure is what lets you test components separately, swap providers, and explain an incident without replaying a chat transcript.
outcomes: Draw an agent's components and state the contract each one exposes to the others.
Separate model judgement from runtime control so limits survive prompt changes and provider swaps.
Instrument one task end to end with a trace that explains every model call and tool result.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The seven components A working agent has a goal specification, a model policy, a tool registry, a loop runtime, a state store, guardrails, and a trace. The goal states the task and definition of done. The policy is the system prompt plus model configuration. Tools expose typed arguments and results. The runtime executes calls and enforces budgets. State carries conversation and task facts. Guardrails validate inputs, outputs, and permissions. The trace records decisions, durations, and costs. Contracts at every boundary The model proposes; the runtime disposes. A tool call must validate against a JSON schema before execution, and its result must be normalised into an observation the model can read. State should be a typed object with explicit fields, not an ever-growing message list. Guardrails sit on both sides: authorisation before a tool runs and schema validation before an answer reaches the user. When a boundary lacks a contract, failures leak across it as confusing text. The trace is a first-class component Each turn should produce a span containing the model, prompt version, token counts, latency, proposed tool, validated arguments, result status, and the next decision. Group spans by task ID and include the user, tenant, and policy version. Without this, a slow task looks like a slow model, and a wrong action looks like a prompt problem. Traces also feed evaluation: you can score trajectories from production samples and turn real failures into regression cases.

key_terms.definition: The system prompt, model identifier, sampling settings, and output schema that shape each decision.
The normalised result of a tool call, returned to the model as the next piece of evidence.

A deterministic check that validates input, output, permission, or budget before an action or response proceeds. MENTAL MODEL An agent is a small distributed system in one process: the model is a remote service, tools are APIs, and the runtime is the only component allowed to enforce a contract.

code.title: A typed state object and a trace span that records steps, tool latency, and failure status for every call.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any, Literal

@dataclass
class AgentState:
  task_id: str
  messages: list[dict[str, str]] = field(default_factory=list)
  steps: int = 0
  status: Literal["running", "done", "blocked"] = "running"

def record(state: AgentState, tool: str, ms: int,
      result: str) -> dict[str, Any]:
  state.steps += 1
  state.messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})
  span = {"task": state.task_id, "tool": tool, "ms": ms,
       "step": state.steps, "ok": not result.startswith("ERROR")}
  return span
what_to_notice: The state object is typed, so a missing task ID or an unexpected status fails at construction rather than deep in a prompt.
The span records whether the result was an error, which keeps failed calls visible instead of letting the model narrate success.

Messages still grow without bound here; production code must summarise or evict old observations under a token budget. Three pages per lesson Page 293 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Putting budgets and permissions in the system prompt, where a persuasive user message can argue with them.
Truncating tool output so aggressively that the model cannot tell success from failure and retries the call.
Logging only the final answer, leaving no record of which tools ran or what they returned.
production_notes: Emit one trace per task with child spans for model calls, tool calls, validation checks, and guardrail decisions.
Version prompts, tool schemas, and model identifiers together so a trace can be replayed against the exact configuration.
Cap observation size per tool and summarise long results, or context growth will silently raise cost and latency.

Guardrails check permissions before tools run and schemas before answers reach users.
A failed task can be explained from its trace without the chat transcript.

What is the risk of truncating a tool observation to a fixed character count?

lessons.title: Agent Loops
lessons.subtitle: Build the loop like a scheduler: every iteration costs tokens, every tool can fail, and every exit must be explicit.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 5 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: The loop is where agents earn their reputation for being unreliable. Each turn appends to the prompt, so cost and latency grow while the context fills with stale observations. Models can repeat a failed call, alternate between two tools, or declare success without evidence. A production loop needs explicit exit conditions and a record of why it stopped. Without them, debugging means reading a long transcript and guessing which turn went wrong.
outcomes: Implement a model-tool loop with step, time, and token budgets enforced by the runtime.
Detect repeated actions and missing progress before the loop burns its full budget.
Return a typed result on success, budget exhaustion, or tool failure instead of an indefinite answer.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One iteration, four decisions Each iteration asks four questions: is the goal met, is there budget left, what does the model propose, and is that proposal allowed? The runtime checks completion and budget before calling the model, validates the proposal after, executes or rejects it, and appends a compact observation. Keeping these checks outside the model makes behaviour predictable across providers and prompt edits. A loop that trusts the model to count its own steps will eventually run until the provider rate-limits it. Progress is measurable Track whether each turn adds new evidence: a new tool, new arguments, or a new result. If the same call and arguments appear twice, return the cached observation with a warning rather than paying for it again. If two consecutive turns produce no new information, stop with a partial result. Token growth is the other signal: when observations exceed roughly 60 percent of the context window, summarise or drop the oldest. These checks turn an open-ended loop into a bounded search. Exit with a typed result The loop should return a result object with status, answer, evidence, steps used, tokens, cost, and a reason. Status values such as completed, budget_exhausted, blocked, and failed let the caller decide whether to retry, escalate, or show partial work. Never let the loop simply stop returning text. The reason field is what turns an incident review from speculation into a fix, because it records which guard fired and what the agent had achieved at that point.

key_terms.definition: One cycle of model decision, optional tool execution, observation, and state update inside an agent task.
A runtime check that stops or warns when consecutive iterations add no new evidence or repeat an action.

A terminal state reached when step, time, token, or cost limits are hit before the goal is complete. MENTAL MODEL An agent loop is a while loop with a credit card attached: every iteration must prove progress, and the runtime must be able to cut it off.

worked_example: A research agent at a market-intelligence firm is asked to compare three competitors' pricing pages. Its first version loops for 47 seconds and 19 model calls, because a fetch tool returns a JavaScript shell and the agent retries the same URL four times. The team adds a repeated-call cache, a rule that two identical observations count as no progress, and a 12-step, 90-second, 40,000-token budget. They also cap each observation at 1,500 tokens and summarise older ones. On the same 40 tasks, median steps fall from 14 to 6, p95 latency from 47 to 18 seconds, and cost per task from USD 0.11 to USD 0.034. Three tasks now end as budget_exhausted with a partial comparison and a clear reason.

Agent Loops
Build the loop like a scheduler: every iteration costs tokens, every tool can fail, and every exit must be explicit.
AI Agents · Lesson 5 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
The loop is where agents earn their reputation for being unreliable. Each turn appends to the prompt, so cost and latency
grow while the context fills with stale observations. Models can repeat a failed call, alternate between two tools, or
declare success without evidence. A production loop needs explicit exit conditions and a record of why it stopped.
Without them, debugging means reading a long transcript and guessing which turn went wrong.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Implement a model-tool loop with step, time, and token budgets enforced by the runtime.
 • Detect repeated actions and missing progress before the loop burns its full budget.
 • Return a typed result on success, budget exhaustion, or tool failure instead of an indefinite answer.
CORE CONCEPTS
One iteration, four decisions
Each iteration asks four questions: is the goal met, is there budget left, what does the model propose, and is that proposal
allowed? The runtime checks completion and budget before calling the model, validates the proposal after, executes or
rejects it, and appends a compact observation. Keeping these checks outside the model makes behaviour predictable
across providers and prompt edits. A loop that trusts the model to count its own steps will eventually run until the
provider rate-limits it.
Progress is measurable
Track whether each turn adds new evidence: a new tool, new arguments, or a new result. If the same call and arguments
appear twice, return the cached observation with a warning rather than paying for it again. If two consecutive turns
produce no new information, stop with a partial result. Token growth is the other signal: when observations exceed
roughly 60 percent of the context window, summarise or drop the oldest. These checks turn an open-ended loop into a
bounded search.
Exit with a typed result
The loop should return a result object with status, answer, evidence, steps used, tokens, cost, and a reason. Status values
such as completed, budget_exhausted, blocked, and failed let the caller decide whether to retry, escalate, or show partial
work. Never let the loop simply stop returning text. The reason field is what turns an incident review from speculation
into a fix, because it records which guard fired and what the agent had achieved at that point.
KEY TERMS
 Iteration                        One cycle of model decision, optional tool execution, observation, and state update inside an agent task.
 No-progress detector             A runtime check that stops or warns when consecutive iterations add no new evidence or repeat an action.
 Budget exhaustion                A terminal state reached when step, time, token, or cost limits are hit before the goal is complete.

  MENTAL MODEL An agent loop is a while loop with a credit card attached: every iteration must prove progress, and the runtime must be
  able to cut it off.

Agent Loops
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A research agent at a market-intelligence firm is asked to compare three competitors' pricing pages. Its first version loops
for 47 seconds and 19 model calls, because a fetch tool returns a JavaScript shell and the agent retries the same URL four
times. The team adds a repeated-call cache, a rule that two identical observations count as no progress, and a 12-step,
90-second, 40,000-token budget. They also cap each observation at 1,500 tokens and summarise older ones. On the same
40 tasks, median steps fall from 14 to 6, p95 latency from 47 to 18 seconds, and cost per task from USD 0.11 to USD
0.034. Three tasks now end as budget_exhausted with a partial comparison and a clear reason.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define the loop's inputs, the result schema, and the four terminal statuses before writing the iteration body.
2.    Check completion, deadline, step count, and token spend at the top of every iteration.
3.    Validate the proposed tool call, execute it with a timeout, and append a capped observation to state.
4.    Fingerprint tool name plus arguments to detect repeats, and stop after two no-progress iterations.
5.    Run 40 tasks and report completion rate, steps, p95 latency, cost, and the distribution of stop reasons.
CODE
A bounded loop that stops on success, repeated evidence, or an exhausted step budget and reports why.
  from dataclasses import dataclass
  from typing import Callable

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Result:
    status: str
    answer: str
    steps: int

  def run(goal: str, step: Callable[[str], tuple[str, str]]) -> Result:
    seen: set[str] = set()
    for n in range(1, 13):
       kind, payload = step(goal)
       if kind == "final":
          return Result("completed", payload, n)
       if kind == "repeat" or payload in seen:
          return Result("blocked", "no new evidence", n)
       seen.add(payload)
       goal = f"{goal}\nOBSERVATION: {payload[:1200]}"
    return Result("budget_exhausted", "partial evidence", 12)
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The loop enforces steps and repeats but not wall-clock or token spend; production must check all four before each model
   call.
 → Observations are truncated to 1,200 characters, which keeps context bounded but can hide the end of a long result.
 → A repeated payload is treated as blocked rather than retried, because retrying the same call spends money without new
   evidence.

lessons.title: Tool Calling
lessons.subtitle: Tool calling is a contract: the model proposes JSON, your code validates and executes it, and the result returns as evidence.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 6 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: The model never executes anything. It emits a structured request, and your application decides whether to run it. That distinction is the whole security model and the main reliability lever. A vague schema invites wrong arguments, an unvalidated call reaches production systems, and an opaque error teaches the model nothing. Treat tool calling as an API boundary you design, test, and monitor, not a magic capability of the provider.
outcomes: Describe the request-response cycle that turns a model's tool proposal into a validated execution.
Write tool schemas that make invalid arguments hard and failure states explicit.
Return errors as observations the model can recover from, without leaking secrets or retrying writes.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The four-message cycle A tool-enabled turn has four parts: the user message, the model's tool call with a name and JSON arguments, the tool result message keyed to that call ID, and the model's next turn. The call ID matters because a model may propose several calls in parallel. Your code validates arguments, checks permissions, executes with a timeout, and returns a serialised result. The model sees only what you send back, so the observation format is part of the interface. Schemas are prompts with teeth Tool names, descriptions, and parameter schemas are the model's only reliable guide to what is callable. Use verbs and nouns precisely: search_orders, not query; require identifiers you cannot safely guess; enumerate status values instead of accepting free text. Keep each tool narrow enough to test, and state limits in the description, such as a maximum of 20 results. A schema that accepts anything turns the model into an optimistic guesser and pushes validation failures into your service. Errors are observations When a tool fails, return a structured error with a stable code, a short message, and whether a retry could help. Do not return a stack trace, SQL, secrets, or an HTML error page. Distinguish validation errors, which the model can fix by changing arguments, from authorisation and outage errors, which it cannot. After two failures of the same kind, the runtime should stop rather than let the model loop. Good error text is often the difference between recovery and a confident wrong answer.

CODE
One Pydantic model generates the tool schema and validates the model's arguments, with structured errors for recovery.
  from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

  class FareArgs(BaseModel):
    origin: str = Field(pattern=r"^[A-Z]{3}$")
    destination: str = Field(pattern=r"^[A-Z]{3}$")
    date: str = Field(pattern=r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$")

  FARE_TOOL = {"name": "get_fare", "parameters": FareArgs.model_json_schema()}

  def dispatch(name: str, raw: dict) -> dict:
    if name != "get_fare":
       return {"error": "unknown_tool", "retryable": False}
    try:
       args = FareArgs.model_validate(raw)
    except ValidationError as exc:
       fields = [e["loc"][0] for e in exc.errors()]
       return {"error": "invalid_arguments", "fields": fields, "retryable": True}
    return {"origin": args.origin, "destination": args.destination,
          "date": args.date, "fare_gbp": 148.20}

lessons.title: Designing Agent Tools
lessons.subtitle: Design tools the model can choose correctly: narrow contracts, honest descriptions, typed arguments, and failures it can
why_it_matters: A tool is the only place where model judgement becomes real action. If the description is vague, the model picks the wrong tool; if the schema is loose, invalid arguments reach your database; if the output is unbounded, one call fills the context window. Tool design is API design for a non-deterministic client that reads the documentation at runtime and never asks a clarifying question.
outcomes: Write tool names, descriptions, and argument schemas that let a model choose the right tool without guessing.
Split broad API surfaces into task-shaped tools that each complete one verifiable unit of work.
Define error contracts, side-effect rules, and output limits so a tool is safe to call unattended.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A tool is a contract, not a wrapper Every tool needs a name that states the action, a description that says when to use it and when not to, a typed argument schema, a bounded result, and a declared error shape. The model sees only that text, so ambiguity in the description becomes a wrong call in production. Write for a competent new colleague: what the tool returns, what it costs, which identifiers it needs, and what it refuses to do. Design for tasks, not endpoints One tool per REST endpoint forces the model to compose multi-step queries and multiplies selection errors. Prefer five task-shaped tools over forty CRUD operations: search_orders(query, status, limit) beats list_orders plus filter_orders plus get_order. Keep each tool at one decision boundary, return only fields the next step needs, and move fixed business rules into the implementation. Surface a new tool only when a measured task fails without it. Failures must be teachable A tool error is a prompt to the model. Return a stable code, a readable message, and a next action, for example INVALID_DATE with 'use ISO 8601, such as 2026-03-04'. Never return a stack trace or an HTML page. Mark each tool read- only or mutating, require an idempotency key for writes, and cap result sizes so one call cannot consume the context budget. The runtime, not the description, enforces those limits.

A tool that completes one user-meaningful operation rather than mirroring a single backend endpoint.

A caller-supplied identifier that lets a mutating tool detect and ignore duplicate executions of the same request. MENTAL MODEL A tool is a shop counter, not a warehouse tour: the model asks for one clearly described item, pays a known price, and gets a labelled package or a useful refusal.

A tool is the only place where model judgement becomes real action. If the description is vague, the model picks the
wrong tool; if the schema is loose, invalid arguments reach your database; if the output is unbounded, one call fills the
context window. Tool design is API design for a non-deterministic client that reads the documentation at runtime and
never asks a clarifying question.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write tool names, descriptions, and argument schemas that let a model choose the right tool without guessing.
 • Split broad API surfaces into task-shaped tools that each complete one verifiable unit of work.
 • Define error contracts, side-effect rules, and output limits so a tool is safe to call unattended.
CORE CONCEPTS
A tool is a contract, not a wrapper
Every tool needs a name that states the action, a description that says when to use it and when not to, a typed argument
schema, a bounded result, and a declared error shape. The model sees only that text, so ambiguity in the description
becomes a wrong call in production. Write for a competent new colleague: what the tool returns, what it costs, which
identifiers it needs, and what it refuses to do.
Design for tasks, not endpoints
One tool per REST endpoint forces the model to compose multi-step queries and multiplies selection errors. Prefer five
task-shaped tools over forty CRUD operations: search_orders(query, status, limit) beats list_orders plus filter_orders plus
get_order. Keep each tool at one decision boundary, return only fields the next step needs, and move fixed business rules
into the implementation. Surface a new tool only when a measured task fails without it.
Failures must be teachable
A tool error is a prompt to the model. Return a stable code, a readable message, and a next action, for example
INVALID_DATE with 'use ISO 8601, such as 2026-03-04'. Never return a stack trace or an HTML page. Mark each tool read-
only or mutating, require an idempotency key for writes, and cap result sizes so one call cannot consume the context
budget. The runtime, not the description, enforces those limits.
KEY TERMS
 Tool schema                      The name, description, and typed argument definition sent to the model so it can request a call.
 Task-shaped tool                 A tool that completes one user-meaningful operation rather than mirroring a single backend endpoint.
 Idempotency key                  A caller-supplied identifier that lets a mutating tool detect and ignore duplicate executions of the same
                                  request.

  MENTAL MODEL A tool is a shop counter, not a warehouse tour: the model asks for one clearly described item, pays a known price, and
  gets a labelled package or a useful refusal.

Designing Agent Tools
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
At a 30-person equity research firm, the agent has 14 tools mirroring the market-data API. On a 120-task benchmark it
chooses the wrong tool 23 percent of the time, mostly between get_prices and get_history. The team replaces them with
four tools: quote_snapshot, price_history, filing_search, and company_profile. Each description now states the unit, the
maximum range, and when to prefer the other tool. Argument schemas require ISO dates and cap history at two years.
Wrong-tool selection falls to 6 percent, median tokens per task drop from 9,400 to 5,100, and the remaining failures are
missing data rather than misselection. The team ships the four tools and logs every rejected argument for the next
review.
STEP BY STEP
1.    List the tasks the agent must complete, then map each to the smallest tool that finishes it without chaining.
2.    Name every tool with a verb and object, and write a description covering purpose, inputs, output shape, and exclusions.
3.    Define a strict argument schema with enums, formats, and limits; reject unknown fields instead of coercing them.
4.    Declare the tool read-only or mutating, require an idempotency key for writes, and cap returned rows and bytes.
5.    Run 30 real tasks against the toolset, count wrong selections and invalid arguments, then merge or rename the worst
      offenders.
CODE
One tool specification: enum-constrained status, capped limit, no extra arguments, and a declared read-only side-effect level.
  SEARCH_ORDERS = {
    "name": "search_orders",
    "description": "Find orders by status. Read-only. Returns at most 25 rows.",
    "mutating": False,
    "schema": {
       "type": "object",
       "required": ["status"],
       "properties": {
          "status": {"enum": ["open", "shipped", "cancelled"]},
          "limit": {"type": "integer", "maximum": 25},
       },
       "additionalProperties": False,
    },
  }

  def search_orders(status: str, limit: int = 10) -> dict:
    rows = [{"id": "A-1042", "status": status}]
    return {"rows": rows[:limit], "truncated": len(rows) > limit}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The schema forbids additional properties and caps limit at 25, so malformed or greedy arguments fail before reaching the
   order database.
 → The description states read-only and result size, which helps the model choose this tool over price_history without
   inventing a filter.
 → The stub returns one synthetic row; wire it to a parameterised query and keep the same validated arguments rather than
   passing raw model text.

Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Wrapping every endpoint one-to-one, leaving the model to chain six calls and invent intermediate identifiers.
2.     Writing 'Gets data' as the description, then blaming the model when it picks the wrong sibling tool.
3.     Letting a mutating tool accept free-text amounts with no idempotency key or confirmation step.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Version tool schemas and log the version with every call; a renamed argument silently breaks transcripts replayed during
      evaluation.
    ◆ Enforce authorisation inside each tool, not in the prompt; the runtime knows the caller identity and must check tenant
      scope per call.
    ◆ Alert on invalid-argument rate and wrong-tool retries per tool; a rising rate usually means description drift or an upstream
      schema change.
CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□      Every tool name is a verb plus object, and its description states when not to use it.
□      Argument schemas constrain formats, ranges, and enums, and reject unknown fields.
□      Each tool is read-only or mutating, and writes require an idempotency key.
□      Result sizes are capped in the implementation, not only described in the prompt.
□      Error responses carry a stable code, a readable message, and one next action.
SHORT QUESTIONS
1.     Why does a vague tool description cause more production failures than a weak model?

2.     When should you expose a single search tool instead of three narrower lookup tools?

3.     What belongs in a tool error so the model can recover without a human?

4.     Why must authorisation live inside the tool implementation rather than the system prompt?

5.     How would you detect that a tool description has drifted away from its implementation?

6.     Which measurements would justify adding a ninth tool to an eight-tool agent?

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Validate before you dispatch Treat every argument as untrusted input from a non-deterministic client. Check types, enums, ranges, and required fields against the same schema sent to the model, then resolve identifiers against your own database rather than trusting a name the model supplied. Reject unknown fields, normalise dates, and cap list lengths. Authorisation comes next: the runtime knows the user, tenant, and scopes, so it must check them before the tool touches a row. A validation failure returns a structured error and never executes code. Run independent calls concurrently but cap fan-out, because six parallel searches can saturate a rate limit or a database. Truncate rows, bytes, and characters, and tell the model what was cut. Stream large artefacts to object storage and return a reference. A tool that hangs consumes the whole run; a tool that returns 200 KB of HTML consumes the context window instead. Retry only idempotent operations or supply an idempotency key the downstream service honours. Wrap each attempt in a trace span with tool name, duration, argument hash, and outcome, but redact secrets and personal data. 2.    Resolve caller identity and tenant from the session, and check required scopes before the tool reads or writes.
3.    Apply a per-tool timeout under the step budget, cap concurrent calls, and truncate results with an explicit marker.

CODE
A single dispatch path with a per-call deadline and a structured error envelope that the agent loop can branch on.
  import asyncio
  from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable

  class ToolError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, code: str, retryable: bool, hint: str) -> None:
       super().__init__(hint)
       self.code, self.retryable, self.hint = code, retryable, hint

  async def execute(name: str, fn: Callable[[], Awaitable[dict]],
            timeout: float = 8.0) -> dict:
    try:
      content = await asyncio.wait_for(fn(), timeout=timeout)
      return {"status": "ok", "content": content}
    except TimeoutError:
      return {"status": "error", "code": "TIMEOUT", "retryable": True,
          "hint": f"{name} exceeded {timeout}s; narrow the query"}
    except ToolError as exc:
      return {"status": "error", "code": exc.code,
          "retryable": exc.retryable, "hint": exc.hint}

   becomes impossible.
 → ToolError carries a stable code and hint; never put a stack trace or raw provider response in hint because it can leak data.
 → The dispatcher does not validate arguments; call the schema validator first, or invalid input reaches fn and raises an

lessons.title: Agent State
lessons.subtitle: Keep the agent's run in an explicit, typed state object so it can pause, resume, audit, and fail without losing its place.
lessons.meta: AI Agents · Lesson 9 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: An agent is a loop, and a loop needs a place to remember where it is. If the transcript is the only state, a restart loses the plan, counters reset, and a retried step can send a second email. If state is scattered across instance variables, you cannot inspect a stalled run or hand it to a human. A typed state object makes progress, budget, and failure visible, which is what turns an unpredictable loop into an operable process.
outcomes: Separate durable run state from the prompt context and from long-term memory, naming what each stores.
Model the run as a small state machine with budgets, guarded transitions, and an explicit terminal condition.
Checkpoint state at step boundaries so a redeploy or approval wait resumes without repeating side effects.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Three different stores Context is what the model sees now: system prompt, recent turns, selected tool results. State is what the runtime knows about the run: goal, plan, step count, tokens spent, pending approval, status. Memory is what survives beyond the run. Mixing them is the usual cause of runaway loops and lost work. Context is rebuilt each step from state; state is checkpointed; memory is written deliberately. Keep the authoritative record outside the model, because the model can forget or contradict it. Make progress and limits explicit Represent the run as a state machine: queued, running, waiting_for_tool, waiting_for_human, completed, failed, cancelled. Each transition validates a guard, such as steps under 12 or spend under USD 0.40, and writes a reason. Store counters for steps, tokens, tool calls, wall-clock seconds, and cost. A terminal state must record why it was reached, so a failure is diagnosable and a cancellation is auditable rather than an empty transcript. Checkpoint at safe boundaries Write state after each tool result and before each model call, keyed by run ID and monotonic version. Use optimistic concurrency so two workers cannot resume the same run. On resume, verify the last completed step and skip side effects already recorded, using the same idempotency keys. Persist a schema version so old checkpoints can be migrated. Keep large blobs in object storage and store references, because checkpoints are read on every step.

key_terms.definition: The durable record of one agent execution: goal, step count, budget, pending actions, status, and outputs so far.
A versioned snapshot of run state written at a safe boundary so work can resume after failure or pause.

A status such as completed, failed, or cancelled after which the loop must not take another step. MENTAL MODEL Agent state is a climber's route card: it records the current pitch, remaining supplies, completed moves, and the turnaround time, so a rescue or a second team can continue safely.

worked_example: A procurement agent runs for up to 40 steps and waits for manager approval before issuing a purchase order. It keeps everything in a Python list held by the worker, so a routine deploy at 14:00 kills 63 in-flight runs; users see spinner timeouts, and three orders are re-created because the loop restarts from the first step. The team moves to a Postgres run_state table with a JSONB payload, a version column, and status waiting_for_human. The worker rehydrates by run ID, resumes after the approved step, and skips completed tool calls through stored idempotency keys. After the change, a deploy during 120 runs loses none, and median resume time is 1.4 seconds.

A procurement agent runs for up to 40 steps and waits for manager approval before issuing a purchase order. It keeps
everything in a Python list held by the worker, so a routine deploy at 14:00 kills 63 in-flight runs; users see spinner

resumes after the approved step, and skips completed tool calls through stored idempotency keys. After the change, a
deploy during 120 runs loses none, and median resume time is 1.4 seconds.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define the state fields: run ID, goal, plan, step and spend counters, pending action, status, and outputs.
2.    Draw the allowed transitions and guards, including terminal states and the reason recorded for each.
3.    Persist the state to a durable store after each tool result and before each model call, with a version column.
4.    Rebuild the model context from state at every step instead of keeping the transcript as the source of truth.
5.    Kill a worker mid-run and verify that resume continues at the right step without repeating a side effect.
CODE
A guarded transition function that enforces allowed status changes and fails the run when either budget is exhausted.
  LIMITS = {"max_steps": 12, "max_spend_usd": 0.40}
  ALLOWED = {
    "running": {"running", "waiting_human", "done", "failed"},
    "waiting_human": {"running", "cancelled"},
    "done": set(),
    "failed": set(),
    "cancelled": set(),
  }

  def transition(state: dict, new: str, reason: str = "") -> dict:
    current = state["status"]
    if new not in ALLOWED[current]:
       raise ValueError(f"cannot move {current} -> {new}")
    if state["steps"] > LIMITS["max_steps"]:
       new, reason = "failed", "step budget exhausted"
    if state["spend_usd"] > LIMITS["max_spend_usd"]:
       new, reason = "failed", "cost budget exhausted"
    return {**state, "status": new, "reason": reason,
          "version": state["version"] + 1}

 → The guard checks budgets only at transition time, so one long tool call can still overspend; also check before each model
   call.
 → The version bumps on every transition, which supports optimistic concurrency; include the expected version in the UPDATE
   where clause.
 → Reason strings are free text here; use enumerated codes if dashboards and alerts need to group failures reliably.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Memory is a policy, not a store Every turn offers candidates: a stated preference, a correction, a completed task, a document. Most should not be stored. Define triggers such as explicit user instruction, repeated behaviour, or a confirmed fact, then require a structured record with source, timestamp, confidence, and scope. Writes should be cheap to reject and easy to inspect. A useful test is whether a future run would make a materially better decision because of this record, not whether it is interesting. Four kinds, four lifecycles Working memory is the current context and dies with the run. Episodic memory stores events and outcomes, such as what was tried and what failed. Semantic memory stores stable facts and preferences. Procedural memory stores learned instructions, tool recipes, or policies. Each has a different write rate, retention period, and retrieval method. Mixing them into one table makes ranking impossible, because a three-year-old event competes with a current correction for the same slot. Retrieve few, forget on purpose Rank candidates by relevance, recency, importance, and confidence, then inject at most three to five memories with visible provenance. Never let memory override the current user message or a policy document. Support updates and contradiction, so a new preference supersedes the old record instead of coexisting. Enforce tenant and user scope at query time, keep deletion jobs and audit records, and measure whether retrieved memories actually improved task success.

code.title: A write gate and a ranking function that combine relevance, recency, importance, and confidence instead of similarity alone.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Memory:
  text: str
  kind: str
  source: str
  confidence: float
  importance: float
  created: datetime

def should_write(text: str, confidence: float, stated: bool) -> bool:
  return stated and confidence >= 0.8 and len(text.split()) >= 3

def rank(m: Memory, relevance: float, now: datetime) -> float:
  age = max(0, (now - m.created).days)
  recency = max(0.0, 1 - age / 180)
  base = 0.5 * relevance + 0.2 * recency + 0.2 * m.importance
  return base + 0.1 * m.confidence
what_to_notice: should_write trusts a stated preference at 0.8 confidence; in practice also require the user to confirm or repeat it before persisting.
The ranking weights are a starting point, not a tuned model; log which memories were injected and whether the answer used them.

Nothing here enforces tenant scope or expiry; those belong in the storage query and a scheduled deletion job, not in scoring. Three pages per lesson Page 311 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.title: Short-Term Memory
lessons.subtitle: Spend the context window like a budget: pin the facts that matter, summarise the history, and drop the rest before quality
why_it_matters: Every turn resends the conversation, tool results, and instructions, so a long agent session costs more per step and eventually exceeds the window. Naive truncation removes the original goal; naive summarisation loses the exact error message needed two steps later. Short-term memory design decides what stays verbatim, what becomes a summary, and what becomes a reference. Getting it right lowers cost and latency while keeping the agent coherent past turn fifty.
outcomes: Explain why the context window is the agent's short-term memory and how token pressure degrades instruction following.
Apply rolling summaries, structured scratchpads, and tool-result pruning inside a fixed token budget.
Measure the quality and cost effect of each compaction strategy on a repeatable multi-turn task set.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The window is a working set The model has no memory between calls; it sees exactly what you send. That makes the context window the whole of short-term memory, and every token competes with instructions and evidence. Long transcripts crowd out the current question, and models attend less reliably to material in the middle. Treat the window as a working set: keep the goal, current plan, recent turns, and selected tool output, then rebuild it each step from state rather than appending forever. Compact in layers Use three layers. Keep pinned invariants verbatim: system rules, user constraints, identifiers, and open approvals. Summarise older turns into a structured scratchpad of decisions, facts, failed attempts, and open questions. Replace bulky tool output with a short summary plus an identifier the agent can re-fetch. Trigger compaction at 70 percent of the window, not at the limit, and keep the last two exchanges untouched so local coherence survives. Measure before you trim Compaction is a lossy operation, so evaluate it. Build a 25-session set with tasks that need facts from early turns, then compare task success, tokens per turn, and p95 latency across strategies. A summary that preserves decisions but drops exact values may pass a chat test and fail a reconciliation task. Log token counts by section and compaction events, and alert when summarisation runs on more than a set share of requests.

key_terms.definition: The maximum tokens a model can attend to in one call, shared by instructions, history, tool results, and the output.
Rewriting older context into a shorter form, such as a summary or reference, to free tokens while preserving key facts.

A structured block in the context holding decisions, confirmed facts, failed attempts, and open questions across turns. MENTAL MODEL Short-term memory is a desk, not a warehouse: keep the current file, the signed page, and a sticky note of decisions on the desk, and return everything else to the archive.

results, averaging 54,000 input tokens by turn 30; the monthly model bill reaches USD 11,800 and p95 latency is 9.2

the team ships the change and monitors compaction rate.

2.    Define what must stay verbatim: system rules, user constraints, identifiers, approvals, and the current plan.
3.    Write a scratchpad schema for decisions, confirmed facts, failed attempts, and open questions, updated each turn.
4.    Summarise history beyond the last six turns and replace large tool results with extracts plus a retrievable reference.
5.    Test on a 25-session set with early-turn dependencies, comparing accuracy, tokens, and latency before release.
CODE
A budgeted context builder that keeps pinned facts and recent turns, stopping before 70 percent of the window is consumed.
  def build_context(pinned: list[str], turns: list[str], scratch: str,
            budget: int = 12_000) -> list[str]:
    def cost(text: str) -> int:
      return int(len(text.split()) * 1.3)

     kept, used = [], cost(scratch) + sum(cost(p) for p in pinned)
     for turn in reversed(turns):
       size = cost(turn)
       if used + size > budget * 0.7:
          break
       kept.append(turn)
       used += size
     return pinned + [scratch] + list(reversed(kept))

   into scratch first.

   budget checks.

   clause instead.

code.code:
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime, timezone

DDL = '''CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS memory (
 tenant TEXT, user TEXT, subject TEXT, predicate TEXT, value TEXT,
 source TEXT, confidence REAL, created TEXT,
 PRIMARY KEY (tenant, user, subject, predicate))'''

def remember(conn, tenant, user, subject, predicate, value, source, confidence):
  sql = '''INSERT INTO memory VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
ON CONFLICT (tenant, user, subject, predicate) DO UPDATE SET
value = excluded.value, source = excluded.source,
confidence = excluded.confidence, created = excluded.created'''
  now = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
  conn.execute(DDL)
  conn.execute(sql, (tenant, user, subject, predicate, value, source,
              confidence, now))
what_to_notice: The primary key enforces one value per subject and predicate, so a new fact supersedes the old without a separate read.
The table has no expiry or provenance columns in this snippet; add expires_at and a source message ID before storing anything personal.

lessons.title: Planning
lessons.subtitle: Make the agent's plan an explicit, inspectable artefact so decomposition, dependencies, and replanning stay under your
why_it_matters: Planning is where an agent's cost and failure modes are decided. A plan implicit in the message history is hard to inspect, resume, or evaluate. Making it explicit lets you validate dependencies before spending tokens, show the intended path to a reviewer, and compare executed work against it. The plan is also the unit you re-run when a tool or model changes.
outcomes: Choose between a static plan-then-execute graph and an interleaved ReAct loop for a given task shape.
Represent a plan as typed steps with dependencies, an owning tool, and a completion check.
Set replan triggers and a replan budget so a failed step does not become an unbounded retry loop.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A plan is data, not prose When the model returns a plan, parse it into steps: identifier, tool, arguments, dependencies, and a success check. Validate the graph before execution: every dependency exists, no cycles, every step names a registered tool. Store the plan beside the run so a reviewer can see intended versus executed work. A prose plan cannot be validated, resumed, or diffed after a prompt change, and it tempts the model to skip steps silently. Plan-and-execute versus ReAct Use plan-and-execute when subtasks are knowable up front, parallelisable, or need approval before spending money; the plan is reviewed once and executed with a scheduler. Use an interleaved reason-act-observe loop when each result changes what to do next, such as debugging or open-ended search. Many production agents combine them: a short plan for the first two levels, then ReAct inside each step. Choosing wrongly yields brittle scripts or runaway loops. Replanning needs a trigger and a budget Replan only on named events: a permanent tool error, a failed success check, new evidence that invalidates an assumption, or a human rejection. Cap replans at two and carry the failed step and its error into the new plan, otherwise the model repeats it. Keep completed steps, mark invalidated ones, and log the reason. Every replan costs a model call and can widen scope, so treat it as an exception with an owner.

key_terms.definition: An agent pattern that produces a complete multi-step plan first, then executes it with a scheduler and replans only on failure.
A directed acyclic graph of steps in which an edge means the target step needs the source step's output.

The maximum number of times an agent may rebuild its plan during one run before stopping or escalating. MENTAL MODEL A plan is a flight itinerary, not a promise: check the legs and dependencies before take-off, and rebook only when a named disruption makes the original route impossible.

worked_example: A research agent at a market-intelligence firm must produce a competitor brief from ten sources. Its first version used ReAct with a 40-step cap; traces showed repeated searches and a cost of USD 1.80 per brief. The team rewrote it as a five- step plan: resolve the company, fetch filings, extract three metrics, cross-check dates, write the brief. Steps two and three run in parallel, and the plan is rejected before execution if a source is missing. Median cost fell to USD 0.55 and p95 latency from 71 to 34 seconds. Replanning is allowed twice, only when a filing returns 404 or the date check fails.

code.title: A dependency-aware plan: steps run only when their prerequisites are done, and completion is asserted rather than assumed.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Step:
  id: str
  tool: str
  needs: tuple[str, ...] = ()

PLAN = [
  Step("search", "web_search"),
  Step("fetch", "fetch_page", ("search",)),
  Step("extract", "extract_claims", ("fetch",)),
  Step("report", "write_report", ("extract",)),
]
done: set[str] = set()
while ready := [s for s in PLAN if s.id not in done and set(s.needs) <= done]:
  step = ready[0]
  print(f"run {step.id} via {step.tool}")
  done.add(step.id)
print("complete:", done == {s.id for s in PLAN})
what_to_notice: The ready-set loop runs any step whose dependencies are complete, so independent fetch steps could execute concurrently with a thread pool.
The final check distinguishes a finished plan from a loop that exhausted its scheduling passes; production code returns a partial result instead.

Nothing here calls a model: the plan is fixed. A real planner must validate model-generated steps against the same rules before dispatch. Three pages per lesson Page 320 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Price a plan before execution by estimating tokens and tool calls; reject plans that exceed the per-request budget.
Run planned steps with a deadline and a per-step timeout; a slow dependency must not consume the whole request budget.

A dependency-aware plan: steps run only when their prerequisites are done, and completion is asserted rather than assumed.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Step:
    id: str
    tool: str
    needs: tuple[str, ...] = ()

  PLAN = [
    Step("search", "web_search"),
    Step("fetch", "fetch_page", ("search",)),
    Step("extract", "extract_claims", ("fetch",)),
    Step("report", "write_report", ("extract",)),
  ]
  done: set[str] = set()
  while ready := [s for s in PLAN if s.id not in done and set(s.needs) <= done]:
    step = ready[0]
    print(f"run {step.id} via {step.tool}")
    done.add(step.id)
  print("complete:", done == {s.id for s in PLAN})

COMMON MISTAKES

WORKED EXAMPLE
A payables agent at a construction firm processes 6,200 invoices a month. Payments under GBP 500 auto-approve when
the purchase order matches; anything above runs through an approval queue. The first release sent reviewers a raw tool

STEP BY STEP
1.    Inventory every tool and classify it as read-only, reversible write, irreversible write, or blocked.
2.    Choose thresholds and argument conditions that route only genuinely risky calls to a person.
3.    Persist run state and the pending call before pausing, including an idempotency key and expiry.

CODE
An approval ticket bound to the exact call arguments and an expiry, so a swapped amount or a late click cannot execute.
  import hashlib, time

  def digest(action: str, args: dict[str, object]) -> str:
    payload = f"{action}:{sorted(args.items())}".encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()[:16]

  def approved(action: str, args: dict, ticket: dict, now: float) -> bool:
    if not ticket or action != ticket["action"] or now >= ticket["expires_at"]:
       return False
    return digest(action, args) == ticket["digest"]

  ARGS = {"invoice": "INV-1042", "amount": 740}
  ticket = {"action": "issue_refund", "expires_at": time.time() + 86400,
        "digest": digest("issue_refund", ARGS)}
  print(approved("issue_refund", ARGS, ticket, time.time()))
  print(approved("issue_refund", {**ARGS, "amount": 9000}, ticket, time.time()))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The digest sorts argument items, so reordered dictionaries still match, but a changed amount produces a different ticket
   hash.
 → Expiry is checked before the digest, and both failures return False; the caller must treat False as deny, never as permission
   to retry.
 → The ticket stores only a digest, not the arguments, so the execution path must reload the original call from persisted run
   state.

lessons.title: Agent Error Handling
lessons.subtitle: Separate transient, permanent, semantic, and budget failures, then answer each with the cheapest recovery that keeps
why_it_matters: Agents fail in layers: the tool times out, the model emits invalid arguments, the plan no longer makes sense, or the budget runs out. A single try/except treats all four the same and usually makes things worse by retrying a permanent error. Dependable agents classify the failure, choose one recovery, record why, and stop with useful partial work when recovery is impossible.
outcomes: Classify tool and model failures by whether retrying, repairing, replanning, or stopping is the correct response.
Return structured, sanitised errors to the model so it can correct arguments without learning internal details.
Bound retries, steps, and spend, and emit partial results with an explicit account of what failed.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Four failure classes Transient failures, such as a 429, 503, or socket timeout, may succeed on retry. Permanent failures, such as a 404, invalid credentials, or a schema violation, will not. Semantic failures return a valid but wrong result, detected only by a check or a reviewer. Budget failures mean steps, tokens, or wall-clock time are exhausted. Each needs a different response: bounded retry, repair or replan, verification, or a clean stop. Misclassifying permanent as transient is the expensive mistake. Errors are prompts, sanitised A tool error is model input, not just a log line. Return a short structured object with the error class, a stable code, the offending field, and one corrective hint, for example invalid_arguments on amount: expected a positive number. Do not paste stack traces, SQL, secrets, or full upstream responses; they waste context and leak internals. Cap repair attempts at two, because a model that cannot fix the arguments after two hints needs a different tool or a human. Stop well, keep partial work Every loop needs a hard step cap, a token budget, and a deadline, checked before the next model call rather than after. When one is hit, stop and return what is verified: completed steps, sources fetched, unresolved questions. Mark the run as partial, not successful, and emit a machine-readable reason. A research brief with three confirmed findings beats a fabricated fourth paragraph. Route repeated failures to a dead-letter queue with the trace identifier.

key_terms.definition: A failure expected to succeed if repeated later, such as a rate limit, timeout, or unavailable upstream service.
A guard that stops calling a failing dependency for a cooldown period after a threshold of consecutive failures.

A store for runs that exhausted recovery so engineers can inspect and replay them without blocking users. MENTAL MODEL Error handling is triage, not optimism: sort the injury, apply the one treatment that fits, and stop before the patient loses more blood.

  import random, time

  class TransientError(Exception):
    pass

  class PermanentError(Exception):
    pass

  def call_with_retry(fn, *args, attempts: int = 3, deadline: float):
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
       try:
         return fn(*args)
       except TransientError:
         if attempt == attempts or time.monotonic() > deadline:
            raise
         delay = min(4.0, 0.5 * 2 ** (attempt - 1))
         time.sleep(delay * (0.5 + random.random()))
    raise AssertionError("unreachable")

  from urllib.parse import urlparse

  ALLOWED_HOSTS = {"api.github.com", "docs.python.org"}

  class PolicyError(Exception):
    pass

  def check_tool(name: str, args: dict, approved: bool) -> None:
    if name in {"read_file", "search"}:
       return
    if name not in {"http_get", "create_issue"}:
       raise PolicyError(f"tool {name} is not permitted")
    if name == "create_issue" and not approved:
       raise PolicyError("create_issue requires human approval")
    if name == "http_get":
       host = urlparse(str(args["url"])).hostname or ""

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A loop with explicit states Model the run as a state machine: receive goal, build context, call model, parse action, authorise, execute, observe, then continue or stop. Deterministic replay before intelligence Start with a scripted fake model that returns a fixed sequence of tool calls and a final answer. Add the real model only after the mechanics pass. Keep the budget checks and the event log in production: they are the difference between an agent you can debug and one you can only re-prompt.

CODE
A minimal loop with a tool registry, step budget, structured tool errors, and a scripted model for deterministic tests.
  TOOLS = {"add": lambda a, b: a + b, "done": lambda answer: answer}

  def run(goal: str, model, max_steps: int = 6) -> str:
    history = [{"role": "user", "content": goal}]
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
       action = model(history)
       name, args = action["tool"], action["args"]
       try:
          result = TOOLS[name](**args)
       except (KeyError, TypeError) as exc:
          history.append({"role": "tool", "error": repr(exc)})
          continue
       if name == "done":
          return f"{result} after {step} steps"
       history.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})
    return "stopped: step budget exhausted"

  script = [{"tool": "add", "args": {"a": 2, "b": 3}},
        {"tool": "done", "args": {"answer": "5"}}]
  print(run("2+3", lambda history: script.pop(0)))

why_it_matters: Every agent framework promises to simplify agents. What they actually provide is an execution model: typed state, deterministic routing, durable checkpoints, streaming events, and a place to pause for human approval. If your loop is fifty lines and loses nothing when the process restarts, a framework adds a dependency without removing work. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The requirements arrive quietly An agent starts as a while loop over messages. Then the product asks for conversation history after a restart, a retry when a tool times out, a branch on the tool result, a progress indicator, a reviewer approval step, and a replay of the run that produced a bad answer. Each request is twenty lines of code. Together they are a runtime with a state model, a scheduler, a persistence layer, and an event stream. Frameworks exist because those pieces must be designed together. What is actually standardised A serious framework defines a state schema, a node contract, an edge or routing function, a checkpoint store, and an event stream. Evaluate it on those five things, not on the demo. Ask how often it checkpoints, whether a node can resume mid-execution, what exactly is serialised, how a paused run is resumed, and whether routing can be tested without calling a model. If the answers are vague, the framework is a prompt wrapper with a marketing site rather than an execution model. The adoption tax Frameworks bring vocabulary, version churn, and a debugging layer between you and the HTTP request. LangChain's 0.1 to 0.3 transition broke imports across partner packages; LangGraph's checkpoint schema has changed with releases. A three-node, ten-minute pipeline rarely repays that tax. Adopt when state or durability is a real requirement, and write the requirement down. The decision record should name the failure it prevents, the weekly maintenance cost you accept, and the signal that would make you remove it.

CODE
The checkpoint code teams write by hand at 2am, which is the moment an orchestration framework starts to earn its dependency.
  import json
  from pathlib import Path
  STORE = Path("runs")

  def resume(run_id: str) -> dict:
    path = STORE / f"{run_id}.json"
    if path.exists():
       return json.loads(path.read_text())
    return {"step": 0, "done": False}

  def save(run_id: str, state: dict) -> None:
    STORE.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (STORE / f"{run_id}.json").write_text(json.dumps(state))

  state = resume("run-8841")
  while not state["done"] and state["step"] < 8:
    state["step"] += 1
    state["done"] = state["step"] >= 3
    save("run-8841", state)
  print(state)
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The write is not atomic, so a crash mid-save leaves a truncated JSON file that resume cannot parse.
 → Two workers using the same run id overwrite each other, because this hand-rolled store has no locking or lease.
 → The loop cap of eight is a budget, not a guarantee: it stops runaway steps but says nothing about cost or time.

lessons.title: Workflows vs Agents
lessons.subtitle: Put control flow in code when the steps are known; put it in the model only when the path genuinely varies per input.
lessons.meta: Agent Orchestration · Lesson 4 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Agent demos optimise for the unknown path, while production traffic is mostly known paths with a messy minority. A workflow is cheaper, faster, and testable because the sequence is code; an agent is flexible because the sequence is a decision. Most teams need both, separated by a router with a measurable rule. Choosing per request, rather than per product, is where the cost and reliability gains are.
outcomes: Distinguish workflows from agents by where the control flow lives, not by which framework is used.
Name the four workflow patterns that cover most production LLM traffic and what each one costs.
Design a router that sends each request to a workflow, an agent, or a human queue on measurable rules.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Where control flow lives In a workflow the developer decides the order and the model fills in content. In an agent the model chooses the next tool at runtime. That single difference drives everything else. Workflows are bounded, replayable, and cheap to evaluate step by step; agents adapt to inputs you did not anticipate but consume more tokens, add latency, and are harder to test because the execution path is data rather than code. Neither is more advanced; each is correct for a different distribution of inputs. The known patterns Five patterns cover most traffic: chain for a fixed sequence, routing to classify then pick one branch, parallelisation to fan out and aggregate, evaluator-optimiser to generate then judge and revise, and orchestrator-workers to plan then delegate. All are deterministic in topology even when a model sits inside a step. Naming the pattern makes design review concrete and tells you what to measure: routing accuracy, join logic, or judge drift across prompt versions. The hybrid default Route every request. If the input matches a known template and confidence is high, run the workflow; otherwise hand off to an agent with a step budget, or to a human when the amount or risk exceeds a limit. Instrument the split, the accuracy per branch, and the cost per branch. When 90 percent is workflow, the agent becomes a bounded exception handler, and the evaluation can concentrate on the genuinely open-ended remainder instead of averaging over everything.

Workflows vs Agents
Put control flow in code when the steps are known; put it in the model only when the path genuinely varies per input.
Agent Orchestration · Lesson 4 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Agent demos optimise for the unknown path, while production traffic is mostly known paths with a messy minority. A
workflow is cheaper, faster, and testable because the sequence is code; an agent is flexible because the sequence is a
decision. Most teams need both, separated by a router with a measurable rule. Choosing per request, rather than per
product, is where the cost and reliability gains are.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Distinguish workflows from agents by where the control flow lives, not by which framework is used.
 • Name the four workflow patterns that cover most production LLM traffic and what each one costs.
 • Design a router that sends each request to a workflow, an agent, or a human queue on measurable rules.
CORE CONCEPTS
Where control flow lives
In a workflow the developer decides the order and the model fills in content. In an agent the model chooses the next tool
at runtime. That single difference drives everything else. Workflows are bounded, replayable, and cheap to evaluate step
by step; agents adapt to inputs you did not anticipate but consume more tokens, add latency, and are harder to test
because the execution path is data rather than code. Neither is more advanced; each is correct for a different distribution
of inputs.
The known patterns
Five patterns cover most traffic: chain for a fixed sequence, routing to classify then pick one branch, parallelisation to fan
out and aggregate, evaluator-optimiser to generate then judge and revise, and orchestrator-workers to plan then
delegate. All are deterministic in topology even when a model sits inside a step. Naming the pattern makes design review
concrete and tells you what to measure: routing accuracy, join logic, or judge drift across prompt versions.
The hybrid default
Route every request. If the input matches a known template and confidence is high, run the workflow; otherwise hand off
to an agent with a step budget, or to a human when the amount or risk exceeds a limit. Instrument the split, the accuracy
per branch, and the cost per branch. When 90 percent is workflow, the agent becomes a bounded exception handler, and
the evaluation can concentrate on the genuinely open-ended remainder instead of averaging over everything.
KEY TERMS
 Workflow                         A pipeline whose step order is fixed in code, with models used inside steps rather than to choose the path.
 Agent                            A loop where the model selects the next action at runtime, within budgets and permissions set by the
                                  runtime.
 Router                           A classification step that sends each request to a workflow, an agent, or a human queue.

  MENTAL MODEL A workflow is a train on fixed tracks; an agent is a taxi. Use the train for the commute and the taxi for the address the
  timetable never covers.

A router that decides from logged fields rather than prose confidence, so every dispatch can be replayed offline.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Invoice:
    layout: str
    pages: int
    confidence: float
    total_eur: float

  def route(inv: Invoice) -> str:
    if inv.layout not in {"acme_v2", "nordic_v1", "scan_std"}:
       return "agent"
    if inv.confidence < 0.80 or inv.pages > 12:
       return "agent"
    if inv.total_eur > 25_000:
       return "human"
    return "workflow"

  print(route(Invoice("acme_v2", 3, 0.94, 1_240.0)))
  print(route(Invoice("scan_std", 2, 0.71, 880.0)))

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Four artefacts, one diagram A graph design has a state schema, a node list, an edge list, and a termination rule. Draw it before coding: boxes for nodes, arrows for edges, labels for routing functions. If the diagram needs a legend to explain recursion, simplify the graph. Any node with more than one responsibility becomes two boxes, because a box that fails should have exactly one reason to fail and one retry policy to apply. Design for the failure boundary Every node is a crash point and a possible duplicate side effect. Decide per node whether it can be retried safely, must be idempotent, or needs a transaction. Make fan-out joins explicit so partial results are representable rather than silently missing. Place checkpoints at step boundaries and define what a partial success returns to the user. A graph that cannot express partial failure will eventually report success while missing half its evidence. Bound the cycles Loops are where agents earn their keep and where budgets die. Every cycle needs a counter in state, a hard maximum, and a fallback answer when the maximum is reached. Prefer a convergence test, such as a score above threshold or no new sources, over a fixed count where the task allows it. Log the reason each iteration continued, so tuning the cap is based on traces rather than guesswork or a bigger model.

Ravi leads four engineers building a research assistant for a media company. The first version was one 300-line node that

2.    Write the state schema and annotate which node writes each key and which node only reads it.
3.    Mark each node retry-safe, idempotent, or transactional, and add the guard it needs.

CODE
A topology as data plus a reachability check that fails CI when a node is orphaned by an edit.
  from collections import deque
  GRAPH = {
    "plan": ["search", "answer"],
    "search": ["extract"],
    "extract": ["synthesise"],
    "synthesise": ["search", "cite"],
    "cite": ["answer"],
    "answer": [],
  }

  def reachable(graph: dict[str, list[str]], entry: str = "plan") -> set[str]:
    seen, queue = {entry}, deque([entry])
    while queue:
       for node in graph[queue.popleft()]:
         if node not in seen:
            seen.add(node)
            queue.append(node)
    return seen

  assert set(GRAPH) == reachable(GRAPH), "graph has unreachable nodes"
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The assertion catches unreachable nodes, not cycles; the synthesise-search loop needs its own counter and maximum.
 → The graph is data, so the validator runs in CI and at import, before any model call or deployment.
 → A node with no outgoing edge silently ends the run, which is right for answer and wrong for extract.

lessons.title: Nodes
lessons.subtitle: A node is one job with a typed input, a partial output, and a failure path; every guarantee in the graph rests on that
why_it_matters: Most graph bugs are node bugs: a function that mutates shared state, does two unrelated things, or repeats a side effect on retry. Because a checkpointer can re-run a node after a crash, a node is never called exactly once by design. Treating each node as a small, idempotent, observable function is what makes the rest of the architecture safe to reason about and safe to resume.
outcomes: Write a node that reads state, performs one bounded operation, and returns only the keys it changed.
Make every side-effecting node idempotent and prove it with a double-invocation test.
Separate recoverable errors recorded in state from unrecoverable errors that must raise.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The node contract A node reads current state and returns a partial update. It must not mutate the input dictionary, must not return the full state, and must name only the keys it owns. Pure transformations are trivial to test: build a state literal, call the function, assert the returned dictionary. Side effects belong at the graph's edges, wrapped so a duplicate call is harmless. Keep conditional logic out of nodes where a routing function can express it, because hidden branches are invisible in the diagram. Retries make idempotency mandatory A crash between a side effect and the checkpoint means the node runs again. Pass an idempotency key derived from stable state, such as an order id, to the downstream API, or check a dedupe table first. For writes you cannot repeat, split the node: record intent in state, execute once, then record the receipt. Tests should invoke the node twice with the same state and assert exactly one external effect. Without that test, replay safety is an assumption rather than a property. One job, one failure mode Nodes named extract_policy, score_draft, or fetch_source tell a reviewer what changed and what can break. A node that plans, retrieves, and writes has three failure modes and no useful retry policy. Capture errors into a declared state key when the graph can recover, and raise when it cannot; never swallow an exception into an empty string. Put a timeout around every I/O call, and keep it shorter than the node budget so the failure surfaces before the graph deadline.

key_terms.definition: A function in a graph that reads state and returns a partial update, optionally performing one bounded side effect.
A stable identifier sent with a write so a retried request produces one effect rather than duplicates.

A dictionary containing only the state keys a node changed, merged by the graph's reducers. MENTAL MODEL A node is a station on an assembly line: it takes the part, performs one operation, stamps the log, and passes the part on without changing anything elsewhere.

worked_example: Lena's team ran order notifications on a three-node graph. During a Kubernetes rollout, a worker was killed after the email provider accepted a receipt but before the checkpoint was written. On resume, send_receipt ran again and 2,100 customers received duplicate receipts; support handled 68 tickets and the team lost a day to reconciliation. The fix was small: the node derived key receipt:order_id and passed it to the provider, which de-duplicated for 24 hours, while state recorded the key before the call. Generating the PDF moved to render_receipt, so send_receipt had one job. A regression test now invokes it twice and asserts a single provider call, and the rollout drains workers before termination.
