A node is one job with a typed input, a partial output, and a failure path; every guarantee in the graph rests on that
contract.
Agent Orchestration · Lesson 6 of 17 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most graph bugs are node bugs: a function that mutates shared state, does two unrelated things, or repeats a side effect
on retry. Because a checkpointer can re-run a node after a crash, a node is never called exactly once by design. Treating
each node as a small, idempotent, observable function is what makes the rest of the architecture safe to reason about
and safe to resume.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write a node that reads state, performs one bounded operation, and returns only the keys it changed.
 • Make every side-effecting node idempotent and prove it with a double-invocation test.
 • Separate recoverable errors recorded in state from unrecoverable errors that must raise.
CORE CONCEPTS
The node contract
A node reads current state and returns a partial update. It must not mutate the input dictionary, must not return the full
state, and must name only the keys it owns. Pure transformations are trivial to test: build a state literal, call the function,
assert the returned dictionary. Side effects belong at the graph's edges, wrapped so a duplicate call is harmless. Keep
conditional logic out of nodes where a routing function can express it, because hidden branches are invisible in the
diagram.
Retries make idempotency mandatory
A crash between a side effect and the checkpoint means the node runs again. Pass an idempotency key derived from
stable state, such as an order id, to the downstream API, or check a dedupe table first. For writes you cannot repeat, split
the node: record intent in state, execute once, then record the receipt. Tests should invoke the node twice with the same
state and assert exactly one external effect. Without that test, replay safety is an assumption rather than a property.
One job, one failure mode
Nodes named extract_policy, score_draft, or fetch_source tell a reviewer what changed and what can break. A node that
plans, retrieves, and writes has three failure modes and no useful retry policy. Capture errors into a declared state key
when the graph can recover, and raise when it cannot; never swallow an exception into an empty string. Put a timeout
around every I/O call, and keep it shorter than the node budget so the failure surfaces before the graph deadline.
KEY TERMS
 Node                             A function in a graph that reads state and returns a partial update, optionally performing one bounded side
                                  effect.
 Idempotency key                  A stable identifier sent with a write so a retried request produces one effect rather than duplicates.
 Partial update                   A dictionary containing only the state keys a node changed, merged by the graph's reducers.

  MENTAL MODEL A node is a station on an assembly line: it takes the part, performs one operation, stamps the log, and passes the part
  on without changing anything elsewhere.

Nodes
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
Lena's team ran order notifications on a three-node graph. During a Kubernetes rollout, a worker was killed after the
email provider accepted a receipt but before the checkpoint was written. On resume, send_receipt ran again and 2,100
customers received duplicate receipts; support handled 68 tickets and the team lost a day to reconciliation. The fix was
small: the node derived key receipt:order_id and passed it to the provider, which de-duplicated for 24 hours, while state
recorded the key before the call. Generating the PDF moved to render_receipt, so send_receipt had one job. A regression
test now invokes it twice and asserts a single provider call, and the rollout drains workers before termination.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Name the node with a verb and one object, then list the state keys it reads and writes.
2.    Write the pure part as a function tested with a state literal and no model or network.
3.    Derive an idempotency key from stable business ids, never from timestamps or attempt numbers.
4.    Wrap each I/O call in a timeout shorter than the node budget and declare which errors it can recover from.
5.    Call the node twice in a test and assert one side effect and one state update.
CODE
A side-effecting node that appends to state without mutating it and reuses one idempotency key across retries.
  import operator
  from typing import Annotated, TypedDict

  class ReceiptState(TypedDict):
    order_id: str
    sent: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]
    errors: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]

  def send_receipt(state: ReceiptState) -> dict:
    key = f"receipt:{state['order_id']}"
    try:
       mailer.send(order_id=state["order_id"], idempotency_key=key, timeout=8)
    except TimeoutError:
       return {"errors": [f"{key} timed out; safe to retry"]}
    return {"sent": [key]}

  state = {"order_id": "ord_5512", "sent": [], "errors": []}
  print(send_receipt(state))
  print(state["sent"]) # unchanged: the node did not mutate its input
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The key comes from order_id, so a retry after a timeout reuses it and the provider collapses the duplicate.
 → The node returns only sent and errors; returning the whole state would overwrite a parallel branch's writes.
 → TimeoutError is recorded for recovery, but a 400 from the provider should raise, because retrying bad input cannot
   succeed.

Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Mutating state in place, so a replayed checkpoint sees values left by the previous attempt.
2.     Building an idempotency key from a timestamp or attempt number, which makes every retry a new write.
3.     Catching every exception and returning an empty result, turning a failure into a silent wrong answer.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Log node name, attempt, duration, idempotency key, and changed keys; those five fields reconstruct most node-level
      incidents quickly.
    ◆ Enforce a per-node timeout below the graph budget so a hung dependency fails the node, not the whole request.
    ◆ Test each side-effecting node for double invocation, and drain workers safely before deploy to shrink the replay window.
CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□      Each node does one job and is named with a verb.
□      Nodes return partial updates and never mutate the input state.
□      Every side effect carries a stable idempotency key derived from business identifiers.
□      Errors are either recorded for recovery or raised, never swallowed.
□      A double-invocation test proves exactly one effect per side-effecting node.
SHORT QUESTIONS
1.     Why must a node return a partial update rather than the whole state?

2.     How does checkpoint replay turn an ordinary retry into a duplicate side effect?

3.     What makes a good idempotency key, and which sources are unsafe?

4.     When should a node record an error in state instead of raising it?

5.     How do you unit-test a node without calling a model or a network?

6.     Why should a per-node timeout be shorter than the whole graph's budget?

TASKS
□      Refactor one multi-purpose node into two single-purpose nodes with disjoint state keys and a test each (40 minutes).
□      Add an idempotency key and a double-invocation test to a node that writes to an external API (45 minutes).
□      Instrument a node with duration, attempt, and changed keys, then replay a failed run and compare logs (30 minutes).

lessons.title: Edges
lessons.subtitle: Wire nodes into a fixed topology, learn what fan-out and fan-in really execute, and know when an edge should stay static.
lessons.meta: Agent Orchestration · Lesson 7 of 17 · study guide
why_it_matters: Most agent bugs are topology bugs: a branch that never runs, a join that fires twice, or a cycle with no exit. Edges are the graph's control flow, and unlike prompt text they are deterministic and reviewable. Reading the diagram before running it turns a class of silent failures into a design conversation, and keeps the model's freedom inside nodes rather than in the wiring.
outcomes: Draw a graph topology with START and END, then read LangGraph's superstep order from the edges alone.
Explain how fan-out branches run in parallel and why a fan-in node waits for every incoming edge.
Choose static edges over conditional routing when the sequence never depends on runtime state.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Static edges are a contract An edge says the target runs after the source completes, always. START marks entry, END stops the run, and every other static edge is unconditional. Because nothing in state can skip or repeat an edge, you can review the sequence in a diff. Use static edges for pipelines whose steps are fixed: load history, retrieve, draft, validate. Push choice into a conditional edge or a node, never into an edge that quietly returns nothing. Fan-out, fan-in and supersteps Two edges from one node run both targets in the same superstep, so they execute concurrently and each sees state as it was when the step began. A node with several incoming edges waits for all of them, then runs once. Ordering between branches is not guaranteed, so never rely on which finishes first. Fan-in is your barrier: merge results there rather than inside either branch. Cycles need a bound An edge can point backwards, which is how LangGraph implements retry and tool loops. Every cycle needs an exit in graph code: a counter in state, a maximum-attempt check in the routing function, or LangGraph's recursion_limit, which defaults to 25 supersteps and raises GraphRecursionError. Document the limit beside the edge, and emit a metric so a graph that keeps looping appears before the invoice does.

key_terms.definition: One round of graph execution in which every node scheduled by the previous step's edges runs, potentially in parallel.

A node with multiple incoming edges that acts as a barrier, running once after all upstream branches complete. recursion_limit LangGraph's cap on supersteps per invocation, raising GraphRecursionError when a cycle fails to terminate. MENTAL MODEL Edges are the rails, nodes are the stations, and supersteps are the timetable: a train only moves along laid track, and two trains on separate rails do not wait for each other.

worked_example: At a legal-tech company, Nadia reviews the retrieval graph for a 40,000-contract assistant. The beta chains dense search into sparse search: 1.4 seconds plus 1.9 seconds, so users wait 3.3 seconds before the model even starts, against a 5- second target. In the review she draws the edges on a whiteboard and finds no dependency between the branches, only habit. Create the nodes, then wire START, the fan-out branches, a fan-in join, and END with plain add_edge calls.

code.title: Parallel retrieval as explicit topology: two branches from START, one join, and END.
code.code:
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class State(TypedDict):
  dense: list[str]
  sparse: list[str]
  merged: list[str]

def dense(state: State) -> dict:
  return {"dense": ["d1", "d2"]}

def sparse(state: State) -> dict:
  return {"sparse": ["s1"]}
g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("dense", dense); g.add_node("sparse", sparse)
g.add_node("join", lambda s: {"merged": s["dense"] + s["sparse"]})
g.add_edge(START, "dense"); g.add_edge(START, "sparse")
g.add_edge("dense", "join"); g.add_edge("sparse", "join")
g.add_edge("join", END)
print(g.compile().get_graph().draw_mermaid())
what_to_notice: Both retrievers start from START, so they receive identical input state; anything dense writes is invisible to sparse in that superstep.
The join node has two incoming edges from one superstep, so LangGraph runs it once after both complete rather than twice.

No cycle appears here deliberately; a back edge would need a state counter and an explicit recursion_limit, which is the next lesson's work. Three pages per lesson Page 354 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Chaining independent branches to force ordering, paying the sum of their latencies instead of the maximum.
Relying on which parallel branch finishes first to populate state that the other branch reads.
Adding a retry edge back to a node without a counter, then meeting the loop at recursion_limit in production.
production_notes: Render the compiled graph in CI and diff the Mermaid output, so an accidental edge change appears in review rather than in an incident.
Give every node a timeout and log its duration per superstep; a slow join usually means one branch is the real bottleneck.
Set recursion_limit from the product's tolerance, alert on GraphRecursionError, and treat that error as a bug report rather than user input.
checklist: I can name the entry, exit, branches, and join in my graph from the diagram alone.
Independent steps share a superstep instead of being chained end to end.
Every join node's incoming edges are intentional and documented.
Every back edge has a counter and an explicit recursion_limit.
I have measured per-branch latency rather than assuming parallelism helped.
questions: Why does a join node wait for all incoming edges, and what breaks if one branch is optional?
What happens to state written by one parallel branch before the other branch reads it?
How would you detect that chaining two 1.5-second calls cost you three seconds?
Why is recursion_limit a graph-level guard rather than a guard inside a single node?
When is a fixed sequence of edges preferable to a conditional edge?
What evidence would justify turning a linear pipeline into a fan-out topology?

lessons.title: Conditional Routing
lessons.subtitle: Turn a state value into a labelled decision, keep the router pure, and make every unresolved label a visible failure rather
why_it_matters: Routing is where an agent's judgement becomes control flow, so it deserves the same treatment as any branch in production code. A router that returns a label nobody mapped silently ends the run, and a threshold guessed inside a prompt cannot be reviewed or tuned. Explicit bands, total mappings, and tests make expensive decisions predictable before a user sees them.
outcomes: Write a router function that reads state and returns a key present in the edge mapping.
Design confidence bands with explicit fallback branches, including a refusal path that is counted.
Test every routing outcome, including an unmapped key, without calling a live model.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A router is a pure function add_conditional_edges takes a source node, a function, and a mapping from returned labels to destinations. The function should read state and return a label or a list of labels for fan-out, and nothing else: no model call, no database write, no exception for ordinary input. Keeping it pure means a unit test can drive every branch from a hand-built state dictionary, and a reviewer can read all thresholds in one place. Bands, not vibes Thresholds belong in configuration with a stated owner. For a support assistant, confidence at or above 0.80 answers directly, 0.45 to 0.80 queues for review, and below 0.45 refuses with a handoff. Each band carries a metric: answer accuracy, reviewer override rate, refusal rate. Tune one band at a time against a labelled set, because a change that lifts automation usually raises the override rate. Put the numbers in graph code, not in the prompt. Every label must resolve The mapping is the contract between router and topology. If the function returns an unknown label, the run fails or ends without an answer, depending on version. Add a test asserting that the label set the router can produce equals the mapping keys. Route unhappy paths into nodes, not straight to END, so refusals and failures are recorded, counted, and visible in traces. A default branch hides bugs; prefer an explicit catch-all with its own metric.

key_terms.definition: A graph edge whose destination is chosen at runtime by a function that maps state to one or more destination labels.
The string a router returns, which must appear as a key in the edge mapping for the run to continue.

An explicit destination that receives unmatched or low-confidence cases so they are handled and counted rather than dropped. MENTAL MODEL A router is a signal box, not a road: it decides which track the train takes, but the points must already exist and every point must lead somewhere.

lessons.mental_model: Think of conditional routing as a building block - once you understand it, you'll use it again and again as you build your AI app.
worked_example: Tomas runs a refund assistant for a payments company handling 6,000 chats a week. The beta answers every question the model returns, and reviewers overrule 9% of answers, most of them policy exceptions. He replaces the single path with three bands: 0.80 and above answers directly, 0.45 to 0.80 goes to a reviewer queue, below 0.45 refuses and offers a callback. On 400 labelled chats the 0.80 boundary holds 97% precision while automation falls from 71% to 58%. The decision is to keep 0.80, absorb the volume with two reviewers, and revisit when the retrieval fix for policy exceptions lands. Six weeks later the override rate is 2.4% and cost per resolved chat is unchanged.
steps: List the decisions the router must make and the state fields carrying the evidence: score, intent, or tool result.
Create each destination as a node whose name states the outcome, such as reply, review, or refuse.
Implement the router as a pure function with thresholds in a module-level config and no I/O of any kind.
Map every label the function can return, including a catch-all, and test that the label set equals the mapping keys.
Replay 200 labelled cases through the compiled graph and record per-band volume, accuracy, and override rate.

code.title: A three-band router with an explicit refusal path and a total label mapping.
code.code:
from typing import Literal, TypedDict
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class State(TypedDict):
  confidence: float
  answer: str
def route(state: State) -> Literal["reply", "review", "refuse"]:
  if state["confidence"] >= 0.80: return "reply"
  if state["confidence"] >= 0.45: return "review"
  return "refuse"
ROUTES = {"reply": END, "review": "human", "refuse": "deny"}

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("answer", lambda s: {"answer": "refund within 30 days"})
g.add_node("human", lambda s: {"answer": "queued for a human"})
g.add_node("deny", lambda s: {"answer": "no verified answer"})
g.add_edge(START, "answer")
g.add_conditional_edges("answer", route, ROUTES)
g.add_edge("human", END); g.add_edge("deny", END)
print(g.compile().invoke({"confidence": 0.62, "answer": ""}))
what_to_notice: The router reads state and returns a literal; putting a database lookup here would force every routing test to mock it.
One branch terminates at END while review and refuse run a node first, so refusals are counted instead of silently dropped.

All three thresholds live in one function, so a reviewer can read the whole policy and change one band without touching the prompt. Three pages per lesson Page 357 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Putting the threshold in the prompt and hoping the model applies it, then watching it drift between requests.
Returning a label no mapping key covers, which ends the run without an answer or an error you can trace.
Routing low-confidence cases straight to END, so refusals never reach a queue and never appear in metrics.
production_notes: Emit the routing key, score, and threshold version as trace attributes; without them you cannot explain a shift in automation rate.
Version thresholds beside the prompt and shadow-run new bands on live traffic before they control customer replies.
Alert on the share of traffic in the catch-all branch; a rising refusal rate is usually a retrieval or provider problem, not policy.

Every label it can return maps to a named node or to END.

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Routing is where an agent's judgement becomes control flow, so it deserves the same treatment as any branch in
production code. A router that returns a label nobody mapped silently ends the run, and a threshold guessed inside a
prompt cannot be reviewed or tuned. Explicit bands, total mappings, and tests make expensive decisions predictable
before a user sees them.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write a router function that reads state and returns a key present in the edge mapping.
 • Design confidence bands with explicit fallback branches, including a refusal path that is counted.
 • Test every routing outcome, including an unmapped key, without calling a live model.
CORE CONCEPTS
A router is a pure function
add_conditional_edges takes a source node, a function, and a mapping from returned labels to destinations. The function
should read state and return a label or a list of labels for fan-out, and nothing else: no model call, no database write, no
exception for ordinary input. Keeping it pure means a unit test can drive every branch from a hand-built state dictionary,
and a reviewer can read all thresholds in one place.
Bands, not vibes
Thresholds belong in configuration with a stated owner. For a support assistant, confidence at or above 0.80 answers
directly, 0.45 to 0.80 queues for review, and below 0.45 refuses with a handoff. Each band carries a metric: answer
accuracy, reviewer override rate, refusal rate. Tune one band at a time against a labelled set, because a change that lifts
automation usually raises the override rate. Put the numbers in graph code, not in the prompt.
Every label must resolve
The mapping is the contract between router and topology. If the function returns an unknown label, the run fails or ends
without an answer, depending on version. Add a test asserting that the label set the router can produce equals the
mapping keys. Route unhappy paths into nodes, not straight to END, so refusals and failures are recorded, counted, and
visible in traces. A default branch hides bugs; prefer an explicit catch-all with its own metric.
KEY TERMS
 Conditional edge                 A graph edge whose destination is chosen at runtime by a function that maps state to one or more
                                  destination labels.
 Routing key                      The string a router returns, which must appear as a key in the edge mapping for the run to continue.
 Catch-all branch                 An explicit destination that receives unmatched or low-confidence cases so they are handled and counted
                                  rather than dropped.

  MENTAL MODEL A router is a signal box, not a road: it decides which track the train takes, but the points must already exist and every
  point must lead somewhere.

Conditional Routing
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
Tomas runs a refund assistant for a payments company handling 6,000 chats a week. The beta answers every question the
model returns, and reviewers overrule 9% of answers, most of them policy exceptions. He replaces the single path with
three bands: 0.80 and above answers directly, 0.45 to 0.80 goes to a reviewer queue, below 0.45 refuses and offers a
callback. On 400 labelled chats the 0.80 boundary holds 97% precision while automation falls from 71% to 58%. The
decision is to keep 0.80, absorb the volume with two reviewers, and revisit when the retrieval fix for policy exceptions
lands. Six weeks later the override rate is 2.4% and cost per resolved chat is unchanged.
STEP BY STEP
1.    List the decisions the router must make and the state fields carrying the evidence: score, intent, or tool result.
2.    Create each destination as a node whose name states the outcome, such as reply, review, or refuse.
3.    Implement the router as a pure function with thresholds in a module-level config and no I/O of any kind.
4.    Map every label the function can return, including a catch-all, and test that the label set equals the mapping keys.
5.    Replay 200 labelled cases through the compiled graph and record per-band volume, accuracy, and override rate.
CODE
A three-band router with an explicit refusal path and a total label mapping.
  from typing import Literal, TypedDict
  from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

  class State(TypedDict):
    confidence: float
    answer: str
  def route(state: State) -> Literal["reply", "review", "refuse"]:
    if state["confidence"] >= 0.80: return "reply"
    if state["confidence"] >= 0.45: return "review"
    return "refuse"
  ROUTES = {"reply": END, "review": "human", "refuse": "deny"}

  g = StateGraph(State)
  g.add_node("answer", lambda s: {"answer": "refund within 30 days"})
  g.add_node("human", lambda s: {"answer": "queued for a human"})
  g.add_node("deny", lambda s: {"answer": "no verified answer"})
  g.add_edge(START, "answer")
  g.add_conditional_edges("answer", route, ROUTES)
  g.add_edge("human", END); g.add_edge("deny", END)
  print(g.compile().invoke({"confidence": 0.62, "answer": ""}))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The router reads state and returns a literal; putting a database lookup here would force every routing test to mock it.
 → One branch terminates at END while review and refuse run a node first, so refusals are counted instead of silently dropped.
 → All three thresholds live in one function, so a reviewer can read the whole policy and change one band without touching the
   prompt.

Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Putting the threshold in the prompt and hoping the model applies it, then watching it drift between requests.
2.     Returning a label no mapping key covers, which ends the run without an answer or an error you can trace.

      automation rate.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: State is a schema, not a bag LangGraph passes a TypedDict or Pydantic model between nodes; a node returns a partial update and the graph merges it into state. Declare every key you rely on and keep the shape flat: messages, query, findings, answer, attempt. Separate what the caller supplies from what the graph accumulates and what the API returns. A flat schema with named owners is easier to validate and to migrate than nested dictionaries that gain a key every sprint. Reducers decide conflicts By default a returned key replaces the previous value. For keys that accumulate, wrap the type in Annotated with a reducer such as operator.add or add_messages, which appends and de-duplicates by message ID. Parallel branches then merge deterministically as LangGraph applies updates, instead of the last write winning. Choose a reducer for every list key on purpose; an unannotated list is a bug waiting for the second branch to finish. Test the collision case. Serialisable and small A checkpointer serialises state on every superstep, so state must survive JSON encoding unless you register a serialiser. Keep model clients, database connections, and API keys out of state; pass them through config or closures. Store large documents by ID or object-store key, never as full text. A 500 KB message history written at every step turns a cheap graph into a storage bill and a slow resume, so trim history with a summarising node.

key_terms.definition: A function attached to a state key that combines the current value with a node's update instead of replacing it.

The dictionary a node returns containing only the keys it changed; untouched keys keep their previous values. add_messages LangGraph's built-in reducer for message lists that appends new messages and replaces existing entries by ID. MENTAL MODEL State is a shared spreadsheet with column rules: anyone may add a row, but each column decides whether a new entry replaces the old cell or is appended below it.

  from operator import add

  class State(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]
    findings: Annotated[list[str], add]

  def analyst(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"findings": ["clause 4.1: assignment allowed"]}

  def checker(state: State) -> dict:
    return {"findings": ["clause 7: no liability cap"]}

  g = StateGraph(State)

lessons.title: Persistence
lessons.subtitle: Give each conversation a durable thread, choose a checkpoint store you can operate, and isolate tenants before the first
why_it_matters: Without persistence every request starts from nothing: no follow-up questions, no resume after a crash, no audit trail. A checkpointer turns a graph run into a resumable record, but it also creates a database you must secure, back up, and prune. The engineering decision is which store, which key, and how long to keep what.
outcomes: Attach a checkpointer and address runs by thread_id so a conversation survives a process restart.
Compare in-memory, SQLite, and Postgres checkpoint stores on durability, concurrency, and operating cost.
Design thread keys, retention, and tenant isolation for a multi-user agent.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Threads are the unit of memory A checkpointer saves state after each superstep under a thread_id supplied in config. The same thread continues a conversation; a new thread starts clean. Thread identifiers are an application concern: use a server-generated UUID combined with tenant and user identifiers, never a raw client-supplied string you trust. One thread equals one conversation rather than one user, so a person with three chats gets three threads and no history bleeds between them. Pick a store you can operate MemorySaver is for tests; it dies with the process. SqliteSaver suits a single-instance tool and local development, with file locking as its concurrency limit. PostgresSaver is the production default when you already run Postgres: transactions, backups, connection pooling, and concurrent writers across replicas. Run its schema setup command once and pin the package version, because checkpointer tables change between releases. A Redis-backed community store trades durability for speed and fits poorly when audits matter. Persistence has a privacy surface Checkpoints hold the full message history, retrieved context, and intermediate drafts, which means customer text and possibly personal data. Encrypt the volume, restrict access with the same rules as the application database, and run a retention job that deletes threads older than policy allows. A user deletion request must remove checkpoints, not just rows in your conversations table. Log thread identifiers, never checkpoint contents, and treat support read access as a privileged action.

key_terms.definition: A LangGraph component that serialises graph state after each superstep and restores it when a run resumes. thread_id The configurable identifier that selects which saved state a run loads and appends to.

The guarantee that committed state survives a process crash, redeploy, or host failure. MENTAL MODEL A checkpointer is a save file and thread_id is the slot name: the game resumes exactly where it stopped, so choose slot names users cannot guess or overwrite.

worked_example: A travel platform's booking assistant kept state in MemorySaver. Every deploy dropped live conversations, and support measured 22% of chats restarting mid-booking during the Thursday release window. The team moves to PostgresSaver on the database they already run, applies the library's schema setup, and schedules a 90-day retention job. Thread keys become tenant, user, and a server-generated UUID, after a pen test shows that a client-supplied thread_id could read another tenant's transcript. Resume after a forced pod kill works on the first attempt. The decision recorded is that checkpoint storage inherits the application database's backup, encryption, and access policy instead of adding a second store.

Run the checkpointer's schema setup, pin the package version, and include its tables in backup and restore drills.

code.title: A Postgres-backed graph addressed by a server-composed thread key, resumed in a later process.
code.code:
import os
from typing import TypedDict
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

class State(TypedDict):
  messages: list

g = StateGraph(State)
g.add_node("reply", lambda s: {"messages": s["messages"] + [("ai", "ok")]})
g.add_edge(START, "reply")
g.add_edge("reply", END)

with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as saver:
  saver.setup()
  graph = g.compile(checkpointer=saver)
  cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1:u9:6f2a"}}
  graph.invoke({"messages": [("human", "hello")]}, cfg)
  print(graph.get_state(cfg).values["messages"])
what_to_notice: thread_id is composed on the server; letting a client supply it would turn conversation storage into a cross-tenant read path.
saver.setup() creates checkpoint tables once per database; calling it per request adds latency and races between replicas.

The compiled graph is reusable while the config carries the thread, so build the graph at startup rather than per request. Three pages per lesson Page 363 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Trusting a thread_id from the request body, which turns conversation storage into a cross-tenant read path.
Keeping checkpoints forever because deletion felt risky, then failing a deletion request or a privacy audit.
production_notes: Include checkpoint tables in backups and restore drills; a resumable agent is only as durable as the last tested restore.
Pool checkpointer connections separately and cap the pool, so agent writes cannot starve the request path of your API.
Run retention as a scheduled job with a volume metric, and log deletions without ever logging the deleted content.

retention job that deletes threads older than policy allows. A user deletion request must remove checkpoints, not just
rows in your conversations table. Log thread identifiers, never checkpoint contents, and treat support read access as a
privileged action.

WORKED EXAMPLE
A travel platform's booking assistant kept state in MemorySaver. Every deploy dropped live conversations, and support
measured 22% of chats restarting mid-booking during the Thursday release window. The team moves to PostgresSaver on

become tenant, user, and a server-generated UUID, after a pen test shows that a client-supplied thread_id could read
another tenant's transcript. Resume after a forced pod kill works on the first attempt. The decision recorded is that
checkpoint storage inherits the application database's backup, encryption, and access policy instead of adding a second
store.

1.    Choose the store from your durability, concurrency, and audit requirements, defaulting to Postgres when it is already in the
      stack.
2.    Run the checkpointer's schema setup, pin the package version, and include its tables in backup and restore drills.
3.    Generate thread_id on the server from tenant, user, and a UUID, and reject client attempts to set it directly.
4.    Pass the config on every invoke and stream call, then restart the process and confirm the same thread resumes.
5.    Add retention and deletion jobs, and verify that deleting a thread removes its checkpoints and any stored blobs.
CODE
A Postgres-backed graph addressed by a server-composed thread key, resumed in a later process.
  import os
  from typing import TypedDict
  from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver
  from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph

  class State(TypedDict):
    messages: list

  g = StateGraph(State)
  g.add_node("reply", lambda s: {"messages": s["messages"] + [("ai", "ok")]})
  g.add_edge(START, "reply")
  g.add_edge("reply", END)

  with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"]) as saver:
    saver.setup()
    graph = g.compile(checkpointer=saver)
    cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "t1:u9:6f2a"}}
    graph.invoke({"messages": [("human", "hello")]}, cfg)
    print(graph.get_state(cfg).values["messages"])

 → thread_id is composed on the server; letting a client supply it would turn conversation storage into a cross-tenant read
   path.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Every superstep is a version With a checkpointer attached, LangGraph writes a snapshot after each superstep carrying an ID, step number, the next nodes, and state values. get_state returns the latest; get_state_history returns the lineage newest first. That lineage is the audit trail for an agent decision: you can see which node produced a value and what state it read. Snapshots are immutable, so time travel means selecting an earlier ID rather than editing history. Keep history long enough for disputes, then prune. Resume, replay, fork Invoking with a null input on an existing thread resumes from the last checkpoint, which is how a crashed run continues after a provider recovers. Passing the checkpoint_id of an older snapshot replays from that point and re-runs downstream nodes with current code. update_state writes a corrected value as if a named node produced it, the mechanism behind human editing before approval. Forking replays into a new thread_id so the original stays intact as evidence while you experiment. Replay makes side effects dangerous A node that sends an email, charges a card, or opens a ticket will do it again on replay, because the graph cannot know the effect already happened. Give every external write an idempotency key derived from thread_id, node name, and a version, and make the downstream service honour it. Record the returned external ID in state so a later node checks instead of duplicating. Read-only tools replay safely; anything with a cost or a customer-visible effect needs this discipline.

  cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "claims-8814"}}

lessons.title: Streaming
lessons.subtitle: Stream the right granularity to the right client, keep the persisted turn consistent with what the user saw, and cancel work
why_it_matters: Users judge latency by the first useful token, not by total run time, and a six-second silent wait feels broken. Streaming also changes your failure model: output is already on screen when validation fails, the client may disconnect mid-run, and the final state must match what was rendered. Consistency requires deliberate choices about granularity, transport, and cancellation.
outcomes: Choose between values, updates, messages, and custom stream modes for a specific interface need.
Expose a graph as server-sent events with a stable event schema and trace identifiers.
Handle disconnect, partial output, and post-stream validation without losing the turn.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Granularity is a product decision values emits the full state after each superstep, updates emits only each node's returned delta, messages emits token chunks plus metadata from inside model calls, and debug adds task metadata. A chat UI needs messages for token feel and updates to show which tool is running. An internal dashboard may need only updates. Custom mode lets a node emit domain events such as retrieved four chunks through a stream writer. Pick the smallest set the interface actually renders; every extra mode costs bandwidth and parsing. Transport and event schema Server-sent events suit one-way token flow over HTTP and reconnect natively, while WebSockets are worth it only when the client also sends mid-stream. Define the envelope once: event type, request ID, sequence number, and payload. Emit a heartbeat every 15 seconds so proxies do not close an idle connection during a slow model call. End with a terminal event carrying the validated answer and citation IDs, and let the UI replace speculative text with that final value. Disconnect, cancel, consistency When the client disconnects, stop the graph rather than paying for an answer nobody reads; in FastAPI check request.is_disconnected, cancel the task, and rely on a checkpointer so a reconnect can resume the thread. Assemble the text server-side and persist only after validation, marking the turn incomplete if the stream breaks. Never let streamed tokens bypass output checks: stream a draft, then confirm citations and schema before the terminal event. Log first-token latency and stream duration separately.

key_terms.definition: A one-way HTTP stream of text/event-stream messages that browsers consume through EventSource and reconnect automatically. stream_mode The LangGraph option selecting what each streamed chunk contains: values, updates, messages, custom, or debug.

The time from request start to the first content chunk reaching the client, which users experience as responsiveness. MENTAL MODEL Streaming is a live broadcast with a published transcript: viewers may tune out at any moment, so the recording must stand alone and the station must stop transmitting to an empty room.

code.title: An SSE endpoint that streams node updates and answer tokens from one compiled graph.
code.code:
import json
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

app = FastAPI()
graph = build_graph() # compiled at startup with a Postgres checkpointer

async def events(payload: dict, config: dict):
  async for mode, chunk in graph.astream(
       payload, config, stream_mode=["updates", "messages"]):
    if mode == "messages":
       token, _ = chunk
       yield f"event: token\ndata: {json.dumps({'t': token.content})}\n\n"
    else:
       yield f"event: node\ndata: {json.dumps(list(chunk))}\n\n"

@app.post("/threads/{thread_id}/messages")
async def send(thread_id: str, body: dict):
  config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}
  return StreamingResponse(events(body, config), media_type="text/event-stream")
what_to_notice: The client sees nothing until the answer node emits tokens, so earlier tool activity must travel through the updates mode as separate events.
Each chunk arrives tagged with its mode; a client assuming every chunk is a token will render a dictionary into the chat window.

There is no heartbeat or cancellation in this snippet; production adds a keep-alive comment line and cancels the graph on disconnect. Three pages per lesson Page 369 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Rendering the streamed draft as final before citation and schema checks pass, then failing to correct the screen.
production_notes: Emit a heartbeat every 15 seconds and a terminal event with the validated answer, so proxies and clients can tell stall from completion.
Track first-token latency, stream duration, cancellation rate, and orphaned runs as separate metrics with their own alerts.
Cancel downstream model work on disconnect and record the partial turn as incomplete rather than silently dropping it.

An SSE endpoint that streams node updates and answer tokens from one compiled graph.
  import json
  from fastapi import FastAPI
  from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

  app = FastAPI()
  graph = build_graph() # compiled at startup with a Postgres checkpointer

  async def events(payload: dict, config: dict):
    async for mode, chunk in graph.astream(
         payload, config, stream_mode=["updates", "messages"]):
      if mode == "messages":
         token, _ = chunk
         yield f"event: token\ndata: {json.dumps({'t': token.content})}\n\n"
      else:
         yield f"event: node\ndata: {json.dumps(list(chunk))}\n\n"

  @app.post("/threads/{thread_id}/messages")
  async def send(thread_id: str, body: dict):
    config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}}
    return StreamingResponse(events(body, config), media_type="text/event-stream")

why_it_matters: An agent that can send money, delete records, or email a customer cannot be trusted to certify its own work. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: An interrupt is a durable state boundary Approval is not a question in the prompt; it is a pause the runtime enforces. Before a side-effecting node runs, the graph writes state to the checkpointer and raises an interrupt carrying the proposed action and its evidence. The process can die for an hour. On resume the runtime loads the checkpoint and injects the decision, so the graph continues from the gate instead of re-running earlier nodes and paying for them twice. Gate by blast radius, not by anxiety Rank actions by reversibility. Reads and drafts need no gate; a refund under GBP 100 may need only a policy check; payments above GBP 5,000, deletions, and permission changes need a human. Gate at the narrowest node that performs the effect and show a diff of what will change. Reject ends the branch and records a reason that feeds evaluation. Every decision stores actor, timestamp, original proposal, final payload, and checkpoint version. Execution after accept must be idempotent, keyed by the approval identifier, because a resumed run can be delivered twice by a queue.

An approval gate that pauses before the payment and resumes from a decision without repeating prior work.
  from langgraph.types import Command, interrupt

  def payment_node(state: dict) -> dict:
    proposal = {"invoice": state["invoice_id"],
           "payee": state["payee"],
           "amount_gbp": state["amount_gbp"]}
    decision = interrupt({"action": "pay_invoice", "proposal": proposal})
    if decision["type"] == "reject":
       return {"status": "rejected", "reason": decision["reason"]}
    payload = decision.get("edited", proposal)
    if payload["amount_gbp"] > 5_000:
       return {"status": "blocked", "reason": "above approval ceiling"}
    key = f"approval:{state['approval_id']}"
    return {"status": "paid", "receipt": payments.transfer(payload, key=key)}

  # app.invoke(state, config) pauses here; resume with:
  # app.invoke(Command(resume={"type": "accept"}), config)

lessons.title: Multi-Agent Systems
lessons.subtitle: Decide when several agents with separate context and permissions beat one agent, and what the extra coordination
why_it_matters: One agent with a large prompt, twenty tools, and a long history degrades: tool selection accuracy drops, the context fills with irrelevant detail, and a single permission scope covers everything. Splitting into specialised agents can restore focus and let you apply least privilege per role. But each handoff loses context, adds a model call, and creates a new place for errors to hide. Multi-agent design is therefore an argument about boundaries and cost, not a default architecture.
outcomes: Justify a multi-agent split by differences in context, tools, permissions, or ownership rather than by task count.
Compare pipeline, supervisor, hierarchical, and peer-handoff topologies and choose one for a stated coupling pattern.
Estimate the token, latency, and failure-propagation cost of adding a second agent before you build it.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A split must earn its keep Two prompts in two files are not a multi-agent system. A real split gives each agent its own context window, toolset, permission scope, and success metric, plus a contract for handing work over. Valid reasons are conflicting permissions, such as a billing agent that may issue refunds beside a research agent that may not; incompatible context, such as a legal corpus versus telemetry; or separate ownership and release cadence. Splitting a job that shares all three adds coordination cost with no isolation benefit. Topologies encode who decides A pipeline passes work in a fixed order and suits staged transforms with no backtracking. A supervisor routes each turn to one worker and owns termination. A hierarchy nests supervisors when a worker's own subtasks need routing, at the price of more hops. Peer handoff lets agents transfer control directly, which is flexible and hard to bound. Choose the least autonomous topology that matches the coupling: fixed order for known stages, a supervisor when the next specialist depends on findings. Coordination has a bill Every delegation sends a prompt and returns a summary, so a five-agent run can cost three to five times a single agent for the same task. Latency adds per hop, and a wrong fact introduced by one worker propagates silently because the next agent trusts its input. Bound it with a delegation cap, a shared budget in tokens and currency, explicit return schemas, and a rule that only verified facts cross a boundary. Measure cost per successful task, not per agent call.

key_terms.definition: The transfer of control and a bounded context payload from one agent to another, including the reason and remaining budget.
The arrangement of agents and the permitted routes between them, such as pipeline, supervisor, hierarchy, or peer mesh.

Giving an agent only the history, tools, and data its role needs, which improves focus and limits blast radius. MENTAL MODEL A multi-agent system is a specialist clinic, not a committee: each desk has its own equipment and authority, patients follow a referral path, and one clinician owns discharge.

code.title: A handoff envelope that carries only verified facts, remaining budget, and the route the receiving agent is allowed to take.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Handoff:
  from_agent: str
  to_agent: str
  reason: str
  facts: tuple[str, ...]
  open_questions: tuple[str, ...]
  budget_tokens: int
  tried: tuple[str, ...] = ()

   def check(self, allowed: dict[str, set[str]]) -> None:
     assert self.to_agent in allowed[self.from_agent], "route not permitted"
     assert self.budget_tokens > 0, "handoff must carry budget"
     assert self.reason and self.facts, "handoff needs reason and facts"
     assert self.to_agent not in self.tried, "do not retry a failed agent"
what_to_notice: The envelope carries claims, not raw transcripts; every fact should name the tool or document that produced it.
The allowed map encodes the routing graph, so an agent cannot invent a peer or escalate to a privileged worker.

Budget travels with the handoff, making cost visible at every hop instead of only at the end of the run. Three pages per lesson Page 375 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

CODE
A supervisor loop with a hop cap and a no-progress counter that ends in an honest partial result.
  DECISIONS = {"search", "filings", "transcripts", "fact_check"}

  def supervise(goal: str, run: dict, workers: dict) -> dict:
    for _ in range(run["max_hops"]):
       decision = route(goal, run["results"], budget=run["budget"])
       if decision["action"] == "finish":
          break
       if decision["worker"] not in DECISIONS:
          break
       result = workers[decision["worker"]](decision["task"], run["budget"])
       run["results"].append(result)
       if result["new_evidence"] == 0:
          run["stale"] += 1
          if run["stale"] >= 2:
             break
       else:
          run["stale"] = 0
    return {"results": run["results"], "complete": run["stale"] < 2}

   budget.

 → The stale counter resets on any new evidence, so a run alternating between two useful workers is not stopped early.

why_it_matters: Once more than one agent works on a task, the hard problem stops being the model and becomes coordination. Two workers research the same company and waste budget; two writers update one memo and lose a section; a fact without provenance gets copied into the final answer. Collaboration design decides what is shared, who may write it, and how a conflict is detected. Get it wrong and the system fails quietly, producing a plausible report assembled from stale and conflicting pieces.
outcomes: Select message passing, a shared blackboard, or an artefact store based on write contention and audit needs.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Three ways to share, three failure modes Message passing keeps agents decoupled: each handoff is an envelope and the receiver owns its own state, which suits supervisor routing but loses a global view. A blackboard gives every agent one readable store, which speeds shared context and invites write conflicts. An artefact store keeps immutable outputs in object storage with a manifest, best for long documents and audit. Most production systems mix all three: envelopes for control, a blackboard for facts, and artefacts for deliverables. A handoff is a contract with provenance The receiver should not need the sender's transcript. Send the task, the constraints, verified facts each tagged with the tool or document that produced them, open questions, what was already tried and failed, and the remaining budget. Unverified model claims must be marked as hypotheses, not facts. This payload is also the unit you log, so a reviewer can see why an agent believed something. Omitting the do-not-retry list practically guarantees a loop. Concurrency needs ownership and versions Parallel workers are safe only when writes are controlled. Give each shared object one writer, or use optimistic concurrency: read a version, compute, then write only if the version is unchanged, otherwise re-read. Merge steps should be explicit and owned by one agent. Duplicate work is cheaper to prevent than to detect, so claim a task with a lease in the blackboard before researching it, and expire the lease so a crashed worker does not block the queue.

key_terms.definition: A shared, readable state store that multiple agents read and write, typically with task leases and version numbers.
A write strategy that commits only if the object's version is unchanged since it was read, otherwise retrying.

The recorded origin of a fact or artefact, including tool, document, timestamp, and agent, used to verify and cite it. MENTAL MODEL Collaboration is a shared kitchen with labelled shelves: anyone may read the stock list, only the assigned cook plates a dish, and every container carries a date and an owner.

A versioned blackboard write that refuses to clobber a concurrent update and returns False for the caller to retry.
  import threading

  class Blackboard:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
       self._data: dict[str, tuple[int, dict]] = {}
       self._lock = threading.Lock()
    def read(self, key: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
       with self._lock:
         return self._data.get(key, (0, {}))
    def write(self, key: str, version: int, patch: dict) -> bool:
       with self._lock:
         current, value = self._data.get(key, (0, {}))
         if current != version:
            return False
         self._data[key] = (version + 1, {**value, **patch})
         return True

  board = Blackboard()
  version, facts = board.read("acme/facts")
  print(board.write("acme/facts", version, {"revenue": "GBP 42m"}))

 → write() returns False instead of overwriting, so the caller must re-read, re-apply its patch, and retry once.

 → The lock protects one process only; with several workers the version check belongs in Postgres or Redis, not in memory.

  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class RunConfig:
    graph_version: str = "2026-10-07.3"
    deadline_s: float = 75.0
    max_tokens: int = 120_000

  def resume_or_restart(checkpoint: dict, config: RunConfig) -> str:
    if checkpoint["graph_version"] != config.graph_version:
       return "restart" # topology or prompts changed; replay unsafe

       return "partial"

why_it_matters: Every assistant eventually needs data and actions it does not own: tickets, repositories, inventory, calendars. Before MCP, each team wrote a private connector, documented it in a wiki, and rebuilt it for the next application. MCP turns that repeated integration work into one versioned contract, so a tool server written once can serve a desktop host, an IDE, and a production agent without changing its transport logic.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One contract, many hosts MCP is an open protocol, not a runtime or a model feature. A host application embeds a client that speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 to a server. The server advertises tools, resources, and prompts; the host decides what the user sees and what the model may call. Because the wire format is standard, a filesystem server built for an IDE also works in a support agent, provided the host implements the same methods and consent rules. Tools, resources, prompts Servers expose three primitives. Tools are callable functions with JSON Schema inputs, such as create_ticket or search_orders. Resources are readable URIs, such as file:///runbooks/oncall.md or crm://accounts/1842. Prompts are reusable templates the user can select. Tools change state, resources read it, prompts shape a request. Keeping that distinction clear prevents a read-only document from becoming an unbounded write endpoint. A resource can be listed and read without granting the ability to mutate it, which keeps reviewable data separate from write paths. Consent sits in the host The protocol carries capability and intent, not trust. A server may offer a destructive tool, but the host must show it, scope credentials per server, and obtain approval where the action is risky. Model output never authorises a call. The client validates arguments, applies timeouts, and records the call. Security depends on host policy and server-side authorisation, not on the description text a model reads.

key_terms.definition: The AI application, such as an IDE or agent runtime, that embeds clients and decides which server capabilities the model may use.
A process that exposes tools, resources, or prompts over MCP and enforces its own authentication, validation, and rate limits.

The byte channel carrying JSON-RPC messages, typically stdio for a local process or Streamable HTTP for a remote service. MENTAL MODEL MCP is a USB-C port for AI tools: the host supplies power and permission, the server supplies a device, and the standard shape means either side can be replaced.

  import json

  def rpc(request_id, method, params=None):
    return {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": request_id, "method": method,
         "params": params or {}}

  initialize = rpc(1, "initialize", {
     "protocolVersion": "2025-06-18",
     "capabilities": {},
     "clientInfo": {"name": "support-console", "version": "1.4.0"},
  })
  print(json.dumps(initialize, indent=2))

  # After the server replies, the client sends this notification:
  initialized = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}
  print(json.dumps(initialized))

  # Discovery is a plain request; the reply contains tool descriptors.
  tools_list = rpc(2, "tools/list", {})
  print(json.dumps(tools_list))

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The N×M tax If three assistants need six systems, bespoke connectors require up to eighteen implementations, each with its own retry logic, pagination, and credential store. A shared protocol reduces that to three shared client implementations and six servers: nine components instead of eighteen edges. The saving compounds as either side grows. from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Estate:
  hosts: int
  systems: int

   def bespoke_edges(self) -> int:
     return self.hosts * self.systems

   def mcp_components(self) -> int:
     return self.hosts + self.systems

estate = Estate(hosts=6, systems=9)
print(f"bespoke connectors: {estate.bespoke_edges()}")
print(f"MCP components: {estate.mcp_components()}")
saved = estate.bespoke_edges() - estate.mcp_components()

lessons.title: MCP Servers
lessons.subtitle: An MCP server owns one system boundary, advertises narrow capabilities, validates every call, and stays observable under
why_it_matters: A server is the only place where the owning team can enforce what an AI may do to their system. If that boundary is vague, every host invents its own rules and the system team loses the ability to audit or revoke access. A good server looks like a small, well-documented API: few capabilities, predictable schemas, explicit errors, and logs that identify the caller. It is infrastructure, not a demo script.
outcomes: Design a server around one bounded system with explicit read and write capabilities.
Implement tool advertisement, validation, error results, and structured logging over stdio or HTTP.
Operate a server with health checks, pagination, rate limits, and graceful shutdown.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One boundary per server Group capabilities by system ownership and data classification, not by assistant feature. A Postgres server that exposes read-only analytics queries has a clear owner, credential, and audit trail; a server that also sends email and refunds has three. Small servers are easier to review, version, and revoke. They also limit blast radius: a prompt injection that reaches the analytics server cannot pivot into payments. When two systems must be composed, let the host or agent orchestrate rather than merging them. Advertise narrowly, validate strictly The server's tools/list response is a contract, so name tools for the action and object, describe when to use them, and publish a JSON Schema with required fields, enums, and bounds. Validate again at execution time: the schema does not prove authorisation or business constraints. Return tool-level failures as isError results with actionable text, and reserve JSON-RPC errors for malformed requests and unknown methods. A server that trusts model-supplied arguments because they passed the schema is an injection path. Run it like a service stdio servers need clean stderr logging, a fast startup, and a parent-death strategy; any print to stdout breaks the protocol. HTTP servers need authentication, per-caller rate limits, health and readiness endpoints, and session expiry. Both need request IDs, latency metrics, and bounded concurrency. Graceful shutdown should stop accepting calls, finish or cancel in-flight work, and close database pools. A server with no health signal becomes invisible until an assistant silently loses a capability.

MCP Servers
An MCP server owns one system boundary, advertises narrow capabilities, validates every call, and stays observable under
concurrency.
MCP · Lesson 5 of 12 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A server is the only place where the owning team can enforce what an AI may do to their system. If that boundary is
vague, every host invents its own rules and the system team loses the ability to audit or revoke access. A good server
looks like a small, well-documented API: few capabilities, predictable schemas, explicit errors, and logs that identify the
caller. It is infrastructure, not a demo script.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Design a server around one bounded system with explicit read and write capabilities.
 • Implement tool advertisement, validation, error results, and structured logging over stdio or HTTP.
 • Operate a server with health checks, pagination, rate limits, and graceful shutdown.
CORE CONCEPTS
One boundary per server
Group capabilities by system ownership and data classification, not by assistant feature. A Postgres server that exposes
read-only analytics queries has a clear owner, credential, and audit trail; a server that also sends email and refunds has
three. Small servers are easier to review, version, and revoke. They also limit blast radius: a prompt injection that reaches
the analytics server cannot pivot into payments. When two systems must be composed, let the host or agent orchestrate
rather than merging them.
Advertise narrowly, validate strictly
The server's tools/list response is a contract, so name tools for the action and object, describe when to use them, and
publish a JSON Schema with required fields, enums, and bounds. Validate again at execution time: the schema does not
prove authorisation or business constraints. Return tool-level failures as isError results with actionable text, and reserve
JSON-RPC errors for malformed requests and unknown methods. A server that trusts model-supplied arguments because
they passed the schema is an injection path.
Run it like a service
stdio servers need clean stderr logging, a fast startup, and a parent-death strategy; any print to stdout breaks the
protocol. HTTP servers need authentication, per-caller rate limits, health and readiness endpoints, and session expiry.
Both need request IDs, latency metrics, and bounded concurrency. Graceful shutdown should stop accepting calls, finish
or cancel in-flight work, and close database pools. A server with no health signal becomes invisible until an assistant
silently loses a capability.

 Bounded context                  A system boundary with one owner, one data classification, and a coherent set of capabilities exposed by a
                                  server.
 isError                          A tool result flag indicating the tool ran but failed, allowing the model to see and possibly correct the
                                  problem.
 Pagination cursor                An opaque token returned by list methods so a client can fetch the next page without loading every
                                  capability at once.

CODE
A read-only FastMCP server with an allowlist and a row cap enforced inside the handler.
  from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

  mcp = FastMCP("warehouse")
  ROWS = {"orders": [{"id": 1, "total": 42}], "refunds": []}
  MAX_ROWS = 1_000

  @mcp.tool()
  def sample_rows(table: str, limit: int = 20) -> dict:
    """Return at most 1,000 rows from an allowlisted table."""
    if table not in ROWS:
       raise ValueError("table not allowlisted")
    capped = min(max(limit, 1), MAX_ROWS)
    return {"table": table, "rows": ROWS[table][:capped], "limit": capped}

  mcp.run(transport="stdio")

lessons.title: MCP Tools
lessons.subtitle: A tool is a named, schema-bound function with a declared side effect; the schema sells it to the model, the handler
why_it_matters: Tools are the part of MCP that changes state. A model chooses them from names and descriptions, fills arguments against a schema, and reads the result as content. Every ambiguity becomes a bad call: a vague description invites the wrong tool, a loose schema accepts a negative quantity, and a bare string result hides whether the refund succeeded. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The descriptor is the prompt A tool definition combines name, description, inputSchema, optional outputSchema, and annotations. The name should be verb_noun and unique: search_orders, not query. The description states when to use it, what it returns, and its limits; often it is the model's only guidance. The schema should mark required fields, constrain enums and ranges, and avoid free-form objects. A tight schema prevents invalid calls; a vague one shifts work to runtime errors. Results, not just strings A tools/call result contains content blocks, such as text, image, or embedded resource, plus optional structuredContent matching outputSchema. Set isError when the tool ran but failed, and include an actionable message so the model can correct it. Protocol errors differ: an unknown tool or malformed params belong in a JSON-RPC error. Never return a stack trace or raw SQL error as success content. Hosts render resources and images, so describe what changed, not only that it worked. Side effects need more than a schema Annotations such as readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, and openWorldHint are hints, not enforcement. A refund tool needs an idempotency key, caps the amount server-side, and returns the ledger reference. Split preview from execute when the user must see consequences: refund_preview calculates fees; refund_execute commits with its token. The host should approve destructive calls, but the server must still authorise the caller and reject replays. Trust the database constraint, not the description.

key_terms.definition: A hint such as readOnlyHint or destructiveHint that helps a host present and gate a tool but does not enforce behaviour.

A caller-supplied identifier that lets a server detect and collapse duplicate write requests caused by retries. MENTAL MODEL A tool is a labelled machine on a factory floor: the label tells operators what it does, the guard stops hands, and the log proves what was produced.

CODE
A destructive tool descriptor and a handler that collapses duplicate calls with an idempotency key.
  TOOL = {
    "name": "refund_execute",
    "description": "Commit a refund after refund_preview; requires approval.",
    "inputSchema": {"type": "object",
             "required": ["preview_token", "idempotency_key"],
             "properties": {"preview_token": {"type": "string"},
                     "idempotency_key": {"type": "string"}}},
    "annotations": {"destructiveHint": True, "idempotentHint": True},
  }
  LEDGER = {}

  def call_refund(args: dict) -> dict:
    key = args["idempotency_key"]
    if not args.get("preview_token"): raise ValueError("preview token required")
    if key in LEDGER:
       return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "duplicate ignored"}],
            "structuredContent": LEDGER[key]}
    LEDGER[key] = {"refund_id": f"RF-{len(LEDGER) + 1:06d}"}

lessons.title: MCP Resources
lessons.subtitle: Resources are addressable, read-only context: a URI the host can list, read, and subscribe to without giving the model a
why_it_matters: Tools let a model act; most requests only need to read. If every document becomes a tool, the model pays tokens to call something a host could have fetched deterministically. Resources separate retrieval from generation: the host resolves a URI, checks permission, and places content in context. That makes context inspectable, cacheable, and reviewable before the model sees it.
outcomes: Distinguish a resource URI from a tool call and choose the right primitive for documents, records, and live state.
Implement resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read with pagination and MIME types.
Apply subscriptions, caching, and URI allowlists so context stays fresh without exposing the filesystem.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The URI is the contract A resource is identified by a URI such as file:///runbooks/oncall.md or crm://accounts/1842, and described by name, description, and MIME type. The scheme encodes the owning system, which keeps routing and authorisation unambiguous. Resources may be fixed or templated: resources/templates/list advertises a pattern like crm://accounts/{id}, and the host fills parameters after checking access. Reading returns text or a base64 blob, never a side effect. List, read, subscribe Clients call resources/list with an optional cursor, then resources/read with one URI. Large trees need pagination or the host stalls on startup. A server advertising resources.subscribe can push notifications/resources/updated when a document changes, letting the host invalidate a cached read instead of polling. Without subscribe, choose an explicit TTL per scheme and record it in the cache entry, because a stale runbook is worse than no runbook. Governance stays in the host A resource URI is an address, not a permission. The host maps schemes to trusted servers, rejects paths that escape a declared root, and limits total bytes placed in context. A model should never invent an arbitrary URI and have the client fetch it: the host resolves candidates, applies allowlists, and ranks them before insertion. Attach provenance, fetch time, and a content hash to every resource block so citation checks can verify what the model actually read.

key_terms.definition: A stable address, such as file:///policies/leave.md, that identifies readable content a host can list and fetch.
A parameterised URI pattern, such as crm://accounts/{id}, advertised so clients can request a known family of records.

A server capability that notifies a client when a subscribed resource changes, allowing cached content to be invalidated. MENTAL MODEL Resources are a library catalogue, not a lending desk: the host chooses which shelf to open, records what was read, and nothing on the shelf changes.

MCP Resources
Resources are addressable, read-only context: a URI the host can list, read, and subscribe to without giving the model a
write path.
MCP · Lesson 7 of 12 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Tools let a model act; most requests only need to read. If every document becomes a tool, the model pays tokens to call
something a host could have fetched deterministically. Resources separate retrieval from generation: the host resolves a
URI, checks permission, and places content in context. That makes context inspectable, cacheable, and reviewable before
the model sees it.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Distinguish a resource URI from a tool call and choose the right primitive for documents, records, and live state.
 • Implement resources/list, resources/templates/list, and resources/read with pagination and MIME types.
 • Apply subscriptions, caching, and URI allowlists so context stays fresh without exposing the filesystem.
CORE CONCEPTS
The URI is the contract
A resource is identified by a URI such as file:///runbooks/oncall.md or crm://accounts/1842, and described by name,
description, and MIME type. The scheme encodes the owning system, which keeps routing and authorisation
unambiguous. Resources may be fixed or templated: resources/templates/list advertises a pattern like
crm://accounts/{id}, and the host fills parameters after checking access. Reading returns text or a base64 blob, never a
side effect.
List, read, subscribe
Clients call resources/list with an optional cursor, then resources/read with one URI. Large trees need pagination or the
host stalls on startup. A server advertising resources.subscribe can push notifications/resources/updated when a
document changes, letting the host invalidate a cached read instead of polling. Without subscribe, choose an explicit TTL
per scheme and record it in the cache entry, because a stale runbook is worse than no runbook.
Governance stays in the host
A resource URI is an address, not a permission. The host maps schemes to trusted servers, rejects paths that escape a
declared root, and limits total bytes placed in context. A model should never invent an arbitrary URI and have the client
fetch it: the host resolves candidates, applies allowlists, and ranks them before insertion. Attach provenance, fetch time,
and a content hash to every resource block so citation checks can verify what the model actually read.
KEY TERMS
 Resource URI                     A stable address, such as file:///policies/leave.md, that identifies readable content a host can list and fetch.
 Resource template                A parameterised URI pattern, such as crm://accounts/{id}, advertised so clients can request a known family of
                                  records.
 Subscription                     A server capability that notifies a client when a subscribed resource changes, allowing cached content to be
                                  invalidated.

  MENTAL MODEL Resources are a library catalogue, not a lending desk: the host chooses which shelf to open, records what was read,
  and nothing on the shelf changes.

MCP Resources
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A support agent answers from 240 runbooks stored in Git. The first build wraps search_docs as a tool, so the model calls it
on 71% of turns and occasionally invents document names. The team replaces it with a filesystem resource server
exposing file:///runbooks/{slug}.md, a manifest resource listing all 240 slugs, and content hashes. The host ranks
candidate slugs from the question, reads at most three, and injects them with fetch timestamps. A subscription
invalidates the cache when the post-deploy runbook changes. Tool calls fall by 64%, p95 latency drops from 3.4 to 1.9
seconds, and the stale-cache wrong-answer incident no longer reproduces.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Inventory read-only content the assistant needs, then assign each set a URI scheme and a responsible server.
2.    Decide which items are fixed resources and which need templates such as ticket://{id}/thread.
3.    Define MIME types, byte caps, and pagination for every listing method before implementing handlers.
4.    Map each scheme to a trusted server, an allowlisted root, and a permission check on the caller.
5.    Add content hashes, fetch timestamps, and TTLs, then test that a subscription notification invalidates the cache.
CODE
A paginated resource listing and a read handler that refuses any path outside the allowlisted root.
  from pathlib import Path

  ROOT = Path("/srv/runbooks").resolve()
  FILES = sorted(p.relative_to(ROOT).as_posix() for p in ROOT.glob("*.md"))

  def resources_list(cursor: str | None = None) -> dict:
    start = int(cursor or 0)
    page = FILES[start:start + 50]
    items = [{"uri": f"file:///runbooks/{s}", "name": s,
           "mimeType": "text/markdown"} for s in page]
    if start + 50 < len(FILES):
       return {"resources": items, "nextCursor": str(start + 50)}
    return {"resources": items}

  def resources_read(uri: str) -> dict:
    path = (ROOT / uri.removeprefix("file:///runbooks/")).resolve()
    if ROOT not in path.parents:
       raise ValueError("uri outside allowlisted root")
    return {"contents": [{"uri": uri, "mimeType": "text/markdown",
                 "text": path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")}]}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The manifest is computed once at startup, so a new runbook needs a restart or a file watcher that emits
   resources/list_changed.
 → Path containment uses resolved parents, so ../ and symlink tricks fail closed rather than reading outside /srv/runbooks.
 → Pagination caps each response at 50 items; without it, a host with hundreds of documents blocks during initial discovery.

lessons.title: MCP Prompts
lessons.subtitle: Prompts are parameterised, server-published templates that give users a reviewed starting point instead of a blank box
why_it_matters: Users type the same requests badly and differently. A prompt template lets the owning team encode domain instructions once, test them, and expose them as a named action such as summarise_incident. The server supplies reviewed text; the host supplies user arguments and consent. Without that boundary, every host copies a prompt from a wiki, drifts, and nobody can tell which wording produced a bad answer.
outcomes: Distinguish a prompt from a system message and from a tool, and decide which belongs to the server.
Implement prompts/list and prompts/get with declared arguments, descriptions, and multipart message content.
