lessons.title: Agent Evaluation
lessons.subtitle: Score the trajectory as well as the answer: tool choice, arguments, step count, state, and the cost of getting there.
lessons.meta: Production AI Engineering · Lesson 18 of 26 · study guide
why_it_matters: An agent can produce the right answer through a lucky, expensive, or unsafe path. Outcome-only scoring rewards a run that deleted the wrong record, retried eight times, or read data it should not have. Agent evaluation must inspect the sequence of decisions and the state they changed. It also needs deterministic replay, because live tools make failures disappear the moment you try to reproduce them.
outcomes: Evaluate an agent on outcome, trajectory, and efficiency rather than judging only the final message.
Replay recorded runs against deterministic tool fakes so tool-call mistakes are reproducible and cheap to test.
Define pass criteria for tool arguments, step limits, and recovery from a failed tool response.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Three layers of score Outcome asks whether the user's goal was met and verified against a source of truth. Trajectory asks whether the agent chose permitted tools with valid arguments in a sensible order. Efficiency asks how many steps, tokens, and seconds it spent. A run passes only when all three meet their thresholds. Report them separately, because a correct answer from a forbidden tool is still a security failure, and a cheap failure is still a failure. Replay instead of live calls Record tool name, arguments, response, latency, and timestamp for every step. Replace the live tools with fakes that return those responses, then run the agent's decision loop against the recording. This makes tests fast, repeatable, and safe for destructive actions. Keep a small live smoke suite to catch schema drift in the tools themselves. Store recordings with the model and prompt versions, since a different model may take a different path. Grade the path, not the prose Check expected tool sets, forbidden tools, argument constraints, and maximum steps with deterministic assertions. Use an LLM judge only for qualities that resist rules, such as whether a plan is coherent, and calibrate it. Score recovery explicitly: inject a 429, a timeout, or an empty result and require a bounded retry or a clear explanation. Termination matters too; an agent that stops without answering should fail, not receive partial credit.

Agent Evaluation
Score the trajectory as well as the answer: tool choice, arguments, step count, state, and the cost of getting there.
Production AI Engineering · Lesson 18 of 26 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
An agent can produce the right answer through a lucky, expensive, or unsafe path. Outcome-only scoring rewards a run
that deleted the wrong record, retried eight times, or read data it should not have. Agent evaluation must inspect the
sequence of decisions and the state they changed. It also needs deterministic replay, because live tools make failures
disappear the moment you try to reproduce them.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Evaluate an agent on outcome, trajectory, and efficiency rather than judging only the final message.
 • Replay recorded runs against deterministic tool fakes so tool-call mistakes are reproducible and cheap to test.
 • Define pass criteria for tool arguments, step limits, and recovery from a failed tool response.
CORE CONCEPTS
Three layers of score
Outcome asks whether the user's goal was met and verified against a source of truth. Trajectory asks whether the agent
chose permitted tools with valid arguments in a sensible order. Efficiency asks how many steps, tokens, and seconds it
spent. A run passes only when all three meet their thresholds. Report them separately, because a correct answer from a
forbidden tool is still a security failure, and a cheap failure is still a failure.
Replay instead of live calls
Record tool name, arguments, response, latency, and timestamp for every step. Replace the live tools with fakes that
return those responses, then run the agent's decision loop against the recording. This makes tests fast, repeatable, and
safe for destructive actions. Keep a small live smoke suite to catch schema drift in the tools themselves. Store recordings
with the model and prompt versions, since a different model may take a different path.
Grade the path, not the prose
Check expected tool sets, forbidden tools, argument constraints, and maximum steps with deterministic assertions. Use
an LLM judge only for qualities that resist rules, such as whether a plan is coherent, and calibrate it. Score recovery
explicitly: inject a 429, a timeout, or an empty result and require a bounded retry or a clear explanation. Termination
matters too; an agent that stops without answering should fail, not receive partial credit.
KEY TERMS
 Trajectory                       The ordered sequence of model decisions, tool calls, observations, and state changes produced during one
                                  agent run.
 Deterministic replay             Re-running an agent against recorded tool responses so a failure reproduces without touching live systems.
 Step budget                      The maximum number of model turns or tool calls allowed before the runtime must stop the agent.

  MENTAL MODEL Judge an agent like a delivery: the parcel must arrive, the route must be legal, and the fuel bill must make sense. A
  lucky shortcut does not earn a pass.

Build it

STEP BY STEP
1.    Write five to ten reference tasks per agent capability, each with a verifiable outcome and an allowed tool set.
2.    Record tool calls, arguments, observations, and state for every step; redact secrets and personal data at capture.
3.    Build fakes that replay those observations, including error cases such as 429, 403, and empty results.
4.    Assert outcome against a source of truth, then assert tool allowlists, argument bounds, and maximum steps.

CODE
A trajectory evaluator that fails a run for a wrong answer, a forbidden tool, an overrun step budget, or an ending on an unhandled tool error.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Step:
    tool: str
    ok: bool

  ALLOWED = {"search_expenses", "get_policy", "summarise"}

  def evaluate(answer, expected, steps, budget=6):
    failures = []
    if answer.strip() != expected.strip():
       failures.append("wrong_answer")
    if {s.tool for s in steps} - ALLOWED:
       failures.append("forbidden_tool")
    if len(steps) > budget:
       failures.append("step_budget")
    if steps and not steps[-1].ok:
       failures.append("unhandled_tool_error")
    return failures

 → The evaluator checks the answer, tool allowlist, step budget, and unhandled errors separately, so a lucky answer cannot
   hide an unsafe path.
 → Recorded 403 and 429 observations turn a rare provider failure into a repeatable test that costs nothing to run.
 → A model change can alter the trajectory even when the outcome is unchanged; re-record and re-score both layers.

lessons.subtitle: Test deterministic code exhaustively, model calls through contracts and fakes, and behaviour with a small evaluation suite.
lessons.meta: Production AI Engineering · Lesson 19 of 26 · study guide
why_it_matters: AI systems combine ordinary code, which deserves ordinary tests, with probabilistic components that cannot be asserted exactly. Testing everything through live model calls produces slow, flaky suites that teams disable. Testing nothing leaves prompt and model changes unguarded. The workable pattern is a pyramid: exhaustive deterministic tests, contract tests at provider boundaries, and a small behavioural suite that runs on every release.
outcomes: Separate unit, contract, integration, and evaluation tests, and place each in the right pipeline stage.
Replace live model calls with fakes and recorded fixtures so tests are fast, repeatable, and cheap.
Test refusals, malformed output, timeouts, and prompt injection as first-class cases, not edge cases.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Test the code you own Most of an AI service is ordinary software: request parsing, auth, retrieval filters, prompt assembly, validation, retries, and persistence. Unit-test those with no model involved. Assert that a chunk outside the tenant filter never reaches the prompt, that a 429 triggers one retry with jitter, and that a missing citation raises the right rule. These tests are fast, deterministic, and catch the majority of regressions before a token is spent. Contracts at the model boundary Wrap the provider in a thin client with a typed request and response. Contract tests run against recorded payloads and a mock server to catch schema changes, missing usage fields, and unexpected finish reasons. A few live smoke tests confirm the real provider still matches. Keep those smoke tests outside the main suite so a provider outage does not block every pull request, but alert when they fail. Behaviour needs scenarios, not assertions For quality, use a small evaluation suite that runs on release candidates: 50 to 200 cases with expected properties, not exact strings. Include refusals, ambiguous requests, prompt injection, long context, and non-English input. Assert thresholds such as 90% schema validity and zero unsafe disclosures, and let a judge or labels score the rest. A failing behavioural test should print the case, the output, and the rule it broke.

key_terms.definition: A test that verifies the request and response shape at a service boundary against a fixed, recorded expectation.
A stored input and expected output pair that lets a test replay a real interaction without a live dependency.

A test whose result changes without a code change, usually because it depends on time, network, or model sampling. MENTAL MODEL Use a test pyramid: many fast checks on your own code, a thin contract layer at the provider edge, and a small, slower suite for behaviour.

code.title: A fake model client that proves the repair path runs exactly once and then raises a typed error, with no network or API key.
code.code:
import pytest
from app.llm import ModelClient, ModelError
from app.service import answer

class FakeModel(ModelClient):
  def __init__(self, reply: str | Exception):
     self.reply = reply
     self.calls = 0

   def complete(self, prompt: str) -> str:
     self.calls += 1
     if isinstance(self.reply, Exception):
        raise self.reply
     return self.reply

def test_repair_is_attempted_once_then_fails():
  fake = FakeModel("{not json")
  with pytest.raises(ModelError):
     answer("Summarise this", client=fake, repair=True)
  assert fake.calls == 2
what_to_notice: The fake counts calls, so the test proves the repair path ran exactly once instead of merely observing an exception.
No network or API key is needed; the failure case runs in milliseconds and behaves the same on every machine.

The fake returns the same malformed payload both times, which tests the bound but not whether a realistic repair can succeed. Three pages per lesson Page 479 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

production_notes: Block merges on the fast deterministic suite and run the full behavioural gate on every release candidate build.
Quarantine flaky tests with an owner and a deadline; silent retries train the team to ignore red builds.
Record the model, prompt hash, and fixture version in failures so a broken test can be traced to a change.

lessons.title: Regression Testing
lessons.subtitle: Compare every prompt or model change against a frozen baseline, and fail the gate when a slice gets worse.
lessons.meta: Production AI Engineering · Lesson 20 of 26 · study guide
why_it_matters: Hosted models change without notice, prompts interact in surprising ways, and retrieval updates alter what the model sees. A system that passed last month can fail today with no commit in between. Regression testing turns that uncertainty into a comparison: same cases, same rubric, old versus new. It is the difference between discovering a quality drop in a dashboard and discovering it in a customer escalation.
outcomes: Freeze a baseline of outputs, scores, latency, and cost, then diff a candidate against it case by case.
Set regression thresholds per slice so aggregate gains cannot hide a serious local failure.
Handle model drift, sampling noise, and flaky cases without turning the gate into a ritual.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Baselines are evidence, not truth Store per-case outputs, scores, latency, token usage, and model version for a known-good release. The baseline is the best evidence you had at that moment, not a guarantee of correctness. When you find a labelling error, fix the dataset and re-baseline deliberately. Never overwrite the baseline during a candidate run, and keep enough history to compare across several releases. A baseline that nobody can reproduce is a rumour with a timestamp. Diff by case and by slice Aggregate scores hide regressions: a two-point overall gain can contain a twenty-point drop for one document type. Compare per-case outcomes, then roll up by intent, language, tenant, and difficulty. Classify each change as fixed, broken, unchanged-correct, or unchanged-wrong. Gate on broken cases and on slice floors, not only the mean. Print the ten most damaging diffs with inputs, outputs, and rule IDs so a reviewer can act. Noise needs a policy Model sampling and judge variance make small differences meaningless. Run at temperature zero where possible, repeat high-variance cases three times, and require a change to exceed the measured noise band. Separate deterministic checks, which should never flake, from judged quality. When a case flips repeatedly, mark it unstable and investigate the rubric rather than loosening the gate. Scheduled re-runs catch provider drift even when your code has not changed.

key_terms.definition: The recorded outputs, scores, latency, and versions from a release accepted as the comparison point.
A subgroup of evaluation cases, such as one language or document type, scored separately.

The range of score variation observed when the same system is evaluated repeatedly. MENTAL MODEL A regression suite is a ratchet: each release may improve the system, but a known-good behaviour should never slip backwards unnoticed.
Page 481 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.mental_model: Think of regression testing as a building block - once you understand it, you'll use it again and again as you build your AI app.
worked_example: A support assistant releases every Thursday. The team keeps 300 labelled cases and a baseline from release 42. Candidate 43 improves aggregate accuracy from 84% to 86%, so the release looks safe. The slice diff shows billing questions fell from 91% to 72% after a prompt edit that shortened policy context. Ten cases now omit the refund window. Because the gate requires every slice to stay within three points of baseline, the release is blocked. The team restores the policy section, re- runs, and gets 85% overall with billing back at 90%. Two cases still flip between runs, so they are marked unstable and reviewed. The decision: ship 43 after the fix, not before.
steps: Freeze a baseline from an accepted release with per-case outputs, scores, latency, cost, and versions.
Run the candidate on the identical dataset and classify every case as fixed, broken, or unchanged.
Roll results up by intent, language, and difficulty, and set a floor for each important slice.
Estimate noise with three repeated runs, then require changes to exceed it before claiming improvement.
Fail the release on broken cases or slice floors, and record the accepted diff in the release notes.

code.title: A candidate-versus-baseline gate that counts broken cases first, then checks every slice against a quality floor.
what_to_notice: The broken-case check runs before any slice average, so a local failure cannot be averaged away by other cases.
The candidate is classified against the baseline, not re-scored in isolation, which makes fixed and broken cases visible.

Two-case examples are illustrative only; real gates need enough cases per slice for the rate to mean something. Three pages per lesson Page 482 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Comparing only aggregate accuracy and missing a large regression in a smaller but valuable slice.
Re-baselining after every run, so the system is only ever compared with itself and drift becomes invisible.
Treating a one-point change as real without measuring run-to-run noise or repeating the evaluation.
production_notes: Schedule the suite against production traffic samples every week to catch provider drift even when no code changed.
Keep baselines and results immutable, tagged with dataset, prompt, and model versions, then expire them on a fixed schedule.
Require an explicit waiver with an owner and expiry date when a known regression is accepted for a release.
checklist: A frozen baseline exists with per-case outputs, scores, latency, and versions.
The candidate runs on exactly the same dataset and rubric.
Every result is classified as fixed, broken, or unchanged before roll-up.
Important slices have their own floors, not just the aggregate score.
Noise is measured, and a waiver is required to accept a known regression.

Regression Testing
Compare every prompt or model change against a frozen baseline, and fail the gate when a slice gets worse.
Production AI Engineering · Lesson 20 of 26 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Hosted models change without notice, prompts interact in surprising ways, and retrieval updates alter what the model
sees. A system that passed last month can fail today with no commit in between. Regression testing turns that uncertainty
into a comparison: same cases, same rubric, old versus new. It is the difference between discovering a quality drop in a
dashboard and discovering it in a customer escalation.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Freeze a baseline of outputs, scores, latency, and cost, then diff a candidate against it case by case.
 • Set regression thresholds per slice so aggregate gains cannot hide a serious local failure.
 • Handle model drift, sampling noise, and flaky cases without turning the gate into a ritual.
CORE CONCEPTS
Baselines are evidence, not truth
Store per-case outputs, scores, latency, token usage, and model version for a known-good release. The baseline is the
best evidence you had at that moment, not a guarantee of correctness. When you find a labelling error, fix the dataset
and re-baseline deliberately. Never overwrite the baseline during a candidate run, and keep enough history to compare
across several releases. A baseline that nobody can reproduce is a rumour with a timestamp.
Diff by case and by slice
Aggregate scores hide regressions: a two-point overall gain can contain a twenty-point drop for one document type.
Compare per-case outcomes, then roll up by intent, language, tenant, and difficulty. Classify each change as fixed, broken,
unchanged-correct, or unchanged-wrong. Gate on broken cases and on slice floors, not only the mean. Print the ten most
damaging diffs with inputs, outputs, and rule IDs so a reviewer can act.
Noise needs a policy
Model sampling and judge variance make small differences meaningless. Run at temperature zero where possible, repeat
high-variance cases three times, and require a change to exceed the measured noise band. Separate deterministic checks,
which should never flake, from judged quality. When a case flips repeatedly, mark it unstable and investigate the rubric
rather than loosening the gate. Scheduled re-runs catch provider drift even when your code has not changed.
KEY TERMS
 Baseline                         The recorded outputs, scores, latency, and versions from a release accepted as the comparison point.
 Slice                            A subgroup of evaluation cases, such as one language or document type, scored separately.
 Noise band                       The range of score variation observed when the same system is evaluated repeatedly.

  MENTAL MODEL A regression suite is a ratchet: each release may improve the system, but a known-good behaviour should never slip
  backwards unnoticed.

Regression Testing
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A support assistant releases every Thursday. The team keeps 300 labelled cases and a baseline from release 42. Candidate
43 improves aggregate accuracy from 84% to 86%, so the release looks safe. The slice diff shows billing questions fell from
91% to 72% after a prompt edit that shortened policy context. Ten cases now omit the refund window. Because the gate
requires every slice to stay within three points of baseline, the release is blocked. The team restores the policy section, re-
runs, and gets 85% overall with billing back at 90%. Two cases still flip between runs, so they are marked unstable and
reviewed. The decision: ship 43 after the fix, not before.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Freeze a baseline from an accepted release with per-case outputs, scores, latency, cost, and versions.
2.    Run the candidate on the identical dataset and classify every case as fixed, broken, or unchanged.
3.    Roll results up by intent, language, and difficulty, and set a floor for each important slice.
4.    Estimate noise with three repeated runs, then require changes to exceed it before claiming improvement.
5.    Fail the release on broken cases or slice floors, and record the accepted diff in the release notes.
CODE
A candidate-versus-baseline gate that counts broken cases first, then checks every slice against a quality floor.
  from collections import defaultdict

  def compare(baseline, candidate, slices, floor=0.85):
    failures = []
    broken = [c for c in baseline if baseline[c] and not candidate[c]]
    if broken:
       failures.append(f"broken:{len(broken)}")
    totals, passes = defaultdict(int), defaultdict(int)
    for case, ok in candidate.items():
       totals[slices[case]] += 1
       passes[slices[case]] += ok
    for name, total in totals.items():
       rate = passes[name] / total
       if rate < floor:
          failures.append(f"slice:{name}={rate:.2f}")
    return failures

  base = {"a": True, "b": True}
  cand = {"a": True, "b": False}
  print(compare(base, cand, {"a": "billing", "b": "billing"}))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The broken-case check runs before any slice average, so a local failure cannot be averaged away by other cases.
 → The candidate is classified against the baseline, not re-scored in isolation, which makes fixed and broken cases visible.
 → Two-case examples are illustrative only; real gates need enough cases per slice for the rate to mean something.

Regression Testing
Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Comparing only aggregate accuracy and missing a large regression in a smaller but valuable slice.
2.     Re-baselining after every run, so the system is only ever compared with itself and drift becomes invisible.
3.     Treating a one-point change as real without measuring run-to-run noise or repeating the evaluation.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Schedule the suite against production traffic samples every week to catch provider drift even when no code changed.
    ◆ Keep baselines and results immutable, tagged with dataset, prompt, and model versions, then expire them on a fixed
      schedule.
    ◆ Require an explicit waiver with an owner and expiry date when a known regression is accepted for a release.
CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□      A frozen baseline exists with per-case outputs, scores, latency, and versions.
□      The candidate runs on exactly the same dataset and rubric.
□      Every result is classified as fixed, broken, or unchanged before roll-up.
□      Important slices have their own floors, not just the aggregate score.
□      Noise is measured, and a waiver is required to accept a known regression.

core_concepts.content: Three signals, three questions Logs answer what happened to one request; metrics answer how often and how bad across the fleet; traces answer where the time went across services. A model call needs all three: an event with model, prompt version, token counts, and finish reason; a histogram of latency by route; a span tree covering retrieval, tools, and generation. Start from the questions you must answer at 03:00, then emit only fields that serve them. AI-specific signals Classic RED metrics — rate, errors, duration — miss the failure that matters most: a confident wrong answer. Add answer quality sampled from production, groundedness or citation coverage, refusal rate, retrieval hit rate, token counts per request, and cost per successful outcome. Track them per route, tenant tier, and model. Quality signals arrive later than latency signals, so pair sampled evaluation with immediate proxies such as empty retrieval or schema repair counts. code.title: One span per answer, carrying the attributes needed to explain latency, model choice, and token spend.
code.code:
import time
from opentelemetry import trace

tracer = trace.get_tracer("support.assistant")
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-4-5"

def answer(question: str, retrieve, generate) -> str:
  with tracer.start_as_current_span("chat.answer") as span:
     span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", MODEL)
     started = time.perf_counter()
     docs = retrieve(question)
     span.set_attribute("retrieval.docs", len(docs))
     text, usage = generate(question, docs)
     span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", usage["input"])
     span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", usage["output"])
     elapsed = (time.perf_counter() - started) * 1000
     span.set_attribute("answer.latency_ms", elapsed)
     return text
what_to_notice: The span records token counts and document volume but no prompt text, so investigators see shape and cost without copying user data into a trace store.
Retrieval is a child operation almost always: when latency jumps, compare its duration with generation before blaming the model provider.

Only low-cardinality attributes belong on metrics; request IDs and user IDs go on spans and logs, where storage cost stays bounded. Three pages per lesson Page 485 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.title: Tracing
lessons.subtitle: Follow one request across retrieval, tools, and model calls so a slow or wrong answer has a visible path, not a mysterious
why_it_matters: A single chat request may touch an auth service, two vector indexes, a reranker, three tool calls, and two model providers. Aggregate latency tells you the total but not the contributor. Tracing records the causal path with timing and attributes for each step, so you can see that generation waited 2.4 seconds on a reranker, or that an agent burned six steps retrying a failing tool. It is the difference between knowing the system is slow and knowing where.
outcomes: Break an AI request into spans with attributes that explain latency, tokens, and tool behaviour.
Propagate trace context through async workers, HTTP calls, and MCP tool servers without breaking the parent chain.
Choose head or tail sampling and redact trace attributes before they leave the process.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A span is a timed operation Each span has a name, start and end time, a parent, a status, and attributes. A root span covers the user request; children cover retrieval, reranking, each tool call, and each model call. Record what you cannot re-derive later: model ID, prompt version, token counts, finish reason, tool name, row counts, and cache hit. Keep names stable and low-cardinality, because span names become the grouping key in every latency chart. Context must travel Trace context is a header pair, trace ID and span ID, passed between processes. Gateways, HTTP clients, queue messages, and MCP calls must forward it, or the trace fractures into orphans. In Python, OpenTelemetry's context is task-local, so create spans inside the same asyncio task and pass a propagated carrier when handing work to a worker. An orphaned span is worse than none: it looks like coverage while hiding the delay between services. Sample and redact deliberately Head sampling decides at request start and is cheap; tail sampling decides after completion, so it can keep every error and every request above a cost threshold. For AI traffic, keep all failures, all guardrail blocks, and a random five percent of successes. Redact before export: hash user IDs, drop raw prompts, and cap attribute length. Budget trace volume by bytes, not span count, because a single agent run with twenty tool results can dwarf a thousand simple chats.

key_terms.definition: A timed operation within a trace, carrying a name, parent, status, and attributes such as model or token count.
The trace and span identifiers propagated in headers so downstream services attach work to the correct parent.

A sampling decision made after a trace completes, allowing retention rules based on errors, latency, or cost. MENTAL MODEL A trace is a receipt for one request: each line is a step, each price is a duration or token, and the total only makes sense when the lines add up.

lessons.mental_model: Think of tracing as a building block - once you understand it, you'll use it again and again as you build your AI app.
worked_example: A four-engineer team ships an agent that books meeting rooms. Users report 20-second waits, but the provider dashboard shows 900 ms median generation. A trace of one run shows 14 spans: two retrieval calls at 300 ms, a calendar tool at 6.8 s with three retries of the same 503, a second model turn at 1.2 s, and a final guardrail at 180 ms. The agent's step budget of 12 let it retry inside the tool without escalating. The decision: cap tool retries at one, move retry to the orchestrator with a 2.5-second deadline, and add a span attribute for attempt count. p95 falls to 5.1 seconds the same afternoon.

code.title: A tool span that injects trace context into the outbound call, records the failure, and keeps the parent chain intact.
code.code:
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.propagate import inject

tracer = trace.get_tracer("agent.booking")

def call_tool(client, name: str, args: dict, timeout: float = 2.5) -> dict:
  headers: dict[str, str] = {}
  inject(headers)
  with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"tool.{name}") as span:
     span.set_attribute("tool.name", name)
     try:
       response = client.post(f"/tools/{name}", json=args, headers=headers,
                     timeout=timeout)
       response.raise_for_status()
       span.set_attribute("tool.status", response.status_code)
       return response.json()
     except Exception as exc:
       span.record_exception(exc)
       span.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR))
       raise
what_to_notice: inject writes traceparent into headers before the call, so the tool server's spans appear under this tool span instead of as a separate trace.
record_exception keeps the stack trace on the span, but the attribute set stays small so a failing tool does not flood the backend.

The timeout is enforced on the client; without it a hung tool produces a long span and no error, which sampling by status would miss. Three pages per lesson Page 488 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

common_mistakes: Starting a new trace in the worker instead of propagating context, so the queue delay disappears from every waterfall.
Putting full prompts, responses, and user emails into span attributes, then exporting them to a third-party collector.
Sampling by head only, which discards the rare failing trace you needed and keeps a thousand boring successes.
production_notes: Set a span budget per request; an agent with unbounded tool loops can generate thousands of spans and a five-figure monthly bill.
Keep the collector inside your network, redact at the SDK boundary, and encrypt exports so trace data never leaves controlled systems.
Alert on orphan rate and missing root spans, because broken propagation silently erodes the coverage you rely on during incidents.
checklist: One trace ID follows the request from gateway to queue worker to tool server.
Every model call span carries model, prompt version, input and output tokens, and finish reason.
Retries appear as separate spans or attempt attributes, not hidden inside one duration.
Sampling keeps all errors and high-cost runs while discarding most successes.
No raw prompt, response, or personal identifier reaches the trace backend.

Tracing
Follow one request across retrieval, tools, and model calls so a slow or wrong answer has a visible path, not a mysterious
total.
Production AI Engineering · Lesson 22 of 26 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A single chat request may touch an auth service, two vector indexes, a reranker, three tool calls, and two model
providers. Aggregate latency tells you the total but not the contributor. Tracing records the causal path with timing and
attributes for each step, so you can see that generation waited 2.4 seconds on a reranker, or that an agent burned six
steps retrying a failing tool. It is the difference between knowing the system is slow and knowing where.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Break an AI request into spans with attributes that explain latency, tokens, and tool behaviour.
 • Propagate trace context through async workers, HTTP calls, and MCP tool servers without breaking the parent chain.
 • Choose head or tail sampling and redact trace attributes before they leave the process.
CORE CONCEPTS
A span is a timed operation
Each span has a name, start and end time, a parent, a status, and attributes. A root span covers the user request; children
cover retrieval, reranking, each tool call, and each model call. Record what you cannot re-derive later: model ID, prompt
version, token counts, finish reason, tool name, row counts, and cache hit. Keep names stable and low-cardinality,
because span names become the grouping key in every latency chart.
Context must travel
Trace context is a header pair, trace ID and span ID, passed between processes. Gateways, HTTP clients, queue messages,
and MCP calls must forward it, or the trace fractures into orphans. In Python, OpenTelemetry's context is task-local, so
create spans inside the same asyncio task and pass a propagated carrier when handing work to a worker. An orphaned
span is worse than none: it looks like coverage while hiding the delay between services.
Sample and redact deliberately
Head sampling decides at request start and is cheap; tail sampling decides after completion, so it can keep every error and
every request above a cost threshold. For AI traffic, keep all failures, all guardrail blocks, and a random five percent of
successes. Redact before export: hash user IDs, drop raw prompts, and cap attribute length. Budget trace volume by
bytes, not span count, because a single agent run with twenty tool results can dwarf a thousand simple chats.
KEY TERMS
 Span                             A timed operation within a trace, carrying a name, parent, status, and attributes such as model or token
                                  count.
 Trace context                    The trace and span identifiers propagated in headers so downstream services attach work to the correct
                                  parent.
 Tail sampling                    A sampling decision made after a trace completes, allowing retention rules based on errors, latency, or cost.

  MENTAL MODEL A trace is a receipt for one request: each line is a step, each price is a duration or token, and the total only makes sense
  when the lines add up.

Tracing
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A four-engineer team ships an agent that books meeting rooms. Users report 20-second waits, but the provider
dashboard shows 900 ms median generation. A trace of one run shows 14 spans: two retrieval calls at 300 ms, a calendar
tool at 6.8 s with three retries of the same 503, a second model turn at 1.2 s, and a final guardrail at 180 ms. The agent's
step budget of 12 let it retry inside the tool without escalating. The decision: cap tool retries at one, move retry to the
orchestrator with a 2.5-second deadline, and add a span attribute for attempt count. p95 falls to 5.1 seconds the same
afternoon.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Draw the request path and mark every network hop, queue handoff, and model call that should become a span.
2.    Wrap the gateway in a root span and give retrieval, reranking, each tool, and each model call their own child span.
3.    Propagate W3C traceparent through HTTP clients, queue payloads, and the MCP client; assert one trace ID in staging.
4.    Attach model, prompt version, token counts, finish reason, attempt number, and cache status to the relevant spans.
5.    Configure tail sampling to keep errors and expensive runs, then verify the collector drops prompt text before export.
CODE
A tool span that injects trace context into the outbound call, records the failure, and keeps the parent chain intact.
  from opentelemetry import trace
  from opentelemetry.propagate import inject

  tracer = trace.get_tracer("agent.booking")

  def call_tool(client, name: str, args: dict, timeout: float = 2.5) -> dict:
    headers: dict[str, str] = {}
    inject(headers)
    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"tool.{name}") as span:
       span.set_attribute("tool.name", name)
       try:
         response = client.post(f"/tools/{name}", json=args, headers=headers,
                       timeout=timeout)
         response.raise_for_status()
         span.set_attribute("tool.status", response.status_code)
         return response.json()
       except Exception as exc:
         span.record_exception(exc)
         span.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR))
         raise
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → inject writes traceparent into headers before the call, so the tool server's spans appear under this tool span instead of as a
   separate trace.
 → record_exception keeps the stack trace on the span, but the attribute set stays small so a failing tool does not flood the
   backend.
 → The timeout is enforced on the client; without it a hung tool produces a long span and no error, which sampling by status
   would miss.

Tracing
Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Starting a new trace in the worker instead of propagating context, so the queue delay disappears from every waterfall.
2.     Putting full prompts, responses, and user emails into span attributes, then exporting them to a third-party collector.
3.     Sampling by head only, which discards the rare failing trace you needed and keeps a thousand boring successes.
PRODUCTION NOTES
    ◆ Set a span budget per request; an agent with unbounded tool loops can generate thousands of spans and a five-figure
      monthly bill.
    ◆ Keep the collector inside your network, redact at the SDK boundary, and encrypt exports so trace data never leaves
      controlled systems.
    ◆ Alert on orphan rate and missing root spans, because broken propagation silently erodes the coverage you rely on during
      incidents.
CHECKPOINT CHECKLIST
□      One trace ID follows the request from gateway to queue worker to tool server.
□      Every model call span carries model, prompt version, input and output tokens, and finish reason.
□      Retries appear as separate spans or attempt attributes, not hidden inside one duration.
□      Sampling keeps all errors and high-cost runs while discarding most successes.
□      No raw prompt, response, or personal identifier reaches the trace backend.
SHORT QUESTIONS
1.     Why does an orphaned span create false confidence during an incident?

2.     Which attributes let you separate provider latency from your own queueing delay?

3.     When does tail sampling beat head sampling for an agent workload?

4.     How would you represent three retries of one tool call in a trace?

5.     What is the risk of putting a user email in a span attribute?

6.     How do you verify propagation across an async worker before production?

TASKS
□      Instrument a three-step chain — gateway, retrieval, model — and export the trace to a local Jaeger or Tempo instance.
□      Break propagation deliberately by dropping the header in the worker, capture the resulting orphan trace, then fix and
       compare.
□      Write a tail-sampling policy for your service with explicit rules for errors, cost, and random successes, then justify each
       threshold.
    CAPSTONE CONNECTION Tracing supplies the causal evidence for the platform's incident runbook: one trace per answer, child spans for
    retrieval and MCP tools, and a retention policy the security review can approve.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: SLIs measure what users feel A service-level indicator is a ratio of good events to valid events. For an assistant, good might mean a complete answer under four seconds with a valid citation and no guardrail block. Valid excludes client cancellations and malformed requests you rejected at the edge. Define the indicator from the user's perspective, then set a service-level objective such as 99% of valid requests are good over 28 days. The error budget that follows is the licence to ship risky changes. Alert on burn, not on spikes A single slow minute is noise. Multi-window burn-rate alerts compare error-budget consumption over one hour and six hours against thresholds: a fast burn pages immediately, a slow burn opens a ticket. For quality, track the rolling score from a nightly evaluation sample and alert when it falls two standard deviations below the fourteen-day mean. Every page needs a runbook entry naming the first three queries, the rollback switch, and the owner. Dashboards are arguments A useful dashboard answers one question per row: are users affected, where is the fault, and what changed. Put the SLO and error budget at the top, then latency by step, error classes, token and cost rate, and quality sample. Annotate deployments, prompt releases, and model changes on the same timeline. Review the dashboard in a weekly operations meeting; if a panel has never informed a decision, delete it so the remaining signals stay legible under pressure.

code.title: Burn rate turns an SLO into two numbers: how fast the budget is going, and whether that justifies waking someone.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Slo:
  name: str
  target: float

   def burn(self, good: int, valid: int) -> float:
     """1.0 consumes the 28-day budget in exactly 28 days."""
     if valid == 0:
        return 0.0
     budget = 1 - self.target
     return (1 - good / valid) / budget

quality = Slo("citation_coverage", 0.99)
fast, slow = quality.burn(142, 200), quality.burn(39_800, 40_000)
print(f"1h burn={fast:.1f}x", "page" if fast > 14.4 else "ticket")
print(f"6h burn={slow:.1f}x", "ticket" if slow > 6 else "ok")
what_to_notice: A 29x burn over one hour with 71% citation coverage pages immediately; the same 0.5x over six hours stays quiet.
The denominator counts valid requests only; bot traffic and client cancellations would otherwise dilute the quality signal.

Threshold 14.4 comes from consuming two percent of a 28-day budget in one hour, not from a round number. Three pages per lesson Page 491 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.title: AI Cost Monitoring
lessons.subtitle: Measure cost per successful outcome, attribute it to the feature and tenant that caused it, and stop a runaway agent
why_it_matters: Token pricing makes cost a runtime property, not a monthly surprise. One retry policy, an unbounded agent loop, or a cache regression can multiply spend overnight while latency and error dashboards stay flat. Cost monitoring turns invoices into a per-request signal you can alert on, attribute to an owner, and compare against the value delivered. Without it, margin disappears quietly and the first warning is finance.
outcomes: Convert provider pricing into per-request and per-outcome cost using recorded token counts and cache hits.
Attribute spend to tenant, route, model, and prompt version without building unbounded metric cardinality.
Set budget guardrails and anomaly alerts that cap damage without blocking legitimate peak traffic.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Unit economics, not totals A monthly total hides the decisions that produced it. Divide spend by successful outcomes: cost per resolved ticket, per booked meeting, per approved claim. Track input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, and reasoning tokens separately, because they carry different prices and different levers. A cheaper model that fails twice is often more expensive than the stronger one that succeeds once. Publish the number beside quality and latency so product trade-offs are explicit. Attribute without exploding cardinality You need to know which tenant, route, model, and prompt version spent the money, but a metric labelled by request ID will destroy the time-series database. Emit a structured cost event per model call to the warehouse, and keep only bounded dimensions — route, model, tier — on metrics. Reconcile the sum of your events against the provider invoice weekly; a two percent gap usually means streaming calls, cached tokens, or image inputs are unaccounted for. Guardrails with a blast radius Budgets work at three levels: a per-request token ceiling, a per-tenant daily cap, and a global monthly alert. Enforce hard limits in code before the call, using the maximum completion tokens and a pessimistic prompt estimate. When a tenant crosses its cap, degrade to a smaller model or queue the request; do not silently drop traffic. For agents, cap steps and total tokens, because loop cost grows with every tool result appended to context.

key_terms.definition: Spend divided by a business outcome such as a resolved ticket, exposing whether the feature earns its margin.
Recording input, output, cached, and reasoning tokens per call so spend can be reconstructed from events.

Reporting attributed spend to the teams or tenants that caused it, without necessarily charging them. MENTAL MODEL Cost monitoring is a household electricity meter with per-appliance plugs: the bill matters, but the decision comes from knowing which appliance ran all night.

code.title: Price cached input separately; on a long transcript the cache discount is the difference between a viable and an unviable unit cost.
code.code:
from decimal import Decimal

PRICES = { # USD per million tokens
  "small": {"in": Decimal("0.15"), "out": Decimal("0.60"), "cached": Decimal("0.04")},
  "large": {"in": Decimal("3.00"), "out": Decimal("15.00"), "cached": Decimal("0.30")},
}

def cost_usd(model: str, in_tok: int, cached_tok: int, out_tok: int) -> Decimal:
  p = PRICES[model]
  fresh = in_tok - cached_tok
  million = Decimal(1_000_000)
  units = fresh * p["in"] + cached_tok * p["cached"] + out_tok * p["out"]
  return units / million

per_call = cost_usd("large", in_tok=18_000, cached_tok=12_000, out_tok=800)
print(f"call=${per_call:.4f}", f"monthly=${per_call * 90_000:.0f}")
what_to_notice: Cached tokens are billed at a lower rate but still appear in the input count, so subtracting them prevents double charging.
The price table is code: a provider change must update it in review, not in a spreadsheet nobody owns.

At this size input still dominates because the transcript is long; shortening retrieved context is the first lever, not the output limit. YOUR WORKING NOTES Three pages per lesson Page 494 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

booked meeting, per approved claim. Track input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, and reasoning tokens separately,
because they carry different prices and different levers. A cheaper model that fails twice is often more expensive than the
stronger one that succeeds once. Publish the number beside quality and latency so product trade-offs are explicit.
Attribute without exploding cardinality
You need to know which tenant, route, model, and prompt version spent the money, but a metric labelled by request ID
will destroy the time-series database. Emit a structured cost event per model call to the warehouse, and keep only
bounded dimensions — route, model, tier — on metrics. Reconcile the sum of your events against the provider invoice
weekly; a two percent gap usually means streaming calls, cached tokens, or image inputs are unaccounted for.
Guardrails with a blast radius
Budgets work at three levels: a per-request token ceiling, a per-tenant daily cap, and a global monthly alert. Enforce hard
limits in code before the call, using the maximum completion tokens and a pessimistic prompt estimate. When a tenant
crosses its cap, degrade to a smaller model or queue the request; do not silently drop traffic. For agents, cap steps and
total tokens, because loop cost grows with every tool result appended to context.
KEY TERMS
 Unit cost                        Spend divided by a business outcome such as a resolved ticket, exposing whether the feature earns its
                                  margin.
 Token accounting                 Recording input, output, cached, and reasoning tokens per call so spend can be reconstructed from events.
 Showback                         Reporting attributed spend to the teams or tenants that caused it, without necessarily charging them.

  MENTAL MODEL Cost monitoring is a household electricity meter with per-appliance plugs: the bill matters, but the decision comes from
  knowing which appliance ran all night.

Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A retail support platform spends USD 4,100 a month on generation. After a prompt change adds the last twelve messages
to every turn, the bill reaches USD 11,800 in three weeks. Latency is unchanged and quality rises one point. Cost events
show 61% of the increase comes from one enterprise tenant whose agents loop through six tool calls, each resending the
full transcript. The team compresses old turns into a summary, caps agent steps at four, and routes simple intents to a
smaller model. Spend settles at USD 5,300 with quality flat, and a per-tenant daily cap prevents a repeat.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Capture token counts, model, cache status, and request ID from every provider response into one cost event.
2.    Join price per million tokens from a versioned table and compute request cost, then aggregate by route and tenant.
3.    Define a successful outcome and report cost per outcome beside quality and latency for each route.
4.    Set request, tenant, and monthly budget limits; decide the degradation path for each before enforcing.
5.    Reconcile event totals with the provider invoice weekly and alert on spend velocity above forecast.
CODE
Price cached input separately; on a long transcript the cache discount is the difference between a viable and an unviable unit cost.
  from decimal import Decimal

  PRICES = { # USD per million tokens
    "small": {"in": Decimal("0.15"), "out": Decimal("0.60"), "cached": Decimal("0.04")},
    "large": {"in": Decimal("3.00"), "out": Decimal("15.00"), "cached": Decimal("0.30")},
  }

  def cost_usd(model: str, in_tok: int, cached_tok: int, out_tok: int) -> Decimal:
    p = PRICES[model]
    fresh = in_tok - cached_tok
    million = Decimal(1_000_000)
    units = fresh * p["in"] + cached_tok * p["cached"] + out_tok * p["out"]
    return units / million

  per_call = cost_usd("large", in_tok=18_000, cached_tok=12_000, out_tok=800)
  print(f"call=${per_call:.4f}", f"monthly=${per_call * 90_000:.0f}")

 → Cached tokens are billed at a lower rate but still appear in the input count, so subtracting them prevents double charging.
 → The price table is code: a provider change must update it in review, not in a spreadsheet nobody owns.

code.title: Immutable prompt files, validated variables, and a content hash that travels with every call.
code.code:
import hashlib
from pathlib import Path
from string import Formatter

PROMPTS = Path("prompts")

class PromptError(ValueError):
  pass

def load(prompt_id: str, version: str, **values: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
  template = (PROMPTS / prompt_id / f"{version}.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
  required = {name for _, name, _, _ in Formatter().parse(template) if name}
  missing = required - values.keys()
  if missing:
     raise PromptError(f"{prompt_id}@{version} missing {sorted(missing)}")
  digest = hashlib.sha256(template.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
  return template.format(**values), digest
what_to_notice: The loaded hash identifies the exact template bytes, so two prompts that look identical but differ in whitespace are distinguishable.
Formatter.parse extracts required variables before rendering; a missing context value raises instead of shipping an empty section.

why_it_matters: Providers retire snapshots, change aliases, and silently update hosted models. Behaviour that passed evaluation in March can drift in June without a line of your code changing. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Aliases move; snapshots stay A provider alias such as gpt-4o or claude-sonnet points at whatever the provider currently serves. A dated snapshot such as gpt-4o-2024-11-20 is immutable and is what you should pin in production. Pin through configuration, not scattered string literals, and record the resolved snapshot on every call. When the provider announces deprecation, you have a known upgrade date and a diff to evaluate rather than an unplanned outage at the retirement hour. Evaluate the upgrade, not the model A newer model is not automatically better for your task. Run the same frozen regression set, then compare overall score, worst slices, refusal rate, format compliance, p95 latency, and cost per outcome. Watch for changed instruction- following, tokeniser differences that alter cost, and stricter safety behaviour that raises refusals. A model that wins overall but loses four points on invoice extraction is not an upgrade for that route; route by task if the evidence supports it. Canary, fallback, rollback Promote a new snapshot to five percent of traffic behind the same abstraction, with automatic rollback when error rate, format failures, or quality scores breach thresholds. Keep a second provider or a smaller local model behind the same interface, and test the fallback monthly; an untested fallback is a rumour. Record model, snapshot, and provider on every trace, so a quality change can be attributed to a model move rather than guessed at during a review.

format failures, or quality scores breach thresholds. Keep a second provider or a smaller local model behind the same
interface, and test the fallback monthly; an untested fallback is a rumour. Record model, snapshot, and provider on every
trace, so a quality change can be attributed to a model move rather than guessed at during a review.
KEY TERMS
 Snapshot                         An immutable, dated model build that the provider will not change, suitable for production pinning.
 Alias                            A provider-managed name that resolves to whichever model build is currently served, and can move without
                                  notice.
 Deprecation window               The period between a provider announcing a model retirement and the date it stops serving requests.

  and the logbook says which one flew.

Model Versioning
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A document-review product pins gpt-4o-2024-08-06 across three routes. The provider announces retirement in 90 days.
The team runs the 480-case regression set against two candidates. Candidate A gains two points overall but drops six on

from 3.8 to 2.9 seconds. They choose B for extraction and summarisation, keep A out, and move chat to a cheaper
snapshot that holds quality. A five percent canary runs for three days, then all routes move. The retirement date passes
with no incident.

1.    Inventory every model identifier in code, config, and prompts, and replace aliases with dated snapshots where available.
2.    Record provider, model, snapshot, and prompt version on every call and in the evaluation report.
3.    Run the frozen regression set against each candidate, comparing overall, worst slice, latency, and cost per outcome.
4.    Canary five percent behind the model interface with automatic rollback on format or quality thresholds.
5.    Rehearse the fallback provider monthly and document the switch, including its quality and latency penalty.
CODE
Routes resolve to pinned snapshots, with a named fallback and an output ceiling that bounds cost per call.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Route:
    primary: str
    fallback: str
    max_output: int = 1200

  ROUTES = {
    "invoice_extract": Route("gpt-4o-2024-08-06", "claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022"),
    "chat": Route("claude-3-5-haiku-20241022", "gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18"),
  }

  def resolve(route: str, primary_healthy: bool = True) -> str:
    spec = ROUTES[route]
    model = spec.primary if primary_healthy else spec.fallback
    print(f"route={route} model={model} max_output={spec.max_output}")
    return model

  resolve("invoice_extract")

 → The print line is the audit trail: every call can be attributed to a route, a snapshot, and a fallback decision.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Drift is the default Code is only one input to a running service. The host contributes the kernel, glibc, OpenSSL, BLAS, GPU driver, locale, and available memory. Upgrading a laptop from Debian 12 to 13 can change a shared object that a wheel expects, and the failure appears only at request time. Containers capture the user-space filesystem, so the difference between environments shrinks to the kernel and the runtime configuration you pass in. Image, container, registry An image is an immutable stack of filesystem layers plus metadata such as the entrypoint and environment. A container is a process started from that image with a thin writable layer, its own network namespace, and resource limits. A registry stores images and serves them by tag or digest. Tags are mutable labels; digests are content hashes. Deploy by digest when you need the same bytes tomorrow, and keep a tag for operators. What a container will not fix A container does not abstract the kernel, GPU driver, or cloud networking, and it is not a hard security boundary. It also does not manage secrets, persistent data, or configuration; those need a secret manager, volumes, and explicit environment variables. Packaging a poorly behaving service changes nothing about its timeouts or connection pools. Treat the image as one reliability tool, not a substitute for designing the request path.

lessons.subtitle: Learn what an image, layer, container, and volume actually are, and read the Docker commands that reveal what is
why_it_matters: Most Docker confusion comes from mixing three objects: an image is the packaged filesystem, a container is a process using it, and a volume is storage that outlives the process. Commands such as run, ps, inspect, and logs expose those boundaries. Once you can read them, debugging a container stops being guesswork and becomes the same work as debugging any Linux process.
outcomes: Explain how image layers, the writable container layer, and volumes divide responsibility for state.
Trace the path from a CLI command through the daemon to a registry pull and a running process.
Use digests, inspect output, and exit codes to verify what a container is really executing.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Layers are a cache and a contract Every Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem creates a layer, keyed by its parent plus the instruction and the files it copies. Docker reuses a cached layer only when everything above it is unchanged, which is why dependency installation must precede source copying. Layers are shared between images on the same host, so ten services on one base image cost less disk than ten independent copies. A lockfile change still invalidates every later layer. A container is a normal process with a view Namespaces hide process IDs, mounts, and network interfaces; cgroups cap CPU and memory. The process sees a filesystem root built from image layers plus a writable layer discarded on removal. It has no init unless you provide one, so PID 1 must reap children and handle SIGTERM. Writing to the container filesystem survives a restart of the same container but not its removal, which is why databases need volumes. Tags move, digests do not A tag such as python:3.12-slim is a pointer that maintainers can repoint after a security rebuild. A digest such as sha256 is the content hash and cannot change. Pulling by tag in CI means two builds a week apart may use different bytes and produce different behaviour. Record the digest in the image label, deploy with it, and let the readable tag serve humans. Apply the rule to every third-party image.

key_terms.definition: A cached filesystem diff produced by one build instruction and shared by every image built on the same parent.
The thin copy-on-write layer a container adds to its image, discarded when the container is removed.

Docker-managed storage mounted into a container whose contents persist independently of the container lifecycle. MENTAL MODEL Images are recipes printed on a page; containers are meals cooked from them; volumes are the boxes you keep leftovers in after the plate is washed.

code.title: A digest and lifecycle probe: what you pin, how many layers you pull, and whether the process is still running.
code.code:
import json
import subprocess

def docker(*args: str) -> str:
  cmd = ["docker", *args]
  return subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout

ref = "python:3.12-slim"
repo = docker("image", "inspect", "--format", "{{index .RepoDigests 0}}", ref)
layers = json.loads(docker("image", "inspect", "--format", "{{json .RootFS.Layers}}", ref))
print("pin:", repo.strip(), f"({len(layers)} layers)", sep="\n")

docker("run", "--detach", "--name", "probe", ref, "sleep", "30")
print(docker("ps", "--filter", "name=probe", "--format", "{{.Status}}").strip())
docker("rm", "--force", "probe")
what_to_notice: The file disappeared because removal, not restart, discards the writable layer; a restart of the same container would have kept it.
The 1.9 GB image was mostly build context, so the fix was a .dockerignore rather than a smaller base image.
Pull time matters in CI and autoscaling; dropping 1.7 GB saves 41 seconds on every cold node. Three pages per lesson Page 507 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

container exited with code 0, so Docker replaced it and discarded the writable layer. The image also weighs 1.9 GB
because COPY . . pulled in .git and 600 MB of test fixtures. Tomas adds a named volume at /app/uploads, writes
a .dockerignore, and moves uploads to object storage in staging. The next redeploy keeps the files, the image drops to
220 MB, and pull time falls from 48 to 7 seconds on the CI runner. The decision: state belongs in a volume or object store,
never in the container.

1.    Pull a small image and record its digest, then pull the same tag again and compare the digest.
2.    Run a container that writes a file, remove it, and start a new one to observe the loss.
3.    Mount a named volume at the write path, repeat the test, and confirm the file survives removal.
4.    Read docker inspect for an image and a container, naming the fields that describe layers, mounts, and limits.
5.    Check exit codes and logs for a deliberately failing command, then explain which Docker component reported it.
CODE
A digest and lifecycle probe: what you pin, how many layers you pull, and whether the process is still running.
  import json
  import subprocess

  def docker(*args: str) -> str:
    cmd = ["docker", *args]
    return subprocess.run(cmd, check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout

  ref = "python:3.12-slim"
  repo = docker("image", "inspect", "--format", "{{index .RepoDigests 0}}", ref)
  layers = json.loads(docker("image", "inspect", "--format", "{{json .RootFS.Layers}}", ref))
  print("pin:", repo.strip(), f"({len(layers)} layers)", sep="\n")

  docker("run", "--detach", "--name", "probe", ref, "sleep", "30")
  print(docker("ps", "--filter", "name=probe", "--format", "{{.Status}}").strip())
  docker("rm", "--force", "probe")

   kept it.

lessons.subtitle: Order instructions for cache hits, split build from runtime, and end with a small non-root image that handles signals.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 3 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: A Dockerfile is a build program, and its instruction order decides both rebuild time and image size. Copying the whole repository before installing dependencies invalidates the dependency cache on every commit. Shipping a compiler and build headers into production adds hundreds of megabytes and attack surface. The difference between a four-minute rebuild and a fifteen-second one is usually ordering, not hardware or network speed.
outcomes: Order Dockerfile instructions so dependency layers survive source changes and rebuilds stay under a minute.
Use a multi-stage build to keep compilers and build caches out of the runtime image.
Run the service as a non-root user with an exec-form entrypoint that receives SIGTERM.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Cache order: dependencies before source Each layer is keyed by its parent, the instruction, and the content it copies. Put COPY requirements.txt and the install step before COPY . so editing a Python file reuses installed dependencies. A wildcard copy of the repository also drags in .git, tests, and datasets unless .dockerignore excludes them, changing the cache key for reasons unrelated to the build. Measure rebuild time after a one-line source change; that is the number developers feel every day. Multi-stage separates build from run A builder stage can install compilers, headers, and build tools, produce wheels or a virtual environment, then disappear. The runtime stage copies only the artefacts and the interpreter it needs. This keeps the final image small, reduces CVE surface, and shortens pulls on cold nodes. Copy the virtual environment to the same absolute path in both stages, or its shebangs and compiled paths will point at a directory that no longer exists. Non-root, exec form, signal handling By default a container runs as root, so a compromised process has more room to move. Create a user with a fixed UID, chown only the files it needs, and switch with USER before CMD. Use exec form so the application is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly; shell form hides it behind /bin/sh. Then handle SIGTERM in the application, stop accepting connections, and finish in-flight requests within the platform grace period.

key_terms.definition: The files sent to the Docker daemon at build time, filtered by .dockerignore and hashed for COPY instructions.
A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where later stages copy only selected artefacts from earlier ones.

A JSON-array ENTRYPOINT or CMD that runs the binary directly as PID 1 instead of through a shell. MENTAL MODEL A Dockerfile is a cooking plan: prep that rarely changes goes first, the plate holds only what is served, and the waiter carries the signal to stop.

code.title: A multi-stage build with dependency-first caching, a non-root runtime, and an exec-form entrypoint.
code.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.7
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
  pip wheel --no-cache-dir -w /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
RUN groupadd -r app && useradd -r -g app app
COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels
COPY --chown=app:app app ./app
USER app
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

The virtual environment is copied to the same absolute path in both stages, so its shebangs still resolve.

lessons.title: Containerizing FastAPI
lessons.subtitle: Make the API container start quickly, report liveness and readiness honestly, and shut down without dropping requests.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 4 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: A FastAPI container that boots is not the same as one that is ready. Model loading, database pools, and Redis connections take seconds, and a liveness probe that checks them will restart a healthy process during a dependency outage. Getting readiness, worker count, and shutdown right prevents crash loops, connection exhaustion, and requests cut off mid- stream during a rollout.
outcomes: Separate build-time packaging from run-time configuration so one image serves every environment.
Design liveness and readiness endpoints that distinguish a dead process from a degraded dependency.
Choose worker count, connection pool size, and shutdown grace from measured concurrency.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One image, configuration at run time Bake code, dependencies, and the interpreter into the image; inject endpoints, credentials, log level, and feature flags as environment variables at start. A settings object built with pydantic-settings validates them once and fails fast with a clear message. Never rebuild for staging, because then the artefact you tested is not the artefact you ship. Use the same digest in every environment and vary only configuration and secrets from the platform secret store. Liveness, readiness, start-up Liveness answers whether the process is wedged; it should check almost nothing and never call Postgres. Readiness answers whether this instance should receive traffic; it can check the connection pool and cache with a 500 ms timeout. Start-up probes cover slow model loading so liveness does not kill the pod first. A failing readiness removes an instance from the load balancer without restarting it, which is what you want during a database failover. Workers, pools, graceful shutdown Each Uvicorn worker is a process with its own memory and connection pool, so four workers multiply connections by four. For async endpoints, one worker with a high concurrency limit often beats four workers competing for CPU. Size the pool from Postgres max_connections divided by total replicas, leaving headroom for migrations and admin sessions. On SIGTERM, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close pools, and exit before the grace period expires.

key_terms.definition: A platform check that restarts the container when the process is unresponsive, deliberately avoiding dependency calls.
A check that controls whether the instance receives traffic, allowed to fail while dependencies recover.

The sequence of refusing new work, finishing in-flight requests, and closing resources after SIGTERM. MENTAL MODEL A container is a new employee: the build is the interview, start-up is the first day, readiness is permission to serve customers, and liveness is whether they are still conscious.

worked_example: Ravi deploys a FastAPI RAG service to a 4-vCPU container with four Uvicorn workers, each opening a 20-connection asyncpg pool. With six replicas that is 480 potential connections against a Postgres limit of 200, and the first spike produces 'too many clients already' with a 34% error rate. The liveness probe also queries Postgres, so a 40-second failover restarts every pod twice. Ravi switches to one worker with concurrency 64, a pool of five per replica, and a /healthz that returns 200 without dependencies. /readyz checks the pool with a 500 ms timeout. A preStop sleep plus lifespan shutdown drains requests. Connections peak at 30, the rollout drops zero requests, and p95 falls from 3.8 to 2.4 seconds.

Implement /healthz with no dependency calls and /readyz with bounded checks of database and cache.

Handle SIGTERM through the lifespan hook: stop accepting, drain in-flight work, then close pools.
Run a rolling deploy under load and confirm readiness changes precede traffic with no failed requests.

Dependency-aware readiness beside a liveness check that stays green, plus pool cleanup on shutdown.
  from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
  from fastapi import FastAPI, Response
  from redis.asyncio import Redis
  @asynccontextmanager
  async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    app.state.redis = Redis.from_url("redis://cache:6379/0", socket_timeout=0.5)
    yield
    await app.state.redis.aclose()
  app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
  @app.get("/healthz")
  async def healthz() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"status": "ok"}
  @app.get("/readyz")
  async def readyz(response: Response) -> dict[str, str]:
    try:

core_concepts.content: Postgres is the system of record Put durable entities, constraints, and transactions in Postgres. Use a migration tool such as Alembic, run migrations as a single job before the new API version, and keep them backward compatible for one release so old and new pods coexist. Set statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a stuck query cannot hold a connection forever. Redis is a cache with an eviction policy Redis holds values you can rebuild: rendered answers, embeddings, rate-limit counters, and job locks. code.title: A bounded start-up that retries transient connection failures, then fails loudly instead of hanging.
code.code:
import asyncio

import asyncpg
from redis.asyncio import Redis

async def connect(url: str, redis_url: str):
  for delay in (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8):
    try:
       pool = await asyncpg.create_pool(url, min_size=2, max_size=5, timeout=3)
       redis = Redis.from_url(redis_url, socket_timeout=0.5)
       await redis.ping()
       return pool, redis
    except (OSError, asyncpg.PostgresError):
       await asyncio.sleep(delay)
  raise RuntimeError("database unavailable after 5 attempts")
what_to_notice: The budget includes autoscaling headroom, so the pool is sized for ten replicas even when six are usually running.
Password-reset tokens moved to Postgres because Redis eviction or restart made them irrecoverable.

lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 6 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: A local stack assembled by hand drifts within days: one developer has Postgres 15, another has 16, and neither remembers the Redis flags. Compose records the images, environment, ports, volumes, and health checks in one reviewed file. That gives every developer and CI job the same stack, and it exposes dependency-ordering problems before they appear in a cluster.
outcomes: Describe a multi-service local stack in Compose and start it reproducibly with one command.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Compose is a development and CI tool Compose runs several containers on one host with a shared network and project namespace. It is excellent for local development, integration tests, and small demos because the file is versioned and the stack starts in one command. It is not a production orchestrator: it has no rolling deploys, multi-node scheduling, or self-healing beyond restart policies. Use it to reproduce the production topology, then deploy the same images with a platform that provides those guarantees. Health gates beat sleep loops depends_on controls start order only unless you request condition: service_healthy. Pair it with a real health check that proves the dependency accepts queries, and set interval, timeout, retries, and start_period from measured start-up time. Even then, application-level retries remain necessary: a dependency can fail after the gate passes, and Compose restarts do not coordinate with your process. Health gates remove the common cold-start race, not every race. Volumes, bind mounts, configuration Named volumes are managed by Docker and persist until explicitly removed; bind mounts map a host path and are useful for live code during development. Mount source in development but never in production, where the image must be the source of truth. Put non-secret defaults in .env, require secrets with ${VAR:?message}, and use separate project names so two branches do not share a database. Seed data belongs in an idempotent script, not a manual step.

key_terms.definition: The Compose namespace that prefixes container, network, and volume names so separate stacks stay isolated.
Docker-managed persistent storage referenced by name and kept until explicitly removed.

A command Compose runs inside a container to decide whether it is healthy enough for dependents. MENTAL MODEL Compose is a stage crew for one theatre: it sets up the same props, lights, and doors every night, but it cannot run a tour across ten cities.

A health-gated stack with pinned database images, persistent Postgres data, and a required password.
  services:
   api:
    build: .
    env_file: .env
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    depends_on:
     db: {condition: service_healthy}
     cache: {condition: service_healthy}
   db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set in .env}"}
    volumes: ["pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]
    healthcheck: {test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"], interval: 5s, retries: 10}
   cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "256mb"]
    healthcheck: {test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"], interval: 5s}
  volumes: {pgdata: {}}

Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
The document-ingestion service at a nine-person legal-tech company ships as a 1.6 GB image built from python:3.12 with
build-essential, git, and the test suite inside. A scan finds 143 CVEs, mostly in compilers the runtime never uses, and cold
