python:3.12-slim, runs as UID 10001, and pins the base digest in CI. The image drops to 210 MB, CVEs to 9, cold start to 6
seconds, and failed uploads to zero after adding a 25-second grace period. The decision: weights stay in object storage,
mounted at boot.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Separate dependency installation into a builder stage and copy only the wheels into the runtime stage.
2.    Pin the runtime base by digest, pass it through a build argument, and add a strict .dockerignore file.
3.    Create UID 10001, copy files with --chown, set USER, and test with a read-only root filesystem.
4.    Switch to exec-form ENTRYPOINT, set a shutdown timeout, and confirm SIGTERM reaches uvicorn mid-request.
5.    Measure image size, scan findings, cold-start time, and shutdown behaviour, then record them beside the Dockerfile.
CODE
A two-stage build that ships only wheels, runs unprivileged, and sends SIGTERM straight to uvicorn.
  ARG BASE=python:3.12-slim
  FROM ${BASE} AS builder
  WORKDIR /build
  COPY requirements.txt .
  RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

  FROM ${BASE} AS runtime
  ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
  WORKDIR /app
  COPY --from=builder /wheels /wheels
  RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/*.whl \
    && rm -rf /wheels
  COPY --chown=10001:10001 app ./app
  USER 10001:10001
  EXPOSE 8000
  HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s \
   CMD python -c "import urllib.request as u;u.urlopen('http://0.0.0.0:8000/ready')"
  ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The builder stage keeps compilers out of the runtime, but only because the final COPY selects wheels rather than the whole
   filesystem.
 → The health check calls a local readiness route with a three-second timeout; it never spends tokens or depends on a provider.
 → USER and exec-form ENTRYPOINT are the two lines most often missing; without them the container runs as root and may
   ignore SIGTERM.

why_it_matters: A pipeline is the only repeatable path from commit to production, and the place where AI services need extra gates: behaviour can change without a code diff when a prompt, dataset, or hosted model changes. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Stages ordered by cost Run cheap deterministic checks first: formatting, lint, type checks, and unit tests finish in under two minutes and catch most mistakes. Then build the image once, scan it, and start Postgres and Redis as service containers for integration tests. Model evaluation comes after that, because it costs money and time. A failed stage must stop promotion; a flaky test that everyone reruns is worse than no test, because it trains the team to ignore red builds. Build once, promote by digest The image built from commit abc123 is the artefact tested in staging and deployed to production; environments differ only in configuration. Retagging by digest preserves identity, while rebuilding per environment introduces a different binary and defeats the test you just ran. Record the digest, SBOM, commit, prompt version, and evaluation report in the release record. Use OIDC federation from the runner to the cloud so the pipeline holds no long-lived keys. Deploy, verify, and roll back A deployment is not finished when the platform reports success. Run a smoke test against the new version: one health check, one authenticated request, and one retrieval query with a known answer. Shift a small share of traffic, watch error rate and p95 latency for ten minutes, then continue. Keep the previous digest deployable and rehearse rollback monthly. Database migrations must be backward compatible for one release so the old and new versions can run together.

key_terms.definition: An image reference that always resolves to the same bytes, usually a digest or a commit SHA.
A deployment that sends a small percentage of live traffic to the new version before widening exposure.

A trust relationship that lets a CI runner obtain short-lived cloud credentials without storing a secret. MENTAL MODEL CI is the inspection line; CD is the crane. Inspect once, stamp the crate, and move that same crate to every shelf.

A pipeline that tests against real services, builds one image, gates on evaluation, and deploys by digest.

   push: { branches: [main] }
  permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }
  concurrency: { group: release, cancel-in-progress: true }
  jobs:
   verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres: { image: postgres:16, env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test } }
      redis: { image: redis:7 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest -q
      - run: |
         docker buildx build --push --iidfile digest.txt \
          -t ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }} .
      - run: python scripts/evaluate.py --gate 0.85 --dataset eval/rag_v7.jsonl
      - run: python scripts/deploy.py --digest "$(cat digest.txt)" --canary 10

lessons.title: Environment Management
lessons.subtitle: Make configuration explicit, typed, and environment-specific so production cannot silently inherit a staging value.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 9 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: Most 'it works in staging' incidents are configuration incidents: a missing variable, a copied bucket name, a default timeout that only matters at production volume. Containers sharpen this because the same image runs everywhere, so behaviour is decided entirely by injected configuration. Treating that configuration as typed, validated, versioned input is cheaper than debugging a silent fallback at 02:00.
outcomes: Separate build-time constants from deploy-time configuration and secrets, and explain why the boundary matters.
Load configuration through one typed settings object that validates at startup and fails fast with a useful message.
Design promotion so staging and production differ only in values, never in code paths or hidden defaults.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Same artefact, different values Twelve-factor configuration lives in environment variables, not in the image, so one digest can run in every environment. Build-time values are limited to things that never vary: the Python version, compiled extensions, and static assets. Everything else, including database URLs, provider keys, bucket names, feature flags, and log levels, arrives at runtime. A .env file is a developer convenience, not a production mechanism; production injects values from the platform or a secret manager. One typed settings object Define settings once with pydantic-settings: field types, required fields, allowed ranges, and explicit aliases. Validate on import, print every invalid key without printing its value, and exit non-zero so a bad deploy fails immediately instead of serving errors. Avoid scattered os.environ lookups with defaults, because a default that is convenient locally becomes a silent production misconfiguration. Tests can construct Settings directly, which removes environment dependence from the suite. Secrets and drift Keep secrets in a managed store, inject them at runtime, and reference them by name rather than value. Rotate on a schedule and after any exposure; a secret in an image layer or CI log is compromised even if it was later deleted. from typing import Literal
from pydantic import AnyUrl, Field, model_validator
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
  model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="APP_", extra="forbid")
  env: Literal["dev", "staging", "prod"]
  database_url: AnyUrl
  storage_bucket: str = Field(min_length=3)
  model_timeout_s: float = Field(gt=0, le=60)

   @model_validator(mode="after")
   def guard_prod(self):
     prod_bucket = self.storage_bucket.startswith("acme-prod-")
     if self.env == "prod" and not prod_bucket:
        raise ValueError("prod bucket must start with acme-prod-")
     return self

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most 'it works in staging' incidents are configuration incidents: a missing variable, a copied bucket name, a default

behaviour is decided entirely by injected configuration. Treating that configuration as typed, validated, versioned input is
cheaper than debugging a silent fallback at 02:00.

Same artefact, different values

Build-time values are limited to things that never vary: the Python version, compiled extensions, and static assets.
Everything else, including database URLs, provider keys, bucket names, feature flags, and log levels, arrives at runtime.
A .env file is a developer convenience, not a production mechanism; production injects values from the platform or a
secret manager.

import, print every invalid key without printing its value, and exit non-zero so a bad deploy fails immediately instead of

silent production misconfiguration. Tests can construct Settings directly, which removes environment dependence from
the suite.

lessons.title: Cloud Deployment
lessons.subtitle: Choose a runtime that fits the team, then wire health checks, secrets, and rollback before the first real user arrives.
lessons.meta: Docker & Deployment · Lesson 10 of 12 · study guide
why_it_matters: Cloud deployment is where architecture meets billing, IAM, and networking. A service that runs locally still needs a load balancer, TLS, a managed database, a secret path, and a rollback plan. Choosing the smallest runtime that meets the availability target keeps the team's attention on the product; choosing Kubernetes for three services converts engineering time into cluster maintenance.
outcomes: Compare virtual machines, container platforms, Kubernetes, and serverless on operational cost and control.
Configure readiness, liveness, and graceful termination so a deploy moves traffic without dropping requests.
Place the API, database, cache, and object storage in a network with explicit ingress, egress, and secret access.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Match runtime to operating capacity A container platform such as Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, or Azure Container Apps gives you HTTPS, scaling, and rolling deploys without a cluster to patch. Kubernetes earns its complexity when you need custom controllers, fine-grained scheduling, or one platform for many teams. Virtual machines remain sensible for GPU workloads and licensed software. Serverless functions suit short, bursty tasks but punish long streaming responses and cold-start-sensitive traffic. Write the choice as an ADR with a revisit trigger. Traffic only reaches ready instances A readiness probe decides whether an instance joins the load balancer; a liveness probe decides whether it is restarted. Confusing them causes restart loops when a dependency is slow. Set initial delay from measured start time, and keep probes cheap and dependency-free so a provider outage does not empty the pool. On termination, remove the instance from rotation, wait for the load balancer to notice, then let in-flight requests finish inside the grace period. Network and identity boundaries Put the API in private subnets behind a load balancer, the database in a data subnet with no route to the internet, and object storage behind a private endpoint. Grant the workload a scoped role, not a user key, so it can read one bucket and one secret. Restrict egress to the model provider and package registries; an open egress policy turns a prompt-injection bug into data exfiltration. Record data residency and retention per environment.

key_terms.definition: A check that controls whether an instance receives traffic, independent of whether the process is running.
A cloud service that operates the orchestration layer so the team manages workloads rather than clusters.

Outbound network traffic from a workload, controlled to limit which external services and data destinations are reachable. MENTAL MODEL Pick the smallest building that fits the work: a rented room, a managed office, or a whole campus you must maintain. Then check the doors, keys, and fire exits.

They compare Cloud Run: the same image, managed HTTPS, minimum two warm instances, Cloud SQL Postgres, and Memorystore Redis in a private VPC. The Cloud Run version costs about EUR 1,700 a month against EUR 1,350 for EKS before engineering time, and removes cluster patching. They choose Cloud Run, keep the image portable, and set a revisit trigger: move to GKE when three teams need shared scheduling. lessons.title: Scaling AI Applications
lessons.subtitle: Scale the queue and the concurrency limit, not the CPU graph, because model latency and provider quotas set your real
why_it_matters: A model call takes seconds and varies in cost, so an AI service rarely saturates CPU the way a CRUD API does. Scaling on CPU therefore reacts late, after users already wait. The real constraints are in-flight provider requests, tokens per minute, connection pools, and memory per stream. Scaling well means measuring those, limiting admission, and moving long work to queues that absorb bursts.
outcomes: Distinguish stateless API scaling from model-bound scaling and identify the actual bottleneck under load.
Apply admission control, queueing, and backpressure so overload degrades predictably instead of collapsing.
Choose autoscaling signals from observed concurrency and queue depth rather than CPU utilisation alone.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Find the constrained resource Load a single instance until latency breaks, recording concurrency, provider latency, tokens per second, CPU, and memory. A streaming endpoint often hits a connection or memory limit first; a batch extraction job hits the provider's tokens-per-minute quota; a retrieval-heavy path hits the database connection pool. The bottleneck determines the fix: more replicas, a queue, smaller payloads, or a cache. Adding replicas to a provider-quota problem increases 429s and cost without improving throughput. Admission control and backpressure A semaphore around provider calls bounds concurrent work per instance and keeps memory predictable. When the semaphore is full, wait with a deadline, return 429 with Retry-After, or push the job to a queue. Unbounded asyncio.gather looks efficient and then exhausts file descriptors and provider quota. Propagate deadlines so a request abandoned by the client cancels its model call; otherwise you pay for tokens nobody reads. Shed load early rather than degrade every request. Scale on the right signal Autoscaling on CPU is a lagging proxy for a system waiting on the network. Use concurrency, queue depth, or tokens per minute, exported as custom metrics, and set a target from the per-instance load test. Keep a minimum replica count for latency-sensitive traffic and a maximum that matches provider quota across all replicas. Scale in slowly, because a replica that exits mid-stream drops a response; finish in-flight work before termination.

key_terms.definition: A gate that limits how many requests enter a service or provider call at once, protecting memory and quotas.
A signal that tells callers to slow down, through a queue, a 429, or a deadline, before the system collapses.

The number of jobs waiting for a worker, a leading indicator of saturation when processing time is variable. MENTAL MODEL Scaling an AI service is managing a queue at a popular counter: add staff when the line grows, but also cap how many orders each cook can hold.
Page 533 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.mental_model: Think of scaling ai applications as a building block - once you understand it, you'll use it again and again as you build your AI app.
worked_example: A research assistant serves 12,000 queries a day with a p95 target of eight seconds. On a launch day traffic triples; CPU stays at 35% while p95 reaches 41 seconds and 9% of calls return 429 from the provider. The team had autoscaled on CPU at 70%, so no new replicas appeared. They add a per-instance semaphore of 16 concurrent model calls, export that gauge, and autoscale at 70% of the limit. Long reports move to a queue with a visible position, and the synchronous endpoint returns 429 with Retry-After when the wait exceeds five seconds. The next spike holds p95 at 7.4 seconds, provider 429s fall below 0.4%, and cost per query rises 6%.
steps: Load-test one instance and record latency, concurrency, tokens per second, CPU, and memory at each step.
Identify the first resource to saturate and state whether replicas, a queue, or a cache can fix it.
Add a semaphore and a request deadline around provider calls, with a visible in-flight gauge.
Move work longer than ten seconds to a queue and expose queue depth and age to users.
Autoscale on the saturation signal, then rerun the load test and compare p95, 429 rate, and cost per request.

code.title: A per-instance admission limit that rejects fast instead of letting a traffic spike exhaust memory and provider quota.

Scaling AI Applications
Scale the queue and the concurrency limit, not the CPU graph, because model latency and provider quotas set your real
ceiling.
Docker & Deployment · Lesson 11 of 12 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A model call takes seconds and varies in cost, so an AI service rarely saturates CPU the way a CRUD API does. Scaling on
CPU therefore reacts late, after users already wait. The real constraints are in-flight provider requests, tokens per minute,
connection pools, and memory per stream. Scaling well means measuring those, limiting admission, and moving long
work to queues that absorb bursts.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Distinguish stateless API scaling from model-bound scaling and identify the actual bottleneck under load.
 • Apply admission control, queueing, and backpressure so overload degrades predictably instead of collapsing.
 • Choose autoscaling signals from observed concurrency and queue depth rather than CPU utilisation alone.
CORE CONCEPTS
Find the constrained resource
Load a single instance until latency breaks, recording concurrency, provider latency, tokens per second, CPU, and
memory. A streaming endpoint often hits a connection or memory limit first; a batch extraction job hits the provider's
tokens-per-minute quota; a retrieval-heavy path hits the database connection pool. The bottleneck determines the fix:
more replicas, a queue, smaller payloads, or a cache. Adding replicas to a provider-quota problem increases 429s and cost
without improving throughput.
Admission control and backpressure
A semaphore around provider calls bounds concurrent work per instance and keeps memory predictable. When the
semaphore is full, wait with a deadline, return 429 with Retry-After, or push the job to a queue. Unbounded
asyncio.gather looks efficient and then exhausts file descriptors and provider quota. Propagate deadlines so a request
abandoned by the client cancels its model call; otherwise you pay for tokens nobody reads. Shed load early rather than
degrade every request.
Scale on the right signal
Autoscaling on CPU is a lagging proxy for a system waiting on the network. Use concurrency, queue depth, or tokens per
minute, exported as custom metrics, and set a target from the per-instance load test. Keep a minimum replica count for
latency-sensitive traffic and a maximum that matches provider quota across all replicas. Scale in slowly, because a replica
that exits mid-stream drops a response; finish in-flight work before termination.
KEY TERMS
 Admission control                A gate that limits how many requests enter a service or provider call at once, protecting memory and quotas.
 Backpressure                     A signal that tells callers to slow down, through a queue, a 429, or a deadline, before the system collapses.
 Queue depth                      The number of jobs waiting for a worker, a leading indicator of saturation when processing time is variable.

  MENTAL MODEL Scaling an AI service is managing a queue at a popular counter: add staff when the line grows, but also cap how many
  orders each cook can hold.

Scaling AI Applications
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A research assistant serves 12,000 queries a day with a p95 target of eight seconds. On a launch day traffic triples; CPU
stays at 35% while p95 reaches 41 seconds and 9% of calls return 429 from the provider. The team had autoscaled on CPU
at 70%, so no new replicas appeared. They add a per-instance semaphore of 16 concurrent model calls, export that gauge,
and autoscale at 70% of the limit. Long reports move to a queue with a visible position, and the synchronous endpoint
returns 429 with Retry-After when the wait exceeds five seconds. The next spike holds p95 at 7.4 seconds, provider 429s
fall below 0.4%, and cost per query rises 6%.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Load-test one instance and record latency, concurrency, tokens per second, CPU, and memory at each step.
2.    Identify the first resource to saturate and state whether replicas, a queue, or a cache can fix it.
3.    Add a semaphore and a request deadline around provider calls, with a visible in-flight gauge.
4.    Move work longer than ten seconds to a queue and expose queue depth and age to users.
5.    Autoscale on the saturation signal, then rerun the load test and compare p95, 429 rate, and cost per request.
CODE
A per-instance admission limit that rejects fast instead of letting a traffic spike exhaust memory and provider quota.
  import asyncio
  from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
  class Admission:
    def __init__(self, limit: int) -> None:
       self._slots = asyncio.Semaphore(limit)
       self.in_flight = 0
       self.rejected = 0
    @asynccontextmanager
    async def slot(self, wait_s: float = 5.0):
       try:
          await asyncio.wait_for(self._slots.acquire(), timeout=wait_s)
       except TimeoutError:
          self.rejected += 1
          raise OverflowError("queue_full") from None
       self.in_flight += 1
       try:
          yield
       finally:
          self.in_flight -= 1
          self._slots.release()
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The semaphore caps work per instance; the autoscaler uses the same gauge, so replicas and admission limits stay
   consistent.
 → A rejected request fails in five seconds instead of occupying a slot for forty, which protects users already being served.
 → The counter is per process; with four uvicorn workers you need four sets of slots or a shared limit at the gateway.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One request path, one diagram Draw the path from client to answer: DNS, load balancer, API, auth, retrieval, model gateway, provider, validation, persistence, and response. Mark synchronous calls, asynchronous hops, caches, and stores. Every box needs an owner, a timeout, a retry policy, and a fallback. The diagram is a review tool, not decoration; if two engineers draw different paths, the system has undocumented behaviour. Keep it in the repository and update it in the same pull request as the change. Availability multiplies along the path Five serial dependencies at 99.9% each give roughly 99.5% end to end, about 3.6 hours of downtime a month. Managed services help, but your own retries and fallbacks decide the user experience. Add redundancy only where the calculation shows it matters, and prefer graceful degradation: serve cached or partial answers with a warning rather than a 500. Measure availability at the user boundary, not per component, because internal dashboards can all look green while requests fail. Cost and security are architecture Every design decision moves cost: replica minimums, cross-region replication, token-heavy prompts, and retained traces all have a monthly price. Put a cost estimate per 1,000 requests beside the diagram and review it when traffic doubles. Security boundaries belong there too: which service holds which secret, where personal data lives, what leaves the network, and how long it is retained. A launch review that cannot answer those questions is a demo with a domain name.

code.title: A serial availability calculation that turns an architecture diagram into a monthly downtime budget.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Hop:
  name: str
  availability: float
  fallback: float = 0.0

def path(hops: list[Hop]) -> tuple[float, float]:
  total = 1.0
  for hop in hops:
    total *= 1 - (1 - hop.availability) * (1 - hop.fallback)
  return total, (1 - total) * 30 * 24 * 60

stack = [Hop("api", 0.999), Hop("postgres", 0.9995), Hop("model", 0.999, 0.95)]
availability, downtime = path(stack)
print(f"{availability:.3%} available, {downtime:.0f} min of downtime/month")
what_to_notice: The model hop improves from 99.9% to 99.995% because a 95% fallback covers most failures; without it the product is 99.5%.
Downtime is computed for a 30-day month, so the number maps to an error budget rather than an abstract percentage.

The calculation assumes independent failures; a shared network or region outage fails several hops together and is worse. Three pages per lesson Page 537 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

why_it_matters: AI system design fails when the model becomes the centre of the diagram. The model is a variable, expensive dependency; the durable parts are contracts, data ownership, state, and failure paths. A design that names those boundaries can swap models without a rewrite. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Constraints before components Start with the user decision, the acceptable error, the p95 latency, the cost ceiling, and the data classification. Those constraints eliminate most architectures before a vendor enters the conversation. A contract review that must cite clauses needs retrieval and provenance; a classification task with 40 fixed labels may need no generation at all. Write the constraints as numbers, because fast and cheap cannot be tested or defended in a review. Three flows, one diagram Draw requests, data, and state separately. Requests show synchronous hops and timeouts; data shows ingestion, ownership, retention, and deletion; state shows where conversation, jobs, and approvals live. Overlay trust boundaries: browser to API, API to provider, worker to tenant data. Most design defects appear as a line crossing a boundary without authentication, or as state stored in a process that can restart. AI System Design
Design the request path, data ownership, and failure behaviour before choosing a model, a framework, or a vendor.
AI System Design · Lesson 1 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI system design fails when the model becomes the centre of the diagram. The model is a variable, expensive
dependency; the durable parts are contracts, data ownership, state, and failure paths. A design that names those
boundaries can swap models without a rewrite. A design that does not will discover its coupling during the first provider
outage, the first tenancy bug, or the first invoice.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Separate product constraints from model choices, and record each decision with an owner and its consequences.
 • Draw the request, data, and state flows, then mark every trust boundary and external dependency on one diagram.
 • Set latency, cost, and failure budgets per stage, and name the degraded behaviour when a dependency is unavailable.
CORE CONCEPTS
Constraints before components
Start with the user decision, the acceptable error, the p95 latency, the cost ceiling, and the data classification. Those
constraints eliminate most architectures before a vendor enters the conversation. A contract review that must cite
clauses needs retrieval and provenance; a classification task with 40 fixed labels may need no generation at all. Write the
constraints as numbers, because fast and cheap cannot be tested or defended in a review.
Three flows, one diagram
Draw requests, data, and state separately. Requests show synchronous hops and timeouts; data shows ingestion,
ownership, retention, and deletion; state shows where conversation, jobs, and approvals live. Overlay trust boundaries:
browser to API, API to provider, worker to tenant data. Most design defects appear as a line crossing a boundary without
authentication, or as state stored in a process that can restart. One diagram, reviewed by an operator, exposes more than
a fifty-page document.
Design the failure, then the feature
For every dependency, state what happens when it is slow, wrong, or gone. Provider timeout: serve a cached answer,
queue the job, or return 503 with a retry hint. Vector store outage: fall back to keyword search with a visible quality
warning. Write these paths as part of the design, not as tickets after launch. Also assign a cost and latency budget per
stage so a regression in retrieval cannot quietly consume the generation budget.

 Trust boundary                   A point where data or control crosses between components with different privileges, requiring

 Failure budget                   The acceptable rate and duration of a dependency failure before the system degrades, queues, or refuses
                                  work.

lessons.title: Designing for Scale
lessons.subtitle: Find the scarce resource before adding replicas, then size capacity from arrival rate, service time, and provider quotas.
lessons.meta: AI System Design · Lesson 2 of 13 · study guide
why_it_matters: Scaling an AI service is not a matter of adding pods. Model calls dominate latency, provider quotas cap throughput, and retries amplify load exactly when capacity is short. A service that scales its API tier but not its token budget will fall over at the first traffic spike. Capacity work starts with measurement: arrival rate, service time, concurrency, and the cost of a rejected request.
outcomes: Apply Little's law and utilisation reasoning to estimate how many concurrent requests a service can hold.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The bottleneck moves Every system has one scarce resource at a time. It may be CPU for parsing, connection pool slots, provider tokens per minute, vector index memory, or the human reviewer behind an approval queue. Fixing the first bottleneck reveals the next. Measure queue wait and service time separately, because a p99 driven by waiting is a capacity problem while a p99 driven by processing is an efficiency problem. Optimise the constraint, not the component that is easiest to tune. Little's law and headroom Little's law says concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by time in system. At 40 requests per second and 2.5 seconds per request, 100 requests are in flight; a 20-worker pool queues immediately. Plan for peak, not average, and keep utilisation below roughly 70% for variable service times. Above that, queue length grows non-linearly and a small latency increase becomes a timeout cascade. Load-test with production-like prompt and output lengths, not one-token pings. Scale the quota, not just the pod Provider limits are expressed in requests per minute, tokens per minute, and concurrent connections. A deployment with 200 workers and a 400,000-token-per-minute quota will spend most of its time backing off. Convert the quota into a work budget: average tokens per call, calls per request, and retry overhead. Then set worker concurrency below the quota ceiling, batch embeddings where the API allows it, and shed load with 429 plus Retry-After before the queue becomes unbounded.

key_terms.definition: The relationship that average concurrency equals arrival rate multiplied by average time spent in the system.
The spare capacity kept unused so that bursts, retries, and slow requests do not saturate a resource.

A mechanism that slows or rejects new work when downstream capacity is exhausted, instead of queueing without limit. MENTAL MODEL Scaling is widening a road: extra lanes help until the bridge, and the bridge is usually the provider quota or the database connection pool.

worked_example: A support SaaS load-tests its assistant before a Monday launch. The API tier handles 120 requests per second on eight pods, but p95 jumps from 2.1 to 9.4 seconds at 35 requests per second. Traces show 6.8 seconds waiting for a database connection, not model time: the pool is 20 connections per pod against a Postgres plan of 100. After moving conversation reads to a replica and pooling at 10 per pod, the service holds 70 requests per second at p95 2.6 seconds. Then the provider quota binds: 3 million tokens per minute allows about 28 average requests per second at 1,800 tokens each. The team adds a token-aware limiter, returns 429 with Retry-After above 24 requests per second, and schedules the launch at 60% of measured capacity.

Fix the constraint, then repeat the test; record the new ceiling and the resource that now binds.

code.title: A capacity check that compares worker concurrency and token quota before a launch.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Capacity:
  rps: float
  seconds: float
  workers: int
  tokens_per_min: int
  avg_tokens: float

def utilisation(c: Capacity) -> tuple[float, float]:
  in_flight = c.rps * c.seconds
  token_rps = c.tokens_per_min / 60 / c.avg_tokens
  return in_flight / c.workers, token_rps / c.rps

plan = Capacity(40, 2.5, 20, 400_000, 1_200)
workers, quota = utilisation(plan)
print(f"workers {workers:.0%} used, quota {quota:.0%} used")
if max(workers, quota) > 0.7:
   raise SystemExit("resize before launch: keep both ratios at or below 0.7")
what_to_notice: The calculation uses average token length; a few long-context requests can consume the minute's quota and starve everyone else.
Little's law measures concurrency, not queue length; a pool at 100% utilisation has unbounded wait, not stable throughput.

The 0.7 threshold is a starting point for variable service times, not a law; measure your own queue growth under load. Three pages per lesson Page 544 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Keep a quarterly capacity review that replays peak traffic and updates the ceiling after prompt, model, or index changes.

lessons.title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous AI
lessons.subtitle: Match the request pattern to the work: answer inside the user's patience window, or acknowledge with a durable job and
why_it_matters: A model call can take 300 milliseconds or three minutes, and the difference is architectural. Holding an HTTP connection open past the edge timeout produces 504s, duplicate work, and users who retry. Moving everything to a queue adds latency and state to simple questions. The design question is not which pattern is modern; it is how long the user will wait and what must survive a restart.
outcomes: Decide between synchronous, streaming, and queued execution using edge timeouts, work duration, and user expectations.
Design a job contract with 202 Accepted, a status resource, idempotency, and a terminal failure state.
Choose the notification path of polling, webhook, or stream to fit the client and the failure model.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Synchronous has a hard ceiling A synchronous request is bounded by the client, the load balancer, the gateway, and the provider timeout. A typical edge allows 30-60 seconds, so a chain of model calls, retries, and tool use must fit inside roughly half of that. Synchronous is right for a single fast completion, a short retrieval pass, or a streaming answer where the first token arrives quickly. It is wrong when work includes batch retrieval, multiple agents, or human approval. Async is a contract, not a queue Asynchronous work needs a submission endpoint that returns 202 Accepted with a job identifier and a Location header, a status resource with queued, running, succeeded, and failed states, and a result that survives worker restarts. Store the request payload, the owner, the idempotency key, and the attempt count. The client needs a defined way to collect the result: polling with backoff, a webhook with signature verification, or a server-sent event stream. Without that contract, a queue is just delayed failure. Hybrid: acknowledge fast, stream progress Many products need both: a fast acknowledgement and visible progress. Synchronous vs Asynchronous AI
Match the request pattern to the work: answer inside the user's patience window, or acknowledge with a durable job and
a way to collect it.
AI System Design · Lesson 3 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A model call can take 300 milliseconds or three minutes, and the difference is architectural. Holding an HTTP connection
open past the edge timeout produces 504s, duplicate work, and users who retry. Moving everything to a queue adds
latency and state to simple questions. The design question is not which pattern is modern; it is how long the user will wait
and what must survive a restart.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Decide between synchronous, streaming, and queued execution using edge timeouts, work duration, and user
   expectations.
 • Design a job contract with 202 Accepted, a status resource, idempotency, and a terminal failure state.
 • Choose the notification path of polling, webhook, or stream to fit the client and the failure model.
CORE CONCEPTS
Synchronous has a hard ceiling
A synchronous request is bounded by the client, the load balancer, the gateway, and the provider timeout. A typical edge
allows 30-60 seconds, so a chain of model calls, retries, and tool use must fit inside roughly half of that. Synchronous is
right for a single fast completion, a short retrieval pass, or a streaming answer where the first token arrives quickly. It is
wrong when work includes batch retrieval, multiple agents, or human approval.
Async is a contract, not a queue
Asynchronous work needs a submission endpoint that returns 202 Accepted with a job identifier and a Location header, a
status resource with queued, running, succeeded, and failed states, and a result that survives worker restarts. Store the
request payload, the owner, the idempotency key, and the attempt count. The client needs a defined way to collect the
result: polling with backoff, a webhook with signature verification, or a server-sent event stream. Without that contract, a
queue is just delayed failure.
Hybrid: acknowledge fast, stream progress
Many products need both: a fast acknowledgement and visible progress. Start the job, return the identifier immediately,
then stream status or partial output over SSE or WebSocket while the worker writes durable checkpoints. If the
connection drops, the client reconnects by job id and resumes from the last checkpoint. Keep the synchronous path for
lightweight status reads, and never make the worker depend on the client staying connected. This pattern protects the
user experience without pretending a long job is a short request.
KEY TERMS
 202 Accepted                     An HTTP status meaning the request is valid and queued or started, but the final result is not yet available.
 Idempotency key                  A client-supplied identifier that lets the server return the same job or result when a request is retried.
 Long polling                     A client request that waits briefly for a state change before returning, reducing empty status checks.

  MENTAL MODEL Synchronous is a phone call; asynchronous is a ticket with a reference number. Use the phone for a quick question and
  a ticket for work that outlives the conversation.

CODE
A 202 submission endpoint and status resource that return the same job for a repeated idempotency key.
  from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException, Response
  from pydantic import BaseModel

  app, JOBS = FastAPI(), {}
  class Briefing(BaseModel):
    topic: str

  @app.post("/briefings", status_code=202)
  def submit(
     body: Briefing, response: Response, key: str = Header(alias="Idempotency-Key")
  ) -> dict:
     job = JOBS.setdefault(key, {"state": "queued", "topic": body.topic})
     response.headers["Location"] = f"/briefings/{key}"
     return job

  @app.get("/briefings/{key}")
  def status(key: str) -> dict:
    if key not in JOBS:
       raise HTTPException(404, "unknown job")
    return JOBS[key]

   with a TTL.

why_it_matters: A queue turns a latency problem into a throughput problem, but it also introduces a new failure surface: messages can be delivered twice, processed out of order, or retried forever. AI workers make this worse because each attempt may cost money and call a rate-limited provider. core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: At-least-once is the default Most queues guarantee at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once. A worker can crash after doing the work but before acknowledging, so the message returns after the visibility timeout. Design every consumer around that fact: write a unique idempotency key, upsert by it, and check whether the side effect already happened. Exactly-once behaviour is a property you build at the effect boundary, not a setting you enable on the broker. Visibility, retries, and poison A received message becomes invisible for a lease period. If the worker finishes, it deletes the message; if it crashes, the lease expires and another worker receives it. Set the lease above p99 processing time, or a slow job will be redelivered while still running. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and route exhausted messages to a dead-letter queue with the error, attempt count, and original payload. Alert on DLQ depth, not only on worker errors. Backpressure and worker sizing Queue depth alone is a poor autoscaling signal because ten fast messages and ten slow ones look identical. Scale on age of the oldest message and on consumer lag, then cap concurrency at the downstream limit. If workers can process 30 jobs per second but the provider allows 400,000 tokens per minute at 1,500 tokens per job, about 4.4 jobs per second is the real ceiling. When the queue grows past a threshold, slow ingestion or return 429 rather than accepting work you cannot finish.

code.title: A leased claim with full-jitter retry, dead-letter routing, and an acknowledgement marker.
code.code:
import random
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

def claim() -> str | None:
  return r.brpoplpush("embed", "embed:working", timeout=5)

def settle(raw: str, status: int, attempt: int) -> str:
  if status in {429, 500, 502, 503, 504} and attempt < 5:
     r.rpush("embed", raw)
     r.lrem("embed:working", 1, raw)
     return f"retry in {random.uniform(0, 2 ** attempt):.1f}s"
  if status >= 400:
     r.rpush("embed:dlq", raw)
     r.lrem("embed:working", 1, raw)
     return "dead_letter"
  r.set(f"done:{raw}", 1, ex=604800)
  r.lrem("embed:working", 1, raw)
  return "ack"
what_to_notice: The claim moves the message to a working list, so a crashed worker leaves it there until a reaper returns it; the lease is not self-healing.
Full jitter reduces thundering herds but makes retry order non-deterministic; use a FIFO queue only where ordering is a product requirement.

lessons.title: Caching Strategies
lessons.subtitle: Cache the deterministic, expensive parts of the AI path, not the whole answer, and make every key depend on the model,
why_it_matters: AI calls are expensive, slow, and often repeated. Caching can cut cost by 30-60% on real support traffic, but a cache that ignores model version or tenant scope becomes a data-leak and correctness bug. The engineering decision is which layer to cache, how to key it, and how to invalidate it when prompts, documents, or permissions change. A high hit rate is only good if the hits are correct.
outcomes: Choose cache layers for embeddings, retrieval, prompts, and final responses by hit rate and invalidation cost.
Design cache keys and TTLs that cannot serve stale, cross-tenant, or wrong-model data.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Cache the narrowest expensive object A final-answer cache has the highest hit value and the highest risk: it can leak another tenant's data or serve a policy that changed this morning. An embedding cache keyed by text hash is deterministic and safe to share across tenants. A retrieval cache keyed by query and index version saves vector search but still needs permission filtering. A prompt-prefix cache works only when the provider supports it and the prefix is byte-stable. Start narrow: embeddings, then retrieval, then whole answers for public content. Keys encode every dependency A cache key must include the model and version, prompt template version, normalised input, tenant or permission scope, and index or document version. Hash the full canonical payload rather than concatenating unchecked strings. If any dependency changes and the key does not, you serve a wrong answer that looks like a hit. Normalise before hashing: trim whitespace, lowercase where the domain allows it, and sort tool arguments. Never include raw personal data in the key or in cache logs. Invalidation, TTL, and stampedes TTL is a blunt but honest invalidation tool: 24 hours for public FAQs, five minutes for account balances, and zero for anything that must reflect a just-completed write. For document updates, bump an index version so old keys become unreachable and expire naturally. Caching Strategies
Cache the deterministic, expensive parts of the AI path, not the whole answer, and make every key depend on the model,
prompt, and data version.
AI System Design · Lesson 5 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
AI calls are expensive, slow, and often repeated. Caching can cut cost by 30-60% on real support traffic, but a cache that
ignores model version or tenant scope becomes a data-leak and correctness bug. The engineering decision is which layer
to cache, how to key it, and how to invalidate it when prompts, documents, or permissions change. A high hit rate is only
good if the hits are correct.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Choose cache layers for embeddings, retrieval, prompts, and final responses by hit rate and invalidation cost.
 • Design cache keys and TTLs that cannot serve stale, cross-tenant, or wrong-model data.
 • Protect origin services from stampedes and measure hit rate, saved cost, and stale-answer rate.
CORE CONCEPTS
Cache the narrowest expensive object
A final-answer cache has the highest hit value and the highest risk: it can leak another tenant's data or serve a policy that
changed this morning. An embedding cache keyed by text hash is deterministic and safe to share across tenants. A
retrieval cache keyed by query and index version saves vector search but still needs permission filtering. A prompt-prefix
cache works only when the provider supports it and the prefix is byte-stable. Start narrow: embeddings, then retrieval,
then whole answers for public content.
Keys encode every dependency
A cache key must include the model and version, prompt template version, normalised input, tenant or permission scope,
and index or document version. Hash the full canonical payload rather than concatenating unchecked strings. If any
dependency changes and the key does not, you serve a wrong answer that looks like a hit. Normalise before hashing: trim
whitespace, lowercase where the domain allows it, and sort tool arguments. Never include raw personal data in the key
or in cache logs.
Invalidation, TTL, and stampedes
TTL is a blunt but honest invalidation tool: 24 hours for public FAQs, five minutes for account balances, and zero for
anything that must reflect a just-completed write. For document updates, bump an index version so old keys become
unreachable and expire naturally. Protect the origin with single-flight: when a key misses, one worker computes while
others wait or receive a stale value. Add jitter to expiry so a popular key does not expire for every request at once.
KEY TERMS
 Hit rate                         The share of requests served from cache rather than recomputed, measured per cache layer and traffic
                                  segment.
 Single-flight                    A pattern where only one caller recomputes a missing key while concurrent callers wait for or reuse that
                                  result.
 Cache stampede                   A surge of concurrent recomputation when a popular key expires or is invalidated.

  MENTAL MODEL A cache is a photocopy on the wall: fast to read, but useless and dangerous once the original changes and nobody
  replaces the copy.

Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A fintech support assistant answers 120,000 questions a week at GBP 0.011 per answer. Logs show 38% exact duplicates,
mostly password resets and card-delivery timelines. The team adds a Redis cache for final answers keyed by tenant,

public FAQs. Hit rate reaches 31% and monthly spend falls by GBP 1,770. A proposal to add semantic caching at 0.92
similarity is rejected after a test returns a cached answer about a different customer's card. The decision: keep exact
caching, add an embedding cache shared across tenants, and require a permission-scope field in every key before any
semantic layer is reconsidered.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Measure duplicate rate, cost per call, and latency by endpoint before choosing a cache layer.
2.    Pick the narrowest object with a high hit rate and a safe invalidation story, usually embeddings first.
3.    Define a canonical key including model, prompt version, tenant scope, and index version; hash it with SHA-256.
4.    Set TTLs per data class and add single-flight plus jitter to prevent stampedes on popular keys.
5.    Load-test hit and miss paths, then track hit rate, stale-answer reports, and saved cost weekly.
CODE
A tenant-scoped response cache with a versioned key and a per-key lock against stampedes.
  import hashlib, json, redis

  r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

  def key(tenant: str, question: str, prompt_v: str) -> str:
    parts = [tenant, " ".join(question.lower().split()), prompt_v, "gpt-4.1-mini"]
    return "ans:" + hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(parts).encode()).hexdigest()

  def answer(tenant: str, question: str, compute) -> str:
    k = key(tenant, question, "v7")
    if (cached := r.get(k)) is not None:
       return cached
    with r.lock(k + ":lock", timeout=30, blocking_timeout=5):
       if (cached := r.get(k)) is not None:
          return cached
       value = compute(question)
       r.set(k, value, ex=600)
       return value
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The key includes tenant, prompt version, and model, so a permission or template change produces a miss instead of a stale
   answer.
 → The lock is per key and bounded at five seconds; a slow compute returns an error or stale value rather than blocking every
   caller.
 → The ten-minute TTL matches account data; public FAQs can use a day, while post-write reads should bypass the cache
   entirely.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One workload per store Postgres handles users, conversations, jobs, and permissions transactionally. Analytics belongs on a replica or a columnar warehouse, not on the primary that serves chat. Vector search belongs in pgvector for modest corpora or a dedicated index when recall, filtering, or scale demand it. Object storage holds documents and generated artefacts. Splitting workloads by access pattern keeps p95 predictable and lets each store scale on its own constraint rather than sharing one. Tenancy is a schema decision A tenant_id column on every row is the minimum, but it is not isolation unless queries enforce it. Enable Postgres row- level security, set the tenant in the session, and test that a missing setting returns zero rows rather than everything. For large tenants, partition by tenant hash or by time, and keep the partition key in every unique index. Shared caches and vector collections need the same tenant filter; a missing WHERE clause is a cross-customer incident, not a performance bug. Transactions do not span model calls Open a transaction, read what you need, commit, call the model, then open a second transaction to write the result with an idempotency key. Holding a transaction across an external call keeps locks and a connection for seconds, and a provider timeout leaves the transaction open until it is killed. For writes that depend on model output, use a unique constraint on request_id and an upsert. Track connection pool saturation and statement timeouts; a 30-second statement timeout is a safety net, not a design.

key_terms.definition: A database policy that filters rows by the current session's identity, enforcing tenant scope inside the engine.
A bounded set of reusable database connections shared by application workers to avoid per-request connection overhead.

A write that inserts a row or updates it when the same key already exists, producing one effect on replay. MENTAL MODEL The database is the ship's log: it must record what happened in order, but you do not hold the pen while the engine room repairs the boiler.

lessons.title: Vector Database Architecture
lessons.subtitle: Treat the vector index as a product with recall, latency, memory, and tenancy budgets, not as a library you install and
why_it_matters: A vector index is approximate. It trades recall for speed and memory, and those trade-offs change as the corpus grows. The failure modes are quiet: recall drops after a bulk insert, a filter is applied after the search so the top ten are empty, or a re-embedding leaves half the corpus on an old model. Vector architecture is the discipline of measuring recall against a labelled set and making index changes reversible.
outcomes: Choose HNSW, IVF, or flat search from corpus size, recall target, latency budget, and memory cost.
Design tenant-safe filtered search and keep embedding versions aligned with index builds.
Plan ingestion, compaction, snapshots, and rebuilds so index maintenance does not take retrieval offline.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Approximate means measurable HNSW builds a graph with a configurable M and ef_construction; higher values improve recall and cost memory and build time. IVF clusters vectors and searches a subset, so recall depends on nprobe. Flat search is exact but linear. Choose by corpus size and recall target, then measure recall@10 against exact search on 500-1,000 labelled queries. A 1536- dimension float32 vector costs about 6 KB before index overhead; 20 million chunks is 120 GB of raw vectors, so memory is usually the first constraint. Filter before or beside the search A metadata filter applied after top-k retrieval can return fewer results than requested, or none, when the filter is selective. Use a store that supports filtered search natively, and keep tenant_id in the filter on every query. Pre-filtering can hurt recall if the index is built across tenants; partitioning by tenant or by a coarse key keeps the search space small. Test a rare tenant with 200 chunks, not only the largest tenant, and assert the result count before sending context to the model. Ingestion and rebuilds are part of the design Embedding model versions change. Store the model name and dimension beside every vector, and never mix versions in one index. New documents should be written to a staging index, validated for count, dimension, and recall, then promoted by alias swap. Keep the raw text and metadata in object storage so a rebuild does not depend on the old index. Budget for compaction and snapshot time: a 20-million-vector snapshot can take minutes and consume IOPS that retrieval also needs.

key_terms.definition: A graph-based approximate index that links nearby vectors across layers to trade memory and build time for fast search.

A stable name that points to a physical index, allowing a rebuild to be promoted by switching the alias atomically. MENTAL MODEL A vector index is a library catalogue built for speed: it usually finds the right shelf, but you must test how often it misses and rebuild it when the books are reclassified.

worked_example: A recruitment platform indexes 18 million CV chunks from 900 employers. The first design uses one HNSW collection with 1536-dimension vectors and no tenant filter; a search for a candidate returns another employer's profile in testing, and the index needs 210 GB of RAM. The team moves to one collection per region, adds tenant_id as a mandatory filter, and tests a rare tenant with 140 chunks. Recall@10 against exact search is 0.91 at ef_search 64 and 0.97 at 128, but p95 rises from 38 to 71 milliseconds. Vector Database Architecture
Treat the vector index as a product with recall, latency, memory, and tenancy budgets, not as a library you install and
forget.
AI System Design · Lesson 7 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A vector index is approximate. It trades recall for speed and memory, and those trade-offs change as the corpus grows.
The failure modes are quiet: recall drops after a bulk insert, a filter is applied after the search so the top ten are empty, or
a re-embedding leaves half the corpus on an old model. Vector architecture is the discipline of measuring recall against a
labelled set and making index changes reversible.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Choose HNSW, IVF, or flat search from corpus size, recall target, latency budget, and memory cost.
 • Design tenant-safe filtered search and keep embedding versions aligned with index builds.
 • Plan ingestion, compaction, snapshots, and rebuilds so index maintenance does not take retrieval offline.
CORE CONCEPTS
Approximate means measurable
HNSW builds a graph with a configurable M and ef_construction; higher values improve recall and cost memory and build
time. IVF clusters vectors and searches a subset, so recall depends on nprobe. Flat search is exact but linear. Choose by
corpus size and recall target, then measure recall@10 against exact search on 500-1,000 labelled queries. A 1536-
dimension float32 vector costs about 6 KB before index overhead; 20 million chunks is 120 GB of raw vectors, so memory
is usually the first constraint.
Filter before or beside the search
A metadata filter applied after top-k retrieval can return fewer results than requested, or none, when the filter is
selective. Use a store that supports filtered search natively, and keep tenant_id in the filter on every query. Pre-filtering
can hurt recall if the index is built across tenants; partitioning by tenant or by a coarse key keeps the search space small.
Test a rare tenant with 200 chunks, not only the largest tenant, and assert the result count before sending context to the
model.
Ingestion and rebuilds are part of the design
Embedding model versions change. Store the model name and dimension beside every vector, and never mix versions in
one index. New documents should be written to a staging index, validated for count, dimension, and recall, then
promoted by alias swap. Keep the raw text and metadata in object storage so a rebuild does not depend on the old index.
Budget for compaction and snapshot time: a 20-million-vector snapshot can take minutes and consume IOPS that
retrieval also needs.
KEY TERMS
 Recall@k                         The share of true nearest neighbours that appear in the first k results returned by an approximate index.
 HNSW                             A graph-based approximate index that links nearby vectors across layers to trade memory and build time for
                                  fast search.
 Index alias                      A stable name that points to a physical index, allowing a rebuild to be promoted by switching the alias
                                  atomically.

  MENTAL MODEL A vector index is a library catalogue built for speed: it usually finds the right shelf, but you must test how often it
  misses and rebuild it when the books are reclassified.

WORKED EXAMPLE
A recruitment platform indexes 18 million CV chunks from 900 employers. The first design uses one HNSW collection with

from 38 to 71 milliseconds. They keep ef_search at 96, accept 0.94 recall, and add a nightly recall probe of 500 queries.

   USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)

  SET hnsw.ef_search = 96;

  SELECT id, document_id, 1 - (embedding <=> %s::vector) AS score
  FROM chunks
  WHERE tenant_id = %s
   AND embedding_model = 'text-embedding-3-small'

why_it_matters: One model cannot be simultaneously the cheapest, fastest, and most capable choice for every request. Routing turns that trade-off into an explicit policy: classify the request, pick the model that clears the quality bar for that class, and record why. Teams that skip routing either overpay for trivial work or under-serve the hard 5% that carries most of the risk. The router is ordinary software, so it can be tested, versioned, and rolled back.
outcomes: Define route classes from task type, input size, risk tier, and tool needs rather than from model fashion.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Routing is a costed classification Routing is a classification problem with a cost function, not a preference. Start by listing the request classes your evaluation already distinguishes: short extraction, long-context summarisation, tool-using agent steps, policy-sensitive answers. For each class, measure pass rate and p95 latency on at least 100 labelled cases for two or three candidate models. The router then encodes the cheapest model that clears the class floor, with the frontier model reserved for classes where the gap is real. Rules first, classifier second Most traffic does not need a model to route it. Deterministic rules cover input length, language, tenant plan, endpoint, attachment presence, and risk tier, and they are cheap, explainable, and easy to audit. Send only the ambiguous remainder to a small classifier or embedding nearest-neighbour lookup trained on labelled route decisions. Keep the rule table and classifier version in configuration, log the chosen route and reason on every request, and shadow new policies before they take traffic. Every route is a separate product Split the evaluation set by route and score each slice independently; an aggregate 94% hides a route that fails 30% of billing disputes. Give each route its own quality floor, p95 target, and monthly cost ceiling, then alert when a slice drifts. Escalate to a stronger model when validation fails, confidence is low, or the request matches a risky intent. Canary a changed policy on 5% of traffic for a day, compare cost and quality, and roll back by flipping the table version.

key_terms.definition: A group of requests sharing a task, size band, risk tier, and quality floor, evaluated and costed separately.
Sending a request to a stronger model after a failed validation, low confidence, or a risky-intent match.

Running a candidate policy on live traffic without serving its output, to compare decisions, quality, and cost. MENTAL MODEL A router is a triage nurse: cheap, fast, and rule-driven for routine cases, escalating the ambiguous or serious ones to a specialist before harm is done.

CODE
A versioned routing table with an explicit risk check, returning the reason alongside the model.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  TIERS = {"small": "gpt-4.1-mini", "large": "gpt-4.1"}

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Request:
    tokens: int
    risk: str    # "low" or "high"
    needs_tools: bool

  def route(r: Request) -> tuple[str, str]:
    if r.risk == "high" or r.tokens > 12_000:
       return TIERS["large"], "risk_or_length"
    if r.needs_tools:
       return TIERS["large"], "tool_use"
    return TIERS["small"], "default_low_risk"

  for req in (Request(800, "low", False), Request(900, "high", False)):
    print(route(req))

lessons.title: Multi-Model Systems
lessons.subtitle: Treat models as a portfolio with contracts and failure domains, not as one vendor you call from ten places in the codebase.
lessons.meta: AI System Design · Lesson 9 of 13 · study guide
why_it_matters: Any serious platform ends up with several models: a frontier reasoner, a cheap bulk extractor, an embedding model, a guard classifier, and a fallback from a second provider. Each has different token limits, JSON behaviour, tool semantics, pricing, and outage patterns. Without a common contract, every new model means edits across the codebase and a fresh round of surprises. Portfolio thinking makes model choice a configuration decision while keeping evaluation, cost, and failure handling in one place.
outcomes: Assign each model in the system a role, an interface, and an owner instead of duplicating provider SDK calls.
Normalise messages, tool schemas, and stop reasons behind adapters that pin model snapshots per environment.
Design cascades, cross-checks, and provider failover, then measure agreement and false-accept rates.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: A portfolio with roles Write down every model role before choosing vendors: reasoning and planning, high-volume extraction, embeddings, moderation or policy classification, and emergency fallback. Give each role an interface describing inputs, output schema, maximum tokens, and timeout. Pin an exact snapshot per environment so an upstream upgrade cannot change behaviour during a release. The portfolio is healthy when no single provider outage removes a capability, and when every role has a measured quality floor and a named cost owner. Adapters absorb the differences Providers disagree about message roles, tool-call formatting, stop reasons, JSON modes, and how they report token usage. Put those differences behind a thin adapter that converts to your internal request and response types, validates the output schema, and records usage. Normalise finish reasons into completed, length, tool_call, and refused so retry logic stays provider-neutral. Keep the adapter small and tested with recorded fixtures, because provider schema drift appears as a parsing bug at 2am, not as a release note. Cascades and cross-checks A cascade runs the cheap model first and escalates when validation fails or confidence is below a threshold, so most traffic stays cheap. A cross-check runs a second model on high-risk output and compares structured fields; disagreement routes to a human. Both add cost, so measure the escalation rate and the false-accept rate before enabling them broadly. A second provider is also a failover path: exercise it on a schedule, because an untested fallback is a design document rather than a capability.

key_terms.definition: A price and latency band of models sharing a role, such as bulk extraction, reasoning, or embedding.
Running a cheap model first and escalating only when its output fails validation or a confidence threshold.

Routing the same internal contract to a second vendor when the primary errors, rate-limits, or times out. MENTAL MODEL A multi-model system is a football squad: defined positions, a shared playbook, substitutes who train weekly, and no plan that collapses when one player is injured.

Multi-Model Systems
Treat models as a portfolio with contracts and failure domains, not as one vendor you call from ten places in the codebase.
AI System Design · Lesson 9 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Any serious platform ends up with several models: a frontier reasoner, a cheap bulk extractor, an embedding model, a
guard classifier, and a fallback from a second provider. Each has different token limits, JSON behaviour, tool semantics,
pricing, and outage patterns. Without a common contract, every new model means edits across the codebase and a fresh
round of surprises. Portfolio thinking makes model choice a configuration decision while keeping evaluation, cost, and
failure handling in one place.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Assign each model in the system a role, an interface, and an owner instead of duplicating provider SDK calls.
 • Normalise messages, tool schemas, and stop reasons behind adapters that pin model snapshots per environment.
 • Design cascades, cross-checks, and provider failover, then measure agreement and false-accept rates.
CORE CONCEPTS
A portfolio with roles
Write down every model role before choosing vendors: reasoning and planning, high-volume extraction, embeddings,
moderation or policy classification, and emergency fallback. Give each role an interface describing inputs, output schema,
maximum tokens, and timeout. Pin an exact snapshot per environment so an upstream upgrade cannot change behaviour
during a release. The portfolio is healthy when no single provider outage removes a capability, and when every role has a
measured quality floor and a named cost owner.
Adapters absorb the differences
Providers disagree about message roles, tool-call formatting, stop reasons, JSON modes, and how they report token
usage. Put those differences behind a thin adapter that converts to your internal request and response types, validates
the output schema, and records usage. Normalise finish reasons into completed, length, tool_call, and refused so retry
logic stays provider-neutral. Keep the adapter small and tested with recorded fixtures, because provider schema drift
appears as a parsing bug at 2am, not as a release note.
Cascades and cross-checks
A cascade runs the cheap model first and escalates when validation fails or confidence is below a threshold, so most
traffic stays cheap. A cross-check runs a second model on high-risk output and compares structured fields; disagreement
routes to a human. Both add cost, so measure the escalation rate and the false-accept rate before enabling them broadly.
A second provider is also a failover path: exercise it on a schedule, because an untested fallback is a design document
rather than a capability.
KEY TERMS
 Capability tier                  A price and latency band of models sharing a role, such as bulk extraction, reasoning, or embedding.
 Cascade                          Running a cheap model first and escalating only when its output fails validation or a confidence threshold.
 Provider failover                Routing the same internal contract to a second vendor when the primary errors, rate-limits, or times out.

  MENTAL MODEL A multi-model system is a football squad: defined positions, a shared playbook, substitutes who train weekly, and no
  plan that collapses when one player is injured.

Claims platform Northgate runs four roles: a small model extracts 42 fields from 90,000 claim forms a month, a frontier

agreement drops from 96% to 92%. The incident review decides to keep the fallback warm with 2% canary traffic, add a
provider-specific golden set of 300 forms, and block automatic promotion of a new snapshot until agreement clears 95%.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Inventory every model role, its owner, token limits, output schema, and current monthly spend.
2.    Define internal request and response types, then wrap each provider in an adapter with fixture tests.
3.    Pin snapshots per environment and record model identifier, adapter version, and usage in every trace.
4.    Build a per-role golden set and record quality, latency, and cost for the primary and the fallback.

CODE
A confidence cascade that escalates to the larger model and refuses to auto-accept disagreement on critical fields.
  def agree(a: dict, b: dict, fields: tuple[str, ...]) -> float:
    hits = sum(a[f] == b[f] for f in fields)
    return hits / len(fields)

  def cascade(text, schema, small, large, critical=()):
    first = small.extract(text, schema)
    if first.ok and first.confidence >= 0.82 and not critical:
       return first.value, small.name
    second = large.extract(text, schema)
    if not second.ok:
       raise ValueError(f"both models failed for {schema.__name__}")
    if critical and agree(first.value, second.value, critical) < 0.9:
       raise NeedsHumanReview(text_id=text.id)
    return second.value, large.name

  value, model = cascade(form_text, Claim, SMALL, LARGE)
  print(model, value["claim_id"])
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The cascade trusts the small model only when validation passes, confidence clears 0.82, and the request carries no critical
   field.
 → The fallback logs which model produced the value, so a provider incident shows up in quality data rather than only in error
   rates.
 → Critical-field disagreement raises a human-review signal and records both answers instead of silently preferring the larger
   model.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The promise comes first An SLI is a ratio you can compute from telemetry, such as successful answers under eight seconds divided by all requests. Define it at the user boundary, not at the model call, so a fast 500 still counts as a failure. A 99.5% monthly target allows about 3.6 hours of full outage, and the error budget is the currency for releases and experiments. Decompose the latency target across edge, auth, retrieval, generation, and validation; if generation gets 3.5 seconds, a 4-second p95 is impossible. Deadlines and retries share one budget Every request carries a deadline that is passed to each dependency, and each layer subtracts its own slice rather than starting a fresh timeout. Retries consume the same budget: two attempts at a 2-second timeout cannot fit inside three seconds. Cap attempts at two or three, retry only 429, 5xx, timeouts, and connection errors, with jittered exponential backoff. Hedge only when the tail matters and you can pay for duplicate tokens; otherwise a hedge doubles spend to protect a few requests. Prove it with deliberate failure Load tests at 1.5 times peak reveal queue growth and quota exhaustion before customers do. Game days inject provider 429s, 30-second latency, a dead replica, and a corrupt cache entry, then check that fallbacks and alerts fire. Canary releases move 5% of traffic for thirty minutes and roll back automatically on error rate, p95 latency, or evaluation score. Record each exercise with detection time, mitigation time, and a follow-up owner; an untested rollback is a hope, not a control.

STEP BY STEP
1.    Define the user-facing success event and compute the SLI from traces, not from infrastructure metrics.
2.    Set an availability target and split the p95 latency budget across edge, retrieval, model, and validation.
3.    Propagate one deadline through every call and cap retries so attempts cannot exceed it.
4.    Load test at 1.5 times peak and run a game day that injects 429s, latency, and a dead dependency.

CODE
One absolute deadline shared by every attempt, with jittered backoff that cannot sleep past the budget.
  import asyncio
  import random

  async def call_with_budget(fn, budget_s: float, attempts: int = 3):
    end = asyncio.get_running_loop().time() + budget_s
    for attempt in range(attempts):
      left = end - asyncio.get_running_loop().time()
      if left <= 0:
         raise TimeoutError(f"budget of {budget_s}s exhausted")
      try:
         return await asyncio.wait_for(fn(), timeout=left)
      except (asyncio.TimeoutError, ConnectionError):
         if attempt == attempts - 1:
            raise
         backoff = 0.25 * 2**attempt + random.random() * 0.1
         remaining = max(0.0, end - asyncio.get_running_loop().time())
         await asyncio.sleep(min(backoff, remaining))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The deadline is absolute, so every retry and backoff is subtracted from the same budget instead of resetting the clock.
 → Only transient exceptions are caught; validation and authentication failures fail fast rather than burning the budget.
 → The backoff wait is capped by the remaining time, so the function cannot sleep past its own deadline.

lessons.title: Fault Tolerance
lessons.subtitle: Assume every dependency will fail: isolate the blast radius, break failing circuits, and recover without duplicating side
why_it_matters: Retries alone turn a slow dependency into a queue of doomed requests. Fault tolerance is the set of mechanisms that keep a partial failure partial: separate pools so one tenant cannot exhaust capacity, breakers that stop calling a failing provider, fallbacks that return something honest, and idempotent writes so recovery does not bill a customer twice. These are ordinary distributed-systems patterns; the AI twist is that a degraded answer may still be useful if it is labelled as degraded.
outcomes: Isolate model, retrieval, and database calls with bulkheads and concurrency limits per dependency and tenant.
Implement circuit breakers with explicit thresholds, half-open probes, and user-visible degraded modes.
Make writes idempotent and drain workers safely so retries and failover cannot duplicate side effects.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Isolate the blast radius Give each dependency its own connection pool, semaphore, and worker pool, and consider a per-tenant concurrency cap on expensive routes. A bulkhead means a provider returning 429s saturates only its own pool while retrieval and cached answers continue. Set queue wait limits, not just execution timeouts, so rejected work fails fast instead of ageing for a minute. Measure saturation per pool; a pool above 80% for five minutes is a capacity signal, not a reason to raise the timeout. Break the circuit, choose the mode A breaker moves from closed to open after a threshold, for example 50% errors across at least 20 requests in 20 seconds, then rejects calls immediately. After a cool-off it enters half-open and admits a few probes; success closes it, failure reopens it for longer. While open, the system must choose a degraded mode: cached answer with a timestamp, a smaller model, a queued job, or a clear apology. Name that mode in the response and the trace so support can explain what the user received. Recover without duplicating effects Failover and retries repeat work, so any write needs an idempotency key derived from the request, stored with the result and reused on retry. Prefer upserts and unique constraints over read-then-write sequences. On shutdown, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight messages inside the visibility timeout, and return the rest to the queue. Send permanently failing messages to a dead-letter queue with payload and error, and alert on depth rather than waiting for a customer to report a missing document.

key_terms.definition: A separate pool or concurrency limit per dependency so one failing resource cannot exhaust shared capacity.
A stateful guard that stops calls to a failing dependency and probes recovery with limited requests.

A defined, labelled response served when a dependency is unavailable, such as a cached answer. MENTAL MODEL Fault tolerance is a ship's watertight compartments: a breach floods one section, the crew seals it, and the vessel keeps moving at reduced speed.
