answers continue. Set queue wait limits, not just execution timeouts, so rejected work fails fast instead of ageing for a
minute. Measure saturation per pool; a pool above 80% for five minutes is a capacity signal, not a reason to raise the
timeout.
Break the circuit, choose the mode
A breaker moves from closed to open after a threshold, for example 50% errors across at least 20 requests in 20 seconds,
then rejects calls immediately. After a cool-off it enters half-open and admits a few probes; success closes it, failure
reopens it for longer. While open, the system must choose a degraded mode: cached answer with a timestamp, a smaller
model, a queued job, or a clear apology. Name that mode in the response and the trace so support can explain what the
user received.
Recover without duplicating effects
Failover and retries repeat work, so any write needs an idempotency key derived from the request, stored with the result
and reused on retry. Prefer upserts and unique constraints over read-then-write sequences. On shutdown, stop accepting
new work, finish in-flight messages inside the visibility timeout, and return the rest to the queue. Send permanently
failing messages to a dead-letter queue with payload and error, and alert on depth rather than waiting for a customer to
report a missing document.
KEY TERMS
 Bulkhead                         A separate pool or concurrency limit per dependency so one failing resource cannot exhaust shared capacity.
 Circuit breaker                  A stateful guard that stops calls to a failing dependency and probes recovery with limited requests.
 Degraded mode                    A defined, labelled response served when a dependency is unavailable, such as a cached answer.

  MENTAL MODEL Fault tolerance is a ship's watertight compartments: a breach floods one section, the crew seals it, and the vessel keeps
  moving at reduced speed.

Fault Tolerance
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
A travel assistant handles 18,000 itinerary requests an hour across three providers. During a regional provider outage,
every request retried twice, worker pools filled with waiting calls, and the whole service returned 504s for eleven minutes
even though retrieval and cache were healthy. The redesign gives each provider its own pool of 40 connections, opens a
breaker after 50% errors across 20 requests, and serves a cached itinerary with a visible timestamp while open. Booking
writes now carry an idempotency key stored in Postgres, and shutdown drains for 25 seconds before requeueing. The
next provider incident produced 3.1% degraded responses and zero duplicate bookings, with p95 at 1.8 seconds.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Map each external dependency and give it a dedicated pool, concurrency limit, and queue-wait ceiling.
2.    Define breaker thresholds from measured error rates and add half-open probes with capped concurrency.
3.    Choose and implement a degraded response per route, labelled in the payload and the trace.
4.    Add idempotency keys to every write and enforce them with a unique constraint in the database.
5.    Drain on SIGTERM, requeue unfinished messages, and alert on dead-letter depth and breaker state.
CODE
A per-dependency circuit breaker with a failure threshold, cool-off, and a limited half-open probe.
  import time

  class Breaker:
    def __init__(self, threshold: int = 5, reset_after: float = 20.0) -> None:
       self.threshold, self.reset_after = threshold, reset_after
       self.failures, self.opened_at = 0, 0.0

     def allow(self) -> bool:
       if self.failures < self.threshold:
          return True
       if time.monotonic() - self.opened_at >= self.reset_after:
          self.failures = self.threshold - 1 # half-open probe
          return True
       return False

     def record(self, ok: bool) -> None:
       self.failures = 0 if ok else self.failures + 1
       if self.failures >= self.threshold:
          self.opened_at = time.monotonic()
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The breaker counts failures but not slow successes; pair it with a latency rule so a 30-second provider also trips it.
 → The half-open probe lowers the count by one rather than resetting it, so a still-broken provider reopens quickly.
 → The breaker is per provider and per operation, not global, so a failing image endpoint does not block text generation.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Cost per successful task Price per million tokens is an input, not a result. Add input and output tokens per call, retry rate, cache hit rate, retrieval and embedding work, evaluation, observability, and human review. Divide by the task success rate to get cost per successful task, then compare candidates on that number. A cheap model that fails 12% of the time and triggers a second call plus a human review can cost more than the frontier model it replaced. Track the figure weekly by route and tenant. Latency is three numbers Users experience time to first token, total completion time, and the tail. Streaming improves perceived speed without reducing total work; shortening context or retrieval improves all three. Prompt caching cuts prefill cost and time-to-first- token when the prefix is stable. For interactive answers, optimise p95 total latency under the four-second budget; for batch enrichment, optimise cost and ignore the tail. Never quote an average that hides a two-second p50 behind a twelve-second p99. Buy quality where it changes outcomes Rank routes by business value and by how much model quality moves the metric. Regulatory answers and billing disputes justify the frontier model; FAQ reformatting and tag extraction rarely do. Set a per-tenant budget, alert at 80%, and degrade non-critical routes to smaller models before failing requests. Re-run the route's evaluation after every downgrade, and keep the previous model configuration one flag away so a regression becomes a rollback rather than a rewrite.

code.title: Ranking two plans by cost per accepted answer, where retries, cache hits, and the pass rate all affect the result.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Plan:
  name: str
  in_price: float # USD per million input tokens
  out_price: float # USD per million output tokens
  quality: float    # pass rate on the route evaluation
  retry_rate: float = 0.06
  cache_hit: float = 0.20

def cost_per_accepted(p: Plan, in_tok: int = 1800, out_tok: int = 220) -> float:
  call = (in_tok * p.in_price + out_tok * p.out_price) / 1_000_000
  per_request = call * (1 + p.retry_rate) * (1 - p.cache_hit)
  return per_request / p.quality

PLANS = [Plan("small", 0.40, 1.60, 0.918), Plan("frontier", 2.00, 8.00, 0.941)]
for plan in PLANS:
  print(plan.name, f"${cost_per_accepted(plan):.5f} per accepted answer")
what_to_notice: The formula divides by quality, so a cheaper model with a lower pass rate can lose on cost per accepted answer.
Retry and cache rates are measured inputs, not assumptions; both change materially after a routing or prompt change.

The comparison excludes retrieval and review cost, so it ranks model choice but does not replace a full unit-cost model. Three pages per lesson Page 574 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.title: Design an AI Platform From Scratch
lessons.subtitle: Turn an ambiguous AI ambition into a one-page brief, five planes, explicit failure behaviour, a budget, and a phased plan
why_it_matters: Most platform failures are decided early: an unstated requirement, a boundary drawn in the wrong place, a cost model that ignores retrieval, or a plan that delivers the demo and defers the hard part. A design written before code is cheap to change and expensive to ignore. This lesson assembles the module into one repeatable process: constrain the problem, draw the flows, design the failure, cost the unit, and sequence the build with evidence gates.
outcomes: Write a one-page design brief covering users, decisions, volume, latency, quality floor, budget, and non-goals.
Draw five planes with contracts, systems of record, and ownership at each boundary.
Produce a phased plan with numeric gates, unit economics, and failure behaviour before any code is written.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Constraints before components Begin with the decisions the platform supports and the cost of being wrong, then quantify volume, concurrency, latency, quality floor, budget, data residency, and retention. Name the non-goals explicitly, because scope creep usually arrives as a reasonable feature request. A claims assistant that must cite policy and survive audit has a different architecture from a marketing copy generator, even if both call the same model. One page of constraints eliminates most component debates before they start. Five planes and their contracts Draw the request plane (edge, auth, rate limits), the orchestration plane (workflow, agents, prompt versions), the model gateway (routing, fallbacks, quotas), the data plane (Postgres, object store, vector index, ingestion), and the operations plane (traces, evaluation, alerts, cost). For each boundary, name the request and response contract, the system of record, and the owner. Move ingestion and evaluation outside the synchronous path, and make every asynchronous handoff idempotent. A box with no owner or metric is a diagram, not a design. Design failure, money, and sequence For each plane write the degraded behaviour, the detection signal, and the recovery action. Budget latency and cost per component so the totals fit the brief, then define the unit metric, such as cost per resolved claim. Sequence delivery in phases that each produce a reviewable artefact: ingestion and evaluation first, then retrieval, generation, agents and MCP, then hardening. Each phase has an exit gate with numbers. Record decisions and rejected alternatives, because the next engineer inherits the reasoning.

key_terms.definition: A one-page statement of users, decisions, volume, latency, quality, budget, and explicit non-goals.
The single authoritative store for a data type, named at every boundary that reads or writes it.

A numeric condition a phase must satisfy before the next starts, such as retrieval recall above 0.85. MENTAL MODEL Designing a platform is drawing a city before pouring concrete: zones, roads, water, and emergency access decided while changes are still cheap.

worked_example: An insurer asks for an AI claims platform in one quarter. The brief narrows scope: 40,000 claims a month, adjusters as users, a 90-second interactive budget, mandatory citations, USD 0.09 per claim, and a non-goal of automated payouts. The review cuts eleven proposed components to six: a FastAPI edge, a Postgres claims store, hybrid retrieval over policy PDFs, a model gateway with two providers, an evaluation service, and a trace pipeline. Two phases slip deliberately: ingestion quality before generation, and human review before agent tool use. The pilot covers two regions and 4,000 claims. Exit gates are recall above 0.9, citation accuracy above 0.95, p95 under 12 seconds, and cost under 0.07 per claim; the platform passes three and misses latency, so asynchronous review ships first.

code.title: A component budget table that turns the architecture's latency and cost targets into a startup assertion.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Budget:
  component: str
  p95_ms: int
  usd_per_1k: float

PLAN = [Budget("auth + edge", 40, 0.00), Budget("retrieval", 220, 0.31),
   Budget("gateway", 60, 0.02), Budget("generation", 2_100, 41.50),
   Budget("validation", 80, 0.07)]

def check(plan, latency_ms: int = 3_000, spend_usd: float = 90.0) -> tuple[int, float]:
  p95 = sum(b.p95_ms for b in plan)
  spend = sum(b.usd_per_1k for b in plan)
  assert p95 <= latency_ms and spend <= spend_usd, (p95, spend)
  return p95, spend

print(check(PLAN))
what_to_notice: The budget sums component p95s and per-thousand costs, so a 2.1-second generation allowance is visible against a 3- second promise.
The assertion runs at startup, turning an architecture decision into a test that fails before deployment.

Validation and tracing are budgeted lines, not free extras; omitting them is how platforms exceed both cost and latency. Three pages per lesson Page 577 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

Design an AI Platform From Scratch
Turn an ambiguous AI ambition into a one-page brief, five planes, explicit failure behaviour, a budget, and a phased plan
you can defend.
AI System Design · Lesson 13 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Most platform failures are decided early: an unstated requirement, a boundary drawn in the wrong place, a cost model
that ignores retrieval, or a plan that delivers the demo and defers the hard part. A design written before code is cheap to
change and expensive to ignore. This lesson assembles the module into one repeatable process: constrain the problem,
draw the flows, design the failure, cost the unit, and sequence the build with evidence gates.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Write a one-page design brief covering users, decisions, volume, latency, quality floor, budget, and non-goals.
 • Draw five planes with contracts, systems of record, and ownership at each boundary.
 • Produce a phased plan with numeric gates, unit economics, and failure behaviour before any code is written.
CORE CONCEPTS
Constraints before components
Begin with the decisions the platform supports and the cost of being wrong, then quantify volume, concurrency, latency,
quality floor, budget, data residency, and retention. Name the non-goals explicitly, because scope creep usually arrives as
a reasonable feature request. A claims assistant that must cite policy and survive audit has a different architecture from a
marketing copy generator, even if both call the same model. One page of constraints eliminates most component debates
before they start.
Five planes and their contracts
Draw the request plane (edge, auth, rate limits), the orchestration plane (workflow, agents, prompt versions), the model
gateway (routing, fallbacks, quotas), the data plane (Postgres, object store, vector index, ingestion), and the operations
plane (traces, evaluation, alerts, cost). For each boundary, name the request and response contract, the system of record,
and the owner. Move ingestion and evaluation outside the synchronous path, and make every asynchronous handoff
idempotent. A box with no owner or metric is a diagram, not a design.
Design failure, money, and sequence
For each plane write the degraded behaviour, the detection signal, and the recovery action. Budget latency and cost per
component so the totals fit the brief, then define the unit metric, such as cost per resolved claim. Sequence delivery in
phases that each produce a reviewable artefact: ingestion and evaluation first, then retrieval, generation, agents and
MCP, then hardening. Each phase has an exit gate with numbers. Record decisions and rejected alternatives, because the
next engineer inherits the reasoning.
KEY TERMS
 Design brief                      A one-page statement of users, decisions, volume, latency, quality, budget, and explicit non-goals.
 System of record                  The single authoritative store for a data type, named at every boundary that reads or writes it.
 Exit gate                         A numeric condition a phase must satisfy before the next starts, such as retrieval recall above 0.85.

  MENTAL MODEL Designing a platform is drawing a city before pouring concrete: zones, roads, water, and emergency access decided
  while changes are still cheap.

Design an AI Platform From Scratch
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
An insurer asks for an AI claims platform in one quarter. The brief narrows scope: 40,000 claims a month, adjusters as
users, a 90-second interactive budget, mandatory citations, USD 0.09 per claim, and a non-goal of automated payouts.
The review cuts eleven proposed components to six: a FastAPI edge, a Postgres claims store, hybrid retrieval over policy
PDFs, a model gateway with two providers, an evaluation service, and a trace pipeline. Two phases slip deliberately:
ingestion quality before generation, and human review before agent tool use. The pilot covers two regions and 4,000
claims. Exit gates are recall above 0.9, citation accuracy above 0.95, p95 under 12 seconds, and cost under 0.07 per claim;
the platform passes three and misses latency, so asynchronous review ships first.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Interview users and write the decisions the platform supports, the error cost, and five explicit non-goals.
2.    Quantify volume, concurrency, latency, quality floor, budget, residency, and retention in one page.
3.    Draw five planes, naming each contract, system of record, owner, and metric at every boundary.
4.    Write degraded behaviour, detection, and recovery for each plane, then budget latency and cost.
5.    Sequence phases with numeric exit gates and a review artefact, starting with ingestion and evaluation.
CODE
A component budget table that turns the architecture's latency and cost targets into a startup assertion.
  from dataclasses import dataclass

  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class Budget:
    component: str
    p95_ms: int
    usd_per_1k: float

  PLAN = [Budget("auth + edge", 40, 0.00), Budget("retrieval", 220, 0.31),
     Budget("gateway", 60, 0.02), Budget("generation", 2_100, 41.50),
     Budget("validation", 80, 0.07)]

  def check(plan, latency_ms: int = 3_000, spend_usd: float = 90.0) -> tuple[int, float]:
    p95 = sum(b.p95_ms for b in plan)
    spend = sum(b.usd_per_1k for b in plan)
    assert p95 <= latency_ms and spend <= spend_usd, (p95, spend)
    return p95, spend

  print(check(PLAN))
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The budget sums component p95s and per-thousand costs, so a 2.1-second generation allowance is visible against a 3-
   second promise.
 → The assertion runs at startup, turning an architecture decision into a test that fails before deployment.
 → Validation and tracing are budgeted lines, not free extras; omitting them is how platforms exceed both cost and latency.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Requirements as testable claims A usable requirement names the actor, the trigger, the observable outcome, and the threshold. "Claims handlers can find the current policy clause in under two minutes with a citation" is testable; "fast, accurate answers" is not. Write each requirement as one sentence plus acceptance criteria a test can evaluate. If you cannot imagine the failing output, the requirement is still a preference. Non-goals and hard constraints Non-goals are requirements with the opposite sign: no autonomous payments, no voice input, no cross-tenant search in v1. Hard constraints come from outside the product: data residency, retention, accessibility, procurement rules, and the classification of the documents being indexed. Naming them early removes architectures that cannot pass a security review, however well they demo. Revisit non-goals at each phase gate rather than silently expanding scope. Traceability from clause to test A traceability matrix maps each requirement to an evaluation case, a metric, an owner, and the phase that delivers it. Orphans are visible in both directions: a requirement without a test will not be checked, and a test without a requirement measures something nobody asked for. Nine requirements with nine tests beat sixty requirements with a demo. Keep the matrix in the repository and make it part of the phase gate.

key_terms.definition: An observable condition, with a threshold, that a test can evaluate to decide whether a requirement is met.
A capability deliberately excluded from the current release, recorded so later scope requests start from an explicit decision.

A table linking each requirement to its test, metric, owner, and delivery phase so gaps are visible. MENTAL MODEL A requirements document is a contract, not a wish list: every clause needs an observable test, a number, and a person who signs it.

from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Requirement:
  id: str
  statement: str
  metric: str
  threshold: float
  tests: tuple[str, ...] = ()

REQS = [
  Requirement("R1", "Cite policy answers", "citation_precision", 0.95,
          ("eval/citations.yaml",)),
  Requirement("R2", "Meet the interactive budget", "p95_latency_s", 6.0,
          ("load/interactive.js",)),
  Requirement("R3", "Refuse without evidence", "false_answer_rate", 0.02,
          ("eval/abstention.yaml",)),

untested = [r.id for r in REQS if not r.tests]
assert not untested, f"requirements without a test: {untested}"

lessons.title: Phase 2 — Architecture
lessons.subtitle: Choose boundaries, synchronous or queued paths, data ownership, and failure behaviour before a framework makes those
why_it_matters: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse: where state lives, which component may call a model, what happens when retrieval is down, and where tenant boundaries are enforced. A diagram alone does not capture them. The phase output is a small design pack: one context diagram, five decision records, and a per-path budget. That pack lets a new engineer predict the system's behaviour under failure without reading every module.
outcomes: Split the platform into edge, orchestration, retrieval, tools, and data planes with explicit interfaces.
Decide which work is synchronous, queued, or streamed, with a latency budget for each path.
Record five architecture decisions as ADRs that include rejected alternatives and operational consequences.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Boundaries outlive models Put the model behind a gateway interface, retrieval behind a retriever interface, and tools behind a registry with schemas. The API layer calls services, services call interfaces, and only adapters know provider names. This is not abstraction for its own sake: it allows a model swap, a second vector store, or a staged migration without editing every route. Enforce the rule with an import test in CI, because diagrams drift. Three paths, three budgets Interactive answers are synchronous and must fit a 6-second p95, so retrieval and generation get 4.5 seconds with 1.5 seconds of headroom. Document ingestion is queued, idempotent, and measured in documents per minute. Streaming improves perceived latency but does not relax the total budget, and validation must still run before the answer is persisted. Assign every path a timeout, a retry policy, and a terminal state. Design the degraded mode For each dependency, write what users see when it is slow, wrong, or absent. Provider timeout: return a cached answer with its timestamp or 503 with Retry-After. Vector store outage: fall back to keyword search and label the result as reduced quality. Queue backlog: accept the job, show its position, and alert at fifteen minutes. Degraded modes are product decisions, so they belong in the ADR, not in a runbook written later.

key_terms.definition: The single internal interface through which all model calls pass, normalising providers, timeouts, retries, usage, and errors.
A short note stating context, choice, alternatives, and consequences, stored with the code it constrains.

The defined behaviour and user-visible quality reduction when a dependency is unavailable or too slow. MENTAL MODEL Architecture is a set of load-bearing walls: the model is furniture you can move, but state ownership and trust boundaries are expensive to relocate.

worked_example: At Corvus Pay, a design review covers the merchant-onboarding assistant four weeks before launch. The first diagram puts PDF parsing, embedding, retrieval, generation, and citation rendering inside one HTTP request with a 90-second provider timeout, stores conversation state in the API process, and uses one database role for every merchant. The review redraws three paths: ingestion is queued and idempotent; answers are synchronous with a 4.5-second internal deadline; long reports stream but are validated before storage. State moves to Postgres with tenant-scoped row-level security, and the model sits behind a gateway with a circuit breaker. Phase 2 — Architecture
Choose boundaries, synchronous or queued paths, data ownership, and failure behaviour before a framework makes those
choices for you.
Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 2 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to reverse: where state lives, which component may call a model,
what happens when retrieval is down, and where tenant boundaries are enforced. A diagram alone does not capture
them. The phase output is a small design pack: one context diagram, five decision records, and a per-path budget. That
pack lets a new engineer predict the system's behaviour under failure without reading every module.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Split the platform into edge, orchestration, retrieval, tools, and data planes with explicit interfaces.
 • Decide which work is synchronous, queued, or streamed, with a latency budget for each path.
 • Record five architecture decisions as ADRs that include rejected alternatives and operational consequences.
CORE CONCEPTS
Boundaries outlive models
Put the model behind a gateway interface, retrieval behind a retriever interface, and tools behind a registry with schemas.
The API layer calls services, services call interfaces, and only adapters know provider names. This is not abstraction for its
own sake: it allows a model swap, a second vector store, or a staged migration without editing every route. Enforce the
rule with an import test in CI, because diagrams drift.
Three paths, three budgets
Interactive answers are synchronous and must fit a 6-second p95, so retrieval and generation get 4.5 seconds with 1.5
seconds of headroom. Document ingestion is queued, idempotent, and measured in documents per minute. Streaming
improves perceived latency but does not relax the total budget, and validation must still run before the answer is
persisted. Assign every path a timeout, a retry policy, and a terminal state.
Design the degraded mode
For each dependency, write what users see when it is slow, wrong, or absent. Provider timeout: return a cached answer
with its timestamp or 503 with Retry-After. Vector store outage: fall back to keyword search and label the result as
reduced quality. Queue backlog: accept the job, show its position, and alert at fifteen minutes. Degraded modes are
product decisions, so they belong in the ADR, not in a runbook written later.
KEY TERMS
 Model gateway                     The single internal interface through which all model calls pass, normalising providers, timeouts, retries,
                                   usage, and errors.
 Architecture decision record      A short note stating context, choice, alternatives, and consequences, stored with the code it constrains.
 Degraded mode                     The defined behaviour and user-visible quality reduction when a dependency is unavailable or too slow.

  MENTAL MODEL Architecture is a set of load-bearing walls: the model is furniture you can move, but state ownership and trust
  boundaries are expensive to relocate.

Phase 2 — Architecture
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
At Corvus Pay, a design review covers the merchant-onboarding assistant four weeks before launch. The first diagram
puts PDF parsing, embedding, retrieval, generation, and citation rendering inside one HTTP request with a 90-second
provider timeout, stores conversation state in the API process, and uses one database role for every merchant. The review
redraws three paths: ingestion is queued and idempotent; answers are synchronous with a 4.5-second internal deadline;
long reports stream but are validated before storage. State moves to Postgres with tenant-scoped row-level security, and
the model sits behind a gateway with a circuit breaker. The team rejects a self-service agent for v1 and records ADR-004
with the reason: there is no approval workflow for refunds.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Draw the context diagram with users, edge API, orchestrator, model gateway, retrieval, tools, queue, and data stores.
2.    Mark every trust boundary and name the authentication and authorisation check enforced on the receiving side.
3.    Classify each operation as synchronous, queued, or streamed, then give it a timeout and a p95 budget.
4.    Write the degraded behaviour for each dependency and decide which failures return 503 rather than a partial answer.
5.    Record five ADRs with alternatives and consequences, then encode the import boundaries as a CI test.
CODE
A dependency test that fails the build when a route imports a provider or retrieval adapter directly.
  import ast
  from pathlib import Path

  FORBIDDEN = ("app.providers", "app.retrieval")

  def check(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    tree = ast.parse(path.read_text())
    hits = []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
       if isinstance(node, ast.ImportFrom) and node.module:
          if node.module.startswith(FORBIDDEN):
             hits.append(f"{path}:{node.lineno} imports {node.module}")
    return hits

  hits = [h for p in Path("app/api").rglob("*.py") for h in check(p)]
  if hits:
     raise SystemExit("boundary violations:\n" + "\n".join(hits))
  print("api layer uses services only")
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The scan catches direct imports only; dynamic imports and framework dependency injection can still cross the boundary.
 → Set the rule at the layer that matters: routes may import services, services may import interfaces, adapters may import
   SDKs.
 → Run the test on every pull request; a boundary check that runs weekly will be bypassed within a month.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: Layout encodes the architecture Use src/app with api, services, providers, retrieval, tools, and domain packages, plus tests/unit, tests/integration, tests/eval, infra, and docs/adr. Keep route modules thin, put orchestration in services, and let only providers import vendor SDKs. Name modules after responsibilities rather than technologies. Avoid a utils package; it becomes the place where boundaries go to die. The tree should let a reader predict where a change belongs before opening a file. Automate the review you would do by hand The pull-request gate runs ruff format and lint, mypy on domain and services, pytest with unit and integration markers, pip-audit, and gitleaks. Target under five minutes so nobody bypasses it. Run the slower evaluation suite nightly and on release branches. A gate that fails on formatting but not on a leaked key has the priorities backwards. Make the same commands available locally through make check so CI and laptop agree. Reproducibility is a build artefact Pin the Python version in .python-version, dependencies in uv.lock, and the base image by digest. A new engineer should reach a passing test run in fifteen minutes from a clean machine. Commit .env.example, never .env, and document every required variable with its type and default. Treat the lockfile as reviewed code: an unexplained dependency upgrade is a supply-chain change, not housekeeping.

key_terms.definition: A generated record of exact dependency versions and hashes so every environment installs the same packages.
A package structure placing importable code under src/ so tests run against the installed package, not the working directory.

Automated detection of credentials and keys in commits and pull requests, usually blocking the merge and requiring rotation. code.title: A repository contract check that fails when required artefacts are missing or a secret is tracked.
code.code:
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

REQUIRED = ["pyproject.toml", "uv.lock", ".python-version", "src/app/main.py",
        "tests", "docs/adr", "eval"]
missing = [p for p in REQUIRED if not Path(p).exists()]
tracked = subprocess.run(["git", "ls-files"], capture_output=True,
                 text=True, check=True).stdout.splitlines()
leaks = [f for f in tracked if f == ".env" or f.endswith(".pem")]
if missing or leaks:
   raise SystemExit(f"missing={missing} tracked_secrets={leaks}")

lessons.title: Phase 4 — Backend
lessons.subtitle: Build the authenticated, tenant-scoped, idempotent request path that every model call, job, and tool will depend on.
lessons.meta: Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 4 of 13 · study guide
why_it_matters: The backend is where the platform becomes a product: it authenticates, authorises, validates, durably records, and admits or rejects work. Model quality cannot compensate for a duplicate charge, a cross-tenant read, or a request that times out after the answer was generated. Phase 4 builds the contract and the safety rails first, then lets the AI layer plug into a path that already behaves correctly under retries, quota limits, and restarts.
outcomes: Implement tenant-scoped authentication, request IDs, and idempotency on every state-changing endpoint.
Define request and response schemas with stable error codes and correct HTTP status mapping.
Move slow work to a queue and expose job status without leaking another tenant's data.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: The backend owns the contract Define request models, response envelopes, and a closed set of error codes before the model layer exists. A successful answer returns content, citations, usage, and a request ID; a failure returns a code such as unauthenticated, forbidden, conflict, rate_limited, or unavailable. Never pass raw provider errors to clients. Version the path and keep additive changes compatible. Contract tests for 401, 403, 409, 429, and 503 catch the failures that demos never show. Tenancy at the data edge Derive tenant_id from the verified token, never from a request body, and set it on the database session so row-level security applies to every query. Use separate roles for migrations, application reads, and workers. Check tool permissions against the same tenant and role, because a model can be persuaded to request another customer's record. Log tenant and request IDs, never document contents. A missing WHERE clause is a breach, not a bug. Slow work leaves the request path Any operation that can exceed two seconds becomes a job: validate, persist, enqueue, return 202 with a job ID, and let the client poll or subscribe. Store an idempotency key per tenant for 24 hours so a retried POST returns the original job rather than a second charge. Workers update job state transactionally and expose queued, running, succeeded, and failed. The request path stays fast while expensive work is retried on its own schedule.

key_terms.definition: A client-supplied identifier stored with a write so retries return the original result instead of creating a duplicate.
A database policy filtering rows by the current session's tenant, enforcing isolation even when application code forgets a filter.

Rejecting or delaying new work with 429 or 503 when capacity or quota is exhausted, rather than queueing without bound. MENTAL MODEL The backend is the building's front desk: it checks identity, records the request, gives a ticket, and refuses to let two people claim the same room.
Page 589 of 618 DYNAMOAI · COMPASS AI Complete lesson guides · 201 lessons

lessons.mental_model: Think of phase 4 — backend as a building block - once you understand it, you'll use it again and again as you build your AI app.
worked_example: Lantern, a 30-person ticketing SaaS, launches an assistant that summarises threads and drafts replies. During a provider slowdown, clients retry POST /v1/answers; the endpoint creates a new job each time. In 40 minutes, 1,400 duplicate jobs consume 2.6 million tokens and GBP 62, and some users see two drafts. The team adds a tenant-scoped idempotency table with a 24-hour TTL, returns 202 with a job ID, and maps provider quota exhaustion to 429 with Retry-After: 30 instead of 503. They also find that a support role could read another tenant's job by guessing the ID, so job lookups gain a tenant predicate. The decision: no synchronous model call on any write path.

Use separate database roles for API, worker, and migrations; an API role with DDL rights turns a bug into an outage.
Record request ID, tenant, route, status, latency, and token usage for every call, but hash or omit prompt contents.

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
The backend is where the platform becomes a product: it authenticates, authorises, validates, durably records, and
admits or rejects work. Model quality cannot compensate for a duplicate charge, a cross-tenant read, or a request that
times out after the answer was generated. Phase 4 builds the contract and the safety rails first, then lets the AI layer plug
into a path that already behaves correctly under retries, quota limits, and restarts.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Implement tenant-scoped authentication, request IDs, and idempotency on every state-changing endpoint.
 • Define request and response schemas with stable error codes and correct HTTP status mapping.
 • Move slow work to a queue and expose job status without leaking another tenant's data.
CORE CONCEPTS
The backend owns the contract
Define request models, response envelopes, and a closed set of error codes before the model layer exists. A successful
answer returns content, citations, usage, and a request ID; a failure returns a code such as unauthenticated, forbidden,
conflict, rate_limited, or unavailable. Never pass raw provider errors to clients. Version the path and keep additive
changes compatible. Contract tests for 401, 403, 409, 429, and 503 catch the failures that demos never show.
Tenancy at the data edge
Derive tenant_id from the verified token, never from a request body, and set it on the database session so row-level
security applies to every query. Use separate roles for migrations, application reads, and workers. Check tool permissions
against the same tenant and role, because a model can be persuaded to request another customer's record. Log tenant
and request IDs, never document contents. A missing WHERE clause is a breach, not a bug.
Slow work leaves the request path
Any operation that can exceed two seconds becomes a job: validate, persist, enqueue, return 202 with a job ID, and let
the client poll or subscribe. Store an idempotency key per tenant for 24 hours so a retried POST returns the original job
rather than a second charge. Workers update job state transactionally and expose queued, running, succeeded, and
failed. The request path stays fast while expensive work is retried on its own schedule.
KEY TERMS
 Idempotency key                   A client-supplied identifier stored with a write so retries return the original result instead of creating a
                                   duplicate.
 Row-level security                A database policy filtering rows by the current session's tenant, enforcing isolation even when application
                                   code forgets a filter.
 Backpressure                      Rejecting or delaying new work with 429 or 503 when capacity or quota is exhausted, rather than queueing
                                   without bound.

  MENTAL MODEL The backend is the building's front desk: it checks identity, records the request, gives a ticket, and refuses to let two
  people claim the same room.

Phase 4 — Backend
Build it
WORKED EXAMPLE
Lantern, a 30-person ticketing SaaS, launches an assistant that summarises threads and drafts replies. During a provider
slowdown, clients retry POST /v1/answers; the endpoint creates a new job each time. In 40 minutes, 1,400 duplicate jobs
consume 2.6 million tokens and GBP 62, and some users see two drafts. The team adds a tenant-scoped idempotency
table with a 24-hour TTL, returns 202 with a job ID, and maps provider quota exhaustion to 429 with Retry-After: 30
instead of 503. They also find that a support role could read another tenant's job by guessing the ID, so job lookups gain a
tenant predicate. The decision: no synchronous model call on any write path.
STEP BY STEP
1.    Define Pydantic request models, a response envelope, and a closed error catalogue with HTTP mappings.
2.    Implement token verification that resolves tenant_id and role, then set both on the database session.
3.    Add an idempotency table keyed by tenant and key, and return the stored job for duplicate writes.
4.    Move model work to a worker, expose job status, and return 202 with a polling or streaming URL.
5.    Write contract tests for 401, 403, 409, 429, and 503, including a cross-tenant lookup attempt.
CODE
A 202 write path that resolves the tenant from the token and collapses retries onto one job.
  from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
  from pydantic import BaseModel
  app = FastAPI()
  JOBS: dict[tuple[str, str], str] = {}

  def tenant_from(token: str = Header(...)) -> str:
    if token != "demo-token":
       raise HTTPException(401, "invalid token")
    return "tenant-a"

  class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str

  @app.post("/v1/answers", status_code=202)
  def ask(body: Ask, idem: str = Header(...), tenant: str = Depends(tenant_from)):
    key = (tenant, idem)
    if key in JOBS:
       return {"job_id": JOBS[key], "duplicate": True}
    JOBS[key] = f"job-{len(JOBS) + 1}"
    return {"job_id": JOBS[key], "duplicate": False}
WHAT TO NOTICE
 → The dependency rejects any token except the demo value; production must verify signature, issuer, audience, and expiry.
 → The idempotency store is in memory here, so it disappears on restart; use Postgres with a unique constraint on tenant and
   key.
 → Returning 202 means the client must poll; include a Location header and a status endpoint that also enforces tenancy.

Operate it
COMMON MISTAKES
1.     Reading tenant_id from the JSON body, then trusting it because the UI normally sends the right value.
2.     Retrying a POST that already created a job, then billing the customer twice for the same question.

    ◆ Use separate database roles for API, worker, and migrations; an API role with DDL rights turns a bug into an outage.
    ◆ Record request ID, tenant, route, status, latency, and token usage for every call, but hash or omit prompt contents.

□      Every write path has a scoped idempotency key and returns the original result on retry.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: One gateway, many providers The gateway accepts a normalised request (system, messages, max tokens, response schema) and returns content, usage, model, latency, and retry count. Adapters translate to each provider. Retry only 429 and 5xx, with jittered exponential backoff and an overall deadline; never retry 400 or 401. Give each attempt a connect timeout and a total timeout. Normalise error classes so the service layer can choose between fallback, queueing, and user-visible failure without importing a vendor SDK. Structured output is a contract Ask for JSON that matches a schema, parse it with Pydantic, and treat validation failure as a first-class outcome. Allow one repair attempt that includes the validation errors, then return a typed failure rather than guessing. Never extract JSON with a regular expression or strip fences by hand. Log the schema version and validator errors, not the full prompt. A model that cannot satisfy the schema should trigger a stronger model or a deterministic fallback, and the decision should be visible in metrics. Budgets before, accounting after Estimate prompt tokens before sending, reserve the output maximum, and reject requests that exceed the task or tenant budget. Track actual usage from the provider response, including cached and reasoning tokens where billed. Set a monthly tenant cap and a per-request ceiling, then alert at 80%. Summarise older context instead of silently truncating it. Cost per successful request, not cost per token, is the number to review with the product owner.

code.title: A pre-call budget reservation that rejects a request before it can exceed the tenant's ceiling.
code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Budget:
  max_input_tokens: int = 8_000
  max_output_tokens: int = 700
  max_usd: float = 0.045

PRICES = {"fast": (0.15, 0.60), "strong": (3.00, 15.00)} # USD per 1M tokens

def reserve(model: str, prompt: str, budget: Budget) -> int:
  input_tokens = len(prompt) // 4 + 1
  if input_tokens > budget.max_input_tokens:
     raise ValueError(f"input {input_tokens} over {budget.max_input_tokens}")
  price_in, price_out = PRICES[model]
  worst = (input_tokens * price_in + budget.max_output_tokens * price_out) / 1e6
  if worst > budget.max_usd:
     raise ValueError(f"worst case ${worst:.4f} over ${budget.max_usd}")
  return input_tokens

print(reserve("strong", "policy preamble " * 700, Budget()))
what_to_notice: The token estimate uses a four-characters-per-token heuristic; production should use the provider tokenizer and include tool schemas.
Prices change and differ by region; load them from configuration and record the price version with each usage event.

Keep one fake provider that returns malformed output, rate limits, and timeouts, and run it in CI.

lessons.title: Phase 10 — Production
lessons.subtitle: Turn the working platform into a service with SLOs, budgets, resilience, evaluation gates, and runbooks that survive a bad
why_it_matters: The demo answers a question; production answers it correctly, quickly, safely, and affordably for every tenant, every day. Probabilistic systems fail in ways that status codes do not capture: a plausible but ungrounded answer, a slow retrieval tail, a retry storm. Production engineering makes those failures measurable, bounded, and recoverable before users report them.
outcomes: Set SLOs for availability, p95 latency, grounded-answer quality, and cost per request.
Add timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, caching, and rate limits around every model and tool call.
Wire evaluation, tracing, and alerting into a release gate that can block a deploy.

core_concepts.title: Concept
core_concepts.content: SLOs for a probabilistic service Availability and latency are necessary but not sufficient. Set a quality SLO on a rolling sample, for example groundedness at or above 0.90 over 500 traces, alongside p95 latency under 3.5 seconds and cost under USD 0.06 per request. Define the window, the sampling method, and the action when the budget burns. A single evaluation score is a release gate; a rolling SLO is how you operate. Resilience at every seam Each model and tool call gets a timeout, a bounded retry, and a breaker. Retry only 429 and 5xx with jittered exponential backoff; never retry validation errors. After ten consecutive failures, open the breaker, serve a cached or extractive answer, and probe recovery with a single request. Cap total attempts per user request so an outage cannot be amplified into three times the traffic. Release gates, not launch day A deploy is an experiment with a rollback plan. CI evaluates the exact image on a 300-case golden set and blocks if groundedness falls more than two points, p95 exceeds 3.8 seconds, or cost exceeds USD 0.08. The canary takes 5% of traffic for ten minutes and compares against a baseline window. Automate rollback on error-rate or quality breach; require a human for judgement calls.

key_terms.definition: A measurable target for service behaviour over a defined window, with an error budget attached.
The allowed shortfall against an SLO, used to decide whether to ship features or fix reliability.

A guard that stops calls to a failing dependency after a threshold and fails fast until recovery. MENTAL MODEL Production is a flight envelope, not a finish line: the aircraft may fly in turbulence, but the crew knows the limits, watches the gauges, and has a diversion plan.

CODE
A CI release gate that blocks deployment when groundedness, latency, or cost breach the service contract.
  import json
  import sys
  LIMITS = {"groundedness": 0.90, "p95_ms": 3500.0, "cost_usd": 0.06}
  def gate(report: dict) -> list[str]:
     failures = []
     if report["cases"] < 300:
        failures.append("fewer than 300 evaluation cases")
     for key, limit in LIMITS.items():
        value = report[key]
        breached = value < limit if key == "groundedness" else value > limit
        if breached:
           failures.append(f"{key}={value} breaches {limit}")
     return failures
  failures = gate(json.load(open(sys.argv[1])))
  if failures:
     raise SystemExit("; ".join(failures))
  print("release gate passed")

code.code:
import pulumi
import pulumi_aws as aws
cfg = pulumi.Config("atlas")
subnets = aws.ec2.get_subnets(filters=[{"name": "tag:tier", "values": ["private"]}])
group = aws.rds.SubnetGroup("atlas", subnet_ids=subnets.ids)
db = aws.rds.Instance(
  "atlas-pg",
  engine="postgres",
  engine_version="16.4",
  instance_class="db.r6g.large",
  allocated_storage=100,
  storage_encrypted=True,
  backup_retention_period=14,
  deletion_protection=cfg.require_bool("prod"),
  db_subnet_group_name=group.name,
  performance_insights_enabled=True,
  skip_final_snapshot=False,
)
pulumi.export("db_endpoint", db.endpoint)

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
Deployment is a control system, not a command. Most rollback failures come from rebuilding artefacts, destructive
schema changes, or canaries judged against the wrong baseline. A pipeline that proves the exact artefact, keeps
migrations compatible, and rolls back on a measured signal turns release from a ceremony into a repeatable operation.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Build one immutable image per commit and promote the same digest across environments.
 • Run migrations, smoke tests, and a 5% canary with automatic rollback on SLO breach.

Build once, promote the digest
CI builds one image per commit, signs it, generates an SBOM, and records the digest. Staging and production receive that
digest; nothing is rebuilt. Configuration arrives through environment variables and secrets, not a new image. A migration
job runs before the new pods start, and the release record names the digest, migration version, and flag state. Rebuilding
per environment invalidates every test you ran on the artefact.
Progressive delivery
Send 5% of traffic to the new version for ten minutes and compare error rate, p95 latency, groundedness, and cost
against a baseline window from the same hour. Promote automatically when the canary is inside tolerance; roll back
automatically when it is not. Feature flags separate deploy from release, so a risky behaviour can be disabled without
rebuilding. A canary without a baseline is just a smaller outage.
Migrations that can go back
Use expand and contract. Add a nullable column, dual-write, backfill in batches, switch reads, then drop the old column in
a later release. Never ship a destructive migration in the same release as the code that stops using it, because old pods
still serve traffic during the canary. Every migration must be safe for both versions and resumable if the job dies halfway.

 Canary release                    Sending a small traffic slice to a new version and comparing metrics before a wider rollout.
 Expand/contract migration         A multi-release schema change that remains compatible with both old and new application code.

code.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Finding:
  area: str
  severity: str
  owner: str
  due: str
FINDINGS = [
  Finding("mcp-auth", "critical", "security", "2026-11-08"),
  Finding("restore-drill", "high", "platform", "2026-11-22"),
  Finding("trace-versioning", "medium", "ai", "2026-12-06"),
]
def verdict(findings: list[Finding]) -> str:
  blockers = [f for f in findings if f.severity == "critical"]
  if blockers:
     return f"conditional: {len(blockers)} blocker(s) due {blockers[0].due}"
  return "approved with tracked risks"
print(verdict(FINDINGS))

Phase 13 — Final Architecture Review
Present the platform as an evidence-backed architecture: decisions, risks, costs, SLOs, and the gaps you chose not to close.
Final Capstone: Build and Review an AI System · Lesson 13 of 13 · study guide

WHY THIS LESSON MATTERS
A final review is not a demo. Reviewers are looking for ownership, evidence, failure behaviour, and honest gaps. A
platform that cannot explain why it chose a vector store, what happens when a provider fails, or who owns a critical
finding is not ready to hand over, regardless of how well the demo answers questions.
WHAT YOU WILL BE ABLE TO DO
 • Run a structured review against requirements, security, reliability, cost, and operability.
 • Defend each major decision with an ADR, a measurement, and the alternative you rejected.
 • Produce a prioritised risk register and a 90-day roadmap that a new owner could execute.
CORE CONCEPTS
Review the system, not the slides

invocation, persistence, and billing. Name the owner and the failure behaviour at each seam. Reviewers learn more from
one trace with timings and token counts than from a deck of component diagrams, because the seams are where the
platform actually fails under load, partial failure, or a bad deploy.
Evidence over assertion
Every claim needs a dated artefact: an evaluation report for quality, a load test for latency, a cost dashboard for spend, a
restore drill for recovery, a threat model and pen-test note for security. Link the commit, dataset version, and trace IDs. If
the evidence is stale, say so and schedule the re-run; an unsupported claim damages trust more than a known gap.
Name the gaps

review date, and status. Separate blockers from accepted risks, and state what would change the decision. 'Future work'
is not a mitigation; a monitored signal with a threshold is. The output is a decision plus a short, owned roadmap, not a
numeric score.

COMMON MISTAKES
